title: ZGCM-1: A Fully Open and Extremely Efficient Foundation Model for Math and Agentic Search
summary: In this work, we present ZGCM-1, a fully open 7B dense foundation model trained from scratch with extreme data, system, and algorithmic efficiency. ZGCM-1 is founded on a core premise: compact models cannot passively memorize the open web, but can overcome parametric capacity limits by coupling deliberate internal thinking with active external tool use. To support this paradigm across a 256K context, we develop an end-to-end, high-efficiency open training recipe: Architecture & System Co-design: interleaved gated sliding-window and full attention, and a stable FP8 Muon optimizer; Progressive Curriculum & MDP Mid-Training: context scaling across 16K, 64K, and 256K, and the reformulation of interaction traces into Markov Decision Processes. Furthermore, we establish an AI-native R&D workflow where agent swarms autonomously manage cluster operations, data curation, and rapid diagnostic evaluation. Extensive evaluations show that ZGCM-1-7B is competitive across 7B model family on general benchmarks. On several challenging mathematical reasoning and agentic search suites, it remains competitive with frontier models orders of magnitude larger, such as Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.1. We also show that our pre-training design offers a ~4.2x efficiency improvement in 16K pre-training time-to-loss. Across the full development lifecycle, we distill eight actionable empirical findings-spanning architectural scaling, SFT quality pruning, long-context generalization, and agentic co-training dynamics. To facilitate community research, we open-source model weights from the pre-training, mid-training, and post-training stages, intermediate checkpoints, training code, per-stage data and data recipes, and W&B logs.

AI.tldr: ZGCM-1 introduces a highly efficient, fully open 7B foundation model with 256K context, designed to overcome small-model capacity limits via internal reasoning and external tool use, supported by an optimized training recipe and AI-native R&D workflow, and released with extensive artifacts for community research.
AI.motivation: Smaller, cost-efficient models struggle to match frontier LLM performance, especially on long-context reasoning and tool-using tasks, because they cannot simply memorize the web or scale parameters indefinitely. The authors aim to show that with carefully designed architecture, training curricula, and AI-automated workflows, a 7B model can approach or match much larger models on demanding benchmarks while being significantly more efficient to train.
AI.method: They build a 7B dense model, ZGCM-1, with a 256K context window, and design: (1) an architecture/system co-design featuring interleaved gated sliding-window and full attention plus a stable FP8 Muon optimizer; (2) a progressive curriculum that scales context from 16K to 64K to 256K and reformulates interaction traces as Markov Decision Processes for mid-training; and (3) an AI-native R&D workflow where agent swarms autonomously handle cluster management, data curation, and rapid evaluations. They train the model from scratch and evaluate it on general, mathematical reasoning, and agentic search benchmarks, while also distilling empirical findings about scaling, SFT pruning, long-context generalization, and co-training dynamics.
AI.result: ZGCM-1-7B performs competitively within the 7B model class on general benchmarks and, on difficult math reasoning and agentic search tasks, achieves performance comparable to much larger frontier models such as Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.1. Their pre-training design yields about a 4.2× improvement in time-to-loss for 16K pre-training. They extract eight empirical lessons on architecture, SFT data filtering, long-context behavior, and agentic co-training from the full development process.
AI.conclusion: A carefully engineered 7B dense model with long-context support, progressive curriculum, MDP-based mid-training, and AI-driven infrastructure can narrow the gap with much larger frontier models while achieving substantial training efficiency gains. By open-sourcing all stages of the model, code, data recipes, and logs, the work provides both a high-performing small model and a comprehensive, reproducible blueprint for efficient, agentic, long-context LLM development.

title: Converge Then Diversify: Decoupling Convergence and Diversity in Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimisation
summary: Multi-objective Bayesian optimisation (MOBO) is a sample-efficient approach for optimising expensive black-box functions with multiple objectives. In MOBO, the goal is to adequately approximate the Pareto front; that is, to obtain a high-quality solution set with 1) good convergence (closeness to the Pareto front) and 2) good diversity (spread across the Pareto front). Existing MOBO methods typically aim to accomplish these two tasks simultaneously, i.e., driving the search towards the Pareto front while maintaining a diverse set of nondominated solutions, such that the solutions, ideally, can gradually approach the entire front. When sufficient search budgets are available, this approach is effective. However, considering both convergence and diversity throughout the search is not easy and requires careful design. Under very tight budgets, there may not be enough solutions generated to be able to simultaneously approach the entire Pareto front. To address this issue, this paper proposes a \textit{converge-then-diversify} (CTD) approach that decouples convergence and diversity into two stages. In the first stage, CTD focuses on convergence, aiming to quickly drive the search toward a single point on the Pareto front. In the second stage, CTD focuses on diversity, aiming to spread solutions across the front. We present two simple instantiations of CTD by using widely adopted acquisition functions in the area. Experimental results show that, across all 446 pairwise comparisons, CTD statistically outperforms state-of-the-art methods in 72.9\% of the cases, performs equivalently in 21.1\%, and is statistically worse in only 6.1\%, with the advantage being particularly evident in settings with very tight evaluation budgets or in high-dimensional problems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage multi-objective Bayesian optimisation strategy, "converge-then-diversify" (CTD), which first focuses purely on convergence to the Pareto front and only later on diversifying solutions along the front. This staged approach improves performance, especially with tight evaluation budgets and high-dimensional problems.
AI.motivation: Existing MOBO methods try to optimise convergence and diversity simultaneously, which works when many evaluations are available but is difficult to design and inefficient when the evaluation budget is very small. Under tight budgets, there may not be enough samples to simultaneously approach and cover the entire Pareto front well, so a new strategy is needed to prioritise convergence first and then diversity.
AI.method: The authors introduce a converge-then-diversify (CTD) framework that splits MOBO into two stages: Stage 1 focuses solely on convergence, quickly driving the search towards a single point (or small region) on the Pareto front; Stage 2 then emphasises diversity, spreading solutions across the front starting from that initial high-quality point. They instantiate CTD using standard MOBO acquisition functions in two simple variants, showing that this decoupling can be implemented with minimal changes to existing pipelines.
AI.result: Through extensive experiments and 446 pairwise comparisons against state-of-the-art MOBO algorithms, CTD is statistically better in 72.9% of cases, statistically equivalent in 21.1%, and worse in only 6.1%. The performance gains are especially strong when the evaluation budget is very tight or the search space is high-dimensional.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling convergence and diversity into sequential stages in MOBO is an effective design, particularly in budget-limited and high-dimensional settings. The proposed CTD framework, even with simple instantiations using standard acquisition functions, consistently outperforms or matches state-of-the-art methods, suggesting that a staged "converge-then-diversify" optimisation strategy is a promising direction for practical multi-objective Bayesian optimisation.

title: Generalized Agent Iteration: One Formal Framework for Iterative Policy Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: When we speak of recursive self-improvement (RSI), are we speaking of a phenomenon, a mechanism, or a prospect? Towards autonomous and evolving intelligence, RSI is being claimed at many scales, while no single framework that formally describes these emerging instances exists. Its counterpart in the classical realm, iterative policy improvement, is characterized by generalized policy iteration (GPI), a framework of broad applicability with well-understood theoretical properties, but only where the update principle and the evaluation base lie outside the agent. In this paper, we propose Generalized Agent Iteration (GAI), a formal framework that describes iterative policy improvement and RSI as two cases of a single learning paradigm. GAI defines the agent as a configuration of modifiable components within a system and models the learning process as a cycle of agent evaluation and agent improvement. Two pivotal dials then distinguish the instances: whether the improving mechanism is part of the agent and whether the standard it is measured against is grounded outside it. The former dial delineates the boundary between GPI and RSI, and the latter determines a system's polarity as anchored, goal drift, or fully self-referential. Moreover, we use these coordinates to place existing systems on the same two axes and make the defects of recursive self-improvement statable one condition at a time. We see this paper as a first step toward exploring a formal characterization of RSI that rests on the classical account, makes existing systems comparable, and provides a principled basis for analyzing and designing new ones.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Generalized Agent Iteration (GAI), a unifying framework that models both classical iterative policy improvement and recursive self-improvement (RSI) as special cases of a single learning paradigm, clarifying how agents can evaluate and modify themselves.
AI.motivation: Current discussions of recursive self-improvement (RSI) are conceptually fragmented: RSI is invoked as a phenomenon, a mechanism, or a speculative prospect, and at many different scales. There is no shared formal framework to describe and compare instances of RSI or to relate them cleanly to the well-understood classical framework of generalized policy iteration (GPI) in reinforcement learning, where learning updates and evaluations are external to the agent. This lack of structure makes it hard to analyze, compare, and reason rigorously about systems that modify themselves.
AI.method: The authors propose Generalized Agent Iteration (GAI), a formal framework that represents an agent as a configuration of modifiable components within a broader system. Learning is modeled as a repeated cycle of (1) evaluating the current agent and (2) improving or modifying that agent. Within this general scheme, they introduce two key binary dimensions ("dials"): (a) whether the mechanism that performs improvement is itself part of the agent, and (b) whether the evaluation standard is grounded outside the agent. By varying these dials, classical GPI and various forms of RSI become special cases of the same iteration process. The authors then map existing systems onto these axes to illustrate the framework's descriptive power.
AI.result: GAI formally unifies iterative policy improvement and recursive self-improvement as instances of a common agent-iteration process, characterized by internal vs. external improvement mechanisms and externally-anchored vs. self-referential evaluation standards. This yields a taxonomy where systems can be classified as classical GPI, anchored RSI, suffering goal drift, or fully self-referential, depending on their positions along the two axes. By placing existing systems in this coordinate space, the authors can express known and potential failure modes of RSI as specific conditions on the dials rather than vague global concerns.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that Generalized Agent Iteration offers a first formal step toward a unified treatment of recursive self-improvement grounded in the established theory of generalized policy iteration. GAI enables systematic comparison of different agent designs, clarifies what is distinctively risky or fragile about various forms of RSI, and supplies a principled lens for analyzing and designing future systems that modify their own decision-making or improvement processes.

title: Vibe Patenting: Evaluating LLM Judges for Professional Patent-Drafting Agents
summary: LLM judges are increasingly used to evaluate and improve AI-generated outputs, yet their reliability for complex professional work remains unclear. We study this problem through Vibe Patenting, an end-to-end patent-drafting testbed for AI-agent evaluation. A separately-invoked LLM judge evaluates generated patent drafts and provides structured feedback for iterative revision. Across multiple inventions and drafting-agent configurations, judge-guided revision consistently improves judge-assessed quality, while unguided revision tends to saturate. Notably, iterative judge feedback enables a low-reasoning agent to approach the performance of a substantially more expensive high-reasoning agent. Stronger models and increased reasoning generally improve judge-assessed drafting quality, while domain-specific agentic workflows provide further gains. We validate the judge against independent evaluation by a professional patent attorney and find meaningful but strongly metric-dependent agreement and systematic calibration differences. These results highlight both the utility and limitations of LLM judges as evaluators and optimization signals for complex professional workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Vibe Patenting, a testbed to study how reliable LLM judges are for evaluating and improving AI‑generated patent drafts, finding they are useful but imperfect optimization signals.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as automatic judges to score, rank, and refine AI‑generated content, but it is unclear whether they are reliable for complex, high‑stakes professional tasks such as patent drafting. The authors want a realistic, end‑to‑end environment to test whether LLM judges can both evaluate drafts and guide iterative improvement, and how their assessments compare with expert human judgments.
AI.method: The authors build Vibe Patenting, an end‑to‑end patent drafting benchmark in which drafting agents generate patent applications for different inventions. A separate LLM judge, called after each draft, evaluates the draft along structured dimensions and provides targeted feedback. Drafting agents then revise iteratively using this feedback. They compare judge‑guided vs unguided revision, vary model strength and reasoning depth (low‑ vs high‑reasoning agents), and explore domain‑specific agent workflows. They also compare the LLM judge’s evaluations to those of an independent professional patent attorney, analyzing agreement, metric dependence, and calibration differences.
AI.result: (1) Iterative revision guided by the LLM judge reliably improves the judge’s own quality scores, whereas unguided revision quickly plateaus. (2) A cheaper, low‑reasoning drafting agent, when iteratively refined with judge feedback, can reach performance close to a much more expensive, high‑reasoning agent. (3) Stronger models and more reasoning generally yield higher judge‑assessed quality, and domain‑tailored agent workflows further improve results. (4) When compared to a professional patent attorney, the LLM judge shows meaningful—but metric‑dependent—agreement and systematic calibration biases, indicating it is neither random nor fully aligned with expert standards.
AI.conclusion: LLM judges are effective optimization signals for improving AI‑generated patent drafts in an end‑to‑end professional setting and can partially substitute for more expensive drafting models, especially when used iteratively. However, their reliability is limited: agreement with human experts depends on the evaluation metric, and systematic calibration differences persist. Therefore, while LLM judges can be powerful tools for scaling evaluation and refinement in complex professional workflows, they should be used with awareness of their biases and validated against expert human judgment.

title: Token Merging for Multilingual Speech Recognition: A Systematic Study Across Model Scale and Fine-Tuning
summary: Leading multilingual speech recognition models like Whisper transcribe diverse, low-resource languages without language-specific training but are computationally expensive to deploy. Token merging mitigates this inefficiency by dynamically combining redundant features, shortening the sequence length during inference without requiring retraining. In this paper, we systematically evaluate token merging on the Whisper model family across sixteen diverse languages and three different model sizes. We also test how token merging interacts with fine-tuning (DoRA) on low-resource languages. Our findings show that merging tokens increases computational efficiency with almost no loss in transcription accuracy across most low-resource languages and model sizes, and it works even after the model has been fine-tuned. Our results demonstrate that token merging is a highly practical method for making multilingual speech recognition faster and cheaper to deploy.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates token merging as a way to speed up Whisper multilingual speech recognition, showing it greatly reduces computation with almost no accuracy loss, even after fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Multilingual speech recognition models like Whisper can handle many low-resource languages but are expensive to run due to long sequence lengths and large model sizes. There is a need for practical methods to reduce inference cost without retraining or sacrificing accuracy, especially for low-resource languages and real-world deployment.
AI.method: The authors apply token merging, a technique that dynamically combines redundant internal token features to shorten the sequence during inference, to different sizes of the Whisper model across sixteen diverse languages. They conduct systematic evaluations of transcription accuracy and computational efficiency, and additionally investigate how token merging behaves when Whisper is fine-tuned on low-resource languages using DoRA.
AI.result: Token merging consistently improves computational efficiency—by reducing effective sequence length and thus inference cost—while causing almost no degradation in transcription accuracy for most tested low-resource languages and for all evaluated Whisper model sizes. The technique remains effective even after models have been fine-tuned with DoRA.
AI.conclusion: Token merging is a practical and robust way to accelerate multilingual speech recognition with Whisper, cutting inference cost while preserving accuracy across languages, model sizes, and even after fine-tuning. This makes Whisper-based systems faster and cheaper to deploy, particularly for low-resource language scenarios.

title: Toward Self-Adaptive Physical AI: Can LLM Agents Manage Long-Horizon Physical Tasks?
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents offer a promising path toward autonomously managing long-term physical tasks without human intervention. However, physical tasks require agents to continuously observe the environment, make consequential actions, and remain effective as the environment changes. Existing approaches either require substantial data and retraining, or primarily focus on agents operating in the virtual world. In this work, we explore the feasibility of building a self-adaptive physical AI agent that manages long-term physical tasks in a zero-shot manner and adapts to environmental changes without human intervention. We design a multi-agent framework that integrates planning, tool calling, observation, and verification, and evaluate it on agricultural tasks against reinforcement learning (RL) agents under different weather patterns. Our results show that zero-shot LLM agents can achieve comparable management outcomes to RL agents under the same weather pattern and adapt more effectively than RL when evaluated under a shifted environment, highlighting a promising path toward self-adaptive physical AI agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a zero-shot, self-adaptive LLM-based multi-agent framework for managing long-term physical tasks, showing it can match RL agents in known environments and outperform them under environmental shifts.
AI.motivation: Physical long-term tasks (e.g., in agriculture) need agents that can continuously observe, act, and adapt to changing conditions without costly retraining or constant human supervision, which current RL or virtual-only LLM approaches do not provide.
AI.method: The authors design a multi-agent architecture around an LLM that combines planning, tool invocation, environment observation, and result verification; they deploy it on agricultural management tasks and compare its performance against reinforcement learning agents under varying and shifted weather conditions.
AI.result: In agricultural simulations, the zero-shot LLM agent achieves management quality comparable to RL agents when evaluated under the same weather regime, and it adapts better than RL baselines when weather patterns change, demonstrating stronger robustness to environmental shifts.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based multi-agent systems can function as self-adaptive physical AI agents, handling long-term tasks in a zero-shot manner and adapting to environmental changes without retraining, suggesting a viable alternative or complement to RL for real-world, dynamic settings.

title: PhysMent: An Interactive Approach For LLM Reasoning In Physics Problems
summary: Large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on static science benchmarks, yet their ability to reason about the physical world through active experimentation remains poorly understood. We introduce PhysMent, a benchmark that evaluates LLM physical reasoning via iterative, toolmediated interaction with a MuJoCo physics simulator. Unlike static benchmarks that supply all quantities upfront, PhysMent requires models to discover information by applying forces, querying object states, advancing time, and modifying scene geometry before answering. The benchmark comprises 105 scenes of classical mechanics, organized across four difficulty regimes (Easy/Hard and Single/Multi), three scene modalities (standard, object creation, hidden objects), and a scene-manipulation category, evaluated with a six-dimensional scoring framework. Results show that current models perform reasonably well on qualitative single-concept tasks (up to 80% accuracy) but degrade substantially on quantitative tasks that demand precise, multi-step experimental procedures: most models fall below 30% on the hardest single-concept category, where the bottleneck is procedural (adaptive multi-step tool use) rather than conceptual load. Across the seven models, accuracy ranges from 25% to 67%, with failures due to premature answer submission, inefficient exploration, and inconsistent grounding in simulator feedback rather than conceptual gaps.

AI.tldr: PhysMent is a benchmark that tests how well LLMs can do hands-on physical reasoning by interactively using a physics simulator, revealing weak performance on complex quantitative, multi-step experimental tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing science benchmarks for LLMs are mostly static question-answer formats where all relevant information is given explicitly. These settings do not capture the process of doing real physical reasoning, which often requires planning, experimentation, interacting with the environment, and gathering missing information. The authors want to understand whether LLMs can behave more like experimental scientists: designing and running experiments in a physics environment, interpreting feedback, and using tools iteratively to reach a conclusion.
AI.method: The authors design PhysMent, a benchmark built around the MuJoCo physics simulator. LLMs interact with scenes via a tool interface that lets them apply forces, query object states, advance time, create or modify objects, and explore the environment. The benchmark includes 105 classical mechanics scenes varying along difficulty (Easy/Hard, Single/Multi concept), scene modality (standard, object creation, hidden objects), and scene-manipulation type. Performance is evaluated through a six-dimensional scoring framework capturing different facets of physical reasoning and tool use. Multiple LLMs are tested on both qualitative (conceptual) and quantitative (numerical, multi-step) tasks.
AI.result: The evaluated LLMs achieve relatively high accuracy (up to about 80%) on easier, qualitative tasks involving single physical concepts. However, their performance deteriorates sharply on more demanding quantitative tasks that require precise measurements and multi-step experimentation, with accuracies dropping below 30% on the hardest single-concept category. Across seven models, overall accuracy spans 25%–67%. Error analysis shows that many failures stem from procedural weaknesses: models answer too early, explore the scene inefficiently, or fail to remain consistent with simulator feedback, rather than lacking the underlying physics concepts.
AI.conclusion: PhysMent demonstrates that LLMs’ current strengths on static physics and science benchmarks do not translate well to interactive, experiment-driven physical reasoning. The main limitations are in procedural and tool-use competence—planning adaptive multi-step experiments, systematically exploring, and grounding conclusions in observed feedback—rather than purely conceptual physics knowledge. This benchmark thus exposes a key gap for future work: improving models’ abilities as active experimenters, not just passive problem solvers.

title: TestHallVQA: Exploring LVLMs' Document-Level Reasoning under Redundant Contexts from Scientific Exams
summary: Large Vision--Language Models (LVLMs) are increasingly expected to perform visual question answering (VQA) over planar media. However, existing planar VQA benchmarks typically emphasize isolated challenges: some emphasize long-document understanding with limited reasoning depth, while others require complex visual reasoning but remain restricted to single-page, noise-free settings. Moreover, through theoretical analysis, we identify the impact of irrelevant visual tokens, which leads to measurable performance degradation but has received little attention with respect to systematic quantification. To address these limitations, we introduce TestHallVQA, a multi-image VQA benchmark that simultaneously embodies document-level scale and the difficulty of human examinations, while providing comprehensive task coverage. Leveraging TestHallVQA's ability to controllably inject multi-level contextual redundancy, we further propose a novel metric, F1-R\textsuperscript{2}, which jointly quantifies LVLMs' computational reasoning capability and their evidence retrieval robustness against document-level redundancy. Extensive experiments and analyses on mainstream LVLMs reveal their latent deficiencies across multiple dimensions, offering concrete insights and directions for future research. The associated datasets, code, and complete theoretical derivations are available at https://github.com/yqyu2317/TestHallVQA-benchmark.

AI.tldr: Introduces TestHallVQA, a multi-image, exam-style VQA benchmark and a new F1-R^2 metric to evaluate LVLMs’ reasoning and robustness to redundant visual context.
AI.motivation: Existing planar VQA benchmarks focus either on long-document understanding with shallow reasoning or on complex reasoning over clean single pages, and they rarely analyze how irrelevant visual tokens and contextual redundancy harm LVLM performance. There is a need for a benchmark that combines document-level scale, exam-like difficulty, and controlled redundancy to systematically probe both reasoning depth and robustness to noisy context.
AI.method: The authors design TestHallVQA, a multi-image VQA benchmark modeled after human examinations that spans diverse task types, document scales, and difficulty levels, and can inject multi-level contextual redundancy across pages. Based on a theoretical analysis of how irrelevant visual tokens affect LVLMs, they formulate a new evaluation metric, F1-R^2, that jointly measures computational reasoning capability and robustness of evidence retrieval in the presence of document-level redundancy. They then run extensive experiments on mainstream LVLMs over this benchmark and analyze their behavior along these dimensions.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show that current large vision–language models suffer significant performance drops when confronted with document-level redundancy and multi-image reasoning, revealing weaknesses both in reasoning depth and in robust evidence localization. The F1-R^2 metric and the structured benchmark expose latent deficiencies that are not apparent under traditional, cleaner VQA settings.
AI.conclusion: TestHallVQA, together with the F1-R^2 metric, offers a more realistic and rigorous way to evaluate LVLMs on planar media by combining document-scale, multi-image, exam-like tasks with controlled redundancy. The findings highlight that existing LVLMs are brittle to irrelevant visual tokens and redundant context, underscoring the need for improved architectures and training strategies targeting robust multi-image reasoning and evidence retrieval.

title: Root-Cause Attribution Is a Search Problem: Continual Search for Long-Horizon Agent Failures
summary: The increasing deployment of AI agents in long-horizon tasks yields massive execution logs. Diagnosing failures within these records is crucial for reliability, as it transforms outcome-level signals into actionable interventions. The sheer scale of the data renders human review impractical, driving the need for automated root-cause attribution (RCA). However, automated RCA methods using LLMs suffer from low diagnostic accuracy, especially as execution traces grow larger. They struggle because relevant information is often sparse, distributed across distant actions, and disconnected from the visible failure, reducing root-cause attribution to a massive search problem. Existing RCA methods typically rely on one-shot LLM judgments to diagnose failures from execution traces. While effective for shorter trajectories, these judges tend to settle on a plausible diagnosis early, leaving critical evidence in longer traces unexamined. We introduce Continual Search, an iterative framework that nudges the judge, over successive turns, to keep searching for unresolved diagnostic evidence. We evaluate Continual Search across four existing RCA benchmarks. Recognizing the lack of massive execution traces in current benchmarks, we introduce MegaRCA-Mix to evaluate RCA at scale. MegaRCA-Mix provides a challenging testbed of 50 human-annotated failure trials spanning long-horizon, execution-heavy tasks. Across multiple benchmark suites and model families, Continual Search consistently improves attribution performance. On MegaRCA-Mix, for example, it improves GPT-5.5's F1 score by more than 40\%, from $0.349$ to $0.498$. More interestingly, within the same model family, lower-tier models can even surpass their higher-tier counterparts, demonstrating that effective search supersedes raw model scale.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Continual Search, an iterative LLM-based framework for root-cause attribution in long AI agent execution logs, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy over one-shot methods, especially on long, execution-heavy traces.
AI.motivation: As AI agents are increasingly used for long-horizon, complex tasks, they generate massive execution logs. When agents fail, understanding why they failed (root-cause attribution) is critical for improving reliability. Manual analysis of these large logs is infeasible, and current automated RCA approaches using LLMs perform poorly on long traces because key evidence is sparse, distant, and disconnected from the visible failure. Existing methods typically rely on a single-pass judgment, which tends to fixate on an early plausible cause and ignore later, crucial evidence. The authors are motivated to design an RCA method that scales to long trajectories and systematically continues searching for evidence instead of settling too early.
AI.method: The authors introduce Continual Search, an iterative LLM-based framework for root-cause attribution. Instead of asking a judge model to diagnose the failure in one shot from the entire execution trace, Continual Search guides the model through multiple rounds of analysis. In each round, the judge is nudged to keep looking for unresolved or missing diagnostic evidence across the trace, treating RCA as an ongoing search over sparse, distributed clues. This process helps the model revisit and integrate information spread across distant actions in long logs. The framework is evaluated on existing RCA benchmarks as well as a new large-scale benchmark, MegaRCA-Mix, which contains 50 human-annotated long-horizon, execution-heavy failure trials.
AI.result: Continual Search yields consistent gains in root-cause attribution performance across several benchmarks and model families. On the newly introduced MegaRCA-Mix benchmark, the method substantially improves the F1 score of GPT-5.5 by more than 40%, increasing it from 0.349 to 0.498. The experiments also reveal that, within the same model family, smaller or lower-tier models equipped with Continual Search can outperform larger or higher-tier models that rely on standard one-shot RCA, indicating that improved search strategy can compensate for or even exceed the benefits of increased model size.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that automated root-cause attribution for AI agents on long, complex execution traces is fundamentally a search problem rather than solely a modeling capacity problem. Their Continual Search framework, which encourages iterative, evidence-seeking analysis, significantly boosts diagnostic accuracy over one-shot LLM judges, particularly at scale. The new MegaRCA-Mix benchmark demonstrates the method’s effectiveness on realistic, long-horizon tasks and highlights that thoughtful search and reasoning procedures can enable smaller models to outperform larger ones for RCA. This underscores the importance of algorithmic frameworks for search and evidence integration in improving AI reliability, beyond simply scaling up model size.

title: Clinical Reasoning Under a Partially Observed Objective in Cone Beam CT Report Generation
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. ODIN 2026 CBCT report generation challenge system. Code: https://github.com/GIND123/CBCT-Clinical-Reasoner
summary: Maxillofacial report generation from cone beam computed tomography is scored here by a composite objective placing 80% of its weight on a large language model judgement of factual entailment and 20% on lexical overlap, of which only the lexical fifth is visible during development. The grader's BLEU-4 and METEOR routines are reproduced in pure Python and match the reference to machine precision, and an offline entailment surrogate, which tells a report written for one patient from one written for another at an area under the curve of 0.987, makes the composite objective cheap enough to optimise directly. Over the 622-case public release, a report selected against the visible lexical ranking scores 0.2909, whereas one selected against the composite objective scores 0.4122, because pursuing n-gram overlap drives entailment precision from 0.522 down to 0.266. A 29 million parameter encoder fine-tuned on the release reaches a prevalence-weighted out-of-fold area under the curve of 0.486 over 985 statements, indistinguishable from the corpus prior, while nine numbers read from the image header reach 0.945 for mandible coverage and 0.872 for condyle coverage, and acquisition centre alone predicts sentence choice at 0.718 against 0.663 for the image-derived model, identifying dictation convention rather than anatomy as the quantity the lexical metrics reward. The delivered system emits eight unconditional statements and five gated on header geometry under polarity, laterality and tooth-level consistency constraints, and reaches METEOR 0.3542 over 50 held-out cases from an unseen centre. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/GIND123/CBCT-Clinical-Reasoner

AI.tldr: They design and validate a new, entailment-focused objective for automatic report generation from CBCT scans, showing that common lexical metrics reward style and site conventions more than factual correctness, and they release data and code.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic report generation for medical images is typically optimized and evaluated using lexical overlap metrics like BLEU and METEOR. In this CBCT maxillofacial setting, the authors suspect that such metrics do not actually capture factual correctness or anatomical adequacy, but instead reward matching local dictation conventions. They want an objective that better reflects whether a generated report is truly entailed by the underlying scan, and they want to understand what current models are really learning when trained against lexical metrics.
AI.method: 1) Define a composite evaluation objective: 80% weight on an LLM-based factual entailment judgement between a candidate report and reference, and 20% weight on lexical overlap (BLEU-4 and METEOR). Only the lexical fifth is exposed during system development to avoid overfitting to the full metric. 2) Re-implement BLEU-4 and METEOR in pure Python to exactly match the original grader. 3) Build an offline entailment surrogate classifier that distinguishes whether a report belongs to a given patient vs another, achieving AUC 0.987, and then use this surrogate to approximate the LLM entailment signal cheaply enough to directly optimize the composite objective. 4) On a 622-case public CBCT dataset, compare reports selected by lexical ranking alone with those selected using the composite objective and analyze the impact on entailment precision. 5) Train a 29M-parameter image encoder on the dataset to predict 985 clinical statements and evaluate its out-of-fold AUC. 6) Compare image-based predictions with simple tabular inputs (nine header fields, acquisition centre) to see what factors drive performance. 7) Design a practical system that emits eight unconditional template-like statements and five statements gated on header-derived geometry, subject to logical constraints, and evaluate it on 50 unseen-centre test cases using METEOR.
AI.result: 1) Composite vs lexical optimization: A report chosen by the visible lexical ranking achieves a composite score of 0.2909, while the one chosen by optimizing the composite objective reaches 0.4122. Chasing n-gram overlap alone drops entailment precision from 0.522 to 0.266, showing that higher BLEU/METEOR can correspond to much worse factual correctness. 2) Entailment surrogate: The offline entailment classifier discriminates correct vs mismatched patient reports with AUC 0.987, making it practical to use as a proxy for the LLM-based entailment component. 3) Image encoder: The 29M-parameter encoder, fine-tuned to predict 985 statements, achieves a prevalence-weighted out-of-fold AUC of 0.486, essentially no better than the corpus prior. 4) Header vs image signals: Simple features from nine header numbers give very strong performance on specific coverage tasks (AUC 0.945 for mandible, 0.872 for condyle), and acquisition centre alone predicts sentence choice with AUC 0.718 compared to 0.663 for the high-capacity image model. This indicates that lexical metrics heavily reward site-specific dictation patterns rather than anatomy-driven content. 5) Deployed system: The final rule/geometry-driven system, combining unconditional and header-gated statements with consistency checks, achieves METEOR 0.3542 on 50 held-out cases from a previously unseen centre. The data and code are released publicly.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing report generation systems against standard lexical overlap metrics can seriously misalign them with factual entailment in CBCT maxillofacial reporting, encouraging models to mimic local dictation conventions instead of accurately reflecting patient anatomy. An entailment-focused composite objective, supported by a high-AUC offline surrogate, yields substantially better factual alignment even when lexical scores may not be maximized. Moreover, a relatively simple system using header-derived geometry and template-like statements generalizes robustly across centres, whereas a sizeable image encoder fails to outperform corpus priors, and acquisition centre alone predicts much of the lexical content. The work argues that future evaluation and training for medical report generation should prioritize entailment-based objectives and carefully control for confounders like site-specific style, and it provides an open dataset and codebase to support such research.

title: RFCLLM: Evaluating LLMs' Reasoning Ability of Network Protocol State Machines
summary: Mapping textual specifications into formal representations is essential for ensuring the correctness of protocol designs and implementations. LLM-generated mappings, used for networking security or testing, are assumed to capture a perfect understanding of the specification, which may not hold in practice. The goal of this paper is to assess the extent to which LLMs can interpret the specification correctly. We examine the degree to which an LLM's implicit representation of a finite-state transition system-defined via natural language descriptions-aligns with a manually generated ground-truth model. We designed 4 tasks and 1482 task queries for 16 protocols. We evaluated different judge biases, observed the inherent difficulty gaps between tasks, looked into the effect of 4 context types, and the influence of protocol characteristics. Our work contributes to a step toward verifying whether LLMs can really be trusted in FSM (Finite State Machine) reasoning of protocol specifications.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how accurately large language models can understand and reason about protocol specifications expressed as finite state machines from natural language descriptions.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to interpret protocol specifications for networking security and testing, with an implicit assumption that they perfectly understand and correctly map textual specs to formal models. However, this assumption is untested and potentially unsafe, especially for security-critical networking protocols. The paper is motivated by the need to rigorously assess whether LLMs’ internal representations of protocol behavior, modeled as finite state machines, actually match ground-truth formal models.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark of 16 protocols, each with manually created ground-truth FSM models, and design 4 distinct task types that probe different aspects of FSM reasoning (e.g., state transitions, reachability, behavior under conditions). They generate 1482 task queries in total, and query LLMs under 4 different context types, systematically varying how protocol information is presented. They also analyze the impact of different judge setups (to evaluate model answers), task difficulty differences, and protocol characteristics on performance.
AI.result: The study finds notable gaps between LLMs’ FSM reasoning and the ground-truth models. Task performance varies significantly by task type and context, revealing inherent difficulty differences. Context design and protocol characteristics substantially influence how well LLMs capture the transition systems, and different judging approaches expose biases in assessing correctness. Overall, LLMs frequently fail to fully align with the formal FSM models, especially on more complex reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: LLMs cannot yet be blindly trusted to accurately and consistently reason about protocol specifications as finite state machines, particularly for safety- and security-critical applications. The work provides empirical evidence, a structured benchmark, and analysis framework as a step toward more rigorous verification of LLMs’ FSM reasoning abilities, highlighting the need for improved methods, guardrails, or hybrid approaches when using LLMs in protocol design and analysis.

title: OrchSLM: Probing the Dynamics of Small Language Model Orchestration
summary: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their reliance on cloud-scale infrastructure poses fundamental challenges for deployment in agentic pipelines, including latency, privacy, connectivity, and substantial computational cost. Small language models (SLMs) offer a compelling alternative: recent studies suggest that many repetitive and narrowly scoped subtasks in agentic workloads may be better served by specialized SLMs than by monolithic LLMs. However, the limited capacity and context windows of SLMs can constrain long-horizon reasoning and interaction-heavy orchestration strategies such as iterative verification and debate. This motivates a complementary, non-interactive paradigm in which heterogeneous SLMs independently generate candidate solutions and a router orchestrates their cached samples without further model interaction. To further understand the mechanisms of such orchestration, we introduce OrchSLM, a routing framework that unifies existing non-interactive orchestration methods and exposes their underlying design choices as controllable parameters. Using OrchSLM as a systematic probe, we reveal how orchestration behavior emerges from diverse knobs, including the task structure, model-pool composition, and multi-agent consensus.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OrchSLM, a routing framework for orchestrating multiple small language models (SLMs) in a non-interactive way, to overcome the latency, privacy, and cost issues of large language models while preserving effectiveness on complex tasks.
AI.motivation: Large language models require heavy cloud infrastructure, causing latency, privacy, connectivity, and cost problems in agentic pipelines. Small language models are cheaper and can handle many narrow subtasks, but their limited capacity and context windows make them unsuitable for long-horizon, interaction-heavy strategies like debate or iterative verification. This gap motivates exploring a non-interactive orchestration paradigm where multiple heterogeneous SLMs work independently and are coordinated via routing, rather than through multi-turn interactions.
AI.method: The authors propose OrchSLM, a unified routing framework for non-interactive orchestration of heterogeneous SLMs. In this setup, SLMs independently generate candidate solutions which are cached; a router then selects and composes these outputs without further LLM/SLM interaction. OrchSLM formalizes and exposes key orchestration design choices—such as task decomposition, routing policies, model-pool composition, and consensus mechanisms—as tunable parameters, enabling systematic experimentation and analysis of how different configurations affect behavior and performance.
AI.result: Using OrchSLM as a probe, the authors empirically study how orchestration behaviors and performance emerge from variations in task structure, the composition and specialization of the SLM pool, and the choice of multi-agent consensus or aggregation strategy. They show that different configurations of these knobs lead to distinct orchestration dynamics and effectiveness profiles, revealing trade-offs and patterns in non-interactive SLM orchestration.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that non-interactive orchestration of heterogeneous SLMs is a viable and flexible alternative to interactive, LLM-centric agent systems. OrchSLM provides a unifying framework to analyze and design such systems, demonstrating that orchestration behavior can be systematically controlled via routing, model selection, and consensus mechanisms, and offering guidance for building efficient, privacy-friendly, and low-latency agentic pipelines using specialized SLMs.

title: CVSS-X: A Multilingual Speech-to-Speech Translation Corpus for 28 Languages
summary: We introduce CVSS-X, a large-scale synthetic speech-to-speech translation corpus that extends CVSS by reversing the translation direction. While CVSS translates from 21 languages into English, CVSS-X enables translation from English into 28 target languages spanning 12 language families. The corpus comprises approximately 240,000 parallel speech pairs per language, totaling over 16,000 hours, eight times larger than CVSS. We provide two variants: CVSS-X-C with two canonical voices per language, and CVSS-X-T with cross-lingual voice cloning, both fully generated. Evaluation shows comparable translation quality to CVSS with consistent performance across typologically diverse languages. Combined with CVSS, this enables research on bidirectional and multilingual speech-to-speech translation. The code is available at https://github.com/ErmisAI/XVSS-X and the dataset under CC-BY-NC 4.0 license at https://huggingface.co/datasets/lgris/XVSS-X.

AI.tldr: CVSS-X is a large-scale, fully synthetic English-to-multilingual speech-to-speech translation corpus, extending CVSS to support bidirectional and multilingual S2ST research.
AI.motivation: Existing CVSS only supports speech-to-speech translation from many languages into English, limiting research on reverse and truly bidirectional/multilingual S2ST systems. There is a lack of large, standardized corpora for English-to-many speech translation at scale, especially with controlled voices and cloning setups for systematic evaluation and modeling.
AI.method: The authors construct a synthetic corpus by generating English speech and its translations as target-language speech for 28 languages. They design two variants: CVSS-X-C, which uses two canonical synthetic voices per language, and CVSS-X-T, which applies cross-lingual voice cloning to better mimic speaker identity transfer across languages. They align about 240k parallel speech pairs per language, totalling over 16k hours, and evaluate translation quality versus the original CVSS benchmarks across typologically diverse languages.
AI.result: CVSS-X reaches translation quality comparable to the original CVSS corpus despite being fully synthetic and targeting more languages and a different translation direction. Performance is consistent over a wide range of language families, and the dataset is substantially larger—about eight times the size of CVSS in hours. The authors release code and data under a permissive research license for community use.
AI.conclusion: CVSS-X fills the gap for English-to-multilingual speech-to-speech translation data by providing a large, synthetic, and systematically designed corpus in two variants (canonical and voice-cloned). Together with CVSS, it enables research on bidirectional and truly multilingual S2ST systems, including evaluation of voice consistency, cross-lingual cloning, and scaling to many target languages.

title: Grounded Adjudication of Variations across Extracted TimeLines (GAVEL): Comparing Clinical Timelines Against Their Case Reports
summary: Existing pipelines for clinical timeline extraction from case reports are evaluated using an expert reference and are limited by imperfect reference annotations and imprecise event alignment. We developed GAVEL, an LLM judge protocol that compares two timelines with the case report and returns a discrepancy type, verdict, and report passage for each difference. We evaluated the event matcher, reviewed 2,738 findings from GPT5.6sol and DeepSeek V3.2, ranked six LLM extractors and two human annotators, and tested GAVEL guided merging. True match rates were 60% immediately below and 48% immediately above the 0.10 cutoff. Manual review confirmed 89.4% and 88.6% of findings. Across 126 reports, merged timelines were preferred in 77.0% of comparisons (95% CI, 69.8 to 84.1%) and reduced discrepancies attributed to the evaluated timeline from 7.63 to 0.85 per report. GAVEL supports report-based comparison and revision without treating either timeline as ground truth.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GAVEL, an LLM-based judging protocol to compare and refine clinical event timelines extracted from case reports, enabling more accurate evaluation and merging of timelines without assuming any single reference is ground truth.
AI.motivation: Existing clinical timeline extraction pipelines rely on expert-annotated reference timelines and simple event matching, which suffer from imperfect annotations and alignment issues. This limits fair comparison among systems and hampers improvement of extracted timelines. There is a need for a more robust, report-grounded way to compare multiple timelines and iteratively refine them without assuming any one is perfectly correct.
AI.method: The authors design GAVEL, an LLM-judge protocol that takes two candidate timelines plus the source case report and, for each detected difference between the timelines, classifies the discrepancy type, issues a comparative verdict (which timeline is better or if they are equivalent), and points to the supporting passage in the report. They evaluate the event-matching component, manually review thousands of LLM-generated findings from different models (GPT5.6sol and DeepSeek V3.2), rank six LLM-based timeline extractors and two human annotators using GAVEL judgments, and apply a GAVEL-guided merging procedure to combine timelines. Metrics such as true match rates at a 0.10 cutoff and confirmation rates from manual review are reported.
AI.result: True match rates around the decision threshold were 60% just below and 48% just above the 0.10 cutoff, indicating meaningful discrimination by the matcher. Manual review confirmed roughly 89% of GAVEL’s findings for both evaluated models, suggesting high reliability. In experiments on 126 case reports, the merged timelines created under GAVEL’s guidance were preferred in 77% of pairwise comparisons (95% CI: 69.8–84.1%) and the average number of discrepancies attributable to the evaluated timeline dropped from 7.63 to 0.85 per report.
AI.conclusion: GAVEL provides a reliable LLM-based framework for comparing and improving clinical event timelines directly against the source report instead of relying on a single ground-truth timeline. It enables robust evaluation, ranking of systems and annotators, and effective timeline merging, substantially reducing discrepancies and producing timelines that human reviewers prefer in most cases.

title: Causal Analysis and Mitigation of Spurious Onsets in Full-Duplex Speech LLMs
summary: Speech-to-speech LLMs like Moshi, and its derivative PersonaPlex, can listen and speak concurrently through full-duplex generation. However, they can begin speaking inappropriately during prolonged user silence: under digital-zero input, Moshi and PersonaPlex initiate speech in 12/40 and 11/40 five-minute continuations, respectively. What causes this spurious speech? We investigate two hypotheses: either repeated sampling selects speech despite persistently low onset probabilities, or conditioning on the model's nonspeech outputs causes an abrupt spike in onset probability. We find that, at every observed onset, speech probability spikes by over nine orders of magnitude in one 80-ms frame, supporting the latter hypothesis. Then, to suppress these onsets without blocking genuine responses, we ask a causal counterfactual question: is the model responding to user speech, or would its next-token distribution remain similar if the preceding user input were muted? Accordingly, we suppress onsets whose distributions change little under this intervention. Across 40 held-out trials per model with realistic microphone noise, our method suppresses 13/13 Moshi and 9/9 PersonaPlex spurious onsets, while preserving 40/40 genuine responses per model. Our inference-time method requires no retraining and runs in real-time, with 95th-percentile decision time below 61 ms, within the 80-ms frame budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/KentoNishi/icassp27-spurious-onsets.

AI.tldr: The paper studies why speech-to-speech LLMs like Moshi and PersonaPlex start talking on their own during user silence, finds that abrupt probability spikes cause these spurious onsets, and proposes a real-time, inference-only causal counterfactual test that reliably suppresses them without hurting genuine responses.
AI.motivation: Speech-to-speech LLMs operate in full-duplex mode, listening and speaking simultaneously. In realistic settings, users may remain silent for long periods, yet models like Moshi and PersonaPlex sometimes start speaking even with no meaningful audio input (digital-zero or just microphone noise). This behavior is undesirable, confusing, and potentially unsafe for deployment. Existing solutions like heuristic thresholds or retraining are either brittle, costly, or harm responsiveness. The paper aims to understand the mechanism behind these spurious speech onsets and to design a principled, low-latency method to suppress them while still allowing prompt, genuine responses.
AI.method: The authors first empirically quantify spurious onset behavior by running 5-minute continuations with digital-zero input on Moshi and PersonaPlex and observing how often they begin speaking. They then formulate two hypotheses: (1) speech eventually appears just from repeated sampling of low-probability onsets; or (2) the model’s own nonspeech outputs shift the context so that speech onset probability suddenly spikes. By analyzing token-level onset probabilities frame by frame (80 ms frames), they show that every observed onset is preceded by an abrupt, >9-order-of-magnitude spike in speech probability within a single frame, supporting the second hypothesis. Building on this, they propose a causal counterfactual inference-time test: they compare the model’s next-token distribution under the actual audio context vs. a counterfactual where the recent user input is muted (replaced with silence). If the distribution changes little, they infer that the response is not actually grounded in user speech and treat the onset as spurious, suppressing it. This method is implemented as a lightweight, real-time check within the frame budget, requiring no retraining of the base models.
AI.result: In experiments on held-out trials with realistic microphone noise, the method is evaluated on Moshi and PersonaPlex. It fully suppresses all detected spurious onsets—13 out of 13 for Moshi and 9 out of 9 for PersonaPlex—while preserving all genuine responses—40 out of 40 responses for each model. Timing measurements show that the counterfactual decision procedure runs in real-time, with a 95th-percentile decision latency under 61 ms, comfortably within the 80-ms frame window used for generation. Additionally, analysis of probability trajectories confirms that speech onsets are preceded by dramatic, sudden spikes in onset probability, refuting the gradual-accumulation-through-sampling hypothesis.
AI.conclusion: Spurious speech during user silence in full-duplex speech-to-speech LLMs arises not from gradual sampling of low-probability tokens, but from abrupt, context-induced spikes in speech onset probability. By explicitly testing whether a potential onset is causally grounded in the recent user audio via a mute-based counterfactual, the authors can reliably distinguish genuine, user-driven responses from spurious ones. Their inference-time, retraining-free method effectively removes spurious onsets in realistic noisy conditions without sacrificing responsiveness, and it operates within strict real-time constraints. This approach provides a practical and principled way to make speech-to-speech LLMs safer and more usable in interactive settings.

title: Token Efficient Task Execution via Application Behavior Modeling for Web Agents
summary: The strong performance of AI Agents across an impressive variety of tasks is driving an unprecedented investment in agentic infrastructures, however the cost of processing tokens is fast increasing. Web agents automate the execution of web-application tasks described in natural language, by analyzing the web-application's user interface (UI) and interacting with it. This work introduces OdoBot, a novel web-agent architecture that completes tasks at a fraction of the cost when compared to conventional web agents. This is achieved by leveraging a behavioral model of the underlying application constructed by analyzing successful task-execution demonstrations. Our experiments with 45 tasks on the Canvas Learning Management System (LMS) demonstrate that OdoBot uses 44% and 80% fewer tokens than two state-of-the-art competitor agents (Agent-E and WebVoyager), while also surpassing WebVoyager in terms of task success rate.

AI.tldr: OdoBot is a web-agent architecture that executes tasks in web applications using significantly fewer tokens than existing agents while maintaining or improving task success rates.
AI.motivation: Processing tokens for AI agents is becoming increasingly costly as their use scales, especially for web agents that need to interpret and interact with complex user interfaces. There is a need for more efficient agents that can complete tasks reliably but with much lower token consumption.
AI.method: The authors propose OdoBot, a web-agent architecture that builds a behavioral model of a target web application by analyzing successful task-execution demonstrations. OdoBot then uses this learned model to interpret natural-language task descriptions and interact with the web application's UI more efficiently, reducing the number of tokens required compared with conventional web agents that rely heavily on repeated full-page reasoning.
AI.result: On 45 tasks from the Canvas Learning Management System (LMS), OdoBot reduces token usage by 44% compared with Agent-E and by 80% compared with WebVoyager. It also achieves a higher task success rate than WebVoyager, demonstrating both efficiency and effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging a learned behavioral model of web applications from demonstrations enables web agents to operate with dramatically lower token costs while maintaining or improving task success. OdoBot shows that demonstration-driven behavioral modeling is a promising direction for scalable, cost-efficient web automation agents.

title: Hindsight Bias in Clinical Temporal Reasoning: How Future Data Exposure Affects Large Language Model Judgment
summary: Clinical decisions are prospective, but clinical language models are often evaluated on retrospective records that reveal the final diagnosis, treatment response, and outcome. Such evaluations may reward the use of future information rather than reasoning under the uncertainty present at the decision point. We introduce a paired benchmark for measuring outcome-conditioned shifts consistent with hindsight bias in clinical temporal reasoning. It contains 171 case reports from the PubMed Central Open Access Subset---40 sepsis and 131 GLP-1/diabetes cases---represented as both textual narratives and human-annotated and LLM-generated textual time series (TTS). For each case, questions are tied to a clinically meaningful cutoff and paired with a prospective reference answer and an outcome-consistent \emph{hindsight trap}. Models answer each question using either a TTS truncated at the cutoff or the complete timeline; additional conditions vary the narrative source (original or synthetic) and TTS annotation source (human or LLM). We evaluate accuracy (Acc), hindsight trap rate (HTR), answer instability rate (AIR), and hindsight bias rate (HBR), each of which captures different signals of hindsight bias. Across GPT 5.6 Sol, Gemma 4, GLM 5.2, and Opus 5, full timeline exposure produces consistent hindsight-sensitive shifts, while temporal masking reduces bias without lowering accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark to detect and quantify hindsight bias in clinical language models by comparing their reasoning with and without access to future outcome information in clinical case timelines.
AI.motivation: Clinical language models are commonly evaluated on retrospective data that include final outcomes, which may let models implicitly use future information instead of reasoning under uncertainty at the actual decision time. This misalignment can mask true clinical reasoning capability and introduce hindsight bias. The authors aim to create an evaluation setup that better reflects prospective clinical decision-making and explicitly measures outcome-conditioned shifts in model behavior.
AI.method: The authors construct a paired benchmark of 171 clinical case reports (40 sepsis and 131 GLP-1/diabetes) from PubMed Central Open Access. Each case is represented as narrative text and as textual time series (TTS) derived from both human annotation and LLM generation. For every case, they define a clinically meaningful temporal cutoff and craft questions with two reference answers: a prospective answer reflecting information available up to the cutoff, and a hindsight trap answer that is only justified by knowledge of the eventual outcome. Models answer questions under multiple conditions: using TTS truncated at the cutoff vs the full timeline, with original vs synthetic narratives, and with human- vs LLM-generated TTS. They then compute four metrics—accuracy (Acc), hindsight trap rate (HTR), answer instability rate (AIR), and hindsight bias rate (HBR)—to quantify different aspects of hindsight bias and temporal reasoning shifts.
AI.result: Across multiple state-of-the-art LLMs (GPT 5.6 Sol, Gemma 4, GLM 5.2, and Opus 5), access to the full clinical timeline systematically alters answers in ways consistent with hindsight bias: models more frequently select outcome-consistent hindsight trap answers and show increased answer instability relative to the truncated condition. Temporal masking (restricting inputs to information available before the decision cutoff) substantially reduces these hindsight-sensitive shifts while preserving overall answer accuracy, indicating that bias can be mitigated without sacrificing performance on the benchmark tasks.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals that current clinical language models exhibit measurable hindsight bias when exposed to complete patient timelines, suggesting that standard retrospective evaluations may overestimate their true prospective reasoning abilities. By pairing prospective and hindsight-trap answers and varying temporal access and representation sources, the framework provides a more faithful assessment of temporal clinical reasoning. The findings support temporal masking and careful dataset design as practical strategies to reduce hindsight bias in clinical model evaluation and encourage future work to adopt prospective-style benchmarks for safer clinical deployment.

title: A Hybrid Hierarchical 1D-CNN-BiLSTM Framework for Extractive Summarization of Biomedical and Clinical Text
summary: Large language models have made abstractive summarization remarkably fluent, but generated summaries can hallucinate facts, posing serious risks in biomedical and clinical domains. We address this by removing generation from the pipeline and framing summarization as extractive sentence selection. Our Hybrid Hierarchical CNN-LSTM Summarizer uses stacked multi-kernel convolutions to compose sentence-level embeddings into richer inter-sentence representations, followed by a bidirectional LSTM to model long-range dependencies across the document. A lightweight scoring head assigns per-sentence importance scores and is trained end-to-end with binary cross-entropy against oracle extractive labels. At inference, a dynamic mean-plus-standard-deviation threshold with a top-3 fallback selects sentences directly from the source and chronologically reorders them into the final summary. Since every output sentence is copied from the input, the model avoids generation-induced factual drift. On PubMed, our architecture outperforms isolated CNN and LSTM baselines, while ablations show that wider convolutional receptive fields improve sentence scoring. On MIMIC-CXR and MIMIC-IV BHC, the model performs well on unstructured narratives but defaults toward positional baselines on highly templated reports. These results suggest that structural constraints can provide a reliable path toward factually grounded summarization systems that are trustworthy by design rather than by correction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an extractive, sentence-selection-based summarization model for biomedical and clinical text to avoid hallucinated content common in abstractive methods.
AI.motivation: Abstractive summarization with large language models often produces factually incorrect (hallucinated) content, which is especially dangerous in biomedical and clinical settings where accuracy is critical. The authors seek a summarization approach that is inherently fact-grounded and minimizes factual drift.
AI.method: They design a Hybrid Hierarchical CNN-LSTM Summarizer. First, stacked multi-kernel CNNs build richer inter-sentence representations from sentence embeddings. Then a bidirectional LSTM captures long-range dependencies across the document. A lightweight scoring head assigns importance scores to each sentence and is trained end-to-end using binary cross-entropy against oracle extractive labels. At inference, sentences are selected via a dynamic threshold defined by mean plus standard deviation of scores, with a top-3 fallback, and selected sentences are copied and chronologically ordered to form the summary.
AI.result: On the PubMed dataset, the hybrid architecture outperforms CNN-only and LSTM-only baselines, and ablations show that wider CNN receptive fields help sentence scoring. On MIMIC-CXR and MIMIC-IV BHC datasets, the model works well on unstructured narratives but tends toward simple positional baselines on highly templated reports.
AI.conclusion: By restricting summarization to extractive sentence selection with a structured hybrid CNN-LSTM architecture and dynamic selection strategy, the system avoids generation-induced hallucinations and offers a more trustworthy, factually grounded summarization method, especially suitable for sensitive biomedical and clinical applications.

title: From Legal Text to AI-specific Risk Sources: A Systematic Analysis of the EU AI Act's High-Risk Requirements
summary: The EU AI Act introduces mandatory requirements for high-risk AI systems with the explicit goal of ensuring the development and operation of trustworthy AI. At the same time, AI risk management practices rely on structured risk taxonomies to systematically identify and treat AI-specific risk sources. As both the AI Act and established risk taxonomies aim to address AI-induced risks, a natural question is whether they align in the risk sources they cover. However, no clear mapping exists between the risks implicitly addressed by the Act's high-risk requirements and established taxonomies, leaving practitioners without a structured basis for aligning regulatory obligations with AI risk management practice. This paper presents a systematic classification of the requirements extracted from the EU AI Act Section 2 (Requirements for high-risk AI systems), revealing that only a minority directly address AI-specific risk sources, while the majority impose organizational process and documentation obligations. From the AI risk-related requirements, a consolidated list of distinct AI-specific risk sources is derived. The resulting EU AI Act Risk Source List takes an important step towards bridging the gap between legal obligation and AI risk management practice, providing a structured reference for explicit comparison between existing AI risk taxonomies and the risk sources implicitly addressed by the EU AI Act. Important Note: This is the authors' preprint. The paper was presented at the 4th International Conference on Frontiers of Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Multidisciplinary Applications. A link to the conference's official proceedings will be provided upon publication.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how the EU AI Act’s high-risk AI requirements map to existing AI risk taxonomies and produces an explicit “EU AI Act Risk Source List” that links legal obligations to AI-specific risk sources.
AI.motivation: Although the EU AI Act and AI risk management taxonomies both aim to tackle AI-induced risks, there is no clear mapping between the Act’s high-risk requirements and established AI risk taxonomies, making it difficult for practitioners to align regulatory compliance with systematic AI risk management.
AI.method: The authors systematically extract and classify the requirements in Section 2 of the EU AI Act (Requirements for high-risk AI systems), distinguish which requirements directly address AI-specific risk sources versus those that impose organizational or documentation obligations, and from the risk-related requirements derive a consolidated list of distinct AI-specific risk sources implicitly covered by the Act.
AI.result: The analysis shows that only a minority of Section 2 requirements directly address AI-specific risk sources, while most focus on organizational processes and documentation; from the identified risk-related requirements, the authors construct an “EU AI Act Risk Source List” that explicitly enumerates AI-specific risk sources embedded in the Act’s obligations.
AI.conclusion: The resulting EU AI Act Risk Source List helps bridge the gap between the legal requirements of the EU AI Act and practical AI risk management, giving practitioners a structured reference to compare existing AI risk taxonomies with the risk sources implicitly addressed by the Act and thereby better align compliance activities with risk-based practices.

title: From Token Probabilities to Semantic Constraints: Towards Declarative Probabilistic Evaluation of Language Models
summary: While Large Language Models have improved rapidly, many fundamental questions remain about how to evaluate the knowledge and reasoning abilities they acquire, and how such evaluations relate to the learning signals used in pre-training. In this paper, we propose ModelLog, a declarative probabilistic framework for pre-training evaluation that makes the semantic structure of model behavior explicit and provides new formal tools for relating evaluation to learning. ModelLog specifies evaluation targets as symbolic constraints over token-level predictions and measures how strongly a model's distribution satisfies those constraints. We explore the framework through a new suite of tasks targeting negation, mutual exclusivity, and consistency, finding systematic failures that are difficult to characterize through token likelihood or answer accuracy alone. We further show that these evaluation scores can also be interpreted as losses, whose gradients reflect logical strength, informativeness, and variable-level sensitivity. This links evaluation and learning through a shared semantics, suggesting evaluation methods that diagnose model behavior while also helping to clarify the semantic structure of learning.

AI.tldr: Proposes ModelLog, a probabilistic, logic-based framework to evaluate LLMs by how well their prediction distributions satisfy symbolic constraints, linking evaluation directly to learning signals.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluations (e.g., token likelihood, answer accuracy) do not expose the underlying semantic structure of model behavior and struggle to diagnose reasoning abilities such as handling negation, mutual exclusivity, and consistency. There is also a conceptual gap between how models are trained (via token-level losses) and how they are evaluated (via task-level metrics). The authors want a principled way to formally relate pre-training signals to higher-level reasoning evaluations.
AI.method: Introduce ModelLog, a declarative probabilistic framework where evaluation targets are expressed as symbolic logical constraints over token-level predictions. For any model and input, ModelLog measures how strongly the model’s output distribution satisfies these constraints. They instantiate the framework in a suite of probing tasks designed around negation, mutual exclusivity, and consistency. They also reinterpret the evaluation scores as differentiable losses and analyze their gradients to understand how they encode logical strength, informativeness, and variable-level sensitivity.
AI.result: Using the ModelLog tasks, they uncover systematic reasoning failures in LLMs that standard metrics (token likelihood, answer accuracy) largely miss. The ModelLog-based scores capture subtler aspects of model behavior such as how consistently the model treats negated statements or mutually exclusive alternatives, and how it propagates constraints across related predictions. They also show that these scores can be differentiated to provide gradients with interpretable logical structure.
AI.conclusion: ModelLog offers a unified, semantics-aware framework that connects evaluation and learning for LLMs. By treating evaluation constraints as probabilistic, differentiable objects over token distributions, it both reveals nuanced reasoning failures and provides losses whose gradients correspond to logical notions like strength and informativeness. This suggests new evaluation methods that are diagnostic while also clarifying and potentially improving the semantic structure of pre-training and fine-tuning objectives.

title: Asclepius: An Adaptive Harness for Long-Horizon Clinical Agents
summary: LLM agents are predominantly benchmarked on short, single-task trajectories, yet real deployments run for hours under contention, surfacing a different class of failures. We use the Clinical Environment Simulator (CES), in which an agent manages an entire emergency-department shift under continuous time and resource pressure, as a testbed: long-horizon execution failures manifest measurably in a single rollout under structured, multi-dimensional grading. On CES, current agents reach the correct diagnosis in most cases yet fail to deliver complete and timely critical actions, revealing an execution gap. We attribute this gap to three long-horizon failure modes, each operationalized as a per-trace counter: instruction-adherence drift, treatment incompleteness, and a severity-equity gap in timeliness. We then introduce Asclepius, an adaptive agent scaffolding with a self-evolving harness that rewrites the operating manual between shifts from trace-level feedback, an externalized clinical skills library for high-stakes regimen knowledge, and three isolated subagents that partition per-turn decisions across the patient queue.
