On held-out batches never observed during harness evolution, Asclepius improves critical-action correctness by 22% (p = 0.024) over a strong baseline agent framework while preserving diagnostic accuracy, with consistent gains across five LLM judges from three model families; on the full ten-batch set, improvements reach 25% on critical actions and 13% on timeliness. The three failure modes form a coupled bottleneck: decisive reductions appear only when all three components act together.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how LLM agents fail on long, realistic clinical simulations and proposes Asclepius, an adaptive scaffolding system that significantly improves timely, critical actions without harming diagnostic accuracy.
AI.motivation: Most benchmarks test LLM agents on short, single tasks, but in real deployments they run for long periods under resource constraints, revealing different failure modes. In emergency-department management, agents might reach the right diagnosis yet still fail clinically by not executing all necessary, time-critical actions. The authors want a realistic testbed and analysis framework to expose these long-horizon execution failures and to design an agent architecture that can adapt and improve from experience.
AI.method: They use the Clinical Environment Simulator (CES), where an agent runs a full emergency-department shift under continuous time and resource pressure, evaluated via structured, multidimensional grading in a single long rollout. They define three quantitative long-horizon failure modes: instruction-adherence drift, treatment incompleteness, and a severity-equity gap in timeliness. They then design Asclepius, an agent scaffolding that: (1) uses a self-evolving harness that rewrites its operating manual between shifts using trace-level feedback, (2) employs an externalized clinical skills library for high-stakes treatment knowledge, and (3) decomposes decision-making across three specialized subagents that handle per-turn choices over the patient queue. Performance is measured on held-out and full batches, with multiple LLM judges from different model families.
AI.result: On held-out batches not used during harness evolution, Asclepius improves critical-action correctness by 22% (p = 0.024) compared to a strong baseline agent framework, while maintaining diagnostic accuracy. Across five LLM judges from three model families, the improvements are consistent. On the full ten-batch evaluation, Asclepius shows a 25% gain in critical actions and a 13% improvement in timeliness. The analysis shows that the three targeted failure modes interact: major performance gains emerge only when all three architectural components are combined.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that standard short-task benchmarks miss key long-horizon execution failures in LLM agents, especially in complex clinical settings like an emergency department. By explicitly modeling and targeting instruction drift, treatment incompleteness, and inequitable timeliness, and by combining adaptive harness rewriting, a clinical skills library, and decision-partitioning subagents, Asclepius closes a substantial portion of the execution gap without sacrificing diagnostic performance. The three failure modes constitute a coupled bottleneck that must be addressed jointly to achieve meaningful gains in real-world, long-horizon agent performance.

title: Domain-Specific Jargon in Large Language Models: A Comparative Analysis between General-Purpose and Specialist Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable proficiency on general-purpose tasks, yet their performance often degrades in highly-specialized technical domains. Moreover, little is known about how parametric knowledge of domain-specific terms is encoded within these models. We address this gap by contributing two novel medical jargon evaluation benchmarks and evaluate a general-purpose Llama-3.1 model against a variant fine-tuned on medical-domain data. Surprisingly, the general-purpose model outperforms the medically fine-tuned model on both tasks. Using mechanistic interpretability tools, we find systematic patterns of miscalibration for the medically fine-tuned model. Instead of reorganizing parametric knowledge, the fine-tuned model places greater emphasis on a small subset of model components associated with jargon-favoring predictions. We find that applying component reweighting strategies against the benchmark tasks successfully suppresses these components and closes the gap with the general-purpose baseline. We also observe that some jargon-sensitive components transfer knowledge to the same tasks involving materials science jargon, suggesting they encode a partially domain-agnostic notion of specialized terminology. Our results provide a case study in which a medically fine-tuned checkpoint does not improve jargon comprehension over its general-purpose counterpart, highlighting that domain adaptation should not be assumed to yield better performance on specialized terminology.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large language models understand specialized medical jargon, creates two evaluation benchmarks, and finds that a general-purpose LLM outperforms a medically fine-tuned version, analyzing why via mechanistic interpretability and proposing component reweighting to fix miscalibration.
AI.motivation: While large language models perform well on general tasks, their behavior on highly specialized technical domains like medicine is less understood, especially regarding how domain-specific terms are encoded and how fine-tuning affects this knowledge. There is a need for principled benchmarks and interpretability-driven analyses to understand and improve domain adaptation for jargon-heavy tasks.
AI.method: The authors construct two medical jargon evaluation benchmarks and compare a general-purpose Llama-3.1 model with a medically fine-tuned variant on these benchmarks. They then use mechanistic interpretability tools to analyze internal model components, studying calibration, the distribution of attention or activation over components, and how fine-tuning changes component usage. Finally, they apply component reweighting strategies to suppress overemphasized jargon-favoring components and test the impact on performance, including transfer to materials science jargon tasks.
AI.result: The general-purpose Llama-3.1 model outperforms the medically fine-tuned model on both medical jargon benchmarks. Mechanistic analysis reveals systematic miscalibration in the fine-tuned model, which relies too heavily on a small subset of components that push it toward jargon-favoring predictions without correspondingly improved understanding. Component reweighting that down-weights these components improves performance and closes the gap with the general-purpose model. Some jargon-sensitive components also transfer to materials science jargon tasks, suggesting partially domain-agnostic encoding of specialized terminology.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning on medical data does not automatically improve jargon comprehension and in this case harms performance relative to a general-purpose model. Fine-tuning can cause miscalibration by overemphasizing a narrow set of jargon-associated components rather than globally reorganizing parametric knowledge. Mechanistic interpretability and component reweighting provide practical tools to diagnose and mitigate these issues. More generally, the work cautions against assuming that domain adaptation will always enhance performance on specialized terminology and shows that some representation of jargon may be domain-agnostic across fields.

title: Toward a Decision-Assurance Layer for AI-Assisted Flight Planning in Air Traffic Management
summary: Generative AI is increasingly being used informally in Air Traffic Management (ATM) for tasks such as flight plan generation, trajectory interpretation, and constraint checking. Although these tools can reduce workload and accelerate planning, their non-deterministic outputs create safety and operational risks in human-in-the-loop settings. This paper proposes the AI Trust and Assurance Layer (ATAL), a model-agnostic decision assurance architecture that evaluates whether AI-generated flight-planning outputs are sufficiently reliable for operational use. ATAL combines semantic stability under prompt variation, operational consistency of structured outputs, and normative constraint validation against domain rules, and maps these signals to a Decision Readiness Level (DRL) for human operators. An ATM-inspired experimental study shows how unsafe, inconsistent, or misleading outputs can be identified before influencing flight-plan validation or execution. Although demonstrated in aviation, the framework is also transferable to other safety-critical decision-support domains that require human oversight under regulatory constraints.

AI.tldr: Proposes a model-agnostic assurance layer to judge when generative AI outputs in air traffic management are safe and ready for operational use.
AI.motivation: Generative AI is already being used informally in air traffic management for tasks like flight plan generation and trajectory analysis. While it can reduce workload and speed up planning, its non-deterministic and sometimes unreliable outputs pose safety and operational risks in human‑in‑the‑loop, safety‑critical contexts. There is a need for a systematic way to decide when AI outputs can be trusted for real operations.
AI.method: Introduce the AI Trust and Assurance Layer (ATAL), a decision-assurance architecture that sits between generative AI systems and human operators. ATAL is model-agnostic and evaluates AI outputs along three axes: (1) semantic stability under prompt variation (does the meaning remain consistent when prompts are perturbed?), (2) operational consistency of structured outputs (are trajectories, constraints, and parameters internally coherent and executable?), and (3) normative constraint validation against domain rules and regulations. These signals are combined into a Decision Readiness Level (DRL) that is presented to human operators. The authors test this in an ATM-inspired experimental setup to see if problematic outputs can be detected before affecting operations.
AI.result: In the ATM-style experiments, ATAL successfully identifies unsafe, inconsistent, or misleading generative AI outputs before they can influence flight-plan validation or execution. The framework demonstrates that combining stability checks, structural consistency checks, and rule-based validation can effectively filter or flag unreliable AI suggestions in flight planning tasks.
AI.conclusion: A model-agnostic assurance layer like ATAL can make the use of generative AI more trustworthy in safety-critical, human-in-the-loop decision-support environments. By quantifying the reliability of AI outputs via a Decision Readiness Level derived from semantic, operational, and normative checks, operators gain a structured basis for deciding when to trust or disregard AI-generated plans. Although showcased in aviation, the approach is generalizable to other regulated domains with similar oversight requirements.

title: A Hybrid Agentic AI Framework for Intelligent Supply Chain Analytics
summary: Efficient utilization of supply chain analytics for decision making remains a significant challenge for planners, as critical tasks such as database querying, key performance indicator (KPI) analysis, demand forecasting, and performance diagnosis require heterogeneous expertise spanning data engineering, operations research, and domain knowledge. In this work, we propose an agentic system for supply chain analytics that bridges the gap between business decision-making and technical expertise, where a coordinator agent interprets user intent and delegates sub-tasks to specialized agents. The system supports both exploratory analysis and deterministic workflows, enabling planners to transition between ad hoc questions and structured processes. Domain logic is encapsulated within specialist agents and prompts, yielding a scalable, modular, and auditable design and lowering the cost of functional extension through prompt-centric development. We evaluate the proposed architecture on a test environment that replicates multi-echelon inventory management operations. Results show that our multi-agent design achieves a 90\% accuracy, which is competitive with a single agent baseline while reducing input token usage by roughly fourfold, substantially improving scalability and cost-efficiency. Furthermore, we provide case studies to demonstrate interpretable suboptimality detection and automated forecast optimization, illustrating how agentic architectures can effectively combine open-ended exploratory analysis and deterministic supply chain analytics workflows, and provide a practical pathway toward more accessible and extensible decision-support systems.

AI.tldr: They design a multi-agent AI system to help planners perform complex supply chain analytics more efficiently, accurately, and cheaply.
AI.motivation: Supply chain planners struggle to use advanced analytics because key tasks—database querying, KPI analysis, demand forecasting, and performance diagnosis—need combined skills in data engineering, operations research, and domain expertise, which few individuals possess. There is a gap between business decision makers and the technical capabilities of analytics tools, limiting effective, scalable use of data-driven decision support.
AI.method: They build an “agentic” multi-agent architecture where a coordinator agent understands user intent and decomposes it into sub-tasks that are passed to specialist agents (e.g., for querying data, analyzing KPIs, forecasting demand, diagnosing performance). The system is designed to support both exploratory, ad hoc questions and deterministic, repeatable workflows. Domain logic and procedures are embedded in specialized agents and prompts, enabling modularity and easier extension via prompt engineering rather than deep system changes. They test the system in a simulated multi-echelon inventory management environment and compare it to a single-agent baseline in terms of accuracy and token usage.
AI.result: In the multi-echelon inventory test environment, the multi-agent system reaches about 90% accuracy, comparable to a single-agent baseline, but uses roughly one-quarter of the input tokens, implying significantly better scalability and lower running cost. Case studies show that the system can perform interpretable suboptimality detection and automated forecast optimization while managing both open-ended exploration and deterministic analytics workflows.
AI.conclusion: A coordinated multi-agent architecture for supply chain analytics can effectively bridge business decision-making and technical analytics expertise. It offers modularity, scalability, and cost-efficiency, achieving competitive accuracy with far lower token usage than a single-agent setup. The pattern of encapsulating domain logic into specialist agents and prompts provides a practical, extensible pathway to more accessible decision-support systems that can handle both exploratory analysis and structured operational workflows.

title: In the Blind: Building Pseudo-References for MT Evaluation
comment: Accepted at Eleventh Conference on Machine Translation (WMT) @ EMNLP 2026
summary: The WMT26 General MT task evaluates systems on 10 language pairs that have no human references (neither translated from scratch nor post-edited from MT output by humans). We describe how we built the pseudo-references for these pairs and six other language pairs (in which some forms of human references are available): seven models translate the 3,277 official documents under up to five prompt conditions, giving a total of 26 system-prompt combinations; then three reference-free quality estimation (QE) models score every candidate; and a per-document selector picks one translation, which GPT-5.5 post-edits where needed. Working without references exposed a failure mode of QE-guided selection: the metrics rank fluent output in the wrong language above correct translations. Adding a confidence-scaled language identification penalty to the score fusion drives the wrong-language count to zero, and the resulting selector still scores better on MetricX than the rank-fusion baseline it replaces. Since no references were available for these pairs while we were building them, we calibrate every selection decision on last year's WMT25 human judgments. The human evaluation, released after construction, shows the cost of getting selection wrong: our references stand with the strongest participating systems when the selector kept a frontier-model candidate, and fall up to 17 ESA points below them when it did not. We release the selection method and the provenance of every reference (https://github.com/surrey-nlp/PseudoRef)

AI.tldr: They build high-quality pseudo-references for WMT26 MT evaluation without human references by combining multiple MT systems, reference-free QE, and GPT-based post-editing, plus a language-ID penalty to avoid wrong-language outputs.
AI.motivation: WMT26 has language pairs with no human reference translations, making standard MT evaluation difficult. The authors need a scalable way to create reliable pseudo-references that approximate human translations, while handling failure modes of reference-free QE such as preferring fluent but wrong-language outputs.
AI.method: Use seven MT models to translate 3,277 documents under up to five prompts (26 system–prompt combos). Score all candidates with three reference-free QE models, then select per-document translations with a score fusion selector. Detect a failure mode where QE prefers fluent wrong-language text; fix by adding a confidence-scaled language-ID penalty to the fused score. When selected, some outputs are post-edited by GPT-5.5. Selection thresholds and penalties are calibrated on WMT25 human judgments since no references were yet available for these pairs. The authors release the method and full provenance of each pseudo-reference.
AI.result: The language-ID penalty eliminates wrong-language selections (wrong-language count goes to zero) and the improved selector outperforms a rank-fusion baseline on MetricX. Post-hoc comparison with WMT26 human evaluation shows that when the selector keeps frontier-model candidates, the resulting pseudo-references match the strongest systems, but when it does not, they can be up to 17 ESA points worse.
AI.conclusion: It is feasible to construct competitive pseudo-references for MT evaluation in the absence of human references by combining multiple MT systems, reference-free QE, language-ID-aware score fusion, and LLM post-editing calibrated on past human judgments. Careful selector design is crucial: mis-selection carries a large quality cost, but with proper penalties and calibration, the approach yields strong, shareable pseudo-references and a reusable selection pipeline.

title: Planning or Learning: Reliability and Cost in Multi-Asset Maintenance
summary: Industrial maintenance systems involve multiple interacting assets and shared resources, making it challenging to balance reliability and operational cost using a single decision framework. While recent work has focused on reinforcement learning (RL) for maintenance scheduling, direct comparisons with planning approaches under identical settings remain limited. In this work, we empirically compare planning and RL for multi-asset bearing maintenance using run-to-failure data. We examine how these methods behave when balancing preventive maintenance against tolerable failures across a range of failure penalty scenarios. We observed a consistent behavioral difference driven by objective formulation. Planning enforces reliability as a hard constraint and produces zero-failure policies whose total cost is largely insensitive to the magnitude of failure penalties. RL agents optimize expected cost and often trade off preventive maintenance against occasional failures as penalties vary, resulting in lower costs under low-penalty regimes but persistent non-zero failures even when penalties are high. We also investigate lightweight constraint mechanisms, including reward shaping and action masking, to encourage RL's reliability. From a practical perspective, planning may be more suitable when strict reliability is required and deployment horizons are short, whereas RL may provide cost-efficient policies when limited failures are acceptable and long-run operational efficiency is prioritized. Overall, this study clarifies the trade-offs between reliability and cost in multi-asset maintenance and suggests that planning and RL are complementary approaches. Beyond these findings, the controlled benchmark protocol itself that unifies environment, cost model, and evaluation across paradigms, offers a reusable template for comparing decision-making approaches in other maintenance settings.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically compares planning and reinforcement learning for multi-asset bearing maintenance, showing that planning yields zero-failure but cost-insensitive policies, while RL flexibly trades failures for cost, highlighting complementary use cases and providing a reusable benchmark for future comparisons.
AI.motivation: Industrial maintenance involves many interacting assets and shared resources, where it is difficult to balance high reliability with low operational cost. Recent works use RL for maintenance scheduling, but there is a lack of controlled, apples-to-apples comparisons against planning approaches under the same assumptions and data. The authors aim to clarify how these paradigms differ in behavior and suitability when managing preventive maintenance versus tolerable failures, and to provide a standard benchmark protocol for fair evaluation.
AI.method: Using run-to-failure data from multi-asset bearing systems, the authors construct a unified benchmark environment with a shared cost model and evaluation protocol. They implement planning methods that treat reliability as a hard constraint and enforce zero failures, and RL agents that optimize expected cumulative cost. They then vary failure penalty levels to examine how each approach trades off preventive maintenance against tolerable failures. They also test lightweight constraint mechanisms for RL, such as reward shaping and action masking, to improve reliability behavior without fully changing the RL objective.
AI.result: Planning methods consistently generate zero-failure policies whose total cost does not significantly change as failure penalties increase, due to reliability being hard-constrained. RL agents, optimizing expected cost, produce policies that allow some failures, reducing preventive maintenance when penalties are low and still exhibiting non-zero failures even under high penalties, although with lower overall cost in low-penalty regimes. Constraint mechanisms can nudge RL toward higher reliability but do not fully eliminate failures in the same way as planning does. The unified benchmark successfully enables controlled, direct comparison between paradigms.
AI.conclusion: Planning and RL exhibit fundamentally different behaviors driven by their objective formulations: planning is reliability-first with hard constraints, leading to robust zero-failure but less cost-sensitive policies, while RL is cost-first, flexibly trading off maintenance and failures. Practically, planning is preferable when strict reliability and short deployment horizons are required, whereas RL is better when limited failures are acceptable and long-term cost efficiency is prioritized. The proposed benchmark framework is a valuable template for systematically comparing decision-making methods in maintenance and potentially other industrial domains.

title: Causal multi-modal AI for personalized chemosensitivity prediction
summary: Chemotherapy improves survival for some patients with breast cancer, but doctors cannot reliably predict who. Current guidelines rely on recurrence scores as a proxy for treatment benefit, which may contribute to the overprescription of chemotherapy. Here we present a causal multi-modal AI model that predicts personalized chemosensitivity using routinely collected pathology and clinical information. We developed our model on a multi-national dataset of 9,141 patients (twelve cohorts, nine countries) and evaluated it on another 1,994 patients (five cohorts, three countries). The model generated treatment-specific recurrence probabilities for each patient, with near-perfect calibration and strong prognostic discrimination across both 5- and 10-year follow-up horizons. Moreover, its chemotherapy benefit predictions demonstrated robust predictive performance, and out-performed existing recurrence-score-based tests. Compared to the standard of care, using the model to support personally tailored therapeutic decisions could reduce the number of patients receiving chemotherapy by 30% while achieving the same recurrence-free rate. Tumors predicted to be highly chemosensitive displayed concordant molecular and morphological programs of proliferation, cell cycle progression, and replication stress. The model's predictive capabilities transferred zero-shot to non-breast cancers, indicating our causal multi-modal AI approach may provide a universal strategy to predict treatment outcomes across cancer types.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a causal multi-modal AI model that predicts which breast cancer patients will benefit from chemotherapy, enabling large reductions in chemotherapy use without increasing recurrence.
AI.motivation: Chemotherapy is life-saving for some breast cancer patients but unnecessary and toxic for others. Current clinical practice mostly relies on recurrence scores, which are only indirect proxies for chemotherapy benefit and can lead to substantial overprescription. A more direct, individualized estimate of chemosensitivity, using data already routinely collected in clinical workflows, is needed to improve decision-making and reduce overtreatment.
AI.method: The authors build a causal multi-modal AI model that integrates routine pathology and clinical data to estimate treatment-specific recurrence probabilities for each patient. They train the model on a large multinational dataset of 9,141 breast cancer patients from 12 cohorts in 9 countries, and evaluate it on an independent set of 1,994 patients from 5 cohorts in 3 countries. The model is designed to output counterfactual, treatment-specific risks (with and without chemotherapy) and is assessed for calibration, prognostic discrimination, and its ability to predict chemotherapy benefit, as well as compared against existing recurrence-score-based tests. Biological correlates of predicted chemosensitivity are examined via molecular and morphological signatures, and the model is also tested zero-shot on non-breast cancers to evaluate generalizability of the causal framework.
AI.result: The model produces treatment-specific recurrence probabilities with near-perfect calibration and strong prognostic discrimination at 5- and 10-year horizons. Its predictions of chemotherapy benefit are robust and outperform current recurrence-score-based tools. Decision simulations suggest that using the model for individualized therapy selection could cut chemotherapy use by 30% without increasing recurrence rates. Tumors predicted as highly chemosensitive show consistent molecular and morphological patterns related to proliferation, cell cycle progression, and replication stress. The modeling approach also transfers in a zero-shot manner to non-breast cancer datasets, indicating cross-cancer applicability.
AI.conclusion: A causal multi-modal AI model leveraging standard pathology and clinical data can directly estimate individual chemosensitivity, outperform recurrence-based proxies, and support major reductions in unnecessary chemotherapy while maintaining clinical outcomes. The consistency of the biological programs associated with predicted chemosensitivity, together with successful zero-shot transfer to other cancers, suggests that this causal AI framework could serve as a general strategy for predicting treatment benefit across cancer types.

title: How User-AI Mistreatment Occurs and Matters in Conversational Systems?
comment: Accepted by the 10th Workshop on Online Abuse and Harms (WOAH 2026) at EMNLP 2026
summary: Safety research often focuses on model-generated harms, but users may also direct hostility, coercion, and adversarial pressure at models. Understanding how and when that occurs is essential for accurately interpreting model behaviour, alignment drift, and real-world deployment risks. In this paper, we audit 777K English LMSYS-Chat-1M conversations with two independent detectors: an eight-category lexicon for hostility directed at the model, and the dataset's moderation signal; and show that they capture different, weakly overlapping phenomena. The lexicon identifies insults, threats, and jailbreak coercion aimed at the assistant, while moderation flags are dominated by toxic-content solicitation rather than hostility at the model. Together, they mark about 5% of user turns; adjusting the narrower lexicon-harassment union for measured precision puts mistreatment aimed at the assistant at 0.90%. These absolute rates describe arena-style evaluation traffic and should not be read as deployment-wide base rates. We find that user hostility varies 13-fold across models, driven largely by who each model attracts rather than by model behaviour: first-turn hostility spreads far wider than post-response hostility, and more than fifteenfold separates the extremes even after deduplicating opening prompts. Within conversations, assistant apologies are consistently associated with higher odds of next-turn hostility under both detectors; the effect survives restricting to non-refused prior turns and to jailbreak-free conversations, and is positive in 20 of 23 models. Yet across models, more apologetic models receive less hostility overall. Finally, hostility also shows temporal structure, with coercive openings front-loading the first turn while affective hostility accumulates over a session. We release the lexicon, the detector cross-validation pipeline, and all derived tables.

AI.tldr: The paper audits a large conversation dataset to quantify how often and in what ways users are hostile or coercive toward language models, showing that different detection signals capture distinct phenomena and revealing systematic patterns across models, turns, and time.
AI.motivation: Most safety work studies harms caused by models, not harms directed at them. However, users frequently display hostility, coercion, and adversarial behavior toward assistants, which can distort evaluations, affect alignment, and pose deployment risks. The authors aim to systematically measure and characterize this understudied form of user behavior in real conversational data.
AI.method: The authors analyze 777K English conversations from the LMSYS-Chat-1M dataset using two independent detectors of user hostility: (1) a custom eight-category lexicon targeting insults, threats, and jailbreak-style coercion directed at the assistant, and (2) the dataset’s existing moderation signal. They compare what each detector captures, estimate precision-adjusted prevalence of model-directed mistreatment, study variation in hostility across different models and across conversation turns, and run within-conversation analyses linking assistant behaviors (especially apologies) to subsequent user hostility, while controlling for factors like refusals and jailbreak attempts. They also examine temporal patterns of different hostility types within sessions. All detectors and derived artifacts are released.
AI.result: Around 5% of user turns are flagged by at least one detector, but the lexicon and moderation signals overlap only weakly and capture different behavioral phenomena. After adjusting for precision, explicit harassment directed at the assistant is estimated at roughly 0.90% of turns in this arena-style setting. Hostility rates differ up to 13-fold across models, mainly due to which users each model attracts rather than to the models’ immediate behavior. First-turn hostility is far more prevalent than post-response hostility, and this pattern remains even after deduplicating opening prompts. Within conversations, assistant apologies reliably predict higher odds of hostility in the next user turn across both detectors and in the majority of models, even when controlling for refusals and excluding jailbreak sequences. Yet at the cross-model level, more apologetic models tend to experience less overall hostility. Hostility also shows temporal structure: coercive behavior is front-loaded in first turns, whereas affective hostility accumulates over the course of a conversation.
AI.conclusion: User mistreatment of language models is measurable, non-trivial, and systematically patterned, but common moderation tools and lexicon-based detectors capture only partially overlapping aspects of it. Hostility is strongly influenced by who a model attracts and by conversational dynamics such as apologies and turn order, with opening prompts being particularly important. These findings have implications for interpreting safety evaluations, understanding alignment drift, and designing deployment and moderation strategies. By releasing their lexicon and validation pipeline, the authors provide tools for future work on modeling and mitigating adversarial and hostile user behavior toward AI systems.

title: FLoKD: Adaptive Knowledge Distillation for Federated Low-Rank LLM over Wireless Networks
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across a wide range of natural language processing tasks. However, conventional fine-tuning typically relies on centralized data collection, bringing in privacy concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative LLM fine-tuning without sharing raw client data, but its deployment over bandwidth-constrained wireless networks is hindered by the communication overhead of model-parameter transmission. Although Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduces the number of trainable parameters, its communication cost still increases with model scale. Knowledge distillation avoids parameter sharing via output logits, but token-level logits in LLMs incur high communication cost due to sequence length and vocabulary size. Reducing logits lowers the cost but weakens supervision and degrades accuracy. To address these limitations, we propose FLoKD, an adaptive knowledge-distillation framework for federated LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs over wireless networks, which communicates intermediate LoRA activations as the distillation signal rather than logits or full parameters. Since transmitting all blocks over the entire public dataset remains costly, we further propose a transformer block importance scoring framework that selectively transmits the most informative blocks, and two dataset selection strategies that discard public samples deviating from the local data distribution and prioritise those most informative for distillation. Extensive experiments across multiple generative language datasets, including WikiText-103, PTB, and Dialog, demonstrate that our proposed framework reduces communication overhead by 50-65% while achieving rapid convergence to competitive perplexity compared to baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FLoKD, a federated LoRA fine-tuning framework for LLMs that uses intermediate activations and selective transmission to drastically cut communication while preserving performance.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning large language models collaboratively with user data faces two key issues: privacy (centralized data collection is undesirable) and communication overhead (federated learning over wireless networks is very costly when transmitting large model parameters or logits). Existing approaches like LoRA, which reduces trainable parameters, and knowledge distillation via logits each still suffer from high communication costs when models, vocabularies, and sequence lengths are large. Reducing the amount of shared information harms model accuracy. The paper is motivated by the need for a privacy-preserving, communication-efficient method to fine-tune LLMs in federated wireless settings without sacrificing performance.
AI.method: They introduce FLoKD, an adaptive knowledge distillation framework built on federated LoRA fine-tuning. Instead of communicating full model parameters or token-level logits, clients send intermediate LoRA activations as the distillation signal. To further cut communication, they (1) design a transformer block importance scoring mechanism to select and transmit only the most informative blocks’ activations, and (2) propose two dataset selection strategies that discard public data samples that diverge from local data distributions and prioritize those samples that are most useful for distillation. The overall method integrates these components into a federated learning protocol tailored to bandwidth-constrained wireless networks.
AI.result: On several generative language benchmarks—WikiText-103, PTB, and a Dialog dataset—the method achieves 50–65% reduction in communication overhead compared to baselines, while still converging quickly and reaching perplexity scores that are competitive with or close to existing methods that use more communication. The experiments indicate that transmitting intermediate activations plus selective block and data sampling effectively preserves model quality under significantly reduced bandwidth usage.
AI.conclusion: FLoKD demonstrates that using intermediate LoRA activations as distillation signals, combined with selective transformer block transmission and informed public-data selection, can substantially reduce communication costs in federated LLM fine-tuning over wireless networks without notable performance loss. This makes privacy-preserving collaborative fine-tuning of LLMs more practical in bandwidth-limited real-world deployments and suggests a promising direction for future communication-efficient FL algorithms for LLMs.

title: When Edit Localization Amplifies Relative Selection Bias: Gradient Geometry, Target Mismatch, and Importance Weighting
summary: Human corrections identify editable spans, but the examples receiving corrections may come from a selective feedback channel. We analyze this interaction at a fixed model checkpoint by decomposing a localized gradient into edited and retained untouched components. Squared relative selection bias is a ratio of quadratics whose derivative has the sign of an explicit quadratic polynomial. Localization can increase, decrease, or nonmonotonically change this diagnostic; its direction depends on component biases and geometry. Oracle importance weighting recovers the population mean for each fixed localization objective, but these objectives have different targets. Against one common full-gradient target, we derive the finite-sample mean-squared error, an analytic optimal retention coefficient, and a fixed-clipping extension. Exact finite-population calculations and 10,000 Monte Carlo repetitions per sample size verify the identities and counterexamples. Public human-post-edit experiments use two translation directions and pretrained models, with declared synthetic selection. An English-German extension differentiates 73.89 million native parameters. In all three declared settings, hard localization has higher relative bias but lower absolute bias than full retention. Untouched-component biases are nonzero and selected component means have negative inner products, so the general criterion applies where the simple unbiased/aligned explanation fails. Output-bias diagnostics show the same endpoint ordering of relative bias across both directions, with one interior maximum. Mechanisms reuse each language's records and include a mixture; they are not independent replications. The evidence separates relative amplification from absolute gradient error and establishes estimation properties, without inferring translation-quality gains or identifying actual complaint propensities.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how selection bias from human feedback affects gradient estimates in localized model updates, and analyzes bias/variance trade-offs of using only edited versus all examples.
AI.motivation: In human-in-the-loop learning, we only see corrections on a subset of model outputs, typically those users choose to edit or complain about. This selection is biased and affects gradient estimates when updating models, especially when focusing on localized editable spans. The paper aims to formally understand how this selection bias interacts with localized gradients and how different retention/localization strategies affect estimation quality.
AI.method: At a fixed model checkpoint, the authors decompose the localized gradient into two components: one from edited spans and one from untouched spans. They define a squared relative selection bias as a ratio of quadratic forms and study how its derivative behaves using an explicit quadratic polynomial. They analyze how different localization objectives (e.g., full retention vs hard localization) change this bias, derive oracle importance weights that would debias estimates for each objective, and compare targets across objectives. For a chosen full-gradient target, they derive finite-sample mean-squared error, an optimal coefficient controlling the retention of untouched components, and a clipped variant. They validate analytic results using exact finite-population calculations and large-scale Monte Carlo simulations. They also run human post-edit experiments in machine translation with synthetic selection mechanisms, including large-scale English-German experiments with a 73.89M-parameter model, and compute gradient-bias and output-bias diagnostics under different localization schemes.
AI.result: Analytically, localization can increase, decrease, or change nonmonotonically the squared relative selection bias depending on the biases and geometry of edited vs untouched components. Oracle importance weighting can recover population means for each localization objective, but these objectives correspond to different targets. They provide explicit finite-sample MSE expressions, the optimal retention coefficient, and a fixed-clipping extension for a common full-gradient target. Empirically, across three declared experimental settings in machine translation, hard localization (using only edited components) yields higher relative bias but lower absolute bias than full retention. They find that biases in untouched components are nonzero and that means of selected components have negative inner products, so a general geometric criterion, rather than a simple unbiased or aligned assumption, explains the observed behavior. Output-level bias diagnostics show consistent ordering of relative bias with one interior maximum as localization strength varies. The experiments distinguish relative amplification of bias from absolute gradient error.
AI.conclusion: Selection bias from human feedback interacts in nontrivial ways with gradient localization. Localized updates (e.g., focusing on edited spans) do not simply reduce or increase bias; their effect depends on the geometry and bias of gradient components. While oracle importance weighting can debias estimates for each localization objective, different localization choices inherently change the learning target. Hard localization tends to reduce absolute gradient error at the cost of higher relative bias, and untouched components cannot be assumed unbiased. Overall, the paper clarifies estimation properties of selective human-feedback training without making claims about downstream translation quality or actual user complaint behavior.

title: $τ$-Elicitation: Benchmarking multi-turn entity extraction in voice agents
summary: Voice agents often need to collect names, addresses, identifiers, dates, and times exactly, yet end-to-end benchmarks obscure where capture fails. We introduce $τ$-Elicitation, a 200-task voice benchmark spanning 10 entity types, controlled difficulty, caller realisms, and three environments. A matched text agent passes all tasks, but four voice configurations achieve robust exact success from 0.14 to 0.41. Agents increase verification for hard and unfamiliar entities and sometimes for incorrect captures, but not for their weakest caller voice; only 24 to 37 percent of verified errors are repaired. A scaffold that prescribes spelling, read-back, correction, and confirmation raises robust Pass$^3$ by 14 to 31 points, at a cost of 21 to 28 seconds per call. Realisms such as spelling variations and restarts do not detectably affect exact success; mispronunciation increases repair effort. These results identify strategy selection and successful recovery as the central bottlenecks in exact spoken entity collection.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces τ-Elicitation, a 200-task benchmark to precisely evaluate how well voice agents collect spoken entities, revealing that current voice setups lag far behind text and mainly fail at strategy choice and error recovery rather than recognition alone.
AI.motivation: Voice agents in real applications must capture critical information—names, addresses, IDs, dates, times—exactly, but existing end-to-end benchmarks hide where and why the system fails. The authors want a controlled way to probe specific weaknesses: which entity types and conversational conditions break exact capture, how verification strategies are used, and where dialogue management rather than raw ASR is the main bottleneck.
AI.method: They construct τ-Elicitation, a 200-task benchmark covering 10 entity types under systematically varied difficulty levels, caller voice realisms (e.g., spelling variants, restarts, mispronunciations), and three environment settings. They compare a text-based agent to four different voice configurations. They analyze robust exact success rates, verification frequency and triggers, and how often verification actually repairs errors. They also design and evaluate a conversational scaffold that enforces a structured strategy (spelling, read-back, correction, confirmation) to see how much performance and time cost it adds.
AI.result: A text-only agent solves all benchmark tasks, whereas four voice agents attain low robust exact success (0.14–0.41). Voice agents verify more for harder or unfamiliar entities and occasionally even for already incorrect captures, but they fail to adapt verification to their weakest caller voice type. When they do verify, only 24–37% of those erroneous cases get successfully repaired. The structured scaffold raises robust Pass^3 by 14–31 percentage points but adds 21–28 seconds to each call. Naturalistic caller behaviors like spelling variations and restarts do not significantly hurt exact success, whereas mispronunciations mainly increase the effort spent on repairs.
AI.conclusion: The key limitations in spoken entity collection are not just in recognition accuracy but in how agents choose interaction strategies and recover from errors. Explicit scaffolding of spelling, read-back, correction, and confirmation substantially improves exact capture but at notable time costs. Future work should focus on smarter, adaptive strategies that retain high repair rates without large latency, targeting strategy selection and recovery as the central bottlenecks revealed by τ-Elicitation.

title: Scaling Hindi Quantum Natural Language Processing through Automatic Pregroup Supertagging
summary: Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP) uses pregroup grammars to translate grammatical structure into diagrammatic representations and quantum circuits. Recent Hindi QNLP work has shown that Hindi-specific pregroup grammars can support grammar-sensitive compositional models, but grammatical type assignment is still largely manual, limiting scalability. This paper formulates automatic Hindi pregroup supertagging as a token-level classification task. Using a manually annotated corpus of 380 Hindi sentences, we evaluate lexical, contextual, prompting-based, lexical-repair, and suffix/morphology-aware methods. Results show that simple lexical and contextual models are strong in this low-resource setting: contextual backoff achieves the best completed accuracy of 64.56\%, while raw Qwen2.5 prompting reaches only 11.65\%. Lexical repair raises LLM-assisted prediction to 64.08\%, demonstrating the value of constraining generative outputs with symbolic grammar knowledge. Diagnostic analysis further shows that seen and unambiguous tokens are much easier than unseen tokens, and suffix/morphology features improve karaka-token accuracy but not overall performance. These results show that automatic Hindi pregroup assignment is feasible and can reduce reliance on manual annotation in future multilingual QNLP pipelines.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates automatic Hindi pregroup grammar tagging for Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP) and finds that simple lexical and contextual models can achieve around 64% accuracy, reducing the need for manual grammatical annotation.
AI.motivation: QNLP relies on pregroup grammars to map sentences to quantum circuits, but for Hindi the assignment of grammatical types has been mostly manual, which is time-consuming and not scalable. To build larger, multilingual QNLP systems, there is a need for an automatic method to assign Hindi pregroup types to tokens while respecting the language’s grammatical specifics.
AI.method: The authors cast Hindi pregroup assignment as a token-level classification (supertagging) task. Using a manually annotated dataset of 380 Hindi sentences, they test several approaches: (1) lexical models that map tokens to types based on a lexicon; (2) contextual models that incorporate surrounding words; (3) prompting-based methods using a Qwen2.5 LLM; (4) lexical-repair methods that constrain or correct LLM outputs using a symbolic grammar lexicon; and (5) suffix/morphology-aware models that incorporate morphological features, particularly for karaka roles. They then compare these methods in terms of tagging accuracy, including a “completed accuracy” metric that accounts for coverage and backoff strategies.
AI.result: Contextual models with backoff achieve the highest completed accuracy at 64.56%. Raw prompting of the Qwen2.5 LLM performs poorly, with only 11.65% accuracy. When LLM predictions are post-processed via lexical repair using the pregroup lexicon, accuracy increases substantially to 64.08%, nearly matching the best contextual model. The analysis reveals that tokens seen in training and tokens with unambiguous types are much easier to tag correctly than unseen or ambiguous tokens. Incorporating suffix and morphological features improves accuracy specifically for karaka-related tokens but does not significantly boost overall tagging performance.
AI.conclusion: Automatic assignment of Hindi pregroup types is practically feasible, even with a relatively small annotated corpus, and can reach mid-60% accuracy with simple lexical or contextual methods. LLMs alone are not sufficient in this low-resource, highly structured setting, but combining them with symbolic grammar knowledge via lexical repair recovers strong performance. While morphology-aware features help certain grammatical roles, they do not yet change the global picture. Overall, automatic pregroup supertagging can substantially reduce manual annotation effort and is a promising component for future multilingual QNLP pipelines that need scalable grammar-sensitive compositional models for languages like Hindi.

title: Identity Is More Than Recall: A Benchmark for Persistent Identity in Deployed AI Agents
comment: 27 pages, 2 figures, including 18 pages of supplementary material
summary: Persistent agents need evaluations that distinguish identity facts they can recall from those they express and enact. We introduce PAI-Bench, a provider-neutral benchmark for fidelity to a versioned, update-governed identity contract. It separates recall, composition, behavioral enactment, resistance, persistence, lineage, and role-conditioned updates while keeping scoring oracles outside the target process. Two frozen campaigns cover sixteen synthetic profiles, thirty-two probes, and three independently initialized target configurations, yielding 1,536 retained responses. A judge-independent literal audit finds direct-parent identifiers in 48/48 atomic responses but only 1/48 implicit self-portraits. On eight profiles, explicit field cues increase joint presence of three identity identifiers from 0/8 to 7/8 under the same four-sentence instruction. A separate startup body-label substitution increases full-designation presence from 1/8 to 7/8 while parents remain absent. These contrasts reveal prompt-dependent component selection and component-specific sensitivity to startup cues in the tested deployments. Replaying identical factorial responses also yields a Claude headline mean 12.5 percentage points below Astra's, demonstrating evaluator sensitivity separately from target behavior. The studies use single target samples per condition, with post-hoc audits and follow-ups. PAI-Bench provides a reproducible evaluation protocol for measuring factual availability, identity expression, and behavioral enactment as distinct aspects of identity-contract fidelity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PAI-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate how well persistent AI agents adhere to a governed identity contract, separating memory, expression, and behavior aspects of identity.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of persistent AI agents often conflate what an agent can remember about its identity with how it expresses and behaves according to that identity. There is a need for a systematic, provider-neutral way to assess identity fidelity, particularly for agents whose identities can be versioned and updated under explicit governance rules. This helps diagnose issues like partial identity recall, inconsistent self-description, and sensitivity to prompts or startup configurations.
AI.method: The authors design PAI-Bench, a benchmark built around a versioned, update-governed identity contract. They construct sixteen synthetic identity profiles and thirty-two probes, and run two fixed evaluation campaigns on three independently initialized target configurations, resulting in 1,536 analyzed responses. The benchmark modularizes several dimensions—recall, composition, behavioral enactment, resistance to change, persistence over time, lineage, and role-conditioned updates—while ensuring that scoring oracles are external to the evaluated agent. They perform literal, judge-independent audits of responses, manipulate explicit field cues in prompts, and alter startup body-labels to study how these factors affect identity expression. They also compare evaluator models (e.g., Claude vs. Astra) on the same replayed response set to analyze evaluator sensitivity separately from target behavior.
AI.result: The literal audits show that direct-parent identifiers are correctly produced in all 48 atomic responses, indicating strong recall for that component, but only 1 out of 48 responses contain implicit self-portraits, suggesting weak spontaneous identity composition. Adding explicit field cues in prompts raises the joint presence of three key identity identifiers from 0/8 to 7/8 for half of the profiles under the same brief instruction, highlighting strong prompt sensitivity. Changing the startup body-label substantially increases full-designation presence from 1/8 to 7/8 while parent identifiers disappear, showing component-specific sensitivity to initial conditions. When the same factorial response set is re-evaluated, a Claude-based evaluator produces headline scores that are on average 12.5 percentage points lower than Astra’s, revealing that benchmark results can vary significantly across evaluators even with identical target behavior. All experiments are based on single target samples per condition with post-hoc audits and follow-ups, so findings are indicative but not statistically exhaustive.
AI.conclusion: PAI-Bench offers a reproducible, provider-neutral protocol to disentangle and measure three distinct aspects of identity-contract fidelity in persistent AI agents: factual availability of identity attributes, explicit identity expression, and behavioral enactment. The empirical results show that identity expression is highly sensitive to prompt design and startup configuration, and that evaluator choice significantly affects measured performance. This underscores the need for standardized, factorized identity benchmarks and careful selection and calibration of evaluators when assessing persistent agent identity behavior.

title: ForeSight: Enhancing Risk Monitoring via Early Safety Signal Distillation
comment: 17 pages, 12 figures. Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed, the generation of harmful content has become a critical safety concern. Existing safeguards operate at the input, output, or streaming-generation stages, while early-risk methods that rely on surface tokens or output logits may suffer from weak initial signals, and internals-based detectors using dense representations may retain highly entangled and redundant safety-irrelevant information. It therefore remains unclear whether the earliest post-generation hidden states already contain reliable signals about final-response harmfulness. To address this gap, we propose ForeSight, a first-token output-risk forecasting framework that distills weak and redundant early safety signals into compact, layer-aware risk representations. Experiments on five safety benchmarks and two target models demonstrate that ForeSight achieves superior and efficient early-risk forecasting while relying solely on first-token hidden states. The code is available at: https://github.com/Scabbards1500/Foresight

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ForeSight, a framework that predicts if an LLM’s final response will be harmful using only the hidden states of the very first generated token.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are more widely deployed, preventing harmful outputs is crucial. Current safety methods act on inputs, outputs, or during generation, but either rely on weak early signals (surface tokens/logits) or on dense internal representations that entangle safety-relevant and irrelevant information. It is unknown whether the earliest hidden states after generation already contain reliable signals of eventual harmfulness, and how to exploit them efficiently. The authors aim to close this gap to enable earlier and more efficient safety interventions.
AI.method: The authors propose ForeSight, a first-token output-risk forecasting framework. It takes the hidden states corresponding to the first generated token from different layers of the LLM and distills them into compact, layer-aware risk representations designed to filter out redundant and safety-irrelevant information. On top of these representations, a lightweight risk predictor is trained to estimate the harmfulness of the eventual full response. The method operates solely on first-token hidden states, avoiding the need to process the full output sequence or dense, unstructured internal embeddings.
AI.result: Across five safety benchmarks and two target LLMs, ForeSight outperforms existing early-risk methods in predicting harmfulness, while being computationally efficient. It can accurately forecast output risk using only the first-token hidden states, indicating that these earliest internal activations already encode strong signals about the safety of the eventual response.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that the earliest hidden states after generation (first token) contain sufficiently rich and structured information to reliably predict whether a final LLM response will be harmful. By distilling these signals into compact, layer-aware risk representations, ForeSight enables more accurate and efficient early-risk forecasting than prior methods. This opens a path toward faster, more proactive safety mechanisms for LLM deployments that can intervene before harmful content is fully generated.

title: Safety as a Constraint: Fine-Tuning a LLM Recommender to Explain Itself
summary: Traditional recommender systems are typically trained to predict what item users will interact with next, but not why. However, offering personalized evidence for why a user might like the predicted item is an important way to enhance the service and to raise the likelihood that the user will be genuinely interested in the recommendation. This service can be delivered by integrating a frontier-model call into the member-facing pipeline, but it will add extra cost and latency. In this paper, we train a recommender LLM to generate personalized explanations for its reccomendation, based on the user's watching history at a large video streaming service. We impose two requirements on the generated explanation: it must be faithful to the elements of the shows it links, and it must be strictly non-harmful to the user. To this end, we first train two LLM-judge reward models covering three specific criteria, and propose constrained GRPO to incorporate these different criteria. On a held-out real-world testing set, our fine-tuned model improves the all-three-criteria PASS rate rises from 0.649 to 0.956 under our own judges and from 0.677 to 0.931 under an independent judge, where as the frontier generator performs similar to the untuned recommender baseline. We conduct further experiments to show that the model's language and recommendation abilities remain unchanged. Based on these results, we conclude that an LLM-based recommender can be fine-tuned on other complex tasks without compromising its original recommendation performance, thus provide insights for further agentic user interface powered by a single model.

AI.tldr: They fine-tune a recommender LLM to generate safe, faithful personalized explanations for recommendations, using LLM-based reward models and constrained optimization, without hurting recommendation quality.
AI.motivation: Current recommender systems predict what to recommend but not why, and explanation can increase user trust and engagement. Calling large frontier models for explanations is expensive and slow, so there is a need for an efficient, in-house model that can both recommend and explain safely and faithfully.
AI.method: They take an LLM-based recommender and train it to generate textual explanations grounded in a user’s watch history. They define three criteria covering faithfulness to show elements and non-harmfulness to users. They train two LLM-judge reward models to evaluate these criteria, then propose a constrained GRPO (a reinforcement-style preference optimization) approach to incorporate multiple reward criteria during fine-tuning, while monitoring that core recommendation and language capabilities remain intact.
AI.result: On a held-out real-world test set from a large video streaming service, the fine-tuned model’s rate of passing all three criteria increases from about 0.65 to around 0.96 under their own reward judges, and from about 0.68 to 0.93 under an independent judge. The frontier generator baseline does not improve over the untuned recommender in terms of explanation quality. Additional experiments show that the model’s recommendation accuracy and general language skills are not degraded by this fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: An LLM-based recommender can be further fine-tuned to produce high-quality, safe, and faithful personalized explanations while preserving its original recommendation performance. This suggests that a single LLM can support both recommendation and more complex explanatory tasks, paving the way for richer, agentic user interfaces without the overhead of separate frontier-model calls.

title: HyperProve: Answer-Guided Hypergraph Expansion for Multi-Hop Question Answering
summary: Multi-hop question answering often fails when retrieval treats evidence as isolated matches to the original question, since the facts needed to answer a complex question are usually connected through intermediate entities, relations, and constraints. We propose HyperProve, a retrieval-augmented QA framework that addresses this challenge by coupling question decomposition with answer-conditioned expansion over a hypergraph of atomic facts. HyperProve does not use atomic facts, hypergraphs, or iterative retrieval in isolation; instead, it carries intermediate answers and supporting hyperedges as retrieval state, then uses that state to bias the next local hypergraph expansion. This design enables HyperProve to construct coherent evidence chains for final answer generation while making the retrieval process stateful and fact-centered. Across multi-hop QA benchmarks, HyperProve achieves the best overall performance in our evaluation, outperforming the strongest baselines by an average relative improvement of 6.2% in answer accuracy and 4.9% in F1.

AI.tldr: HyperProve is a multi-hop QA framework that builds coherent evidence chains by performing stateful, answer-conditioned retrieval over a hypergraph of atomic facts, leading to significant gains in accuracy and F1 over strong baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard multi-hop QA systems often fail because their retrievers treat each piece of evidence as an independent match to the original question. However, answering complex questions usually requires connecting multiple facts via intermediate entities, relations, and constraints. Existing methods that use atomic facts, hypergraphs, or iterative retrieval typically do so in isolation and lack a mechanism to carry intermediate reasoning state through the retrieval process. The authors aim to design a retrieval mechanism that can construct coherent evidence chains by explicitly modeling and propagating intermediate answers and the supporting structure that links facts together.
AI.method: The authors introduce HyperProve, a retrieval-augmented QA framework that integrates question decomposition with answer-conditioned expansion over a hypergraph of atomic facts. The system represents knowledge as a hypergraph where hyperedges capture atomic facts and their relations. During multi-hop reasoning, HyperProve maintains a retrieval state consisting of intermediate answers and their supporting hyperedges. It iteratively expands the hypergraph conditioned on this state, biasing the retrieval of new facts toward those that are most relevant to the current partial reasoning chain. This approach makes retrieval stateful and fact-centered, ensuring that each new retrieval step builds directly upon the existing evidence chain rather than re-querying the entire corpus independently.
AI.result: On multiple multi-hop QA benchmarks, HyperProve achieves the best overall performance among evaluated systems. It yields an average relative improvement of 6.2% in answer accuracy and 4.9% in F1 score compared to the strongest existing baselines, demonstrating that its stateful, hypergraph-based retrieval leads to more effective evidence chaining and better final answers.
AI.conclusion: HyperProve shows that coupling question decomposition with answer-conditioned hypergraph expansion, while explicitly carrying intermediate answers and supporting hyperedges as retrieval state, substantially improves multi-hop question answering. By making retrieval stateful and centered around coherent evidence chains rather than isolated matches to the query, the framework outperforms strong baselines across benchmarks, indicating that structured, stateful retrieval is a promising direction for complex reasoning tasks.

title: Cost Characterization of Vertically Partitioned Federated Knowledge Graphs
comment: Accepted at DMKG'26: 2nd International Workshop on Data Management for Knowledge Graphs, co-located with ISWC 2026; to appear in CEUR-WS proceedings
summary: Knowledge graphs are increasingly distributed across autonomous organizations that share an entity space but own disjoint subsets of relations, forming a vertical partition. Answering a multi-hop query may require combining facts from several silos, making the partitioning strategy a key data management decision that affects communication, indexing, load balance, and query latency. However, the costs associated with different partitioning strategies remain insufficiently studied. We formalize vertical partitioning as a design space and compare four strategies: semantic domain grouping, frequency-balanced partitioning, co-occurrence graph-cut partitioning, and random partitioning. We evaluate them using five metrics: communication cost, candidate index size, cross-silo path length, load balance, and end-to-end query latency. Three of the five prove to be determined by the graph and the silo count rather than by the partition, which reduces the design problem to two conflicting axes, cross-silo path length and load balance. Experiments on MetaQA and PathQuestion use a fixed federated knowledge graph question-answering architecture based on TransE embeddings and a frozen BERT encoder across three silo configurations. By keeping the learning model unchanged, we isolate the effect of partitioning and show that the trade-off between locality and balance holds only where each silo can hold several relations, weakening as the number of silos increases. The study provides practical guidance for deployments constrained by cross-silo reasoning or by silo load.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different ways of vertically partitioning knowledge graphs across multiple silos impact communication, indexing, load balance, and query latency, revealing that only cross-silo path length and load balance are truly affected by partition choices under a fixed QA architecture.
AI.motivation: Distributed knowledge graphs are often split across autonomous organizations (silos) that share entities but own different relations. Multi-hop queries must traverse these silos, and the way relations are partitioned critically impacts communication overhead, indexing complexity, load distribution, and response time. Despite this importance, the actual costs and trade-offs of different vertical partitioning strategies have not been systematically compared or formalized as a design space, leaving practitioners without clear guidance for real deployments.
AI.method: The authors formalize vertical partitioning of knowledge graphs as a design space over relation-to-silo assignments and instantiate four concrete strategies: (1) semantic domain grouping (group relations by semantic domains), (2) frequency-balanced partitioning (balance relation frequencies across silos), (3) co-occurrence graph-cut partitioning (use a relation co-occurrence graph and cut it to minimize cross-silo connections), and (4) random partitioning. They define five evaluation metrics—communication cost, candidate index size, cross-silo path length, load balance, and end-to-end query latency—and analyze which of these are structurally determined by the underlying graph and the number of silos versus which depend on the partitioning. They then conduct experiments on MetaQA and PathQuestion datasets using a fixed federated KG question-answering pipeline: TransE embeddings for KG reasoning and a frozen BERT encoder for question understanding, evaluated under three silo configurations. By holding the model architecture and parameters constant, they attribute performance differences solely to partitioning strategies.
AI.result: The analysis shows that three of the five metrics—communication cost, candidate index size, and one additional structural factor—are primarily determined by the intrinsic properties of the knowledge graph and the number of silos, not by the particular partitioning strategy. Consequently, only cross-silo path length and load balance remain as true degrees of freedom in the partition design space, and they conflict with each other: improving locality (shorter cross-silo paths) often worsens load balance and vice versa. Empirical results on MetaQA and PathQuestion with the fixed TransE+BERT QA pipeline corroborate this: strategies that cluster related relations reduce cross-silo hops but can create skewed silo workloads, whereas more balanced schemes may increase cross-silo reasoning. The trade-off is most pronounced when each silo contains multiple relations, and it weakens as the number of silos grows and each silo holds fewer relations.
AI.conclusion: Vertical partitioning of distributed knowledge graphs is constrained more by the graph structure and silo count than by specific partition heuristics, leaving only a fundamental trade-off between cross-silo path length and load balance as tunable design levers. Under a fixed federated QA architecture, partitioning choices matter primarily in regimes where silos can each store several relations; as the number of silos increases, all strategies converge in behavior and the locality–balance trade-off diminishes. The paper offers practical guidance: deployments where cross-silo reasoning is expensive should favor locality-oriented partitions, while environments constrained by silo capacity or fairness should prioritize balanced partitions, recognizing that many other considered metrics cannot be significantly optimized via partitioning alone.

title: GeoSkill:Experience-Driven Hierarchical Skill Learning with Collaborative Revision forGeospatialAgents
summary: Geospatial agents are increasingly expected to support recurring and evolving analytical tasks rather than execute isolated workflows. In such settings, effective agents must distill prior execution experience into reusable geospatial procedural knowledge to guide future planning and tool use. However, existing memory-augmented paradigms struggle to summarize both long-horizon tool-chain orchestration experience and tool-level invocation constraints in geospatial analysis, while directly relying on LLM self-reflection to update experience often leads to misattribution and unreliable revisions. To address these challenges, we propose GeoSkill, an experience-driven hierarchical skill learning framework for geospatial agents. GeoSkill comprises two core components: (i) a Hierarchical Skill Bank (HSB), consisting of a Planning Skill Bank and a Tool Skill Bank, which respectively distill high-level task-planning experience and tool usage constraints, enabling structured representation and cross-task reuse of historical execution experience; and (ii) a Collaborative Trace-driven Skill Revision (CTSR) mechanism, where Judge, Critic, and Refiner collaboratively perform error identification, skill-level defect localization, and targeted modification, preventing misattributed and unreliable revisions from polluting the skill bank. GeoSkill learns and validates skills from historical executions during development, and freezes the skill bank for retrieval-only guidance on unseen tasks during deployment. Extensive experiments on EarthBench and ThinkGeo demonstrate that GeoSkill effectively transforms historical execution experience into reusable hierarchical skills, improving both end-to-end task accuracy and tool-execution reliability in geospatial tasks.

AI.tldr: GeoSkill is a hierarchical skill-learning framework that converts past tool-use traces of geospatial agents into reusable planning and tool-usage skills, with a collaborative mechanism to safely revise these skills and improve future task performance.
AI.motivation: Geospatial agents increasingly handle recurring, complex analytical tasks that require chaining multiple tools over long horizons. Current memory-augmented approaches struggle to (1) summarize long tool-chain experiences into reusable knowledge, (2) capture detailed constraints for individual tools, and (3) reliably update that knowledge—LLM self-reflection often misattributes errors and corrupts memories. There is a need for a structured, robust way to distill past execution traces into reusable procedural knowledge for geospatial analysis.
AI.method: The paper proposes GeoSkill, composed of: (i) a Hierarchical Skill Bank (HSB) with two layers: a Planning Skill Bank that encodes high-level task-planning experience (how to orchestrate multi-step workflows) and a Tool Skill Bank that captures tool-specific usage constraints and patterns; and (ii) a Collaborative Trace-driven Skill Revision (CTSR) process, where three roles—Judge, Critic, and Refiner—work together over execution traces to identify errors, localize which skills are defective, and revise them in a targeted way. Skills are learned and validated from historical execution logs during development, and then the resulting skill bank is frozen and used only for retrieval-guided planning on new tasks.
AI.result: On the EarthBench and ThinkGeo benchmarks, GeoSkill improves end-to-end task accuracy and the reliability of tool executions compared to prior baselines. The framework successfully converts historical execution experiences into effective hierarchical skills, leading to better planning and fewer tool-use errors in geospatial tasks.
AI.conclusion: GeoSkill demonstrates that hierarchically structuring experience into planning and tool-level skills, combined with a collaborative, trace-driven revision mechanism, yields more reliable and reusable procedural knowledge for geospatial agents. Once learned and frozen, this skill bank can robustly guide agents on unseen geospatial tasks, improving both task outcomes and tool-chain reliability.

title: Understanding the Limits of Agentic ICD Coding
summary: ICD-10-CM codes are alphanumeric codes used in the US to classify diagnoses and injuries for medical billing and epidemiological reporting. Standard ICD-10-CM benchmarks report aggregate metrics that obscure performance on complex coding scenarios. We evaluate neural, workflow, and agentic systems on a rarity-stratified set of MIMIC-IV discharge summaries and identify two orthogonal failure modes. Neural classifiers exhibit a 0.43 micro-F1 gap between rare and common codes. Workflow systems handle rare codes well but score near zero on injury and external cause codes that require multi-step guideline following. A tool-augmented agentic configuration with structured access to official ICD-10-CM reference materials recovers up to 0.34 micro-F1 on this subset. No single system dominates across all conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper compares neural, rule-based workflow, and tool-augmented agentic systems for assigning ICD-10-CM codes, revealing complementary strengths and weaknesses, especially on rare and complex codes.
AI.motivation: Existing ICD-10-CM coding benchmarks report only aggregate results, hiding how systems behave on challenging cases such as rare diagnoses, injuries, and codes requiring nontrivial guideline application. This makes it unclear which methods are reliable in real-world, high-stakes clinical coding scenarios.
AI.method: The authors create a rarity-stratified evaluation set from MIMIC-IV discharge summaries and test three system types: (1) neural classifiers, (2) workflow systems that follow explicit rules, and (3) tool-augmented agentic systems with structured access to official ICD-10-CM reference materials.
