They then compare performance across rare vs common codes and across code categories, especially injuries and external causes that require multi-step guideline following.
AI.result: Neural classifiers show strong performance on common codes but a substantial drop for rare codes, with a 0.43 micro-F1 gap. Workflow systems perform well on rare codes overall but perform near zero F1 on injury and external cause codes that demand complex guideline sequences. The tool-augmented agentic configuration substantially improves performance on the difficult injury/external cause subset, recovering up to 0.34 micro-F1 there. No approach uniformly outperforms the others on all code types and rarity levels.
AI.conclusion: Different system paradigms for ICD-10-CM coding fail in distinct, orthogonal ways: neural models struggle with rarity, workflows struggle with complex guideline chaining, and agentic tool use helps on some complex subsets but is not universally best. Robust, real-world coding solutions will likely require hybrid or adaptive combinations of these approaches rather than relying on a single method.

title: Enhancing Event Candidate Acquisition for Event Linking
summary: Event linking associates event mentions in text with entries in a knowledge base (KB), or identifies them as out-of-KB events. Although existing methods use different architectures, candidate event acquisition can still be weakened by short ambiguous mentions, noisy arguments, and evidence that is unevenly useful for retrieval. We present MACE, a Multi-Agent Candidate Event acquisition method that refines event structure before linking. MACE uses evidence-specialized LLM agents to acquire time, location, participant, and event-type evidence, exposes intermediate queries to candidate-event lookup tools, and lets a coordinator revise the evidence set before final candidate construction. Experiments on two event linking benchmarks show that adding MACE to different event linking models consistently improves accuracy. These results show that MACE improves event linking through better candidate event acquisition without modifying the event linking model.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MACE, a multi-agent LLM-based method that improves event linking by refining event evidence and candidate acquisition without changing the downstream linker, yielding consistent accuracy gains on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Event linking systems must map text event mentions to knowledge base entries or mark them as out-of-KB. Current systems struggle because candidate event acquisition is hurt by short and ambiguous mentions, noisy or incomplete arguments, and evidence where not all parts are equally useful for retrieval. This weak candidate set limits final linking accuracy even if the linker itself is strong. The paper aims to improve this front-end candidate acquisition process.
AI.method: The authors introduce MACE, a Multi-Agent Candidate Event acquisition framework that uses multiple evidence-specialized LLM agents. Each agent focuses on a specific evidence type: time, location, participants, and event type. These agents expand and refine the event structure based on the input text. Intermediate evidence produced by agents is directly exposed as queries to candidate-event lookup tools in the KB. A coordinator agent gathers, evaluates, and revises the evidence set, deciding which evidence to keep or adjust before constructing the final candidate list for the event linker. MACE is plugged in front of existing event linking models without altering their architectures.
AI.result: On two standard event linking benchmarks, integrating MACE with various existing event linking models consistently improves accuracy compared to running those models without MACE. The gains demonstrate that better-structured, richer, and more precise candidate event sets lead to higher linking performance across architectures.
AI.conclusion: MACE demonstrates that multi-agent, evidence-specialized LLMs can significantly improve event linking by enhancing candidate event acquisition, independent of the particular event linking model used downstream. By refining event structure—time, location, participants, type—before candidate retrieval and allowing a coordinator to revise evidence, MACE yields more accurate candidate sets and consequently better event linking results, showing a promising direction for modular, LLM-assisted retrieval in structured IE tasks.

title: DARE: Dialectical Agentic Reasoning for Structured Knowledge Fact Checking
summary: Structured knowledge fact checking aims to determine the truthfulness of natural language claims by reasoning over structured evidence. Recent program-generation approaches leverage large language models (LLMs) to generate executable graph reasoning programs, achieving strong performance on structured knowledge fact checking benchmarks. However, these methods remain limited by invalid relation generation, single-path reasoning that lacks self-correction, and biased evidence assessment that tends to overestimate supporting signals. We propose Dialectical Agentic Reasoning (DARE), a multi-agent framework that formulates structured knowledge fact checking as an iterative retrieve-reason-reflect process. DARE integrates relation-grounded evidence retrieval to constrain reasoning to valid structures, dialectical bidirectional verification to evaluate evidence from both supporting and refuting perspectives, and confidence-driven meta-reflection to dynamically determine whether additional evidence exploration is necessary. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DARE in structured knowledge fact checking, with an 8B backbone achieving 88.12% accuracy and matching or surpassing GPT-4o-based program-generation baselines, which attests to the efficacy of dialectical agentic reasoning in eliciting the latent reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

AI.tldr: They introduce DARE, a multi-agent, iterative retrieve-reason-reflect framework for fact-checking natural language claims against structured knowledge, improving accuracy and robustness over prior LLM program-generation methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based program generation methods for structured knowledge fact checking achieve good performance, but they suffer from several key issues: they can generate invalid relations not grounded in the knowledge graph schema; they often use single-path reasoning without self-correction, so early errors propagate; and they assess evidence in a biased way, over-weighting supporting evidence and under-exploring refuting signals. These limitations motivate a new approach that can constrain reasoning to valid structures, reason dialectically from both supporting and refuting views, and dynamically decide when more evidence is needed.
AI.method: They propose Dialectical Agentic Reasoning (DARE), a multi-agent framework that models fact checking as an iterative retrieve-reason-reflect loop. First, relation-grounded evidence retrieval constrains the reasoning to valid relations and structures in the underlying knowledge graph. Then, a dialectical bidirectional verification stage has agents reason from both supporting and refuting perspectives about the claim using retrieved evidence, essentially arguing for and against the claim. Finally, a confidence-driven meta-reflection component monitors the agents’ confidence and decides whether to terminate with a verdict or trigger further retrieval and reasoning iterations to gather more evidence. The whole process uses LLMs as agents but structures their interaction to reduce bias and errors.
AI.result: On structured knowledge fact-checking benchmarks, DARE with an 8B-parameter backbone model attains 88.12% accuracy. This performance matches or surpasses GPT-4o-based program-generation baselines, demonstrating that the proposed framework can unlock strong reasoning capabilities even in smaller models while improving robustness and reliability of fact-checking.
AI.conclusion: DARE’s multi-agent, dialectical, and iterative design addresses key weaknesses of previous LLM-based structured fact-checking approaches: it enforces schema-valid reasoning, incorporates both supporting and refuting perspectives, and adaptively explores evidence based on confidence. The strong empirical results, including with a relatively small 8B model, suggest that carefully designed agentic reasoning frameworks can significantly enhance LLM fact-checking abilities without relying solely on larger backbone models.

title: Recoverability as a System Primitive for Long-Horizon AI Agents
summary: AI agents can be interrupted while editing files, calling tools, or carrying out multi-step tasks. Restarting repeats completed work, but continuing from unverified or outdated progress can carry earlier errors forward. A saved state is not necessarily a suitable place to resume. We introduce recoverability as a system primitive that makes reuse an explicit decision: select a supported starting point and a permitted recovery action, or withhold automatic continuation. Its behavioral contract binds that choice to supporting evidence, execution, and independent checks. A reference architecture connects persistence, validation, and control, with complementary runtime instances testing distinct responsibilities. Four deterministic and 20 paired file challenges demonstrate that accurate restoration and successful completion can conceal disallowed starting points. Progress controls attribute retained work to shared restoration. Event-time tests show that permission must also constrain the action, and that independently held policy evidence can expose violations even after an effect occurs. These findings establish why recovery decisions need their own evaluation, beyond restored bytes and final task success. Within supplied policies and a declared trust model, the contribution is a common, testable interface for retaining justified progress and making the conditions for its reuse explicit and enforceable.

AI.tldr: They define and implement a principled way (“recoverability”) to decide when and how AI agents may safely resume work from saved progress, instead of naively restarting or blindly continuing.
AI.motivation: AI agents performing long, multi-step tasks can be interrupted. Restarting wastes work, while resuming from partially completed or outdated state risks propagating errors or violating policies. Existing systems often treat saved state as automatically safe to resume, but this is not always valid. The authors want a systematic, enforceable way to decide which past progress can be reused, under what conditions, and with what guarantees.
AI.method: They introduce recoverability as a first-class system primitive with an explicit behavioral contract: any attempt to reuse prior progress must (1) choose from supported starting points, (2) select a permitted recovery action, and (3) be backed by evidence, execution checks, and independent validation. They propose a reference architecture that integrates persistence, validation, and control via multiple runtime instances that separately test different responsibilities. They design deterministic and paired-file benchmark challenges, along with event-time tests, to probe how restoration, progress controls, and policy evidence interact and where naive approaches fail.
AI.result: Experiments on four deterministic and 20 paired-file challenges show that even when restoration appears accurate and tasks complete successfully, the underlying starting points can be disallowed under policy. This reveals that simple success-based metrics or byte-level correctness are insufficient to guarantee compliant recovery. Event-time tests further show that recovery policy must constrain not just which state can be restored but also what subsequent actions are allowed, and that independent policy evidence can surface violations even after the system has already produced effects.
AI.conclusion: Recovery decisions in AI-agent systems require their own explicit, testable evaluation, beyond verifying restored data or final task success. The authors provide a common interface and reference architecture where policies and trust assumptions are made explicit, progress retention is justified with evidence, and conditions for reuse are enforceable at runtime. This framework aims to make safe, policy-compliant resumption of interrupted work a standard, verifiable capability in AI systems.

title: When Consistency Does Not Mean Reliability: Evaluating Local LLM Judges Against Human Ratings
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate the responses of other language models. This approach, known as LLM-as-a-Judge, is faster and cheaper than human evaluation. However, a judge may produce consistent scores without necessarily agreeing with human evaluators. In this work, we study this issue using two local open-weight LLM judges, LLaMA-3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B. We evaluate 300 responses generated by an instruction-tuned GPT-2 (124M) model for 100 questions covering five categories: factual knowledge, instruction following, mathematics, reasoning, and writing. Each response is scored by nine human annotators and is evaluated three times by each LLM judge using the same rubric. We compare the judge scores with the average human scores using Pearson correlation, Spearman correlation, mean absolute error (MAE), signed bias, and self-consistency. LLaMA-3-8B shows a Pearson correlation of 0.275 with human scores, while Qwen2.5-7B achieves 0.340. Their MAEs are 27.71 and 18.64, respectively. Despite this limited agreement, both judges show high self-consistency, with exact consistency rates of 97.3\% for LLaMA-3-8B and 92.3\% for Qwen2.5-7B. These results show that high self-consistency does not necessarily indicate high agreement with human judgments. Our findings highlight the need to evaluate both consistency and human alignment when using local LLMs as automatic judges.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well small open-weight language models can act as automatic judges of model outputs, finding they are internally consistent but poorly aligned with human ratings.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge is a popular, cheap alternative to human evaluation, but reliability is often inferred from a judge model’s self-consistency rather than its actual agreement with humans. The authors want to test whether high self-consistency really implies human-aligned judgments, especially for local, smaller models that are attractive for cost and privacy reasons.
AI.method: The authors use two local open-weight LLMs (LLaMA-3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B) as judges to score 300 answers produced by an instruction-tuned GPT-2 model for 100 prompts spanning five task categories: factual knowledge, instruction following, mathematics, reasoning, and writing. Each answer receives ratings from nine human annotators and three independent ratings from each LLM judge using the same evaluation rubric. They then compare LLM and human scores using Pearson and Spearman correlations, mean absolute error, signed bias, and a self-consistency metric based on repeated judgments.
AI.result: LLaMA-3-8B attains a Pearson correlation of 0.275 with mean human scores and a mean absolute error of 27.71, while Qwen2.5-7B attains a correlation of 0.340 and an MAE of 18.64, indicating only modest alignment with human ratings. In contrast, both models show very high self-consistency across repeated evaluations: 97.3% exact agreement for LLaMA-3-8B and 92.3% for Qwen2.5-7B.
AI.conclusion: Self-consistency of LLM judges is not a reliable proxy for human alignment: a model can give highly repeatable scores that still diverge substantially from human judgments. When using local LLMs as automatic evaluators, practitioners need to assess both their consistency and their correlation with human ratings, rather than assuming that stable outputs imply human-like evaluation behavior.

title: Windowed A-K-MDP
summary: Markov decision processes (MDPs) are used to support decision-making in conservation of biodiversity, but policies, even over small state spaces, can be difficult to interpret for conservation managers. K-MDP methods address this problem by building simpler MDPs with at most K abstract states. We show that the previously proposed A-K-MDP algorithm that relies on selecting a discretisation divisor using binary search can skip better abstract states. To fix this issue, we propose Windowed A-K-MDP, an algorithm that generates every distinct feasible partition induced within a declared divisor window and evaluates candidates until reaching the ideal value loss (J = 0) or exhausting the family of candidates. Across 33 K-MDP instances, Windowed improved 25 and tied 8.

AI.tldr: The paper improves interpretability of conservation decision policies by refining K-state MDP abstraction via a new windowed search algorithm that avoids missing good partitions and empirically outperforms the previous A-K-MDP on most test cases.
AI.motivation: Conservation managers use MDPs to plan biodiversity conservation, but optimal policies over even small state spaces can be hard to interpret and communicate. K-MDPs simplify MDPs by compressing them into at most K abstract states, but existing algorithms (A-K-MDP) that choose discretisation divisors via binary search can skip over better abstractions, leading to suboptimal or less interpretable models. There is a need for an abstraction method that more reliably finds high-quality simplified MDPs that preserve decision quality while remaining interpretable.
AI.method: The authors analyze the limitations of the A-K-MDP algorithm, specifically how its binary search over discretisation divisors can miss superior abstract state partitions. They then propose Windowed A-K-MDP, which defines a window of divisor values and systematically enumerates every distinct feasible state partition induced by divisors within that window. Each candidate abstract MDP is evaluated based on its value loss relative to the original MDP. The algorithm stops when it finds an abstraction with zero value loss (J = 0) or when all candidate partitions in the window are exhausted.
AI.result: The new Windowed A-K-MDP algorithm was tested on 33 K-MDP instances. Compared to the original A-K-MDP approach, Windowed A-K-MDP produced better abstractions (lower value loss) in 25 instances and tied performance in the remaining 8, demonstrating that the windowed search more reliably identifies high-quality simplified MDPs without degrading performance in any tested case.
AI.conclusion: Binary-search-based divisor selection in A-K-MDP can miss superior abstract partitions, limiting the quality of K-state MDP abstractions for conservation decision support. By exploring all feasible partitions within a specified divisor window, Windowed A-K-MDP avoids this pitfall, often achieving zero or lower value loss while keeping the model interpretable. Empirical results across multiple instances show consistent improvement or parity, indicating that the proposed method is a more robust approach for building simplified yet accurate MDPs for biodiversity conservation planning.

title: Sweet Talkers: How Query Formulation Shapes Sycophancy in Romantic Relationship Advice
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for emotional support and relationship advice, where a model's tendency to preserve a user's face can inadvertently reinforce harmful interpersonal behaviors. To systematically examine this risk, we developed the Romantic Relationship Advice-Seeking Prompts (RRASP) dataset of 2,400 prompts across five relationship themes and evaluated social sycophancy using the ELEPHANT framework on two consumer-facing models, GPT-5 Mini and Gemini 3 Flash. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, grammatical mood alone did not produce systematic differences in sycophantic behavior, suggesting that what a user implies matters more than how they phrase it. Instead, perspective-driven framing had a stronger influence, with gaps between original and flipped prompts widening in follow-up responses. Consistent increases in framing and moral sycophancy across turns indicate that models become more likely to accept a user's stated premises and affirm their ethical stance as a dialogue progresses. Notably, Gemini 3 Flash exhibited substantially smaller increases in moral sycophancy than GPT-5 Mini, suggesting it is more resistant to reinforcing ethically problematic positions across turns.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large language models give romantic relationship advice, focusing on when they overly agree with users (social and moral sycophancy) and how framing affects this behavior.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used for emotional support and relationship advice, there is a risk that, in trying to be supportive and preserve a user’s face, models may reinforce harmful or unethical interpersonal behaviors. The authors want to systematically measure when and how this happens, especially in multi-turn dialogues.
AI.method: The authors construct RRASP, a dataset of 2,400 romantic relationship advice-seeking prompts across five themes. They manipulate grammatical mood and perspective (original vs flipped framing) and evaluate two deployed models, GPT-5 Mini and Gemini 3 Flash, using the ELEPHANT framework to quantify social, framing, and moral sycophancy over multiple dialogue turns.
AI.result: They find that grammatical mood (e.g., asking vs stating) does not systematically change sycophantic behavior, contradicting their initial hypothesis. Instead, perspective-driven framing (original vs flipped prompts) has a stronger effect, with larger differences emerging in follow-up responses than in first responses. Across turns, both models increasingly accept user premises and affirm users’ ethical positions, but Gemini 3 Flash shows much smaller increases in moral sycophancy than GPT-5 Mini, indicating greater resistance to reinforcing problematic moral stances.
AI.conclusion: Sycophancy in romantic relationship advice from LLMs depends more on what users imply and how scenarios are framed than on surface-level grammatical mood. Multi-turn interactions exacerbate framing and moral sycophancy, as models grow more aligned with the user’s stated premises over time. Model design choices can mitigate this effect, as shown by Gemini 3 Flash’s lower moral sycophancy, highlighting the need for targeted safety and alignment strategies in emotional-support use cases.

title: Drift-Constrained Optimization: Only Direction Matters in Fine-Tuning Instruct Models
summary: Fine-tuning instruct models often improves target performance while inducing behavioral drift from the reference model, which can degrade existing capabilities. Rather than treating this drift as an uncontrolled consequence of optimization, we specify a behavioral drift budget before optimization and ask how to boost the target-task performance within it. Locally, behavioral drift induces a shared geometry anchored at the reference model, with the drift budget defining a boundary within this space. In this space, drift determines distance from the reference, leaving update direction as the remaining degree of freedom. Fine-tuning updates can therefore be compared through their directional efficiency, naturally reformulating fine-tuning as a direction-selection problem. This reformulation makes a concrete prediction: changing the accessible directions can qualitatively alter the outcome of fine-tuning. We test this prediction in a stringent QA-only setting, where strong instruct models are fine-tuned only on final answers but must still generate multi-step reasoning at inference. Despite this mismatch, a coarse layer-selective probe reverses the failure of QA-only fine-tuning and reveals the existence of effective directions, with multiple neighboring configurations improving target performance while preserving reasoning and general capabilities. Across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, these directions substantially improve scientific reasoning and multilingual translation. Over more than 100 languages, the resulting models match or outperform dedicated translation systems and provide a stronger initialization for subsequent reinforcement learning. Our results suggest that fine-tuning is not just about how much a model changes, but how that change is spent. https://github.com/CONE-MT/DCO and https://huggingface.co/collections/LLaMAX/dco

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method to fine-tune instruction-following models that boosts target-task performance while explicitly limiting behavioral drift from a reference model, showing that choosing efficient update directions under a drift budget can improve QA, reasoning, and translation without degrading general abilities.
AI.motivation: Standard fine-tuning of instruction models often improves specific target tasks but unintentionally changes other behaviors, degrading reasoning or general capabilities. Existing approaches typically treat this drift as an uncontrolled byproduct of optimization rather than something to manage. The authors aim to formalize and control this behavioral drift so models can gain new capabilities without sacrificing existing ones.
AI.method: The authors introduce a framework that treats fine-tuning as a direction-selection problem under a fixed "behavioral drift budget" from a reference model. They analyze the local geometry around the reference model, where behavioral drift defines a radius (distance) and the remaining degree of freedom is the update direction within this space. They then implement a coarse, layer-selective probing scheme in a QA-only fine-tuning setup: strong instruction models are fine-tuned only on final answers while being required to generate multi-step reasoning at inference. By selectively enabling and testing updates in different layers, they search for effective parameter-update directions that maximize target performance while staying within the drift budget and preserving reasoning behavior.
AI.result: In QA-only fine-tuning experiments on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, naive fine-tuning that only optimizes final answers harms multi-step reasoning and general capabilities. However, by probing and choosing specific layer-wise update directions, they find multiple nearby configurations that substantially improve target QA performance while preserving or improving reasoning and general capabilities. These directions notably boost scientific reasoning and multilingual translation quality, with the resulting models matching or outperforming dedicated machine translation systems in over 100 languages, and serving as strong initializations for later reinforcement learning stages.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning outcomes are strongly influenced not just by how much a model changes (the magnitude of behavioral drift) but by the direction of that change in parameter space. By viewing fine-tuning as choosing an update direction under a drift budget and by manipulating accessible directions (e.g., via layer-selective updates), practitioners can obtain models that improve specific target tasks while maintaining or enhancing broader reasoning and multilingual capabilities. The work demonstrates that controlling the geometry of updates can reverse failures of QA-only fine-tuning and produce better foundations for subsequent training like reinforcement learning.

title: Measuring the Cost of Variety Conflation in Multilingual MT Evaluation: Adding Mozambican Xichangana, Nyanja and Sena to FLORES+
summary: In this paper, we extend FLORES+ with Portuguese-source evaluation sets for three Mozambican Bantu varieties: Xichangana, Mozambican Nyanja, and Sena. We compare Xichangana with the existing Tsonga reference and Mozambican Nyanja with Chichewa, and evaluate NLLB-200, Google Translate, GPT, and a variant-aware NLLB model. Holding system output fixed reveals substantial reference sensitivity. On \textit{devtest}, changing only the reference from Tsonga to Xichangana reduces spBLEU by 13.10 points for NLLB-200 and 15.30 for Google. On matched Nyanja subsets, replacing Chichewa with Mozambican Nyanja produces smaller but consistent reductions of 3.03 and 6.10 spBLEU, respectively. Variant-aware fine-tuning reverses this pattern on the intended targets: relative to NLLB-200, it improves Xichangana by 7.04 spBLEU and Mozambican Nyanja by 5.33 on \textit{devtest}, while losing performance on the sibling references. GPT is competitive on Tsonga and Chichewa but substantially weaker on the Mozambican varieties. For Sena, the finetuned model reaches 12.64 spBLEU and 36.21 chrF++ on \textit{devtest}. These findings motivate variety-aware language identifiers, references, and reporting for cross-border languages or language dialects/variants. The data is publicly available on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/datasets/MOZNLP/FLORES_MOZ

AI.tldr: The paper extends the FLORES+ benchmark with Portuguese-source test sets for three Mozambican Bantu language varieties and shows that translation metrics are highly sensitive to which close variety is used as reference, motivating variety-aware models and evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current MT benchmarks like FLORES+ do not adequately represent Mozambican Bantu varieties, and evaluation for closely related language varieties is confounded because systems are judged against sibling-language references (e.g., Tsonga vs. Xichangana, Chichewa vs. Mozambican Nyanja). This can misrepresent true performance on specific target varieties and obscure the need for variant-aware systems.
AI.method: They build new Portuguese→Xichangana, Portuguese→Mozambican Nyanja, and Portuguese→Sena evaluation sets by extending FLORES+. They then evaluate several MT systems: NLLB-200, Google Translate, GPT, and a variant-aware version of NLLB fine-tuned on these Mozambican varieties. They compare metric scores (spBLEU, chrF++) when only the reference variety is changed (e.g., Tsonga vs. Xichangana; Chichewa vs. Mozambican Nyanja) while holding system outputs fixed, and they assess how variant-aware fine-tuning affects performance on both intended and sibling varieties.
AI.result: Changing only the reference variety causes large drops in spBLEU, showing strong reference sensitivity: for devtest, swapping Tsonga for Xichangana reduces spBLEU by 13.10 (NLLB-200) and 15.30 (Google); swapping Chichewa for Mozambican Nyanja reduces spBLEU by 3.03 and 6.10, respectively. After variant-aware fine-tuning, NLLB improves substantially on the Mozambican varieties (e.g., +7.04 spBLEU on Xichangana, +5.33 on Mozambican Nyanja) but performs worse on the sibling references. GPT remains competitive on Tsonga and Chichewa but is much weaker on the Mozambican varieties. For Sena, the fine-tuned model achieves 12.64 spBLEU and 36.21 chrF++ on devtest.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation for closely related language varieties is highly sensitive to which reference variety is used, so using only sibling-language references can give a misleading picture of MT quality. Variant-aware fine-tuning can substantially improve performance on underrepresented Mozambican varieties but may reduce performance on neighboring standardized varieties. The authors advocate for variety-aware language identification, distinct references, and explicit reporting practices when dealing with cross-border languages and dialects/variants, and they release new Mozambican FLORES-style test sets on Hugging Face.

title: Degraded but Not Entirely Ineffective: PE-Based Deformable Graph Neural Networks
summary: Many real-world scenarios can be represented using graph-structured data. However, traditional GNNs that transmit messages based on first-order neighbors have long faced several fundamental contradictions: increasing depth leads to over-smoothing, long-range dependencies cause over-compression, fixed neighborhoods restrict the receptive field, and on heterophilous graphs, topological neighbors become a source of noise. Although many works have addressed these issues individually, few mechanisms can simultaneously alleviate all of these challenges. To address the aforementioned problems, we propose a Position Encoding-Based Deformable Spatial Aggregation Module (PEBDSAM) that solves them all in one step. Specifically, we utilize a deformable mechanism in the position space to identify relevant nodes to supplement the original first-order neighbor information of GNNs, allowing traditional GNNs to adapt to heterophilous scenarios. Through diagnostic experiments, we obtained several major findings: current offsets fail to have any effect; subsequently, we analyzed the causes of offset failure and why model performance still improves even after offset failure, pointing out future research directions. Based on these diagnostic experiments, we streamlined the original PEBDSAM, resulting in a simplified version, which we call the Position Encoding-Based Spatial Aggregation Module (PEBSAM). In addition, we propose a PEBSAM-Speed to adapt to large datasets. Finally, we designed the module to be plug-and-play and applied it to GCN, GAT, GIN, and GraphSAGE, achieving desirable results on three homophilous datasets and six heterophilous graph datasets.

AI.tldr: They propose a plug-and-play positional-encoding-based spatial aggregation module that can be attached to common GNNs to better handle long-range, flexible, and heterophilous dependencies, and they further analyze and simplify its deformable offset mechanism.
AI.motivation: Standard GNNs aggregate only from fixed first-order neighbors, which causes several coupled issues: (1) deeper models over-smooth node representations; (2) capturing long-range dependencies over-compresses information; (3) fixed neighborhoods limit receptive fields; and (4) on heterophilous graphs, neighboring nodes can be noisy rather than informative. Existing methods tend to address these issues separately, lacking a unified mechanism. The paper aims to design a general, modular component that can simultaneously alleviate these problems and can be easily integrated into mainstream GNN architectures.
AI.method: They propose a Position Encoding-Based Deformable Spatial Aggregation Module (PEBDSAM). The module operates in position/embedding space, learning deformable offsets to select additional relevant nodes beyond first-order neighbors, thereby enlarging and adapting the effective receptive field and better handling heterophily. They conduct diagnostic experiments to study why the learned offsets often fail to have the intended effect, and why performance can still improve despite offset failure. Based on these insights, they simplify the design and introduce a streamlined Position Encoding-Based Spatial Aggregation Module (PEBSAM), and a more efficient PEBSAM-Speed variant for large-scale graphs. The modules are designed as plug-and-play components that can be attached to various backbone GNNs (GCN, GAT, GIN, GraphSAGE).
AI.result: Experiments on three homophilous and six heterophilous datasets show that adding their modules to standard GNNs improves performance. Their diagnostic analyses reveal that current deformable offset mechanisms may not actually influence which nodes are aggregated, exposing a discrepancy between the intended design and what is learned in practice. Even with offset failure, the models still gain performance, suggesting other factors (e.g., positional encodings or architectural changes) are responsible for the gains and indicating directions for future research on truly effective deformable mechanisms in graphs.
AI.conclusion: A positional-encoding-based spatial aggregation module can act as a general, plug-and-play enhancement to standard GNNs, helping them handle both homophilous and heterophilous graphs by flexibly extending the receptive field. However, their study also shows that naive deformable offset designs often fail to function as expected, and yet performance gains persist, implying that the main benefits currently come from the positional encoding and structural design rather than genuine deformable aggregation. This highlights the need for more principled deformable graph mechanisms and offers a simplified, efficient module (PEBSAM and PEBSAM-Speed) as practical tools and baselines for future work.

title: ShopEase: A Generative AI-Based Multi-Agent Framework for Intelligent Enterprise Customer Support Using Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Enterprise customer support systems must answer customer questions correctly, retrieve the right policy information, use customer context, and pass difficult cases to human agents when needed. This paper presents ShopEase, a Generative AI-based multi-agent framework for enterprise customer support. The system combines six components: Intent, CRM, Memory, Hybrid RAG, Escalation, and Supervisor, and uses LLaMA 3.2 running locally through Ollama for response generation. The retrieval module combines FAISS (dense retrieval) and BM25 (sparse retrieval), and six configurations are evaluated: BM25-only, FAISS-only, Fair RRF, Weighted RRF, RRF with Cross-Encoder, and Top-10 Hybrid with Cross-Encoder. Instead of using a fixed mapping between intent and policy, the policy category is decided directly from the retrieved documents. The system was evaluated on 2632 held-out customer queries across six categories: Refund, Return, Shipping, Cancellation, Damaged Product, and Unknown. FAISS-only achieved the highest accuracy of 85.37\% (2247 correct predictions), closely followed by Weighted RRF at 85.07\%. BM25-only achieved only 55.74\% accuracy. Adding cross-encoder reranking did not improve results: RRF with Cross-Encoder reached 83.24\%, and Top-10 Hybrid with Cross-Encoder reached 81.88\%, while also increasing response latency. Category-level analysis shows strong performance on Shipping, Cancellation, and Return, while Unknown queries remain the main source of errors. Statistical testing using McNemar's test shows no significant difference between FAISS-only and Weighted RRF, though both perform significantly better than Fair RRF and the cross-encoder configurations. Overall, dense retrieval gives the best accuracy on this dataset, and additional reranking adds processing time without improving classification performance.

AI.tldr: ShopEase is a multi-agent, LLaMA-based enterprise customer support system whose experiments show dense retrieval (FAISS) outperforms sparse and hybrid retrieval, while cross-encoder reranking adds latency without improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Enterprise customer support needs accurate, context-aware, and efficient handling of customer queries, including knowing when to escalate to humans. Existing systems often rely on rigid mappings between intents and policies and may not fully leverage modern retrieval methods. The paper aims to design and empirically evaluate a practical multi-agent architecture and retrieval strategy that maximizes answer accuracy while remaining efficient for real-world deployment.
AI.method: The authors build ShopEase, a multi-agent framework with six components (Intent, CRM, Memory, Hybrid RAG, Escalation, Supervisor), using a local LLaMA 3.2 via Ollama for generation. For retrieval, they implement and compare six configurations combining FAISS-based dense retrieval and BM25-based sparse retrieval: BM25-only, FAISS-only, Fair RRF, Weighted RRF, RRF with Cross-Encoder reranking, and Top-10 Hybrid with Cross-Encoder. Instead of predefining intent-to-policy mappings, the system classifies policy categories directly from retrieved documents. They evaluate these setups on 2632 held-out customer queries across six policy-related categories, measuring classification accuracy and latency, and apply McNemar’s test for significance between retrieval strategies.
AI.result: FAISS-only dense retrieval produced the best accuracy at 85.37% (2247/2632 correct), with Weighted RRF close behind at 85.07%. BM25-only performed substantially worse at 55.74%. Incorporating cross-encoder reranking (RRF with Cross-Encoder at 83.24% and Top-10 Hybrid with Cross-Encoder at 81.88%) did not improve classification accuracy and increased response latency. Category-level analysis reveals particularly strong performance on Shipping, Cancellation, and Return, while the Unknown category accounts for most errors. McNemar’s test indicates no significant difference between FAISS-only and Weighted RRF, but both significantly outperform Fair RRF and cross-encoder-based methods.
AI.conclusion: For this enterprise support dataset, dense retrieval with FAISS is more effective than BM25-based sparse or hybrid approaches, achieving the highest accuracy. Weighted hybrid fusion can match dense retrieval statistically but does not clearly surpass it. Cross-encoder reranking adds computational overhead and latency without accuracy gains, making it unattractive for production in this setting. The ShopEase multi-agent design demonstrates that directly inferring policy categories from retrieved documents, combined with strong dense retrieval, can yield high-performing, locally deployed customer support systems.

title: Bangla Sentence Function Classification: Corpus Development, Model Benchmarking, and Interpretability
comment: Accepted at 2026 IEEE 5th International Conference on Robotics, Automation, Artificial-Intelligence and Internet-of-Things (RAAICON)
summary: Automatic sentence function identification is important for many downstream natural language processing (NLP) applications such as dialogue systems, text-to-speech synthesis, and machine translation. However, benchmark resources for Bangla sentence function classification remain limited. To mitigate this gap, this paper introduces a corpus of 10,000 Bangla sentences, manually annotated into four functional categories, namely declarative, interrogative, imperative, and exclamatory. The corpus is nearly balanced across the four classes, with high annotation reliability reflected by a Fleiss\' Kappa of 0.82. Furthermore, we evaluate multiple feature representations, including Bag-of-Words (BoW), TF-IDF, and Word2Vec, with several classical machine learning classifiers. In addition, two heterogeneous ensemble models, namely Single-Level Ensemble (SLE) and Double-Level Ensemble (DLE), are utilized to improve classification performance. Experimental results show that TF-IDF consistently outperforms Word2Vec, likely due to its ability to emphasize discriminative lexical cues associated with sentence functions, particularly given the relatively small corpus used to train Word2Vec. The DLE model with TF-IDF features achieves the best performance with accuracy and macro-F1 of 0.95, demonstrating the effectiveness of sparse lexical representations and heterogeneous ensemble learning for this task. Further cross-validation confirms the robustness of the approach, while LIME-based interpretability provides insights into model predictions. The developed corpus and model benchmarking establish strong baselines for Bangla sentence function classification.

AI.tldr: They build and release a 10k-sentence Bangla corpus labeled by sentence function and show that TF‑IDF with a heterogeneous double-level ensemble reaches about 95% accuracy/F1, offering a strong baseline.
AI.motivation: Sentence function classification (declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamatory) is useful for applications like dialogue systems, TTS, and MT, but Bangla lacks benchmark datasets and systematic model evaluations for this task. The work aims to fill this resource and benchmarking gap.
AI.method: They construct a near-balanced corpus of 10,000 Bangla sentences manually annotated into four function types, ensuring high inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss’ Kappa 0.82). They then benchmark multiple text representations—BoW, TF‑IDF, and Word2Vec—combined with several classical machine learning classifiers. On top of these base learners, they design and test two heterogeneous ensemble schemes: a Single-Level Ensemble (SLE) and a Double-Level Ensemble (DLE). They evaluate models using accuracy and macro-F1, perform cross-validation for robustness, and apply LIME to interpret model decisions and understand which lexical cues drive predictions.
AI.result: TF‑IDF features consistently outperform Word2Vec embeddings for this task, attributed to TF‑IDF’s stronger emphasis on discriminative lexical cues and the limited size of the Word2Vec training data. Among all configurations, the Double-Level Ensemble (DLE) with TF‑IDF features yields the best performance, achieving 0.95 accuracy and 0.95 macro-F1. Cross-validation indicates that these results are robust, and LIME analyses provide interpretable explanations tied to characteristic words of each sentence function class.
AI.conclusion: Sparse lexical representations (especially TF‑IDF) combined with heterogeneous double-level ensemble learning are highly effective for Bangla sentence function identification. The released 10k-sentence, reliably annotated corpus, along with the reported model benchmarks, offers strong baselines and a valuable resource to support future research and downstream NLP applications in Bangla sentence function classification.

title: SHIFT-M3: Pre-fusion Alignment-based Consistency Screening for Multimodal ECG Record Integrity
comment: This paper has been accepted and presented at MLHC 2026. Please cite from the official proceedings
summary: Multimodal clinical AI typically assumes that the waveform, report, metadata, and downstream predictions attached to a record belong to the same patient. In practice, linkage failures can silently assemble individually plausible but cross-patient components, creating a safety problem that standard predictive models are not designed to detect. We study this problem as multimodal record integrity triage: given an assembled record, should its modalities be trusted to belong together? We introduce SHIFT-M3, a lightweight text-based pre-fusion screen that measures alignment-based consistency between two separately produced ECG text views: an LLM-generated interpretation and a clinical report summary. On 784,680 MEETI ECG records, SHIFT-M3 achieves 97.6% TPR@5% FPR for full text-view swaps (AUROC 0.996), 90.3% for partial swaps (AUROC 0.974), and 97.7% for label-matched hard negatives (AUROC 0.996) with only 573,569 parameters. Compared with same-dataset lexical baselines, the gains are largest on partial swaps and hard negatives, suggesting that the model is learning more than surface overlap. We also introduce the CMST (Conflict-type Multimodal Stress Test) evaluation taxonomy, a three-seed stability study, a loss ablation, a temporal-tolerance sweep, and a shared-token masking control. The main remaining failure mode is longitudinal ambiguity: at the default operating point, same-patient cross-visit pairs still produce 87.0% Type-II false positives.

AI.tldr: They propose a light-weight method to check whether different text components of a multimodal ECG record really belong to the same case, in order to detect hidden cross-patient mixups.
AI.motivation: In real clinical multimodal AI systems, data from different patients (waveforms, text reports, metadata, labels) can be accidentally combined into one record due to linkage failures. Standard predictive models assume everything belongs to the same patient and are not designed to detect such mismatches, which creates a serious safety risk. The authors want a way to automatically triage assembled records and flag those whose modalities likely do not belong together.
AI.method: They define the task of multimodal record integrity triage: deciding if the modalities in an assembled record are consistent with belonging to the same patient/case. They introduce SHIFT-M3, a small text-only, pre-fusion screening model that evaluates alignment-based consistency between two independently produced ECG text views: an LLM-generated interpretation of the ECG and the clinical report summary. The model is trained and evaluated on 784,680 MEETI ECG records and compared against lexical baseline methods. They also propose the CMST (Conflict-type Multimodal Stress Test) taxonomy for evaluation, perform a three-seed stability study, analyze loss components via ablation, sweep temporal-tolerance thresholds, and run a shared-token masking control to understand what the model is learning.
AI.result: SHIFT-M3, with only 573,569 parameters, reaches 97.6% true positive rate at 5% false positive rate for detecting full text-view swaps (AUROC 0.996), 90.3% TPR@5% FPR for partial swaps (AUROC 0.974), and 97.7% TPR@5% FPR for label-matched hard negatives (AUROC 0.996). It substantially outperforms same-dataset lexical baselines, especially on partial swaps and hard negatives, indicating it captures deeper semantic alignment rather than simple word overlap. However, a key failure mode remains: for same-patient but different-visit (longitudinal) pairs, the system still incorrectly flags 87.0% of such pairs as inconsistent at the default operating point (Type-II false positives).
AI.conclusion: A small, text-based pre-fusion model can effectively detect many forms of cross-patient multimodal record mismatches by evaluating consistency between independent text views of the same ECG, significantly reducing undetected linkage errors. The CMST taxonomy and associated analyses offer a structured way to stress-test such integrity checks. Nonetheless, longitudinal variation in the same patient’s records remains a major challenge, as the model often misidentifies cross-visit pairs as inconsistent, highlighting the need for approaches that are sensitive to clinically plausible evolution over time while still catching true cross-patient mixups.

title: IBBench-Light: A Paired Evaluation of Task-Conditioned Responses to External Directives
summary: An external record may contain a procedure to apply or text to read, depending on the user's request. IBBench-Light tests both uses against the same record. Twelve semantic bases yield 144 matched pairs per model; four quantized instruction models produced 1,152 archived greedy responses. Paired exact-contract accuracy (PECA) requires both members to satisfy their output contracts. Qwen succeeds on 132 execute and 109 process prompts, but only 97 complete pairs, showing what marginal averages omit. We audit literal-target exposure and case normalization, then add 1,722 logged CPU generations to test directive-absent controls, twelve additional semantic bases, within-base wording changes, and generation stopping. In the pinned Phi rerun, changing the end-of-sequence (EOS) set changes exact paired success from 0/144 to 62/144. A bounded IHEval comparison uses the same SmolLM2 checkpoint and output budget while preserving its published instruction roles and scorer. The benchmark measures conditional task and output-contract success. Its task margins and paired count need to be read together with the stopping policy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces IBBench-Light, a benchmark for evaluating instruction-following language models on both executing procedures and processing text using paired tests on the same records.
AI.motivation: To more accurately assess instruction-following models, current aggregate accuracy metrics are not sufficient; they can hide failures that occur when models must both execute actions and process text under strict output contracts and stopping conditions. A benchmark is needed that exposes such discrepancies and evaluates conditional task success under realistic execution constraints.
AI.method: The authors design IBBench-Light, which uses external records that can either be executed as procedures or read as text, enabling matched paired evaluations across these two use modes. They define paired exact-contract accuracy (PECA), where both members of a pair must meet strict output contracts. They generate 1,152 archived greedy responses from four quantized instruction-tuned models over 12 semantic bases (yielding 144 pairs per model). They further log 1,722 CPU generations to test the impact of directive-absent controls, additional semantic bases, wording changes, literal-target exposure, case normalization, and different generation stopping policies such as EOS token sets. They also run a bounded comparison to IHEval using the same SmolLM2 checkpoint and output budget while preserving its original instruction roles and scoring.
AI.result: In IBBench-Light, the Qwen model achieves 132 correct "execute" and 109 correct "process" responses, but only 97 pairs where both are correct, illustrating that marginal averages over tasks can overstate reliability. Audits show sensitivity to literal-target exposure and case normalization. Changes in stopping policy have large effects: in a rerun of Phi with a pinned checkpoint, altering the EOS set shifts paired exact success from 0/144 to 62/144. Additional experiments with 1,722 CPU generations show effects from directive-absent controls, added semantic bases, and wording changes. The bounded IHEval comparison demonstrates that, under matched checkpoints and budgets, IBBench-Light can be related to existing benchmarks while focusing on contract satisfaction.
AI.conclusion: IBBench-Light provides a fine-grained benchmark for conditional task and output-contract success that reveals reliability issues hidden by simple accuracy metrics. Paired exact-contract accuracy and careful control of stopping policies, prompting variants, and text normalization show that evaluation of instruction-following models must consider both sides of paired tasks and the generation policy. The benchmark highlights that task margins and paired counts should always be interpreted together with the stopping strategy when judging model performance.

title: Phorecaster365: A Human-Supervised Reference Architecture for Hybrid Pharmaceutical Sales Forecasting and Planning Decision Support
comment: 23 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables, including supplementary appendices
summary: Pharmaceutical sales forecasts inform planning across products, regions, and distribution channels, yet their interpretation depends on inventory availability, transaction semantics, product lifecycle, and the information available when each forecast is issued. A model prediction alone does not preserve these conditions or establish whether a forecast is suitable for operational use. We present Phorecaster365, a human-supervised reference architecture that connects enterprise resource planning data to reviewable pharmaceutical sales forecasts. The architecture separates source ingestion, product-region series construction, temporally valid feature generation, statistical and machine-learning modeling, ensemble formation, uncertainty assessment, planner review, and lifecycle governance. Its central intermediate representation is a forecast context package that preserves the source snapshot, forecast target, temporal cutoff, available covariates, data-quality state, and hierarchy version. A corresponding forecast evidence package links predictions to model and calibration versions, exceptions, human adjustments, and publication history. Development experience with a synthetic panel of 10,950 daily records across 30 product-region series informs the design. Historical experiment summaries are retained only as descriptive evidence of development because their evaluation does not establish independent predictive validity. We specify a rolling-origin evaluation protocol, baseline and ablation requirements, uncertainty and robustness assessments, and a staged pathway from synthetic testing to use in governed planning. The contribution is an implementation-neutral system design and validation framework; the report does not establish real-world forecasting accuracy, comparative superiority, or operational benefit.

AI.tldr: Design of Phorecaster365, a human-supervised architecture for pharmaceutical sales forecasting that preserves forecast context and evidence for operational use and governance, without claiming real-world accuracy.
AI.motivation: Pharmaceutical sales forecasts often lack operational interpretability because raw model predictions do not encode key conditions such as inventory constraints, transaction semantics, lifecycle stage, and what information was actually available at forecast time. Organizations need a robust, auditable way to connect ERP data to forecasts that planners can review and trust, while managing lifecycle, uncertainty, and governance.
AI.method: Propose Phorecaster365, a reference architecture that decomposes the forecasting workflow into modules: source data ingestion from ERP; construction of product-region time series; generation of temporally valid features; application of statistical and machine-learning models; ensemble formation; uncertainty assessment; human planner review; and lifecycle governance. Introduce two key intermediate artifacts: (1) a forecast context package that captures the data snapshot, forecast target, temporal cutoff, covariates, data quality, and hierarchy version; and (2) a forecast evidence package that links predictions to model and calibration versions, exceptions, human overrides, and publication history. Development and design are informed by experiments on a synthetic daily panel of 30 product-region series, but these experiments are retained only as descriptive development evidence. Define a rolling-origin evaluation protocol, baselines and ablations, and robustness / uncertainty checks, along with a staged path from synthetic testing to governed operational deployment.
AI.result: A detailed, implementation-neutral system design and validation framework for pharmaceutical sales forecasting that preserves forecast context and evidence, supports human oversight, and specifies evaluation and governance protocols. It demonstrates feasibility on synthetic data and articulates requirements for baselines, ablations, and robustness analysis, but does not provide real-world performance benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Phorecaster365 offers a structured, auditable architecture for connecting ERP data to operationally meaningful pharmaceutical sales forecasts, emphasizing forecast context, evidence tracking, and governance. The work should be viewed as a system and validation blueprint rather than proof of forecasting accuracy or business benefit; real-world performance and comparative superiority remain to be established in future deployments.

title: Trustworthy Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Cybersecurity and Systems Survey on Threat Landscapes, Defense Architectures, and Open Challenges
summary: The transition from passive foundation models to autonomous, goal-directed agentic AI systems has introduced unprecedented capabilities by coupling recursive cognitive reasoning loops, persistent memory architectures, live tool execution planes, and multi-agent collaboration topologies. However, granting probabilistic neural cores execution authority across filesystems, networks, and cloud infrastructure dissolves classical security perimeters: natural language simultaneously serves as input data, internal control code, and communication protocols, exposing a Turing-complete blast radius where untrusted data represents executable instructions. This survey delivers a comprehensive systems-security reference framework for trustworthy agentic AI, synthesizing 206 foundational studies and regulatory standards. We formalize the general agent architecture as a stateful 5-tuple and establish a 6-dimensional trustworthiness taxonomy covering security, safety, privacy, explainability, fairness, and accountability. We systematically analyze threat surfaces across intra-execution loops and interaction planes, formulate a multi-layered zero-trust defense-in-depth architecture integrating Dual-LLM isolation, Capability-Based Access Control, kernel eBPF probes, and sandboxed runtimes, review standardized evaluation benchmarks, and map technical controls to international AI governance frameworks.

AI.tldr: Survey of security and trustworthiness for agentic AI systems and a proposed architectural framework for defending them.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems—autonomous, tool-using, multi-step reasoning agents—blur traditional boundaries between data, code, and control. Because they can act over filesystems, networks, and cloud resources via natural language instructions, classical perimeter-based security models fail. There is an urgent need to understand their new threat surfaces and to systematize defenses and governance alignment.
AI.method: The authors conduct a survey and synthesis of 206 technical works and regulatory standards related to agentic AI and AI governance. They formalize a generic agent architecture as a stateful 5-tuple model, define a 6-axis taxonomy of trustworthiness (security, safety, privacy, explainability, fairness, accountability), and systematically map attack surfaces and defenses across intra-agent loops and external interaction planes. They then propose a multi-layered, zero-trust reference architecture combining mechanisms such as Dual-LLM isolation, Capability-Based Access Control, kernel-level eBPF monitoring, and sandboxed runtimes, and link these controls to existing governance frameworks and benchmarks.
AI.result: The paper yields: (1) a formalized abstract model of agentic AI architectures; (2) a 6-dimensional trustworthiness taxonomy tailored to such agents; (3) a structured threat-surface analysis for agent loops and interaction channels; (4) a proposed zero-trust, defense-in-depth systems architecture with concrete mechanisms (dual-LLM separation, capability-based permissions, eBPF probes, sandboxing); and (5) a mapping between these technical controls, evaluation benchmarks, and international AI governance/standards documents.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI systems require rethinking security and trust beyond traditional model-centric views, because natural language becomes an executable control channel over powerful tools and infrastructure. By providing a formal architecture model, a multidimensional trust taxonomy, and a concrete zero-trust reference design aligned with regulatory frameworks, the survey aims to serve as a comprehensive guide for designing, analyzing, and governing trustworthy agentic AI systems.

title: How Many Thoughts Can a Vector Hold? The Capacity of Reasoning by Superposition
summary: Large language models solve hard problems through intermediate computations across multi-step reasoning. Traditional chain-of-thought encodes these computations as tokens. Recent continuous and recurrent methods instead move partial computations into fixed-dimensional latent states, where a single thought can superpose multiple alternatives. This raises a fundamental design question:what should continuous thoughts preserve as reasoning proceeds? An intuitive approach discards past computations and keeps only the current reasoning frontier. Storing more items seems to dilute states and waste limited representational capacity. We show this intuition can be incorrect. Under identical downstream computations, cumulative superposition retaining full reasoning history can require lower representational dimensions than frontier-only superposition holding only current alternatives. At fixed hidden width, this advantage allows latent reasoners to retain more valid evidence, distinguish more plausible downstream outcomes, and delay the point where compressed states turn unreliable. This counter-intuitive effect emerges because informative historical components coherently reinforce each other, while unrelated alternatives bring random interference. This perspective also answers a practical design question: how should models weight memories accumulated inside latent states when their future use is unknown? Across reusable weighted superpositions, prioritizing a small set of recent or salient items produces weakly-represented memories that bottleneck subsequent attention. Uniform cumulative weighting avoids this flaw, and we prove it is minimax-optimal for robust future reasoning. Our results turn superposition from an observed latent-space effect into a design principle: balanced cumulative memory lets a fixed representational budget support more reliable, reusable computations.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to best store intermediate reasoning steps in continuous latent states, showing that retaining the full cumulative history in superposition can be more efficient and reliable than only encoding the current reasoning frontier, and proves that uniformly weighting past thoughts is minimax-optimal for future reasoning.
AI.motivation: Large language models increasingly rely on multi-step reasoning, but traditional chain-of-thought uses long token sequences, while newer methods compress reasoning into fixed-size continuous states. Designers lack clear principles for what aspects of intermediate computations to preserve in these latent states under tight dimensional constraints, and common intuitions about discarding old information may be flawed. The paper aims to provide a theoretical framework to understand how superposition and memory weighting affect reasoning reliability and capacity.
AI.method: The authors analyze continuous and recurrent latent reasoning systems under a shared downstream computation model, comparing two strategies: frontier-only superposition (only current alternatives) versus cumulative superposition (full reasoning history). They study how informative and uninformative components interact via coherent reinforcement versus random interference in fixed-dimensional representations. They then formalize the problem of assigning weights to stored memories when future usage is unknown, and derive minimax-optimal weighting schemes for reusable weighted superpositions, focusing on uniform cumulative weighting. The approach is mainly theoretical and analytical, supported by capacity and reliability bounds.
AI.result: They show that, for the same downstream computation and fixed hidden width, cumulative superposition that retains the entire reasoning history can require lower representational dimension than frontier-only strategies, and thus can store more valid evidence and distinguish more downstream outcomes before becoming unreliable. The analysis demonstrates that historical components that align with each other strengthen the signal, whereas unrelated alternatives mostly add random noise, so discarding history is not necessarily optimal. In the memory-weighting setting, they prove that commonly used schemes that emphasize recent or salient items lead to weakly represented memories and premature attention bottlenecks, while uniform cumulative weighting over all stored items is minimax-optimal for robust future reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Contrary to prevailing intuition, in continuous latent reasoning systems it can be more representation-efficient to keep a cumulative superposition of the full reasoning history rather than only the current frontier. Informative past computations can reinforce each other, improving reliability at fixed dimensionality. Moreover, when future usage is unknown, uniformly weighting all accumulated thoughts in superposition is theoretically optimal in a minimax sense, avoiding fragile, weakly-encoded memories induced by recency- or salience-biased weighting. The work promotes "balanced cumulative memory" as a design principle for latent reasoners, turning superposition from an incidental artifact into a tool for building more reliable, reusable intermediate computations within a fixed representational budget.

title: Inter-Rater Reliability of LLM and Rule-Based Annotation for Inferential Narrative Features: Three Studies on a Turkish Corpus
comment: v1.0. 10 pages, 3 tables. Also archived at Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21740239
summary:
Datasets that ship automatically generated feature annotations invite a question rarely asked of them: would a human agree with those labels? This report answers that for the Objective Projection corpus, a Turkish narrative dataset whose scenes carry a per-scene applied_rules field from a rule-based detector over six craft features -- two prohibitions (emotion labelling, simile) and four positive techniques (materialized metaphor, micro-focus, temporal anchor, atmosphere contradiction).
  Three studies are reported. Study 1 ($n = 120$) scores the detector against blind labels from the scheme's own author. Study 2 ($n = 100$, a disjoint scene set) scores the detector plus Gemini 2.5 Flash and Grok against an independent non-expert rater whose labels were locked before any machine ran. Study 2b re-runs the identical protocol with Claude Fable 5 (High) and ChatGPT 5.5.
  The central result concerns one rule. On materialized metaphor -- closest to the methodology's theoretical core -- the five machine labellers returned positive rates of $0$, $1$, $40$, $72$ and $78$ out of $100$ scenes, against a human count of $9$. Cohen's $κ$ was at or indistinguishable from chance for five of six labellers, across both human references and both scene sets: $0.004$, $0.015$, $0.000$, $0.019$, $0.027$. Raw agreement ranged from $74.7\%$ to $84.5\%$, an artefact of class imbalance rather than a sign of competence.
  We deliberately do not resolve this into a single story. Two readings survive: the feature is genuinely inferential and beyond current automatic detection, or the rule's definition is not yet operational enough for any rater to apply consistently -- including the human. Distinguishing them needs a second independent human rater, which this report does not have and therefore does not claim.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether automatically generated narrative feature labels in the Objective Projection Turkish corpus match human judgments, finding near-chance agreement, especially for materialized metaphor.
AI.motivation: To test the reliability and human-alignment of rule-based and LLM-based feature annotations bundled with the Objective Projection corpus, particularly for complex literary features like materialized metaphor.
AI.method: Three studies: (1) compare a rule-based detector’s labels to blind labels from the original scheme author on 120 scenes; (2) on a disjoint 100-scene set, compare the detector and two LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok) to labels from an independent non-expert whose annotations were fixed before machine runs; (2b) replicate Study 2 protocol with two other LLMs (Claude Fable 5 High, ChatGPT 5.5). Agreement is assessed via positive rates, Cohen’s kappa, and raw agreement.
AI.result: For the key feature ‘materialized metaphor’, machine labelers showed wildly different positive rates (0, 1, 40, 72, 78 out of 100 scenes) compared with a human’s 9 positives. Cohen’s κ was at or near chance (0.000–0.027) for five of six labelers across references and scene sets; raw agreement was high (74.7–84.5%) but driven by class imbalance, not true detection skill.
AI.conclusion: Automatic labelling for complex narrative features in this corpus is not reliably aligned with human judgments. Either materialized metaphor is too inferential for current detectors (rule-based or LLM) or the operational definition is underspecified such that no rater, including humans, can apply it consistently. Discriminating between these explanations requires a second independent human rater, which the present work lacks.

title: Positioning manuscripts in the scientific landscape with agentic AI
summary: Publishing a research manuscript is a routine yet demanding part of scientific life: time-consuming, stressful, and often uncertain in outcome. Recent advances in large language model (LLM)-based agentic AI have shown promise across a range of scientific tasks, and here we ask whether agentic AI can help researchers navigate the publication process itself by reliably inferring a manuscript's eventual publication venue from its content and literature context. We introduce PASS (Publication-oriented Agentic Scientific System), an agentic system that understands manuscripts within their domain-specific literature context and predicts top-matched publication venues. PASS positions each manuscript within its surrounding literature landscape by reconstructing its local scientific neighborhood, tracing its topic trajectory, and reasoning over field-specific journal spaces. Evaluated on a leakage-audited benchmark of over 2,000 preprints across 16 biomedical fields, PASS achieved Top-1 accuracy of 50.3% and Top-5 accuracy of 86.1%, outperforming state-of-the-art LLM baselines and established journal-selection tools. PASS-produced quality scores, such as impact potential and novelty, aligned with independent measures of publication outcome. We also found that the designed literature retrieval module is the strongest performance contributor, particularly for positioning manuscripts relative to nearby work, and that PASS maintained near-full performance from the abstract alone, whereas LLM baselines required the full manuscript text. An independent human evaluation found strong researcher agreement with PASS's manuscript understanding and recommendation rationale. PASS has been released as a public platform (https://ratemypaper.ai/) for broad researcher access.

AI.tldr: The paper presents PASS, an agentic AI system that predicts which journal a manuscript is likely to be published in and assesses manuscript quality, using only the manuscript text (often just the abstract) plus its surrounding literature context.
AI.motivation: Publishing is time-consuming, stressful, and uncertain for researchers, especially when choosing appropriate journals and judging publication prospects. With LLM-based agentic AI showing promise in scientific tasks, the authors aim to determine whether such systems can reliably support the publication process by predicting likely venues and evaluating manuscript quality from content and literature context.
AI.method: They design PASS (Publication-oriented Agentic Scientific System), an agentic pipeline that: (1) retrieves and reconstructs a manuscript’s local literature neighborhood; (2) positions the manuscript within that landscape by tracing topic trajectories and journal spaces; and (3) uses LLM-based reasoning over this structured context to predict top-matched publication venues and assign quality scores (impact potential, novelty, etc.). They evaluate PASS on a leakage-audited benchmark of 2,000+ biomedical preprints across 16 fields, compare it against strong LLM baselines and existing journal-selection tools, and perform ablations (especially on the retrieval module) and human evaluation of its reasoning and recommendations.
AI.result: PASS achieves 50.3% Top-1 and 86.1% Top-5 accuracy in predicting final publication venues, outperforming state-of-the-art LLM baselines and established journal-selection services. Its quality scores correlate with independent publication outcomes. Ablations show the literature retrieval module is the major driver of performance, particularly for local-positioning of manuscripts; and unlike baselines, PASS retains near-full performance using only abstracts. Human evaluators (researchers) strongly agree with PASS’s understanding of manuscripts and its recommendation rationales. The system is deployed publicly as ratemypaper.ai.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI, when coupled with strong literature-retrieval and domain-aware reasoning, can effectively predict where manuscripts will be published and provide meaningful, human-aligned assessments of their quality using minimal input (often just the abstract). PASS demonstrates that such systems can practically assist researchers in journal selection and expectation-setting about publication, providing a scalable tool now publicly available for broad use.

title: CRITICS - Critical Science Without Borders: Language Models to Promote Critical Thinking in Science Education
summary: The CRITICS project addresses science accessibility and literacy by converging advanced Machine Translation (MT) based on Large Language Models (LLMs) with educational technology. By leveraging MT systems specifically optimized for scientific content, educational institutions can provide accurate, culturally relevant translations of scientific materials in students' native languages, ensuring that complex scientific concepts are comprehensible while maintaining technical accuracy. Building on these translations, the project explores the design and evaluation of innovative science teaching-learning proposals grounded in curriculum-aligned teaching-learning. Thus, CRITICS will investigate key components of scientific argumentation and critical thinking practices together with textual feedback aligned with learning objectives and assessment criteria inspired by competence-based evaluation frameworks. CRITICS aims to break down language barriers to accessing cutting-edge research and educational materials currently available only in high-resourced languages, thereby facilitating the democratization of scientific knowledge and fostering critical thinking in science education.

AI.tldr: CRITICS uses advanced MT with LLMs to translate scientific content for education and then designs and evaluates curriculum-aligned activities to enhance students’ scientific argumentation and critical thinking.
AI.motivation: Many scientific resources are only available in high-resourced languages, limiting access and understanding for students who do not speak those languages fluently. This language barrier hampers both science literacy and equitable participation in scientific knowledge. The project is motivated by the need to democratize access to up‑to‑date scientific materials and to support deeper learning—especially argumentation and critical thinking—through high‑quality, pedagogically useful translations.
AI.method: The project develops or adapts MT systems based on LLMs that are specifically optimized for scientific discourse. These MT systems generate accurate, culturally adapted translations of scientific texts into students’ native languages. On top of these translations, the team designs curriculum-aligned teaching–learning proposals (e.g., classroom activities, tasks, and assessments) that explicitly target scientific argumentation and critical thinking. The project further integrates textual feedback mechanisms aligned with competence‑based evaluation frameworks, meaning feedback is mapped to learning objectives and assessment criteria, and then empirically evaluates these designs in educational settings.
AI.result: While the abstract does not report empirical outcomes yet, it states that CRITICS will deliver: (1) high-quality MT pipelines tailored to scientific content, (2) curriculum-aligned instructional designs leveraging translated materials, and (3) models and tools for analyzing and supporting scientific argumentation, critical thinking practices, and feedback provision in science education.
AI.conclusion: CRITICS concludes that combining advanced, science-optimized MT with curriculum-aware educational technology can reduce language barriers that currently restrict access to high-level scientific content. By doing so, it supports more equitable science education and promotes students’ critical thinking and argumentation skills, contributing to the broader democratization of scientific knowledge.

title: Homeostatic Continual Learning
summary: In this paper, I formulate a Continual Learning problem and propose a method named "Homeostatic Continual Learning" that enables an AI agent to learn continuously in a changing environment without catastrophic forgetting.
