AI.conclusion: Lightweight LoRA fine-tuning can effectively adapt open-source instruction-tuned LLMs to the specific language, notation, and structured-solution format used in a university Linear Control Systems course. This yields more reference-like and consistently formatted answers without full model retraining. However, the chosen metrics focus on textual similarity and formatting rather than deep domain reasoning or mathematical correctness, so comprehensive evaluation still requires expert-designed rubrics and human assessment.

title: Corpus Characterization and Inverse Constitutional Fine-Tuning for Style-Aware Radiology Reports
summary: Automated radiology report generation has advanced rapidly in diagnostic accuracy, yet generated reports frequently diverge from the stylistic conventions of authentic radiologist writing in structure, diction, and uncertainty language, a gap which has direct implications for clinician trust and user experience. To address this, we characterize stylistic variation across 2,000 reports from the CheXpert Plus dataset using Bio-ClinicalBERT embeddings, UMAP dimensionality reduction, and HDBSCAN clustering, identifying five distinct reporting patterns differing in pathology focus, narrative structure, and lexical preference. Drawing on these findings, we adapt the inverse constitutional AI framework to derive a style-focused constitution from radiologist-written report pairs without requiring a formal preference dataset. This constitution, encoding conventions of tone, diction, uncertainty calibration, and report structure, is incorporated into the supervised fine-tuning of a MedGemma-4B base model on 25,245 CheXpert Plus training pairs. Constitutional fine-tuning produces a substantial increases in text alignment (BLEU-4: 0.006 to 0.308; ROUGE-L: 0.171 to 0.484) relative to the untuned baseline. These gains show a qualitative shift in structural and lexical alignment rather than marginal improvement, as the baseline model produces near-zero scores due to format mismatch. Overall, we establish corpus-level style characterization and constitutional modeling as an effective and data-efficient strategy for producing radiology reports that conform to authentic radiologist writing conventions.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes stylistic patterns in real radiology reports and uses them to constitutionally fine‑tune a vision–language model so its generated reports better match authentic radiologist writing style and structure, greatly improving text alignment metrics.
AI.motivation: Despite progress in automated radiology report generation, model outputs often fail to match the stylistic norms of real radiologists—such as report structure, tone, lexical choices, and how uncertainty is expressed—leading to mistrust and poor user experience even when diagnostic content is accurate. The authors aim to systematically characterize these stylistic patterns and build a data‑efficient way to enforce them during model training.
AI.method: 1) Extract Bio‑ClinicalBERT embeddings for 2,000 reports from CheXpert Plus; 2) apply UMAP for dimensionality reduction and HDBSCAN for clustering to discover distinct stylistic/reporting patterns; 3) interpret clusters in terms of pathology focus, narrative structure, and lexical preferences; 4) adapt the inverse constitutional AI framework to automatically derive a style‑focused “constitution” from pairs of radiologist‑written reports, encoding tone, diction, uncertainty calibration, and structure; 5) incorporate these constitutional rules into supervised fine‑tuning of a MedGemma‑4B base model on 25,245 CheXpert Plus training pairs; 6) evaluate text alignment using BLEU‑4 and ROUGE‑L between model outputs and reference reports.
AI.result: The style‑aware, constitutionally fine‑tuned MedGemma‑4B model shows large improvements in alignment with reference radiology reports: BLEU‑4 increases from 0.006 to 0.308 and ROUGE‑L from 0.171 to 0.484. The improvement is primarily due to correcting major structural and lexical mismatches between the baseline model and authentic radiologist report format, rather than minor incremental gains on already‑aligned text.
AI.conclusion: Corpus‑level analysis of reporting style and an adapted inverse constitutional AI framework can be combined into a practical, data‑efficient training strategy that substantially improves the stylistic fidelity of automated radiology report generation. By encoding radiologist conventions for tone, diction, uncertainty, and structure into a learned constitution and using it in supervised fine‑tuning, models can produce reports that better resemble authentic radiologist writing, potentially improving clinician trust and usability.

title: SAILOR: Solver-Assisted Interactive LLM-based Optimization Recovery
summary: Natural-language descriptions of optimization problems may be incomplete or vague about numerical information that a solver requires, including costs, capacities, demands, bounds, and penalties. A language model can translate the description into code, but when a required value is absent it must either stop or guess. We present SAILOR, a proof-of-concept system that detects such unsupported numerical choices, asks the user targeted follow-up questions, and updates the optimization model before returning a solution. Questions are prioritized using uncertainty and solver-derived estimates of how strongly each missing value affects the current model. We evaluate the pipeline on 1,723 instances from seven masked benchmarks using an idealized simulator that returns ground-truth values. Exact objective-value agreement ranges from 27.0% to 87.6% across datasets, with 1.4--5.7 questions per instance on average. These results establish feasibility under controlled branch-and-reveal feedback; they do not measure performance with human users or general structural model repair. Code is available at: https://github.com/sshaghayeghs/SAILOR.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SAILOR, a system that turns vague natural-language optimization problem descriptions into precise models by detecting missing numerical values, querying the user for them, and updating the model iteratively.
AI.motivation: Natural-language problem descriptions often omit or vaguely specify crucial numerical parameters (e.g., costs, capacities, penalties) needed by optimization solvers. Existing LLM-to-code pipelines either have to hallucinate these values or fail. The authors want a principled way to handle missing numeric information by interacting with the user instead of guessing, thereby making language-based optimization more reliable and practical.
AI.method: They build SAILOR, a pipeline where (1) a language model converts a natural-language description into an optimization model, (2) the system detects numerical parameters that are unsupported by the text, (3) it ranks these missing values for clarification using a combination of LLM-estimated uncertainty and solver-based sensitivity/importance measures, and (4) it asks the user targeted follow-up questions to obtain the missing values, iteratively updating and re-solving the model. They test this using an idealized simulator that provides ground-truth answers instead of humans, across seven benchmark datasets where key numbers are artificially masked.
AI.result: On 1,723 benchmark instances with masked numerical parameters, SAILOR achieves exact objective-value agreement with the ground-truth models on 27.0%–87.6% of instances across datasets, while requiring on average only 1.4–5.7 clarification questions per instance. This empirically demonstrates that the approach can often recover the correct optimization behavior with a modest amount of interactive querying under the controlled simulation setup.
AI.conclusion: SAILOR shows that interactive clarification of missing numerical information in natural-language optimization problem descriptions is feasible and can substantially recover correct solutions under a branch-and-reveal simulator. However, the study is limited to controlled benchmarks and simulated feedback; it does not yet address real human users or broader forms of model repair beyond missing numerics, leaving these as directions for future work.

title: The Attribution-Compression Frontier in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
comment: Accepted to GroundLM 2026 Workshop at EMNLP
summary: Context compression reduces generator input in retrieval-augmented generation, but answer quality alone does not characterize citation attribution. We measure citation attribution across compression methods and budgets, comparing reranking, extractive selection, abstractive summarization, token pruning, and an extract-cluster-rewrite construction on ASQA and QASPER under a fixed generator and primary entailment evaluator. On ASQA at a nominal 0.25 budget (achieved compression 0.08), a RECOMP-style compressor's citations score 0.86 precision against its summaries but 0.12 against source spans under our re-attributability protocol. These estimates depend on a shared NLI model for span recovery and citation scoring and lack independent human calibration. Extractive selection's observed grounded precision ranges from 0.43 to 0.49 across nominal budgets from one-half to one-tenth of the ASQA context, while answer quality declines. For the same RECOMP setting, claim verification after source recovery yields an unsupported rate of 0.88 versus 0.17 when checking summaries. This gap persists beyond structural rejection of missing provenance, but remains evaluator-dependent. A 200-question TRUE T5-XXL audit also finds emitted--grounded gaps under both fixed and recomputed source mappings, without establishing human-calibrated support rates.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how different context compression methods in retrieval-augmented generation affect not just answer quality but the correctness of citations back to original sources, finding large gaps between apparently good summaries and truly grounded, source-attributable content.
AI.motivation: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), long retrieved contexts are often compressed to fit model input limits or improve efficiency. Prior work typically evaluates compression via answer quality alone, assuming that if answers look good, the system remains faithful to its sources. However, compressed contexts can lead to hallucinated or misattributed citations, undermining trust, auditability, and factual grounding. This paper is motivated by the need to systematically measure how different compression strategies impact citation attribution and grounding, not just surface-level answer quality.
AI.method: The authors compare multiple context compression strategies—reranking, extractive selection, abstractive summarization, token pruning, and an extract-cluster-rewrite scheme—within a controlled RAG setup using a fixed generator and a primary NLI-based entailment evaluator. They run experiments on ASQA and QASPER datasets under various compression budgets (fractions of the original context). They introduce a re-attributability protocol that first recovers supporting spans from the original sources using an NLI model, then measures citation precision both against compressed summaries and against the true source spans. They also conduct claim verification after source recovery and perform a 200-question audit using TRUE T5-XXL to probe discrepancies between emitted citations and grounded evidence under both fixed and recomputed source mappings.
AI.result: For ASQA at a nominal 0.25 context budget (effective compression 0.08), a RECOMP-style abstractive compressor achieves high citation precision (0.86) when evaluated against its own summaries but extremely low precision (0.12) when evaluated against the original source spans under the re-attributability protocol, revealing major overestimation of grounding if summaries are treated as truth. Extractive selection shows grounded precision between 0.43 and 0.49 as the nominal budget decreases from one-half to one-tenth of the context, but answer quality worsens with more aggressive compression. For the same RECOMP setting, claim verification after source recovery yields 0.88 unsupported rate when checking against recovered sources versus 0.17 when checking against summaries, showing a large emitted–grounded gap. These patterns hold even after accounting for structurally missing provenance but remain sensitive to the chosen NLI evaluator. The TRUE T5-XXL 200-question audit similarly finds gaps between emitted citations and truly grounded evidence under both fixed and recomputed source mappings, though it does not pin down human-calibrated support levels.
AI.conclusion: Answer quality and summary-level citation metrics substantially overstate the true grounding of RAG systems that use aggressive context compression. Abstractive and construction-style compressors, in particular, can maintain seemingly good answers and high citation scores relative to their own summaries while being poorly attributable to original sources. Extractive selection offers better grounding but at the cost of answer quality as compression increases. Reliable assessment of citation attribution requires protocols that trace claims back to original source spans, not just to compressed intermediates, and current NLI-based evaluators still introduce dependence and uncertainty. Overall, the paper warns that compression pipelines can create large hidden gaps between what models emit and what is actually supported by retrieved documents, calling for more cautious evaluation and human-calibrated auditing of grounding in compressed RAG systems.

title: Synthetic Data in Marketing Research: How to Evaluate and When to Trust
summary: Debate over synthetic data in marketing research has polarized between claims that large language models (LLMs) make human respondents obsolete and calls to avoid them entirely. We argue that both positions obscure the more useful question: not whether synthetic respondents work, but when. Building on Brand, Israeli, and Ngwe (2026), we make three contributions. First, we distinguish three types of synthetic data (ungrounded LLM responses, segment-level personas, and individual-level digital twins) and map each to the decisions it can support. Second, we develop a taxonomy of four families of accuracy measures and suggest that the wide range of reported twin accuracy, from near-perfect to near-chance, largely reflects differences in what is being measured rather than in method quality. Aggregate measures often perform well even when little information is supplied to the LLM, and can mask a complete absence of respondent-level differentiation. Third, we introduce the forgotten question problem, in which a question is omitted from a fielded study, as a setting for twin-based augmentation of existing data. We propose an ex-ante answerability diagnostic that requires no ground truth: the R^2 of a random forest predicting twin outputs from the data used to construct the twins. Across 108 attitude questions from a nationally representative survey (N = 3,063), screening at R^2 above 0.7 raises the mean twin-human individual-level correlation by 15% and reduces the share of poorly answered questions from 25.9% to 4.3%. Embedding similarity and experienced-researcher judgment provide correlated but weaker screens.

AI.tldr: The paper clarifies when and how different kinds of LLM-based synthetic respondents are useful in marketing research, proposes a framework for evaluating their accuracy, and introduces a practical diagnostic to decide which survey questions can be reliably imputed with digital twins.
AI.motivation: Debate about synthetic data in marketing research is stuck between extreme positions: that LLM-based synthetic respondents can fully replace human respondents or should never be used. Existing results on the accuracy of digital twins are highly inconsistent, with some studies reporting very high accuracy and others near-chance, creating confusion about their practical value. Researchers also lack tools for using twins to fix common data-collection problems, such as omitted survey questions, in a principled way. The paper aims to move the discussion from “whether” to use synthetic respondents to “when and for what decisions,” and to provide diagnostics that make twin-based augmentation safer and more interpretable.
AI.method: The authors conceptually distinguish three kinds of synthetic data—ungrounded LLM responses (no real respondent data), segment-level personas (cluster or segment summaries), and individual-level digital twins (LLM personas tied to specific respondents)—and link each to appropriate decision contexts. They construct a taxonomy of four families of accuracy metrics for twins, showing how different metrics can yield very different conclusions about performance. Methodologically, they define the “forgotten question” setting where a survey item is missing from the fielded study and must be imputed using digital twins. For this setting, they propose an ex-ante answerability diagnostic: train a random forest to predict twin answers to a target question from the variables used to build the twins, and use the resulting R^2 as a screen for whether that question is answerable by the twin model. They empirically apply this on 108 attitude questions from a large, nationally representative survey, comparing the diagnostic to alternatives such as embedding similarity and expert judgment.
AI.result: The taxonomy clarifies that wide variation in reported digital-twin accuracy across studies largely reflects differences in what is being evaluated (e.g., aggregate vs. individual-level, directional vs. exact match), not necessarily differences in modeling quality. In empirical tests using 108 attitude items and N = 3,063 respondents, aggregate metrics look strong even when LLMs are given very limited respondent information, but such metrics can hide almost nonexistent individual-level differentiation. In the forgotten-question setting, the proposed ex-ante answerability diagnostic (R^2 from a random forest predicting twin outputs) is effective: restricting to questions with R^2 > 0.7 increases mean twin–human individual-level correlation by about 15% and reduces the share of poorly answered questions from 25.9% to 4.3%. Alternative screening approaches based on embedding similarity and experienced-researcher judgment are positively correlated with this diagnostic but less effective at filtering out poorly answered items.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based synthetic respondents are not universally good or bad; their usefulness depends on how they are constructed, what decisions they inform, and which accuracy metrics are used. Ungrounded responses, segment personas, and individual-level digital twins support different kinds of marketing decisions and should not be treated as interchangeable. Reported performance of digital twins must be interpreted in light of the specific accuracy family being measured, with aggregate metrics providing an overly optimistic view of respondent-level fidelity. In practical applications such as recovering omitted survey questions, digital twins can be valuable if paired with an ex-ante answerability diagnostic like the proposed random-forest R^2 screen, which substantially improves reliability relative to naive use of twins or weaker heuristics. The paper thus reframes the debate toward context-dependent use and offers concrete tools for safer deployment of synthetic respondents in marketing research.

title: Document Topic Alignment Metrics for Evaluating Topic Models of Short-Text Public Health Communications on Social Media
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 60th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS 2027)
summary: Topic models are widely used to analyze public health-related social media short texts, yet their evaluation remains dominated by metrics that focus entirely on generated topics alone. There is a lack of metrics that quantitatively assess whether assigned topics meaningfully represent the corresponding short-text posts. We propose Document-Topic Alignment metrics (DoTA), an assignment-aware evaluation framework comprising metrics that measure semantic alignment between documents (posts) and their assigned topics. We also introduce margin-based and discriminative variants that capture topic assignment confidence and distinguishability. We evaluate DoTA across five topic models on three public health-related social media datasets from X and compare DoTA metrics with conventional topic-based metrics. Results show that DoTA provides complementary evaluation cues and aligns meaningfully with human evaluations. These findings establish the need for assignment-aware evaluation and demonstrate that the addition of DoTA enables a more comprehensive and practically meaningful evaluation for assessing short-text topic modeling performance.

AI.tldr: They introduce new metrics (DoTA) to evaluate how well topic models’ assigned topics actually match each short social media post, showing these metrics complement existing topic-level evaluations and align with human judgments.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation of topic models on short social media texts mostly uses topic-level metrics (e.g., topic coherence), which ignore whether the topic assigned to each individual post truly reflects that post’s content. For public-health applications where per-post interpretation matters (e.g., understanding specific concerns or misinformation), it is important to know if document–topic assignments are semantically meaningful. There is thus a need for assignment-aware, quantitative metrics that evaluate the quality of document–topic alignment, not just the quality of topics in isolation.
AI.method: The authors propose Document-Topic Alignment (DoTA), a framework of assignment-aware metrics that compute semantic similarity between a document (short social media post) and its assigned topic representation. They further design margin-based variants that consider how much more aligned a document is with its assigned topic than with other topics, and discriminative variants that quantify how well the metrics distinguish between correct and incorrect topic assignments. They apply DoTA to outputs of five different topic models on three public health-related Twitter/X datasets and compare DoTA’s behavior with conventional topic-based evaluation metrics.
AI.result: Across the different models and datasets, DoTA metrics capture aspects of performance that are not reflected by traditional topic-based metrics. DoTA scores correlate well with human judgments about how appropriate topic assignments are for specific posts. The margin-based and discriminative extensions help quantify assignment confidence and distinguishability between topics in practice.
AI.conclusion: Assignment-aware evaluation via DoTA is both feasible and informative for short-text topic modeling. Incorporating DoTA alongside conventional topic-level metrics yields a more complete and practically useful assessment of topic models, especially in public health social media analysis where accurate document–topic alignment is critical.

title: Convergent Emergence of In-Context Learning Across Modalities
summary:
Few-shot in-context learning (ICL), the capacity of a model to infer abstract patterns from input-output examples provided in its prompt and apply them to new inputs, has been extensively studied in large language models trained for next-token prediction on human text. Recently, few-shot ICL has been demonstrated in autoregressive genomic models as well. This raises a question: does ICL emerge broadly across domains, and if so, what common structure is shared?
  To address both, we develop a controlled cross-modality framework that instantiates the same task suite in a variety of modalities to test what we call the Convergent Emergence Hypothesis: the idea that few-shot ICL, when it emerges, shares a common cross-modality difficulty profile - i.e., tasks that benefit from ICL in one modality tend to benefit in others. We show that paired-mapping ICL emerges across six modalities (language, genome, integer sequences, time series, images, and proteins), surpasses controlled baselines, and has correlated per-task effects across five of them. Together, these results provide support for the Convergent Emergence Hypothesis in some modalities, but not all.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether few-shot in-context learning (ICL) arises similarly across very different data types and tasks, and finds that a shared difficulty pattern often, but not always, appears across modalities.
AI.motivation: Few-shot in-context learning has been observed in large language models and, more recently, in genomic models, but it is unclear whether this phenomenon is specific to certain domains or reflects a general property of sequence models. The authors want to understand whether ICL emerges in a common way across very different modalities and what structural similarities underlie this behavior.
AI.method: The authors design a controlled, cross-modality framework where the same underlying task suite is instantiated in multiple data modalities. They focus on paired-mapping ICL tasks, in which models see several example input-output pairs in-context and must generalize to a new input. They then train or evaluate autoregressive models across six modalities—language, genome, integer sequences, time series, images, and proteins—and compare ICL performance to controlled baselines, measuring and correlating per-task ICL effects across modalities.
AI.result: Paired-mapping ICL emerges robustly in all six tested modalities and outperforms the controlled baselines. Moreover, the per-task gains from ICL are correlated across five of the six modalities, indicating that tasks which are ICL-friendly in one modality tend to be ICL-friendly in others, though this convergence is not universal.
AI.conclusion: The findings support a Convergent Emergence Hypothesis for few-shot ICL: when ICL arises in autoregressive models, it often exhibits a shared difficulty profile across diverse modalities. However, the convergence is incomplete—some modalities deviate—suggesting that while there is a common structural basis for ICL across domains, modality-specific factors also play an important role.

title: DenMark: Robust Semantic Watermarking for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Semantic text watermarks encode signals in meaning rather than surface token choices, offering robustness to paraphrasing and other semantic-preserving edits. Existing semantic watermarking methods are primarily designed for autoregressive language models (ARLMs), where completed candidate units can be generated and scored before generation proceeds. This paradigm does not naturally extend to diffusion language models (DLMs), where semantic units remain incomplete during intermediate denoising steps and tokens may be updated in flexible orders. We propose DenMark, a semantic watermarking framework that injects key-dependent signals directly into the DLM denoising process. DenMark partitions the output into fixed token regions and uses temporary rollouts as semantic lookahead: conditional completions estimate the eventual semantics of an incomplete region, enabling DenMark to select local updates with higher estimated semantic watermark scores. Repeating this procedure across denoising steps progressively accumulates watermark evidence in the final output. For detection, DenMark uses calibrated scanning over candidate unit sizes to remain robust to boundary shifts introduced by semantic attacks. Across four DLMs, three datasets, and four semantic attacks, DenMark achieves the best results across all reported detection metrics in all 48 backbone-dataset-attack combinations. These results demonstrate that DenMark provides an effective mechanism for robust semantic watermarking in DLMs.

AI.tldr: DenMark is a semantic watermarking framework tailored for diffusion language models (DLMs), embedding and detecting robust meaning-level watermarks during the denoising process.
AI.motivation: Existing semantic watermarking methods work well for autoregressive language models, which generate text sequentially and can score completed candidate units before continuing. However, these methods do not naturally apply to diffusion language models, where text is refined through denoising steps, semantic units are incomplete for most of the process, and tokens can be updated in flexible, non-sequential orders. There is a need for a watermarking approach that fits the generative dynamics of DLMs while remaining robust to paraphrasing and other semantic-preserving attacks.
AI.method: The authors introduce DenMark, which injects key-dependent semantic watermark signals directly into the DLM denoising procedure. The method partitions the output sequence into fixed token regions. During denoising, it uses temporary rollouts as a semantic lookahead: for each incomplete region, the model generates conditional completions to estimate the final semantics. Based on these estimates, DenMark chooses local token updates that increase an estimated semantic watermark score. This process is repeated across denoising steps so that watermark 'evidence' accumulates progressively. For detection, DenMark performs calibrated scanning over different candidate unit sizes, allowing it to handle boundary shifts caused by semantic-preserving attacks such as paraphrasing or local edits.
AI.result: Evaluated on four different diffusion language models, three datasets, and four types of semantic attacks, DenMark consistently outperforms prior methods. It achieves the best performance across all reported detection metrics in all 48 combinations of model, dataset, and attack configuration, indicating strong robustness and reliability of watermark detection under a wide range of conditions.
AI.conclusion: DenMark effectively adapts semantic watermarking to diffusion language models by integrating watermarking decisions into the denoising process and using semantic lookahead via temporary rollouts. Its strong empirical performance across multiple models, datasets, and attack scenarios shows that it provides a robust and practical solution for embedding and detecting semantic watermarks in DLM-generated text.

title: Schizophrenia Detection from EEG Signals: A Transformer Framework with Spectrogram Representation
summary: Schizophrenia is a serious psychiatric disorder that affects millions of people worldwide, and its diagnosis remains primarily dependent on clinical assessment. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive approach to investigate brain activity and has shown potential to support automated Schizophrenia detection. However, existing EEG-based classification studies often suffer from limitations including small datasets, inconsistent preprocessing strategies, and evaluation protocols that may not adequately prevent subject-related data leakage. In this study, we propose an EEG-based Schizophrenia classification framework that transforms preprocessed EEG recordings into time-frequency representations using the Short-Time Fourier Transform. The generated spectrogram images are classified using both conventional Machine Learning algorithms, including Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, and XGBoost, and Deep Learning models, including convolutional architectures and CNN-Transformer hybrids. To ensure reliable evaluation, all data partitions are performed at the subject level. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves competitive classification performance, with the CNN-Transformer (CT-SZ) model achieving an AUC-ROC of 88.41% and the CNN + Squeeze and Excitation + Transformer (CST-SZ) achieving an AUC-ROC of 92.88% on the independent test set.

AI.tldr: The paper builds an EEG-based framework that converts signals to spectrograms and classifies schizophrenia using both traditional ML and CNN-Transformer models, achieving up to ~93% AUC with strict subject-level evaluation.
AI.motivation: Schizophrenia diagnosis currently relies on clinical assessment, which can be subjective and time-consuming. EEG is a non-invasive, relatively inexpensive tool that could support automated diagnosis, but prior works often use small datasets, inconsistent preprocessing, and flawed evaluation that allows subject data leakage, inflating performance. The authors aim to create a more reliable and scalable EEG-based schizophrenia classifier with rigorous evaluation.
AI.method: Preprocessed EEG recordings are converted to time–frequency representations via Short-Time Fourier Transform to form spectrogram images. These images are then fed into several classifiers: classic ML models (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost) and deep learning models, including CNNs and CNN-Transformer hybrid architectures (CT-SZ and CST-SZ). Data splitting is done strictly at the subject level to avoid leakage between train, validation, and test sets.
AI.result: The proposed framework yields competitive performance in distinguishing schizophrenia from controls. Among all methods, CNN-Transformer models perform best: the CT-SZ model reaches an AUC-ROC of 88.41%, while the enhanced CST-SZ (CNN + Squeeze-and-Excitation + Transformer) model achieves 92.88% AUC-ROC on an independent test set, indicating strong generalization under subject-level evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Transforming EEG signals into STFT-based spectrograms and classifying them with CNN-Transformer hybrids is an effective strategy for schizophrenia detection. Rigorous subject-level data partitioning produces credible performance estimates, and the CST-SZ model in particular shows promising potential as a tool to support clinical diagnosis, though further validation and real-world testing will be needed.

title: Editorial routing shapes how computational results are qualified in AI-assisted scientific writing
summary: Large language models increasingly analyze computational results and draft manuscripts, making reliable communication as important as correct analysis. Using fixed computational evidence, we tested whether assigning comparisons across modeling choices elsewhere in a research workflow changes manuscript reporting. In constrained sentence-writing tasks, Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5 often omitted numerical qualifications when detailed comparisons were assigned to a group repository, but retained them more often when the same comparison was assigned to Supporting Information or its own working notes; Claude Opus 5 was less sensitive. These effects did not follow a simple accessibility ordering. A targeted placement rule largely restored sentence-level qualification, whereas a generic accuracy reminder did not. Longer contributions retained numerical qualifications, although some summaries across computational settings were still redirected to the repository. Thus, documenting context within an AI workflow does not ensure its communication where readers encounter the result.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the placement of model-comparison details in an AI-assisted research workflow affects whether large language models accurately communicate numerical qualifications in manuscripts.
AI.motivation: As large language models are increasingly used to interpret computational results and draft scientific text, there is a risk that important numerical details and caveats may be lost or underreported depending on how information is organized in the workflow. Understanding how documentation placement influences what LLMs report is critical for trustworthy scientific communication.
AI.method: Using fixed underlying computational evidence, the authors designed constrained sentence‑writing tasks for large language models (primarily Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5). They systematically varied where detailed numerical comparisons across modeling choices were stored in the workflow: in a group repository, in Supporting Information, or in the model’s own working notes. They then measured how often generated sentences preserved numerical qualifications. They also tested interventions: a targeted rule about where to place certain comparisons versus a general reminder to be accurate.
AI.result: Claude Sonnet 5 frequently dropped numerical qualifications when the detailed comparisons were only in a group repository but preserved them more when the same information was placed in Supporting Information or its own notes. Claude Opus 5 showed smaller sensitivity to placement. The pattern of omissions did not simply track how “accessible” the information appeared to be. A specific rule about how to place comparison information substantially improved the retention of qualifications, whereas a vague accuracy reminder had little effect. Longer generated passages tended to keep numerical details, though some cross-setting summaries were still shunted to the repository instead of being stated explicitly.
AI.conclusion: The way context and numerical comparisons are documented within an AI-assisted research workflow strongly affects whether LLMs actually communicate those details in the parts of the manuscript readers see. Merely recording information in shared or background locations does not guarantee that models will surface it where needed. Carefully designed placement rules and workflow structures are necessary to preserve important numerical qualifications in AI-generated scientific writing.

title: VeriDx: Earning the Right to Diagnose with Disease-Centric Verification
comment: accepted by EMNLP 2026, 17 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
summary: A correct diagnosis can still be reached for the wrong reasons. In clinical reasoning, every disease hypothesis creates obligations: key evidence must be checked, alternatives must be ruled out, contradictions must be resolved, useful tests must be considered, and closure must be justified. Current evaluations of medical LLMs mostly focus on final answers, local steps, or isolated facts, and therefore miss these hypothesis-induced commitments. We introduce \textbf{VeriDx}, a disease-centric verification framework that links free-form diagnostic reasoning to structured disease profiles. VeriDx tracks whether each hypothesis is satisfied, unresolved, or violated its clinical obligations, exposing failures such as missing critical tests, unresolved differentials, ignored contradictions, unsupported claims, and premature closure. We instantiate VeriDx for complex respiratory diagnosis using guideline-derived disease profiles and expert-annotated longitudinal cases. Our results show that many diagnostic errors are not isolated mistakes, but broken commitments made earlier in the reasoning process.

AI.tldr: VeriDx is a framework to verify whether diagnostic reasoning about diseases fulfills key clinical obligations, not just whether the final diagnosis is correct.
AI.motivation: Existing medical LLM evaluations mostly check final diagnoses or isolated reasoning steps, missing whether a model properly follows through on the obligations that each disease hypothesis entails (e.g., ruling out alternatives, ordering key tests, resolving contradictions). There is a need for a more faithful assessment of clinical reasoning quality that can reveal when correct answers are obtained for the wrong reasons.
AI.method: The authors propose VeriDx, a disease-centric verification framework that maps free-form diagnostic reasoning onto structured disease profiles derived from clinical guidelines. For each disease hypothesis in a case, VeriDx checks whether required clinical obligations are satisfied, unresolved, or violated, including checking key evidence, ruling out alternatives, addressing contradictions, considering necessary tests, and providing justified closure. They instantiate and evaluate this framework on complex respiratory diagnosis using expert-annotated longitudinal patient cases and guideline-derived profiles.
AI.result: Using VeriDx on complex respiratory cases shows that many diagnostic errors stem from earlier failures to satisfy hypothesis-specific obligations. These include missing critical tests, failing to rule out differential diagnoses, ignoring contradictory evidence, making unsupported claims, and stopping the reasoning process prematurely. Errors appear as patterns of broken commitments rather than isolated local mistakes.
AI.conclusion: VeriDx reveals that diagnostic quality cannot be reliably judged from final answers alone; instead, one must track whether each disease hypothesis fulfills its associated clinical obligations. The framework exposes systematic reasoning failures in LLM-based diagnosis and suggests that improving and evaluating medical AI should focus on maintaining and honoring these hypothesis-driven commitments throughout the reasoning process.

title: E2A-Bench: Benchmarking Evidence-to-Action Reliability in Financial Chart Reasoning
summary: Can financial vision-language models (VLMs) turn chart evidence into reliable action recommendations? Existing hallucination evaluations are mostly claim-centric; they assess whether generated statements are supported, but not whether evidence remains traceable through rationale, confidence, and final action. We introduce E2A-Bench, a 969-query benchmark for financial chart reasoning, constructed from 323 HS300 constituents under three input modalities with deterministic OHLCV-derived evidence anchors. E2A-Bench evaluates grounding, reasoning-action consistency, evidence-confidence calibration, and directional coverage through UCR, RCI, ECI, and NDR, where NDR measures coverage-aware evidence-to-action reliability rather than realized trading performance. Evaluating 20 VLMs reveals three failures hidden by scalar hallucination scores: the lowest-UCR model ranks near the bottom by NDR due to only 6.4% directional coverage; oracle-aided verification reduces unsupported claims but can collapse coverage; and financial fine-tuning amplifies the BUY:SELL ratio by factors of 4.21 to 4.68 across strict base-fine-tuned pairs. These results show that financial VLM evaluation should trace the full evidence-to-action chain rather than rely on a single hallucination score. Code and data: https://github.com/wanng-ide/E2A-Bench

AI.tldr: The paper introduces E2A-Bench, a benchmark to test whether financial vision-language models can turn chart evidence into reliable trading-like action recommendations, emphasizing the entire chain from evidence to action rather than only hallucination rates.
AI.motivation: Most evaluations of hallucinations in language and vision-language models focus on whether generated statements are supported by evidence (claim-centric), but they do not check if the underlying evidence is consistently and traceably propagated through the model’s rationale, confidence, and final action decisions, especially in high-stakes financial settings. The authors aim to fill this gap for financial chart reasoning.
AI.method: They construct E2A-Bench, a benchmark of 969 financial chart reasoning queries built from 323 HS300 index constituent stocks, with three input modalities and deterministic OHLCV-derived (open-high-low-close-volume) evidence anchors. The benchmark defines four metrics: UCR for grounding, RCI for reasoning–action consistency, ECI for evidence–confidence calibration, and NDR for coverage-aware evidence-to-action reliability. NDR is designed to measure how reliably recommended actions align with anchored evidence under varying coverage, not to simulate actual trading performance. They then evaluate 20 different vision-language models on these metrics.
AI.result: When evaluating 20 VLMs, they uncover three important failure patterns that are not visible from a single scalar hallucination score: (1) a model with the lowest unsupported-claim rate (best hallucination score) still ranks near the bottom in NDR because it only gives directional recommendations in 6.4% of cases (very low coverage); (2) giving the model oracle-like verification ability reduces unsupported claims but can severely shrink coverage; and (3) financial-domain fine-tuning systematically skews models toward much more aggressive BUY recommendations, inflating the BUY:SELL ratio by factors between 4.21 and 4.68 compared to their unfine-tuned base versions.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-to-action reliability in financial VLMs cannot be adequately evaluated with a single hallucination score. Proper assessment must track how evidence flows through rationale, confidence estimates, and action recommendations, considering coverage and directional balance. The E2A-Bench benchmark and its metrics provide a more nuanced and realistic framework for evaluating financial chart reasoning models in this end-to-end manner.

title: Semantic Knowledge Technologies: what the Semantic Web lost sight of, and what it never had
summary: The Semantic Web set out to give information a machine-interpretable form so that software could integrate and reason over it. Its standards became scientific knowledge infrastructure, but the machine competence it promised did not follow, and the systems now answering questions over scientific knowledge are language models holding no inspectable account of what they know. This paper argues the original goal was right and the technical programme incomplete, states what is missing, and names the extended programme Semantic Knowledge Technologies: the same technical core carried out of its web-publishing origin and applied to knowledge wherever held. The diagnosis is that the standards formalised truth while omitting three things: the conditions under which a claim holds, the operations its terms permit, and any account of what a base covers. Without conditions, contradiction and applicability cannot be judged; without operational grounding, holding a statement confers no ability; without declared coverage, a system cannot recognise the boundary of its own content, which under the open-world assumption cannot be inferred. The paper fixes the word understanding to five measurable tests (check, connect, derive, act, delimit) and sets out a seven-layer architecture in which the first three layers are enabling and the rest the cognitive capabilities they make possible. It then defines three terms the programme implies: Large Knowledge Model, a model whose unit of output is a reference to an addressable claim, not a token; SLKM, the knowledge base an agent builds for itself from declared sources; and Semantic Artificial General Intelligence, stated as a falsifiable position about necessary conditions, not a system. A graded ladder replaces the untestable word general. It is offered as a research agenda, with its weakest points and refutation condition named.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the original vision of the Semantic Web—machine-understandable scientific knowledge—was correct but incomplete, and proposes an expanded research agenda, Semantic Knowledge Technologies, to enable measurable machine understanding beyond current language models.
AI.motivation: Although Semantic Web standards became core scientific knowledge infrastructure, they failed to deliver genuine machine competence or understanding. Meanwhile, large language models can answer questions but lack explicit, inspectable knowledge representations and guarantees. There is a need to revisit and complete the original Semantic Web programme to achieve robust, testable machine understanding of knowledge.
AI.method: The paper conceptually analyzes the limitations of existing Semantic Web standards, especially their focus on truth without modeling conditions of validity, operational grounding of terms, or coverage boundaries. It proposes a formal notion of ‘understanding’ defined by five tests (check, connect, derive, act, delimit) and introduces a seven-layer architecture separating enabling layers from cognitive capabilities. It then introduces and defines three new conceptual constructs: Large Knowledge Model, SLKM (self-built knowledge base from declared sources), and Semantic Artificial General Intelligence (SAGI), formulated as falsifiable necessary conditions rather than as a concrete system.
AI.result: The paper identifies three critical omissions in Semantic Web standards and derives five measurable tests for machine understanding, along with a seven-layer reference architecture connecting enabling technologies to cognitive capabilities. It also defines Large Knowledge Models, SLKMs, and SAGI as key constructs in a new research programme and provides a graded ladder in place of the vague notion of general intelligence. Weak points and explicit refutation conditions for the programme are articulated.
AI.conclusion: The Semantic Web’s failure to deliver machine understanding stems not from a flawed goal but from an incomplete technical programme that ignored conditions of validity, operational grounding, and coverage of knowledge. By extending the programme into Semantic Knowledge Technologies, defining measurable tests of understanding, and introducing structured concepts such as Large Knowledge Models, SLKMs, and SAGI, the paper offers a falsifiable, graded research agenda for building truly semantic machine intelligence and invites the community to test and refine this framework.

title: SpectralShift: Effective Context Window Extension of Gated DeltaNet via Spectral Reparameterization
summary: Recently, linear attention layers have been increasingly adopted to replace softmax attention at scale for long-context modeling. However, existing context extension approaches typically apply continued pretraining directly without modifying these layers, overlooking the spectral properties of linear attention state dynamics. In this work, we study long-context extension of Gated DeltaNet (GDN) from a spectral perspective of transition matrix and identify two essential factors governing long-range information retrieval: (1) a sufficiently broad slow spectral band aligned with the target dependency length, and (2) the preservation of fast-decaying modes for state clearing and context switching. Based on this observation, we propose SpectralShift, a spectral reparameterization approach for long-context continual pretraining of GDNs. Specifically, SpectralShift reparameterizes the alpha projections initialization to reshape the decay spectrum by enhancing slow propagation capacity, and further introduces a learning-rate scaling for alpha projections to facilitate long-context training. Experiments show that SpectralShift consistently improves long-context capabilities over training, providing an effective and efficient solution for extending context windows of linear attention models. The code has been open-sourced at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/GDN-SpectralShift.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes and improves long-context capabilities of Gated DeltaNet (a linear attention model) via spectral analysis of its state transition matrix, and proposes SpectralShift, a spectral reparameterization and learning-rate scaling scheme that enables more effective long-context continual pretraining.
AI.motivation: Linear attention layers are increasingly used for long-context modeling, but standard context extension methods simply continue pretraining without accounting for the spectral (eigenvalue) properties of the state dynamics, which determine how information propagates and decays over long sequences. This can limit long-range information retrieval and context switching in models like Gated DeltaNet when extending the context window.
AI.method: The authors study Gated DeltaNet from a spectral perspective by analyzing the transition matrix governing its state dynamics. They identify key spectral properties needed for effective long-range modeling: a sufficiently broad band of slowly decaying eigenmodes tailored to the desired dependency length, and fast-decaying modes for quick state clearing. Based on this, they propose SpectralShift, which (1) reparameterizes the initialization of alpha projection matrices to reshape the decay spectrum and strengthen slow information propagation, and (2) applies a dedicated learning-rate scaling to the alpha projections during continual pretraining to better adapt the spectrum for longer contexts.
AI.result: Across experiments on long-context benchmarks, applying SpectralShift during continual pretraining of GDNs leads to consistent improvements in long-context performance over training compared to baseline linear-attention models that do not use this spectral reparameterization. The approach is effective and efficient for extending context windows without architectural overhauls.
AI.conclusion: Spectral properties of linear attention state dynamics are crucial for successful long-context extension. By explicitly controlling the decay spectrum of Gated DeltaNet through reparameterized alpha projections and tailored learning-rate scaling, SpectralShift enhances long-range information retrieval and context switching, offering a practical way to extend context windows of linear attention models. The implementation is publicly available for further use and research.

title: MOSCOPT: Mixture-of-Skills Collective Optimization for LLM Agents
summary: Natural language prompts and skills serve as the strategic backbone of LLM-based agents. Recent advances in prompt and skill optimization have achieved notable gains, yet all existing methods optimize a \emph{single} text template---missing the synergy among multiple complementary strategies. We propose MOSCOPT, a text-native, parameter-free algorithm that jointly optimizes a pool of $N$ skills and a gating skill $G$ that dynamically selects $K$ skills per step. To effectively optimize the skills, we build the EditAdam with internally maintained dual states. Through the three-phase interleaved updates with EditAdam, the system monotonically improves without gradient or parameter tuning. Extensive experiments and detailed ablations across 5 benchmarks and 3 target LLMs demonstrate that MOSCOPT consistently outperforms all baselines, and confirm that both the mixture-of-skills architecture with selective activation and the collective evolution with three-phase interleaving are essential to its superior performance. Code is released https://github.com/zhangzhenyu13/SummerClaw/tree/master/summerclaw/agent_trainer/algorithms/moscopt.

AI.tldr: MOSCOPT is a parameter-free algorithm that jointly optimizes multiple text-based skills and a gating skill for LLM agents, yielding consistent performance gains over existing single-prompt optimization methods.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt and skill optimization methods focus on improving a single text template, neglecting the potential synergy and complementary strengths of multiple skills. There is a need for a method that can jointly optimize a set of skills and a mechanism that selects which skills to use at each step, without requiring gradient access or parameter tuning, to better leverage LLM agents in complex tasks.
AI.method: MOSCOPT introduces a mixture-of-skills architecture with a pool of N textual skills and a gating skill G that chooses K skills at each step. It employs EditAdam, a text-native optimization procedure with dual internal states, to iteratively edit and refine these skills. The optimization proceeds via three-phase interleaved updates over the skills and the gating skill, allowing the system to improve monotonically without gradients or model parameter updates.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks and three different target LLMs, MOSCOPT achieves consistent performance improvements over all baseline methods. Ablation studies show that both the selective mixture-of-skills design and the three-phase interleaved collective evolution are critical for achieving the observed gains.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing multiple complementary skills together with a gating skill in a text-native, parameter-free way leads to superior LLM agent performance compared with single-prompt optimization. The mixture-of-skills architecture and the EditAdam-based three-phase interleaving form an effective strategy for scalable, gradient-free skill optimization in LLM-based agents.

title: Formal Properties of Language as Constraints on Neural Dynamics
summary: What must a neural system be capable of to implement language? Current research annotates stimuli with linguistic variables and tests which electrodes, voxels, or language-model layers predict neural activity. Yet predictive success leaves mechanisms under-constrained. Here, we show that algebraic properties of language specify invariants that mechanisms must preserve: non-associative hierarchical grouping, commutativity, recursive closure, access to substructures, and structured workspace transitions. We term this the Neural Admissibility Program (NAP). Syntactic structure building is analyzed algebraically, with candidate mechanisms offered for each requirement: content-addressable workspace memory, graph-structured transient dynamics scheduling structure-building operations (e.g. stable heteroclinic channels), and a phase-coupled sealing operation recording grouping. Simulations show that a corrected Marcolli-Berwick entropy-optimized binding gate preserves grouping only within a narrow commitment band. As an alternative, we propose a novel neural binding operation we term 'Meld': two constituent populations converge through shared synapses, integrate sublinearly, and saturate. Meld is, to our knowledge, the closest neurally plausible composition law to syntactic Merge. It preserves every NAP invariant, uses known cortical operations, and recovers hierarchical structure at every tested depth and temperature. It predicts that effective population dimensionality separates alternative bracketings and that the composite depends on constituent disagreement. Importantly, the laws decoding bracketing most accurately are a priori inadmissible, showing that decoding accuracy alone cannot adjudicate between mechanisms. By specifying how neural dynamics can remain faithful to linguistic structure, the NAP changes the criterion by which neural implementations of cognition are evaluated.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a formal program (Neural Admissibility Program, NAP) specifying algebraic constraints that any neural mechanism for syntax must satisfy and introduces a neurally plausible binding operation, Meld, that meets these constraints better than prior proposals.
AI.motivation: Current neuroscience of language focuses on whether neural signals or model layers predict brain activity, but this leaves the underlying neural mechanisms under-specified. There is a need for principled constraints—derived from the algebraic properties of language—on what any candidate neural implementation of syntax must do, so that decoding accuracy is not the only evaluation criterion.
AI.method: The authors characterize syntactic structure-building using algebraic properties and derive a set of invariants (non-associative hierarchical grouping, commutativity, recursive closure, substructure access, and structured workspace transitions) that neural mechanisms must preserve. They analyze candidate neural mechanisms—including content-addressable workspaces, graph-structured transient dynamics like stable heteroclinic channels, and binding gates such as the Marcolli-Berwick entropy-optimized gate—via simulations. They then design and simulate a new neural binding operation, Meld, evaluating whether it preserves all specified invariants and can recover hierarchical structure across depths and noise (temperature) levels.
AI.result: They find that the corrected Marcolli-Berwick entropy-optimized binding gate preserves syntactic grouping only in a narrow range of parameter settings (a narrow "commitment band"), making it fragile as a general mechanism. In contrast, the proposed Meld operation—where two neural populations converge via shared synapses, integrate sublinearly, and saturate—preserves all the NAP invariants, robustly recovers hierarchical structure across tested depths and temperatures, and yields testable predictions: (i) effective dimensionality of population activity separates different syntactic bracketings; and (ii) the resulting composite representation depends on disagreement between constituents. They also show that the best-performing decoding laws for bracketing are, by NAP’s criteria, inadmissible, demonstrating that decoding accuracy can favor mechanisms that are structurally wrong.
AI.conclusion: The Neural Admissibility Program (NAP) provides a principled, algebraic framework for constraining which neural mechanisms can plausibly implement syntactic structure, shifting the evaluation standard from mere decoding accuracy to preservation of linguistic invariants. Within this framework, their new Meld operation emerges as a neurally plausible binding mechanism closely analogous to syntactic Merge, offering specific dynamical and representational predictions about cortical population codes for hierarchical syntax.

title: Dynamic Learning Solutions: A System for Personalized Educational Video Generation
summary: We present an automated pipeline that converts NCERT textbooks into interactive video explanations that respond directly to user queries. A user uploads a PDF and asks a question; the system then generates a video-based explanation as output, handling both text and visual elements from the PDF for multi-modal retrieval and response generation. The pipeline combines a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) model with generative multimedia components. The RAG stage is optimized for the structure of NCERT textbooks and performs best on content from those books. Given a user query, the RAG model retrieves relevant content from the PDF and generates a multi-scene script containing narrative explanations and structured visual prompts aligned with the textbook's explanatory style. These prompts are passed to a Stable Diffusion module, implemented layer by layer for interpretability and control, which generates contextually relevant images. The images are then processed by DynamiCrafter to produce animated sequences. Finally, a Google Text-to-Speech module generates synchronized narration, aligning speech with the visual scenes through time-based control. The result is a coherent video explanation integrating animation, narration, and textbook-aligned visuals, transforming static educational material into an engaging learning experience. By combining multi-modal document retrieval, generative visual models, animation frameworks, and speech synthesis, this pipeline demonstrates a scalable approach to delivering interactive, personalized digital education content.

AI.tldr: Automated pipeline that converts NCERT PDFs into query-driven, interactive video explanations using RAG and generative multimedia models.
AI.motivation: Traditional NCERT textbooks are static and may not support interactive or personalized learning. There is a need to automatically transform textbook content into engaging, multi-modal explanations that can respond to specific learner queries at scale.
AI.method: The system takes a user-uploaded NCERT PDF and a natural language question. A RAG model, tuned to NCERT structure, retrieves relevant passages and generates a multi-scene script with narrative text and visual prompts. These prompts feed a layer-wise controllable Stable Diffusion pipeline to create images, which are animated with DynamiCrafter into sequences. Google Text-to-Speech then produces narration, which is temporally aligned with the animated scenes to form a coherent explanatory video.
AI.result: The pipeline produces coherent, question-specific video explanations that combine textbook-aligned narration, generated visuals, and animations, effectively turning static NCERT content into dynamic, interactive educational videos. It shows that combining RAG with generative image, animation, and TTS modules can provide scalable, automated video explanations.
AI.conclusion: A multi-stage, RAG-driven multimedia pipeline can automatically convert NCERT textbooks into interactive, personalized video explanations by integrating multimodal retrieval, script generation, controllable image synthesis, animation, and speech synthesis. This approach offers a scalable path to richer digital learning experiences from existing static educational materials.

title: Policy Loopholes in Agent Evaluation: When Policy Ambiguity Masquerades as Agent Error
summary: Agent benchmarks evaluate policy compliance but assume each policy determines a unique correct action. Natural-language policies can violate this assumption through silence, ambiguity, or contradiction, admitting multiple defensible readings that a single gold trajectory cannot capture. Auditing two $τ^2$-bench domains, we develop a taxonomy of such policy loopholes and show that affected tasks produce unreliable scores: they lower scores across different models in different ways and make every model less consistent across repeated trials. A cross-domain comparison reveals that exploitability requires both policy ambiguity and tool permissiveness: when policy complexity exceeds what tools can enforce, agents resolve gaps inconsistently and scores become unreliable. Policy specification quality sets the ceiling on evaluation quality. Benchmark developers should audit policies before collecting gold annotations.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that current agent benchmarks can be unreliable because natural-language policies often allow multiple reasonable behaviors, so a single “gold” answer is insufficient.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for AI agents assume each policy yields one uniquely correct behavior, which is then used to compute scores. However, real-world natural-language policies are frequently incomplete, ambiguous, or even contradictory, allowing multiple defensible interpretations. This mismatch can make evaluation scores misleading, but it has not been systematically analyzed.
AI.method: The authors audit two τ^2-bench domains, carefully examining their natural-language policies and associated tasks. They construct a taxonomy of policy loopholes—cases of silence, ambiguity, or contradiction—and measure how these loopholes affect evaluation outcomes. They then perform a cross-domain comparison to study how policy ambiguity interacts with the permissiveness of available tools to impact score reliability and model consistency across repeated runs.
AI.result: They find that tasks affected by policy loopholes yield unreliable benchmark scores: different models are penalized in different, inconsistent ways, and all models become less stable across repeated trials. The analysis shows that exploitability arises when ambiguous or underspecified policies are paired with tools that cannot fully enforce the intended rules, causing agents to “fill in the gaps” idiosyncratically.
AI.conclusion: The quality of policy specification fundamentally limits the quality of agent evaluation. If policies are ambiguous or under-specified relative to what the tools can check, benchmark scores become unreliable. Therefore, benchmark creators should rigorously audit and refine their natural-language policies for clarity and enforceability before generating gold trajectories or annotations.

title: Question's Gambit: The First Move Matters in Agentic Deep Search
summary: Deep research agents answer complex questions through iterative loops of searching, reading, and reasoning. Recent work on reasoning-intensive benchmarks such as BrowseComp-Plus shows that well-configured lexical retrieval can surface high-quality evidence, yet agents may still fail to connect documents carrying evidence to the gold documents. We identify a deep research agent's first retrieval move as an important design decision for this setting. We introduce Question's Gambit, a first-move retrieval module that decomposes the question into a set of clues, reformulates them into complementary searches, consolidates the retrieved results, and reranks the candidate pool before the agent begins its iterative search-and-reasoning process. This produces an opening context designed to support both clue aggregation and final-answer verification. We further evaluate on MultiHop-RAG to test whether these benefits transfer beyond BrowseComp-Plus to a more conventional multi-hop question structure. Experiments on BrowseComp-Plus show that Question's Gambit improves retrieval recall and downstream agent accuracy over strong baselines, improving answer accuracy from 83.1% to 90.5% with gpt-5.5 over Pi-Serini, the strongest reported agentic baseline. Our results confirm that effective agentic deep research depends not only on the tools available inside the loop, but also on the quality of the first move. We published our implementation publicly at https://github.com/radinhamidi/Question-s-Gambit.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Question's Gambit, a first-move retrieval module that improves deep research agents by creating a stronger initial evidence context, significantly boosting accuracy on complex question benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Deep research agents often fail not because of poor tools during iterative reasoning, but because their initial retrieval step does not surface or organize the right evidence. Even with strong lexical retrieval, agents struggle to connect evidence-bearing documents to gold answers. The authors aim to improve this crucial first retrieval move to enhance downstream reasoning and accuracy.
AI.method: The authors design Question's Gambit, a first-move retrieval module that: (1) decomposes the input question into multiple clues, (2) reformulates these clues into complementary search queries, (3) retrieves and consolidates results from those queries, and (4) reranks the combined candidate pool before the agent begins its standard search–read–reason loop. This curated opening context is optimized for aggregating clues and verifying final answers. They evaluate the method on BrowseComp-Plus and MultiHop-RAG, comparing against strong agentic baselines like Pi-Serini using models such as gpt-5.5.
AI.result: On the BrowseComp-Plus benchmark, Question's Gambit improves retrieval recall and downstream agent accuracy compared to strong baselines. In particular, it raises answer accuracy from 83.1% to 90.5% with gpt-5.5 over the prior best agentic baseline, Pi-Serini. It also shows benefits that transfer to MultiHop-RAG, indicating effectiveness beyond a single benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that the effectiveness of deep research agents depends critically on the design of their first retrieval move, not just their in-loop tools and reasoning strategies. By structuring a high-quality opening retrieval context via Question's Gambit, agents achieve significantly better performance on complex, multi-hop questions. The authors release their implementation publicly for further research and application.

title: NeuroActiSep: Detecting Factual Hallucinations from Feed-Forward Neurons in a Single Pass
summary: Hallucination in large language models reduces their reliability and slows adoption. Various white-box studies have used internal representations to detect patterns of truthfulness and factuality. A less-studied approach is to identify feed-forward neurons correlated with hallucination. We propose a method to rank feed-forward neurons at the final prompt token using a custom neuron selection dataset. We transfer the selected neuron identities to train hallucination classifiers on other factual question answering datasets. Our work provides empirical evidence that probes trained using the features from the selected neurons perform on par with probes trained on internal states. We also analyze the distribution of selected neurons and the effect of layer depth on detection performance.

AI.tldr: They identify and rank specific feed-forward neurons linked to hallucination in large language models and use them to build hallucination detectors that work as well as detectors using full internal states.
AI.motivation: Hallucinations in large language models undermine trust and slow their real-world adoption. While prior work often uses rich internal representations in a white-box fashion to detect hallucinations, there has been limited focus on which individual neurons are most associated with hallucinations. Finding such neurons could enable more efficient, interpretable, and potentially transferable hallucination detectors.
AI.method: They construct a custom neuron selection dataset to identify and rank feed-forward neurons at the final prompt token that correlate with hallucination behavior. Using this ranking, they select specific neurons and use their activations as features to train hallucination classifiers on separate factual QA datasets. They then compare these neuron-based probes to standard probes trained on full internal states and analyze how the selected neurons are distributed across layers, studying how layer depth influences detection performance.
AI.result: Probes that use only the activations of the selected feed-forward neurons achieve performance comparable to probes trained on the full internal model states for hallucination detection. The analysis also reveals systematic patterns in where these influential neurons are located in the network and how layer depth affects detection quality.
AI.conclusion: A relatively small subset of carefully selected feed-forward neurons at the final prompt token is sufficient to build effective hallucination detectors, performing on par with detectors using full internal states. This suggests that hallucination-relevant information is concentrated in specific neurons and that neuron-level analysis is a viable and efficient route for hallucination detection and interpretability in large language models.

title: Safety Signals to Verify NetOps Agents with Action-Level Granularity
summary: Agentic Network Operations (NetOps) are an emerging paradigm promising to enable workload-aware, self-adjustable, and reliable autonomous networks. While agents have proven their value in incident summarization and telemetry signal extraction, their effectiveness as autonomous control-loop engines heavily relies on their long-horizon reliability. One such setting is the datacenter fabric, where an agent must respond to alarms and operator intents while abstaining from high-risk actions that may cause or extend downtime. Abstention, however, presupposes that an action's impact is known pre-execution, which necessitates a per-action ground truth that NetOps agent benchmarks do not provide. We construct such a ground truth for the network repair task of NetArena. A symbolic replay of the emulated network, validated against the environment at every turn, yields the exact value of every action. From the action-level value, we derive two pre-execution targets, namely whether an action reduces the repair distance (progress) and whether it increases it (harm). We show across 10 agent models, that agent verifiers leveraging internal signals predict both harm and progress more reliably than a baseline using observable signals only. Perspectively, we aim to use these signals as safety feedback to an agent harness to abstain from risky actions and protect the target system.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a per-action ground truth for network repair in NetArena to evaluate and improve the safety and reliability of autonomous NetOps agents, focusing on predicting when actions help or harm before execution.
AI.motivation: Existing NetOps agents are good at summarizing incidents and extracting signals but lack robust, long-horizon reliability as autonomous controllers, especially in high-stakes datacenter environments where unsafe actions can cause downtime. Current benchmarks do not provide per-action ground truth needed to know an action’s impact pre-execution, which is essential for safe abstention and risk-aware control.
AI.method: The authors construct a per-action ground truth for the NetArena network repair task by symbolically replaying the emulated network and validating against the environment at each step, determining the exact value of each action. From these values they derive two pre-execution labels: whether an action reduces the repair distance (progress) or increases it (harm). They then compare agent verifiers that leverage agents’ internal signals to a baseline that uses only observable signals, testing 10 different agent models on their ability to predict progress and harm.
AI.result: Symbolic replay provides precise per-action value labels, enabling the definition of progress and harm targets. Across 10 agent models, verifiers that use internal agent signals more reliably predict both harmful and progress-making actions than verifiers based solely on observable external signals.
AI.conclusion: Per-action ground truth via symbolic replay allows the definition and measurement of pre-execution safety targets (progress and harm) for NetOps agents. Internal-signal-based verifiers outperform purely observable-signal baselines in predicting risky or helpful actions, suggesting these internal signals can serve as effective safety feedback. The authors plan to use such feedback within an agent harness to abstain from risky actions and better protect production network systems.

title: Theseus in the Graph: Towards Traceable Multi-Hop Graph Navigation
summary: Multi-Hop Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) tasks require models to assemble relational evidence along paths in a KG to answer natural-language questions. However, existing KGQA systems typically focus on predicting the final answer without explicitly modeling or validating the intermediate reasoning steps, obscuring whether the correct answers arise from faithful multi-hop reasoning. To address this limitation, we re-frame multi-hop KGQA as a question-conditioned graph navigation problem. We refer to this formulation as THESEUS - Traceable Hop-wise Evidence SEarch in a Unified Semantics. In this setting, an agent receives a KG, a question, and a topic entity, and traverses a sequence of relations towards the answer, making the reasoning path explicit. To systematically study this formulation, we provide three key contributions. (i) We augment the existing KINSHIP and MQuAKE resources into navigation-ready KGQA datasets with annotated evidence paths and paraphrased questions. (ii) We design evaluation protocols to measure path fidelity, robustness to linguistic variation, and performance across multi-hop and multi-answer questions. (iii) We adapt established path-based KG completion agents - MINERVA, MultiHopKG, and SQUIRE - to operate on full question embeddings rather than symbolic single-relation queries, enabling their trajectories to be guided by natural-language semantics. Together, these contributions advance KGQA research toward systems where traceability is fundamental: answers are accompanied by explicit reasoning paths whose agreement with reference evidence can be systematically evaluated.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes multi-hop knowledge graph QA as explicit question-guided graph navigation so that models produce both answers and traceable reasoning paths, and it benchmarks adapted agents on new navigation-ready datasets and protocols.
