AI.motivation: Existing multi-hop KGQA models usually predict only final answers and do not explicitly model or validate intermediate reasoning steps, making it unclear whether correct answers result from genuine multi-hop reasoning or shortcuts; the authors want a framework where reasoning paths are explicit, traceable, and evaluable against reference evidence while being robust to linguistic variation.
AI.method: They formulate multi-hop KGQA as a question-conditioned graph navigation task (THESEUS), where an agent receives a KG, a question, and a topic entity, and then traverses relations to reach an answer. They (i) convert KINSHIP and MQuAKE into navigation-ready datasets with annotated evidence paths and paraphrased questions, (ii) define evaluation protocols for path fidelity, robustness to paraphrasing, and multi-hop / multi-answer performance, and (iii) adapt existing path-based KG completion agents (MINERVA, MultiHopKG, SQUIRE) to consume full natural-language question embeddings instead of single symbolic relations so that navigation is directly guided by question semantics.
AI.result: They obtain KGQA agents that, given a question and topic entity, output both an answer and an explicit traversal path whose agreement with gold evidence paths can be automatically assessed; the adapted agents can be evaluated on how faithfully they follow multi-hop reasoning, how robust they are to linguistic variation, and how they handle multi-hop and multi-answer questions on the new KINSHIP and MQuAKE benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Recasting multi-hop KGQA as question-conditioned graph navigation and equipping existing path-based agents to operate on natural-language embeddings enables traceable KGQA systems where answers are supported by explicit, evaluable reasoning paths, moving the field toward more faithful and interpretable multi-hop reasoning over knowledge graphs.

title: When does a scaling result justify a different allocation? A critical review of resource-allocation evidence for AI systems
summary: AI scaling studies increasingly evaluate systems that combine a pretrained model with retrieval, search, verification, tools, and interaction. Yet a higher score under a larger budget does not by itself show where additional resources are best spent. This critical integrative review asks when a reported scaling result supports a resource-allocation decision. It compares evidence across pretraining, test-time computation, retrieval, and agent evaluation, distinguishing the performance of a tested procedure from the best performance achievable under a resource limit. The synthesis shows that three mismatches recur across this evidence: success counted before an answer is chosen, information a deployed system will not have, and costs left out of the comparison. A capability surface expresses performance as a function of budgets, mechanisms, and available information. Worked analytical examples show how the evaluation metric, deployment volume, selection rule, and stopping policy can alter an allocation conclusion. A resource envelope provides a structured record of the task, development and run-time resources, information access, and procedure behind a reported score. Its application to a published comparison illustrates which conclusions the evidence supports and which deployment questions remain unresolved. The resulting framework specifies the comparisons needed to choose among feasible systems and motivates experiments on the transfer of allocation rules across tasks and operating conditions. It does not propose a universal scaling law or infer general intelligence from benchmark gains.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques how AI scaling results are interpreted for resource allocation and proposes a framework (capability surfaces + resource envelopes) to make comparisons that truly inform where to spend compute, data, and engineering effort.
AI.motivation: Current AI scaling studies often report higher benchmark scores obtained with larger budgets (more parameters, more compute, more tools, more retrieval, etc.), but these scores alone do not tell practitioners where to invest limited resources (pretraining, test-time compute, retrieval, agents, etc.). There is a gap between reported experimental setups and the real deployment constraints (costs, information availability, and decision rules). The authors aim to clarify when a scaling result is actually informative for making resource-allocation decisions.
AI.method: The paper conducts a critical integrative review across four areas: pretraining scaling, test-time compute scaling, retrieval-augmented systems, and agent-style evaluations. It identifies recurring mismatches between reported metrics and deployment realities, and formalizes these issues using a capability surface: performance expressed as a joint function of budgets, mechanisms (e.g., retrieval, tools, agent loops), and information available at inference. The authors provide analytical worked examples to show how different evaluation choices (metric, deployment volume, selection rule, stopping policy) can qualitatively change optimal resource allocations. They introduce the concept of a resource envelope—a structured description of task, development and run-time resources, information access, and procedure—to systematically document what a reported score actually represents. They then apply this framework to an existing published comparison to demonstrate how conclusions change when analyzed through resource envelopes and capability surfaces.
AI.result: The review identifies three recurring mismatches in existing scaling and system-comparison work: (1) success is often counted before an answer is actually selected or committed (e.g., intermediate reasoning traces judged rather than final outputs), (2) evaluations rely on information that real deployments will not have (e.g., ground-truth labels, hindsight signals, or oracle tools), and (3) important costs (compute, latency, annotation, tool calls, human oversight) are frequently omitted or inconsistently accounted for. Through analytical examples, the authors show that these mismatches can reverse or obscure which system is actually preferable under realistic resource constraints and deployment scales. Applying their framework to a published comparison reveals which resource-allocation conclusions are supported by the data and which remain underdetermined.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that many current AI scaling results are insufficient for principled resource-allocation decisions because they do not clearly relate performance to budgets, mechanisms, and available information under realistic deployment conditions. The proposed framework—capability surfaces plus resource envelopes—specifies what comparisons and documentation are needed to make such decisions soundly. It emphasizes that responsible evaluation must align metrics, information assumptions, and cost accounting with intended use cases. The authors explicitly state that they are not proposing a universal scaling law or making claims about general intelligence from benchmark improvements; instead, they motivate targeted experiments to understand how allocation rules transfer across tasks and operating conditions, enabling more rational design and deployment of AI systems under resource constraints.

title: Neyshekar: An Open Persian Read-Speech Corpus for Automatic Speech Recognition
comment: 24 pages, 6 figures; dataset and code available at https://github.com/amirivojdan/neyshekar
summary: Neyshekar is presented as an open Persian read-speech corpus designed for coverage of both formal and informal language, named entities, and longer utterances. In version 6, 62,279 validated recordings totalling 99.02 hours are provided from 190 contributors, with 34,541 distinct recorded prompts. The prompt pool was assembled from human-written material, contextualised homographs, and reviewed language-model-generated text. Text entries were normalised with the shekar library, which supports both formal and informal Persian, and every submitted recording was reviewed against a common validation rubric. About 24% of released clips are classified as informal by an automatic classifier; these register labels are not human-validated. Item-level rater labels are provided for reproducible agreement estimation, opaque per-clip contributor identifiers make the speaker-disjoint partitioning auditable and support contributor-clustered uncertainty estimates, and a text-disjoint test subset is included for evaluation beyond previously seen prompts. Per-contributor recording load and reference-free signal quality are characterised for every released clip. Corpus characteristics are compared with Persian Common Voice under shared processing. Utility is assessed through two ASR architectures, three optimisation seeds, WER and CER, and independent evaluation on the public PSRB sample. Against duration-matched Common Voice training at approximately 32 hours, in-domain WER is reduced by 9.5 points for Whisper and 11.6 points for XLS-R, and by approximately eight points for both architectures on the independent PSRB sample. Transfer and mixture benefits are not consistently observed across architectures and training budgets. The corpus is released under CC0; code and data are made available through the project repository at https://github.com/amirivojdan/neyshekar.

AI.tldr: Neyshekar is an open 99-hour Persian read-speech corpus, carefully curated for both formal and informal language, with detailed metadata and evaluations showing clear ASR performance gains over a duration-matched Persian Common Voice subset.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of high-quality, openly available Persian speech corpora that (1) balance formal and informal language, (2) provide longer and more complex utterances, (3) include systematic metadata for robust experimentation, and (4) allow reproducible comparisons across ASR architectures. Existing resources like Persian Common Voice are valuable but have limitations in register coverage, prompt design, and documentation of contributor- and clip-level characteristics. The paper aims to create a well-documented, CC0-licensed corpus that can serve as a strong baseline and benchmark for Persian ASR research and downstream tasks.
AI.method: The authors (1) assemble a prompt pool from multiple sources: human-written texts, contextualised homographs, and reviewed language-model-generated sentences; (2) normalise all text with the `shekar` library that supports both formal and informal Persian; (3) collect crowd-sourced read-speech from 190 contributors; (4) validate every recording using a common rubric, yielding 62,279 accepted clips (≈99 hours, 34,541 unique prompts); (5) automatically classify clips as formal vs informal (≈24% informal, with the caveat that these labels are not human-validated); (6) attach item-level rater labels, anonymised per-clip contributor IDs, per-clip signal quality metrics, and per-contributor recording load statistics; (7) construct a text-disjoint test set for robust evaluation; (8) process Neyshekar and Persian Common Voice under a unified pipeline and train two ASR architectures (Whisper and XLS-R) with multiple random seeds and training budgets; and (9) evaluate via WER/CER on both in-domain data and the independent PSRB sample to quantify gains and investigate transfer and data mixture effects.
AI.result: Neyshekar v6 consists of 62,279 validated recordings, totalling 99.02 hours from 190 speakers and 34,541 unique prompts, with about 24% of clips automatically labelled as informal. The corpus includes rich metadata (rater labels, contributor IDs, quality estimates, and test splits) and is fully CC0-licensed with open code and data. When using roughly 32 hours of Neyshekar to match the duration of Persian Common Voice training data, ASR models trained on Neyshekar achieve substantially better recognition: in-domain WER is lower by 9.5 absolute points for Whisper and 11.6 points for XLS-R, and on the external PSRB evaluation both models see about an 8-point WER reduction. However, combining Neyshekar with other data or transferring across settings does not yield consistent additional benefits across all architectures and training budgets.
AI.conclusion: Neyshekar is a high-quality, openly licensed Persian read-speech corpus that provides better ASR training signal than a duration-matched subset of Persian Common Voice, as shown by large WER improvements for two state-of-the-art architectures on both in-domain and external evaluations. Its careful text design, inclusion of informal language, rich and auditable metadata, and text-disjoint test set make it a strong and transparent benchmark resource for Persian ASR research. Nonetheless, the mixed and transfer-learning results suggest that optimal use of Neyshekar in combination with other corpora is architecture- and budget-dependent, pointing to future work on data selection and training strategies.

title: Beyond Scene Description: Multi-Agent Orchestration for Non-visual Access to Virtual Worlds
summary: Virtual worlds now host classrooms, meetings, conferences, shops, and social venues, and nearly every interaction they expose assumes a user who can scan a three-dimensional scene, follow avatars, and read floating panels. Blind and visually impaired (BVI) users are left with assistive tools that each solve one task in isolation: naming an object, reading text, describing a scene, or planning a route. A live virtual room defeats that model: obstacles, speakers, gestures, chat, slides, and notifications arrive together, and a tool that narrates all of them trades a visual barrier for an auditory one. This paper presents MetaBlind, an architecture that distributes nonvisual access across eight specialized agents, spanning perception, navigation, social and object interaction, communication, safety and trust, memory, and personalization, and that places an Accessibility Orchestrator between those agents and the user. Agents publish candidate information into a shared accessibility context instead of speaking to the user directly. The orchestrator scores each candidate on safety relevance, goal relevance, urgency, confidence, user relevance, and estimated listening load, then releases only the items it judges relevant at that moment through speech, structured audio, or haptic output. We give the selection step a formal statement, specify the orchestration cycle as an algorithm, and define an evaluation protocol against a single-agent assistant. MetaBlind is reported at the design stage, with no prototype measurement or user study, and the protocol states which outcomes would support the design and which would refute it.

AI.tldr: MetaBlind proposes a multi-agent, orchestrated accessibility architecture for blind and visually impaired users in virtual worlds, replacing single-task tools and naive narration with a context-aware selection mechanism for what information to present, when, and how.
AI.motivation: Existing assistive tools for blind and visually impaired users each handle only one function (e.g., object recognition, text reading, navigation). In dynamic virtual environments where many events (obstacles, speech, gestures, chat, slides, notifications) occur simultaneously, these isolated tools fail: narrating everything overwhelms users with auditory clutter, while narrating too little misses critical information. There is a need for a coordinated, scalable approach that can integrate multiple perception and interaction capabilities while controlling information overload.
AI.method: The paper introduces MetaBlind, a conceptual architecture composed of eight specialized agents covering perception, navigation, social and object interaction, communication, safety and trust, memory, and personalization. Instead of directly communicating with the user, these agents publish candidate informational items into a shared accessibility context. An Accessibility Orchestrator evaluates each item based on dimensions such as safety relevance, goal relevance, urgency, confidence, user relevance, and estimated listening load. It then selects and delivers only the most relevant items at a given moment through speech, structured audio, or haptics. The authors formally define the selection step, describe the orchestration cycle as an algorithm, and propose an evaluation protocol that compares MetaBlind to a single-agent assistant.
AI.result: At this design stage, there are no empirical results from prototypes or user studies. The main result is the detailed architectural design, the formalization of the orchestration problem, and a specified evaluation protocol that outlines how future work should measure and compare MetaBlind’s effectiveness against a single-agent baseline.
AI.conclusion: MetaBlind offers a structured, multi-agent, and orchestrated approach to nonvisual access in virtual worlds that aims to reduce auditory overload while preserving critical and goal-relevant information for blind and visually impaired users. The contribution is currently conceptual: a formal selection framework, an orchestration algorithm, and a testable evaluation protocol. Future empirical studies are required to validate whether this architecture truly improves usability, safety, and efficiency compared to existing single-task tools or naive narration systems.

title: TATK: Triple-Aware Top-K Learning with Knowledge-Grounded Verification for LLM-based Sequential Recommendation
comment: Accepted at EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. 23 pages, including references and appendix
summary: LLM-based sequential recommenders usually cast next-item prediction as text generation, but this interface is poorly matched to full-catalog top-K ranking. We propose TATK, a Triple-Aware framework that couples Top-K Learning (TKL) with Knowledge-Grounded Verification (KGV) for LLM-based sequential recommendation. Top-K Learning combines context-aware metadata-KG prompt grounding with position-aware top-K rewards, aligning training with ranking utility; Knowledge-Grounded Verification then applies structure-aware reranking over the top-M candidates after a single LLM forward pass, using the same metadata-derived item graph. We evaluate TATK on Musical Instruments, CDs and Vinyl, and Video Games from Amazon Reviews 2023 under a matched R2ec-style full-catalog protocol. Experiments use Gemma-2-2B-It and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct backbones, compare against sequential, generative, KG-augmented, and reasoning-enhanced baselines, and include component, reward-shape, sequence-perturbation, reranking, relation-quality, and candidate-pool diagnostics. TATK improves over the matched R2ec reproduction on all 36 reported metrics. On NDCG@10, it improves Qwen by 8.05%, 4.26%, and 3.78% on the three datasets, and improves Gemma by 27.03%, 10.52%, and 10.23%, while keeping inference within 1.17x of Base RecPO latency. The diagnostics show that structural evidence is most useful for recoverable top-M candidates with reliable KG support, and should be gated when metadata relations are sparse or noisy.

AI.tldr: The paper presents TATK, a triple-aware framework that aligns LLM-based sequential recommendation with full-catalog top-K ranking via top-K aware learning and knowledge-grounded reranking.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based recommenders typically formulate next-item prediction as free-form text generation, which does not align well with full-catalog top-K ranking needs and practical efficiency constraints. There is a gap between sequence modeling as language modeling and the ranking-oriented objectives and structures used in recommender systems. The authors aim to better exploit item metadata and knowledge graphs while keeping inference efficient and improving ranking metrics.
AI.method: The authors propose TATK, which has two core components: (1) Top-K Learning (TKL), which grounds prompts using context-aware metadata and knowledge graph information, and optimizes with position-aware top-K rewards so that training is directly aligned with ranking utility; and (2) Knowledge-Grounded Verification (KGV), which performs a structure-aware reranking of the top-M candidates obtained from a single LLM forward pass. Both components rely on a metadata-derived item graph (knowledge graph). The system runs with LLM backbones (Gemma-2-2B-It and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) and plugs into a full-catalog recommendation protocol similar to R2ec.
AI.result: On three Amazon Reviews 2023 domains (Musical Instruments, CDs and Vinyl, Video Games) and under a full-catalog evaluation protocol, TATK consistently outperforms baselines including sequential, generative, KG-augmented, and reasoning-enhanced recommenders. It surpasses a matched R2ec reproduction on all 36 reported metrics. For NDCG@10, Qwen-based TATK yields relative improvements of 8.05%, 4.26%, and 3.78% on the three datasets, while Gemma-based TATK improves by 27.03%, 10.52%, and 10.23%. These gains are achieved with inference latency within 1.17x of the Base RecPO method.
AI.conclusion: TATK shows that explicitly aligning LLM-based recommenders with top-K ranking via position-aware rewards, and leveraging knowledge-grounded structure for post-hoc verification and reranking, can significantly improve full-catalog recommendation quality with only modest inference overhead. Structural (KG) evidence is especially helpful when candidate items have strong and reliable metadata relations, but its use should be modulated or gated in settings where the metadata graph is sparse or noisy.

title: OptoAgent: A Trustworthy Multi-Agent Framework for Opportunistic Vision Micro-Screening in Classroom Environments
summary: A child with reduced distance vision often does not know that anything is wrong. Children adapt, move closer, and rarely report the difficulty, so the problem can survive years of schooling before an adult notices. School screening addresses part of this, but it runs on a schedule, depends on staffing, and is separated from the classroom moments where the difficulty appears. Smartphone and web-based acuity tests have widened access, yet every one of them still needs somebody to start a test. We present SightSentinel, an architecture that turns a wall display a child already reads from into a recurring screening site. Ordinary educational content carries short calibrated optotype probes, and eight specialized agents divide the work. Perception agents recover viewing distance, recognition accuracy, approach behavior, gaze stability, response latency, and interocular difference from each encounter. A quality agent discards observations taken under bad geometry, poor lighting, or inattention. A longitudinal agent accumulates only the surviving evidence against the child's own baseline, and an orchestrator reports a Vision Concern Score routed through a safety gate whose output range excludes diagnosis, refraction, prescription, and reassurance. The design question is whether many cheap, noisy, well-gated encounters can reach a referral decision that one scheduled test reaches late or misses. We state the formulation, the architecture, a four-stage validation protocol against clinical reference standards, and the conditions under which the approach should be rejected.

AI.tldr: SightSentinel embeds tiny vision tests into everyday classroom displays to continuously screen children’s eyesight without explicit testing sessions.
AI.motivation: Many children with reduced distance vision are unaware of their problem and compensate rather than complain, so issues can go unnoticed for years. School screenings are infrequent, resource‑dependent, and detached from the classroom situations where difficulties manifest. Existing smartphone and web-based tests still require someone to initiate a test session, leaving gaps in early detection. The authors aim to create a passive, recurrent, classroom-embedded screening system that can flag potential vision problems earlier and more reliably, without relying on scheduled tests or self-report.
AI.method: They propose SightSentinel, an architecture that converts ordinary classroom wall displays into continuous screening sites by embedding short, calibrated optotype probes into regular educational content. Eight specialized software agents process each encounter: perception agents estimate viewing distance, recognition accuracy of the optotypes, the child’s approach behavior, gaze stability, response latency, and interocular differences. A quality-control agent filters out low-quality observations (bad geometry, poor lighting, inattention). A longitudinal agent aggregates valid observations over time relative to each child’s own baseline, and an orchestrator computes a Vision Concern Score. A safety gate constrains outputs so they only express concern levels suitable for referral decisions and never act as a diagnostic, refractive, or prescriptive tool. They outline a four-stage validation protocol comparing the system’s outputs against clinical reference standards and specifying failure conditions.
AI.result: As this is an abstract, definitive empirical results are not reported. Instead, the paper delivers: (1) a formal problem formulation for passive, classroom-based vision screening; (2) the detailed SightSentinel architecture with its multi-agent design, quality gating, and longitudinal evidence accumulation; and (3) a planned four-stage validation framework against clinical benchmarks, including clearly stated criteria for when the method should be considered unsuccessful or rejected.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that many low-cost, noisy but well-gated observations, collected opportunistically during normal classroom activities, may be sufficient to reach timely and appropriate referral decisions—potentially earlier than conventional, scheduled screenings that may be late or miss cases. They emphasize that SightSentinel is designed as a screening and concern-raising tool, not a diagnostic or prescriptive system, and that its validity hinges on rigorous comparison with clinical standards and on honoring predefined rejection conditions if performance proves inadequate.

title: Disentangling Topology and Diversity in Multi-Agent LLMs for Multilingual Low-Resource Emotion Detection
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures, 25 tables. Accepted at the REALM Workshop at EMNLP 2026. Code: https://github.com/eracoding/topologyxdiversity
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems combine multiple inference calls, but prior work often confounds how calls are connected with how they are diversified. We study these factors independently: inference topology and source of inter-agent diversity. In a controlled $2 \times 3$ matrix, we cross parallel aggregation and sequential refinement with stochastic sampling, role prompting, and learned QLoRA specialization, under a fixed three-call budget and output protocol within each backbone. Using Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we evaluate all six configurations on multilingual low-resource emotion detection across nine languages. Parallel learned specialization is strongest on Qwen at 52.83 Macro-F1 and reaches 52.94 on Llama. On Qwen it also exceeds same-backbone zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, and seven-call self-consistency baselines. The preferred topology depends on diversity source: sequential refinement helps stochastic and prompted settings, while the learned Width advantage shrinks from 2.83 points on Qwen to 0.17 on Llama. Depth-wise analysis suggests that later learned specialists can overwrite correct early predictions, although the aggregate effect is backbone-dependent. Overall, how agents are differentiated produces larger performance shifts than topology, which should be evaluated jointly with specialization.

AI.tldr: The paper disentangles and compares the effects of inference topology (parallel vs. sequential) and inter-agent diversity (sampling, role prompts, learned specialization) in multi-agent LLM systems, showing that how agents are differentiated matters more than how they are connected.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM work mixes two factors—how multiple LLM calls are wired together (topology) and how the individual agents are made diverse—making it hard to understand what really drives gains. The authors want to provide a controlled comparison that isolates these dimensions and offers practical guidance on designing multi-call systems, especially for low-resource multilingual tasks.
AI.method: They construct a controlled 2×3 experimental grid: two inference topologies (parallel aggregation vs. sequential refinement) crossed with three diversity mechanisms (stochastic sampling, role prompting, and learned QLoRA-based specialization), under a fixed budget of three calls and a fixed output aggregation protocol per backbone. Using Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as backbones, they evaluate all six configurations on a multilingual low-resource emotion detection benchmark spanning nine languages, and compare against strong baselines (zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, and multi-call self-consistency). They also perform depth-wise analyses of how later agents affect earlier predictions.
AI.result: Parallel learned specialization is the best-performing configuration, reaching 52.83 Macro-F1 on Qwen2.5-14B and 52.94 on Llama-3.1-8B. On Qwen, this setup outperforms zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and a seven-call self-consistency baseline using the same backbone. The optimal topology (parallel vs. sequential) depends on the diversity mechanism: sequential refinement benefits stochastic sampling and role prompting, while the advantage of parallel learned specialization is pronounced on Qwen but almost disappears on Llama (Width advantage shrinking from 2.83 to 0.17 points). Depth-wise analysis shows that in sequential learned specialization, later specialists can overwrite correct earlier predictions, and the net effect varies across backbones.
AI.conclusion: The main driver of performance in multi-agent LLM systems is how the agents are differentiated, not merely how their calls are interconnected. Inference topology (parallel vs. sequential) interacts with the diversity mechanism, so both should be designed and evaluated jointly. Learned specialization via QLoRA is particularly strong in parallel setups, though its benefits and the risks of sequential overwriting depend on the backbone model. This suggests future multi-agent LLM designs should prioritize principled diversity mechanisms and consider backbone-specific behavior when choosing between width and depth.

title: AI Deployment Accountability Engineering: A Vision for Accountable AI in Safety-Critical Socio-Technical Systems
comment: Appeared in ACM AI Summit 26, Atlanta, GA as a vision paper
summary:
Artificial intelligence systems are rapidly becoming critical components in healthcare, finance, public services, and other safety-critical domains. Yet the engineering practices used to evaluate these systems remain predominantly model-centric, emphasizing properties such as accuracy, robustness, fairness, and interpretability before deployment. These properties are necessary but insufficient once an AI system operates within an ever changing socio-technical environment characterized by distribution shifts, institutional constraints, human feedback loops, privacy requirements, and interactions among multiple AI agents.
  This vision paper introduces AI Deployment Accountability Engineering (ADAE), a proposed AI engineering subdiscipline concerned with establishing measurable, continuous, and actionable accountability for deployed AI systems. ADAE treats accountability as a deployment-layer property rather than solely as a property of an individual model. It seeks to determine whether an AI-enabled system continues to operate within acceptable risk limits, identify the contexts in which failures emerge, attribute failures across interacting technical and human components, translate technical failures into downstream consequences, and support timely intervention.
  We articulate a research agenda built around four interconnected pillars: structured discovery of context-dependent failure modes, privacy-preserving accountability measurement, system-level risk analysis for agentic AI, and translation of technical failures into operational, and institutional risks. The broader goal is to establish foundational principles, mathematical tools, and system architectures for accountable AI deployment across safety-critical applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AI Deployment Accountability Engineering (ADAE), a framework for continuously ensuring and measuring accountability of AI systems after deployment, beyond traditional model-centric evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing AI evaluation focuses on pre-deployment model properties (accuracy, robustness, fairness, interpretability) and overlooks how AI systems behave and fail over time within complex, changing socio-technical environments. There is a gap in methods and tools to systematically monitor, attribute, and manage real-world risks and failures once AI is deployed, especially in safety-critical domains.
AI.method: The paper is a vision / position piece, not an empirical study. It defines ADAE as a new AI engineering subdiscipline and structures a research agenda around four pillars: (1) methods for systematically discovering context-dependent failure modes in deployment, (2) privacy-preserving approaches for ongoing accountability measurements, (3) system-level risk analysis techniques tailored to agentic and multi-agent AI systems, and (4) frameworks for mapping technical failures to operational and institutional risks to guide interventions.
AI.result: As a vision paper, it does not present experimental results. Its main outputs are the conceptualization of ADAE, a formal framing of accountability as a deployment-layer system property, and a structured research agenda with key problem areas and directions for future work.
AI.conclusion: Accountability for AI in safety-critical domains must be engineered as a continuous, system-level deployment property rather than a one-time, model-level checklist. By developing foundational principles, mathematical tools, and system architectures under the ADAE framework—centered on continuous monitoring, privacy-aware measurement, system-level risk analysis, and translation of technical failures into institutional risk—AI deployments can be made more trustworthy and governable in real-world settings.

title: Domain-specific Pretraining Profile and Transformer Performance: Evidence from Modeling Digital Pragmatics in Arabic-English Code-switching
summary: This study highlights the role of domain-specific pretraining profile (DSPP) in Transformer performance for modeling digital pragmatics in Arabic-English code-switched discourse. It evaluates MARBERT and XLM-R(oBERTa), with BERT serving as a general-purpose baseline. The models were evaluated on their ability to classify context-sensitive pragmatic functions in code-switched social-media discourse. 11695 unique X posts were collected via Python and utilized for the study. The study employs a quantitative and qualitative NLP approach, following a supervised pipeline. Findings unveil that MARBERT consistently surpasses XLM-R with validation Macro F1 increasing from 0.39 to 0.84 and validation loss decreasing from 0.55 to 0.19. On an independent test set, it achieved 0.96 accuracy, 0.83 macro precision, 0.87 macro recall, and 0.85 Macro F1, while XLM-R achieved 0.92 test accuracy but a substantially lower Macro F1 of 0.52. This was also supported by class-level performance where MARBERT outperforms XLM-R considerably with F1 improvements ranging from +0.33 to +0.60, demonstrating a clear advantage in modeling Arabic digital pragmatics. The study concludes that Transformer performance depends more on DSPP than multilingual coverage alone, as the latter does not guarantee optimal performance on a highly specialized pragmatic classification task.

AI.tldr: The paper compares Transformer models for classifying pragmatic functions in Arabic-English code-switched social media posts and finds that domain-specific pretraining is more important than broad multilingual coverage.
AI.motivation: To understand how the pretraining profile of Transformer models affects their ability to capture subtle, context-dependent pragmatic functions in Arabic-English code-switched social media discourse, where digital pragmatics and code-switching pose challenges for general-purpose or purely multilingual models.
AI.method: The authors collect 11,695 unique X (Twitter) posts of Arabic-English code-switched discourse via Python, label them with context-sensitive pragmatic functions, and train/evaluate three Transformer models (MARBERT, XLM-R(oBERTa), and BERT). They follow a supervised NLP pipeline with both quantitative evaluation (accuracy, macro precision/recall/F1, loss) and qualitative analysis of model outputs, comparing overall and class-level performance.
AI.result: MARBERT, a model pretrained on Arabic social media, consistently outperforms XLM-R(oBERTa) and the BERT baseline. MARBERT’s validation Macro F1 rises from 0.39 to 0.84 with validation loss dropping from 0.55 to 0.19. On an independent test set, MARBERT achieves 0.96 accuracy, 0.83 macro precision, 0.87 macro recall, and 0.85 Macro F1. XLM-R achieves similar accuracy (0.92) but much lower Macro F1 (0.52). Class-level F1 gains for MARBERT over XLM-R range from +0.33 to +0.60, particularly for specialized pragmatic categories.
AI.conclusion: Transformer success in modeling Arabic digital pragmatics in code-switched social media is driven more by domain-specific pretraining profiles than by multilingual coverage alone. A multilingual model like XLM-R cannot guarantee strong performance on specialized pragmatic classification tasks without appropriate domain and discourse-specific pretraining, whereas a domain-tuned model like MARBERT yields substantially better and more balanced performance across pragmatic classes.

title: CompCQR: Compositional Query Generation for Training-Free Conversational Search
summary: Multi-turn interactions with LLMs are becoming increasingly common in information-seeking scenarios. However, user queries are often ambiguous and context-dependent, making them ill-suited for direct use as retriever queries. Conversational query reformulation (CQR) addresses this issue by rewriting the current utterance into a stand-alone query grounded in the dialogue history. Recent LLM-based CQR approaches achieve strong performance; however, their repeated LLM invocations and misalignment with downstream retrievers remain challenges. In this work, we begin from the observation that retrievers are highly sensitive to content ordering: simply reordering the same content can lead to changes in retrieval coverage and performance. Based on this, we propose a novel training-free method that generates a very large number of queries with minimal LLM usage by compositionally combining a small set of atomic components. We further apply LLM reasoning to construct a high-quality document set that balances precision and recall while capturing the user's core intent. Our framework generalizes across both open- and closed-source LLMs as well as dense and sparse retrievers. It achieves strong performance on four widely used conversational benchmarks, with up to 22.5% relative MRR improvement over the previous state-of-the-art baseline with far fewer LLM calls.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free conversational query reformulation framework that massively expands candidate queries via recombining a few atomic components and uses LLM reasoning to select documents, yielding large MRR gains with far fewer LLM calls.
AI.motivation: In multi-turn, information-seeking conversations with LLMs, user questions are often ambiguous and highly context-dependent, making them poor inputs for retrieval models. Existing LLM-based conversational query reformulation methods can rewrite these questions into stand-alone queries, but they usually require many LLM calls and are not well aligned with the behavior and sensitivity of downstream retrievers, especially regarding content ordering. This leads to inefficiencies and suboptimal retrieval performance in conversational systems.
AI.method: The authors first observe that dense and sparse retrievers are very sensitive to the ordering of content in queries: reordering the same elements can change which documents are retrieved. Leveraging this, they propose a training-free framework that (1) uses an LLM minimally to identify or generate a small set of atomic components capturing the user’s intent and dialogue context, (2) compositionally combines these components in many different orders and configurations to produce a very large number of candidate stand-alone queries without additional model training, and (3) applies LLM-based reasoning to select or aggregate a high-quality set of retrieved documents that balances precision and recall while preserving the user’s core information need. The method is designed to work with both open- and closed-source LLMs and with different types of retrievers (dense and sparse).
AI.result: On four standard conversational information-seeking benchmarks, the proposed framework achieves strong retrieval performance. It yields up to a 22.5% relative improvement in Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) over the previous state-of-the-art conversational query reformulation baseline, while also requiring far fewer LLM invocations overall, demonstrating both effectiveness and efficiency gains.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that carefully exploiting retrievers’ sensitivity to content ordering, combined with minimal but strategic use of LLM reasoning, enables an effective training-free approach to conversational query reformulation. By generating many compositional query variants from a small set of atomic components and constructing a balanced, high-quality document set, the framework improves retrieval quality across multiple benchmarks and retriever types, all while substantially reducing reliance on repeated LLM calls.

title: DynSTEER: Dynamic Stage-wise Trajectory Evaluation and Execution-time Review for Agents
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed for long-horizon task execution. However, current evaluation paradigms face three major limitations: terminal-only assessment ignores intermediate processes and struggles to localize errors efficiently and accurately, single-reference matching penalizes valid alternative solution paths, and post-hoc trajectory judging incurs high costs without the ability to halt failed runs early. To address these issues, we propose DynSTEER, a dynamic stage-wise trajectory evaluation framework for agents. DynSTEER segments rollouts into stages anchored by key completed actions, focusing evaluation on essential milestones with adequate context while enabling targeted strategy adjustments. It compiles a path-tolerant milestone graph from public task views to respect diverse legitimate strategies without leaking ground truth. Furthermore, it adaptively routes evaluation queries across multi-tier judges and halts unrecoverable executions online to curb resource waste. Experiments demonstrate that DynSTEER improves evaluation discriminability across LLM agents by 85.2\% over native evaluation, separates all model pairs with statistical significance, and saves 34.51\% of execution steps on failed rollouts.

AI.tldr: DynSTEER is a dynamic, stage-wise evaluation framework for long-horizon LLM agents that improves discriminability and efficiency by milestone-based, path-tolerant, and adaptive multi-tier judging with early halting.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations for long-horizon LLM agents mostly focus on final outcomes, rely on single-reference solutions, and use expensive post-hoc judging, which makes it hard to localize errors, unfairly penalizes valid alternative strategies, and wastes computation on doomed trajectories. There is a need for an evaluation framework that can assess processes, handle multiple valid paths, and stop failed runs early while remaining efficient and scalable.
AI.method: DynSTEER segments agent trajectories into stages defined by key completed actions (milestones), forming a milestone graph derived from public task views that encodes multiple legitimate solution paths without revealing ground-truth answers. At each stage, the framework evaluates progress with sufficient context, dynamically adjusts strategy focus, and adaptively routes evaluation requests across a hierarchy of judges with varying cost and capability. It also includes an online decision mechanism to detect unrecoverable executions and halt them early, reducing unnecessary computation on failing rollouts.
AI.result: In experiments across multiple LLM agents and tasks, DynSTEER increases the discriminative power of evaluations by 85.2% compared with native evaluation schemes, is able to statistically significantly distinguish all tested model pairs, and reduces the number of execution steps spent on ultimately failed trajectories by 34.51%, demonstrating both better evaluation quality and improved efficiency.
AI.conclusion: DynSTEER offers a more informative and efficient way to evaluate long-horizon LLM agents by focusing on milestone-based, path-tolerant, and dynamically routed stage-wise assessments. This framework resolves key limitations of terminal-only, single-reference, and purely post-hoc evaluations, enabling finer-grained error localization, fairer treatment of diverse solution strategies, and substantial savings in computation through early stopping of unrecoverable runs.

title: Optimizing Sparse Outcomes Through Dense Behavioral Signals via Value-Guided Preference Distillation
summary: Aligning multi-turn dialogue agents is usually framed as matching turn-level human preferences, yet direct optimization of long-term outcomes is often ineffective and prone to reward hacking. We formulate long-horizon dialogue optimization as a multi-objective reinforcement learning problem and train a multi-head value model that predicts a vector of observed user behaviors across multiple look-ahead horizons. Our findings demonstrate that a scalarized composite of dense auxiliary behavioral signals enables effective credit assignment and optimization of sparse outcomes. However, optimizing unconstrained single-objective proxies might induce policy degradations that are harmful when the agent is exposed to real users. To identify these failure modes prior to deployment, we establish a safety framework combining counterfactual user simulation with a validated dialogue-level outcome model to evaluate preference weightings and policy optimization methods. Finally, we demonstrate that distilling multi-objective value preferences into the policy via reference-anchored preference optimization matches on-policy online RL at a small fraction of its compute budget. Live A/B testing confirms that our distilled policy significantly improves long-term user retention, while simultaneously enhancing the positive behaviors and therapeutic-process markers.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-objective reinforcement learning framework for aligning multi-turn dialogue agents to long-term user outcomes, using behavioral signals, safety evaluation via simulation, and preference distillation to achieve better user retention and positive behaviors at low compute cost.
AI.motivation: Existing alignment approaches mainly optimize for turn-level preferences, which often fail to capture and improve long-term user outcomes in multi-turn dialogues and can lead to reward hacking. There is a need for methods that can handle long-horizon credit assignment, avoid policy degradation when optimizing proxy rewards, and be evaluated for safety and effectiveness before deployment with real users.
AI.method: The authors cast long-horizon dialogue optimization as a multi-objective reinforcement learning problem. They train a multi-head value model that predicts a vector of user behavior signals across different look-ahead horizons. They use scalarized combinations of these dense behavioral signals for credit assignment toward sparse long-term outcomes. They then develop a safety framework that uses counterfactual user simulation and a validated dialogue-level outcome model to assess different preference weightings and policy optimization methods. Finally, they distill the learned multi-objective value preferences into the dialogue policy using reference-anchored preference optimization, aiming to approximate online RL performance cheaply.
AI.result: Using scalarized auxiliary behavioral signals improves credit assignment and enables optimization of sparse long-term outcomes. However, they find that naïvely optimizing unconstrained single-objective proxies can degrade policy quality in ways that would be harmful for real users. Their safety evaluation framework can expose such failure modes before deployment. The distilled policy, obtained via reference-anchored preference optimization, matches the performance of on-policy online RL while using only a small fraction of its compute budget. In live A/B tests with real users, this distilled policy increases long-term user retention and improves markers of positive behavior and therapeutic process.
AI.conclusion: Multi-objective RL with dense behavioral signals is an effective strategy for aligning dialogue agents to long-term user outcomes, but care is needed to avoid harmful proxy optimization. A safety pipeline based on simulation and outcome modeling can identify risky configurations before deployment. Preference distillation from multi-objective value functions into a dialogue policy offers a compute-efficient alternative to online RL, achieving comparable performance and yielding empirically verified gains in user retention and positive, therapeutically relevant behaviors.

title: Diffusion-Based Generation of Gait Trajectories
comment: International Conference on NeuroRehabilitation (ICNR2026), September 29-October 2, 2026, Seoul, South Korea
summary: Generation of musculoskeletal gait trajectories conditioned on patient-specific parameters remains a key challenge for wearable robotics and rehabilitation. Assistive systems such as lower-limb exoskeletons require reference trajectories that adapt to individual morphology and therapeutic goals while preserving biomechanical realism. Traditional approaches rely on hand-crafted gait templates or optimization procedures that scale poorly across subjects and walking conditions. In this work, we explore conditional diffusion models for generating lower-limb joint-angle trajectories conditioned on gait parameters such as step length. We compare a baseline transformer diffusion model with a controllable diffusion transformer variant incorporating adaptive normalization and classifier-free guidance. Experiments on a dataset of 4,590 gait cycles show that diffusion models can generate realistic periodic gait trajectories while enabling some controllability variation in gait characteristics, highlighting their potential for personalized gait synthesis in assistive robotics.

AI.tldr: They use conditional diffusion models to generate realistic, patient-specific musculoskeletal gait trajectories for assistive robotics, improving controllability and personalization over traditional template or optimization methods.
AI.motivation: Wearable robots and rehab exoskeletons need joint-angle reference trajectories that adapt to each patient’s body and therapy goals. Existing hand-crafted templates or optimization-based approaches do not scale well across individuals and walking conditions and may lack biomechanical realism or flexibility.
AI.method: They train conditional diffusion models to generate lower-limb joint-angle time series conditioned on gait parameters like step length. They compare a baseline transformer-based diffusion model with a controllable diffusion transformer that adds adaptive normalization and classifier-free guidance to improve controllability over generated trajectories.
AI.result: On a dataset of 4,590 gait cycles, the diffusion-based models produce realistic, periodic joint-angle trajectories and allow controlled variation with respect to conditioning parameters such as step length. The controllable diffusion variant improves control over gait characteristics compared to the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Conditional diffusion models are promising for synthesizing individualized, biomechanically realistic gait trajectories for exoskeletons and other assistive devices, offering better personalization and controllability than traditional template or optimization-based methods.

title: The Garden of Forking Prompts: How Users Explore Narrative Space in Story Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have changed the way people engage with stories. Drawing on public chatbot logs, we can see that when users generate stories, they iteratively edit their prompts to explore narrative possibilities, adjusting characters, redirecting plots, and swapping fictional universes. As aggregated data, these prompts represent rich traces of creative preference at scale. Yet story generation evaluation benchmarks rely on static, one-shot prompts that cannot capture this exploratory behavior. In this work, we study how users revise consecutive story prompts in the wild. Using a dataset of naturally occurring user-chatbot conversations, we construct WildStories, a sample of 275,635 story generation prompts (labeled with story format, prompt components, and explicitness), and WildEdits, a collection of 24,291 edit trees that model how users iteratively edit base story prompts and explore branching story possibilities. From these trees we develop a framework of edit types crossing four directions (adding, removing, changing, and extending) with fourteen targets (e.g., plot, character, genre). We then use our datasets and this framework to analyze user behavior in navigating narrative space via LLMs. Finally, we show how automated permutations based on the framework can be used for story generation benchmarking. Content Warning: This paper works with "wild" chatbot logs, which often include toxic and sexually explicit themes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces datasets and an edit-framework to study how real users iteratively edit prompts for LLM-based story generation, and shows how this can improve evaluation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing story generation benchmarks use static, one-shot prompts and fail to capture how people actually use LLMs to explore stories via iterative prompt editing. There is a need to understand real-world creative behavior and to design evaluation methods that better reflect this exploratory process.
AI.method: The authors collect and annotate a large-scale dataset of real user–chatbot story prompts (WildStories) and construct edit trees from consecutive prompts in conversations (WildEdits). They label prompts with features like story format, components, and explicitness, and derive a taxonomy of edit types based on four edit directions (add, remove, change, extend) and fourteen narrative targets (e.g., plot, character, genre). They then analyze user behavior using this taxonomy and demonstrate how to automatically generate prompt permutations following the framework to build more realistic story generation benchmarks.
AI.result: They produce two main resources: (1) WildStories, containing 275,635 labeled story prompts, and (2) WildEdits, comprising 24,291 edit trees capturing iterative prompt modifications. From these they develop a systematic framework of edit types (4 directions × 14 targets) and empirically characterize patterns in how users navigate narrative space with LLMs. They further show that automatic prompt permutations based on this framework can be used to create benchmark tasks that reflect real-world editing behavior.
AI.conclusion: User interactions with LLMs for story generation are highly iterative and exploratory, and cannot be adequately represented by static, one-shot prompts. Modeling this behavior through large-scale wild data, edit trees, and a structured edit framework yields new insights into narrative exploration and enables more realistic benchmarks for evaluating story generation systems.

title: Lightning Weave: Improving the Accuracy-Efficiency Frontier of Reasoning Models through Capability Composition
summary: A core goal of efficient reasoning is to improve the accuracy-efficiency frontier. However, jointly improving reasoning accuracy and inference efficiency can be challenging, as the two objectives can favor different reasoning behaviors. Independently post-trained models already offer distinct strengths in accuracy and efficiency. We introduce Lightning Weave, a post-training framework that extracts and composes these independently learned capabilities in a single student through on-policy distillation. Each acquired capability is represented by the policy shift from the model before post-training to the resulting specialist. Lightning Weave combines aligned log-ratio shifts at shared student token states and uses Tilted-Target DOPD to convert the cached signals into a stable learning target. Each anchor pair scores the cached trajectories once, enabling subsequent student training without serving multiple live anchor models concurrently. Across diverse student models and benchmarks in mathematics and code, Lightning Weave substantially improves upon the base students and achieves a state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency frontier. On Qwen3.5-4B, it raises HMMT 2025 accuracy from 59.2% to 64.0% with 10.7% fewer response tokens, and LiveCodeBench v5 accuracy from 41.7% to 54.2% with 9.6% fewer response tokens. Adjusting the relative strengths of the anchor signals yields a strong empirical accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier. These results establish Lightning Weave as a new practical route to efficient reasoning through capability composition. Code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: Lightning Weave is a post-training framework that combines the strengths of multiple specialist models into one student to achieve better accuracy with fewer tokens for reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing models face a trade-off between reasoning accuracy and inference efficiency; specialists can be accurate but slow or efficient but less capable. There is a need for a systematic way to combine independently post-trained capabilities into a single model that sits on a better accuracy-efficiency frontier.
AI.method: Lightning Weave treats each specialist model as defining a policy shift from a base model. It caches log-ratio shifts (aligned policy changes) between base and specialist at shared token states, then composes these shifts for a student model via on-policy distillation. A Tilted-Target DOPD procedure converts these cached shifts into a stable learning signal, allowing the student to be trained without running all anchor models live during training. Anchor strength weights are tunable to explore the accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
AI.result: Applied to various student models and benchmarks in math and code, Lightning Weave significantly outperforms base students and prior approaches on the accuracy-efficiency frontier. For Qwen3.5-4B, it improves HMMT 2025 accuracy from 59.2% to 64.0% while cutting response tokens by 10.7%, and boosts LiveCodeBench v5 accuracy from 41.7% to 54.2% with 9.6% fewer tokens.
AI.conclusion: Lightning Weave demonstrates that post-hoc capability composition via policy-shift distillation can yield state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-offs for reasoning models. Its cached-anchor design and adjustable anchor strengths make it a practical, flexible route to building efficient reasoners from multiple specialized post-trained models.

title: One Feedback System Does Not Fit All: Localising Data-to-Text Driver Coaching for the United Kingdom and Nigeria
summary: Data-to-text driver coaching is often presented as a generic pipeline from telematics events to advice. This paper argues that its content requires localisation because usefulness and credibility depend on drivers' knowledge, prevalent risks, regulation, infrastructure, and available data. Two independently developed systems in the United Kingdom and Nigeria are compared by tracing requirements through content selection, generation, and field evaluation. The UK system prioritises post-trip reflection, explanations tied to road and place context, and tone-sensitive wording. The Nigerian system combines legally grounded, once-daily Tips based on detected events with weekly persuasive Reports; it foregrounds safety education and alcohol-related risk in response to reported gaps in formal training and traffic-rule knowledge, as well as local road-safety priorities. Reliable speed-limit metadata supported speeding feedback in the UK, whereas its scarcity led the Nigerian evaluation to exclude speeding from its outcome metric. Both interventions were associated with reduced distance-normalised unsafe-event rates in their own field studies, although their designs and metrics preclude an effect-size comparison. The analysis yields a requirements-to-content design process for localising safety-critical NLG without treating a high-income deployment as the default.

AI.tldr: The paper compares two localized data-to-text driver coaching systems in the UK and Nigeria, showing that safety-critical natural language generation must be tailored to local context rather than reusing a one-size-fits-all pipeline.
AI.motivation: Existing data-to-text driver coaching is typically treated as a generic pipeline from telematics events to advice, implicitly assuming that a system designed in one context (often high-income countries) can transfer elsewhere. The authors argue this is problematic because what makes advice useful and credible varies with drivers’ prior knowledge, main risks, infrastructure, legal frameworks, and data availability. There is a need to understand how to systematically derive localized NLG content requirements for safety-critical applications, and to avoid taking high-income deployments as the default template.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comparative analysis of two independently developed data-to-text driver coaching systems: one deployed in the UK and one in Nigeria. They trace requirements from contextual analysis of each setting through concrete design decisions in content selection, message generation, and field evaluation. They examine how differing constraints (e.g., regulations, driver training levels, metadata availability) shaped each system’s architecture, message types, tone, and metrics, and then analyze field-study outcomes in terms of unsafe-event rates per distance driven.
AI.result: The UK system was designed to support post-trip reflection with context-rich explanations linked to specific roads and places, emphasizing tone-sensitive wording. The Nigerian system instead used legally grounded daily Tips and weekly persuasive Reports, focusing on safety education and alcohol-related risk, to compensate for gaps in formal training and traffic-rule knowledge. Reliable speed-limit data in the UK enabled specific speeding feedback; in Nigeria, limited speed-limit metadata forced speeding to be omitted from outcome measures. Both systems, in their respective field evaluations, were associated with reductions in distance-normalised unsafe-event rates, although differences in design and metrics prevent a direct comparison of effect sizes.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that effective, trustworthy safety-critical NLG for driver coaching must be localized to contextual factors such as legal frameworks, infrastructure, driver knowledge, and data availability. It proposes a requirements-to-content design process that systematically connects local constraints and priorities to NLG content and evaluation choices, explicitly rejecting the assumption that a high-income deployment is the universal default. This process supports more equitable and context-sensitive design of data-to-text driver coaching systems.

title: Depth and Scale in the Sub-150M Regime: JugnuLM-53M vs JugnuLM-110M
summary: We scale our conventional sub-150M pretraining recipe from 53.5M to 109.7M parameters, holding the method fixed (Qwen3-style decoder with grouped-query attention, RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, QK-Norm, and a z-loss; FineWeb-Edu data) and changing only the geometry to a deep-and-thin 23-layer x 576-hidden design. The larger model improves across the board -- BLiMP 78.1 -> 81.3, ARC-Easy 51.4 -> 52.5, WikiText-2 byte-perplexity 2.04 -> 1.95 -- and its 81.3% BLiMP essentially matches GPT-X2-125M (81.28) at about 12% fewer parameters. Notably the 110M model achieves this on fewer training tokens (about 8B vs 12B), so the gain is attributable to capacity and depth, not more data. Both models are deliberately conventional; this report is a clean scaling control and the baseline rung (R0) of an ablation study of what further improves models in this regime. An ablation ladder follows: value residuals (R1) and the Muon optimizer (R2) lift ARC-Easy by a cumulative +3.6 (52.5 -> 56.1) at a near-flat BLiMP and are kept; a diverse data blend (R3) and two logit-distillation settings (R4a/R4b) are not kept -- honest negatives. R3 pins ARC-Easy to FineWeb-Edu's educational filtering rather than raw diversity; distillation from a 1.7B teacher can reach the class-leading ARC-Easy (56.99, matching GPT-X2-125M) but only at a perplexity cost that dialing KD down then erases -- so R2 remains the best kept stack.

AI.tldr: The paper scales a small language model from 53.5M to 109.7M parameters while keeping the training recipe fixed, showing consistent performance gains and then runs an ablation ladder (R0–R4) to identify which architectural and optimization changes further help in this regime.
AI.motivation: To provide a clean, controlled baseline for understanding how conventional sub-150M language models scale with increased depth and capacity, and to rigorously test which additional techniques (architecture tweaks, optimizer choice, data mixtures, and distillation) genuinely improve performance without confounding factors such as more data or exotic recipes.
AI.method: Start from a conventional Qwen3-style decoder-only transformer (grouped-query attention, RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, QK-Norm, z-loss) trained on FineWeb-Edu. Scale parameters from 53.5M to 109.7M solely by changing the geometry to a deeper, thinner configuration (23 layers × 576 hidden), keeping all other training details fixed. Measure performance on BLiMP, ARC-Easy, and WikiText-2. Then run an ablation ladder: R0 is the baseline; R1 adds value residuals; R2 switches to the Muon optimizer; R3 swaps to a more diverse data blend; R4a/R4b apply different logit-distillation settings from a 1.7B-parameter teacher, tracking both accuracy and perplexity.
AI.result: Scaling to 109.7M parameters yields broad improvements: BLiMP from 78.1 to 81.3, ARC-Easy from 51.4 to 52.5, and WikiText-2 byte-perplexity from 2.04 to 1.95, essentially matching GPT-X2-125M BLiMP performance with fewer parameters and fewer training tokens (8B vs 12B). In the ablations, adding value residuals and the Muon optimizer (R1+R2) cumulatively increases ARC-Easy by +3.6 points (to 56.1) with almost unchanged BLiMP. A diverse data blend (R3) does not help, as performance appears tied to FineWeb-Edu’s educational filtering. Logit distillation from a 1.7B teacher can match state-of-the-art ARC-Easy (56.99) but only at the cost of worse perplexity; reducing KD strength removes the perplexity hit but also the accuracy gain.
AI.conclusion: Simply scaling depth and capacity within a conventional recipe improves small language models consistently and can match larger peers with fewer parameters and tokens. Among tested modifications, value residuals plus the Muon optimizer give robust gains without harming linguistic benchmarks, while naive data diversification and strong knowledge distillation introduce trade-offs or regressions. The authors select R2 (value residuals + Muon) as the preferred stack and establish this setup as a clean, reproducible baseline for future improvements in the sub-150M parameter regime.

title: Building Legal Reward Models for Grounding and Abstention
summary: Large language models are increasingly used in high-stakes domains such as law, where systems must ground their reasoning in retrieved evidence and abstain when that evidence is insufficient. However, existing reward models are largely optimised for general preferences rather than contextual grounding, limiting their ability to evaluate these behaviours in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) settings. We introduce a framework for transforming existing legal QA datasets into contextual preference data and use it to construct LegalRewardBench (LRB), a benchmark for evaluating grounded legal generation under noisy and insufficient retrieval conditions. Across general and legal contextual evaluation, we find that contextual DPO improves grounded evaluation, but performance is sensitive to preference-data construction. Length-balanced augmentation substantially improves grounded legal evaluation, with the strongest configuration combining length-balanced legal and general contextual preference data and improving performance by up to $\mathbf{+25.6}$pp over baseline. We further find evidence of cross-jurisdiction transfer: models contextually refined primarily on Victorian criminal-law data improve grounded evaluation on external US legal benchmarks, including a $\mathbf{+16.2}$pp improvement on \textsc{Housing Statute QA}. Together, these results provide a reproducible foundation for constructing and evaluating grounded legal reward models in retrieval-augmented settings.

AI.tldr: They build and evaluate reward models tailored for legal retrieval-augmented generation, showing that contextual preference data and length-balanced augmentation greatly improve grounded legal reasoning, with transfer across jurisdictions.
AI.motivation: General-purpose reward models don’t reliably evaluate whether a legal RAG system is correctly grounding its answers in retrieved evidence or abstaining when evidence is insufficient. Legal domains have high stakes and noisy/insufficient retrieval, but there is no standard way to build or assess specialized reward models for this setting.
AI.method: They propose a framework that converts existing legal QA datasets into contextual preference data suitable for training/evaluating reward models. Using this, they build LegalRewardBench (LRB), a benchmark for grounded legal generation under noisy and insufficient retrieval. They train and compare reward models using contextual DPO and various preference-data constructions, including length-balanced augmentation and combinations of legal and general contextual preference data. They also test cross-jurisdiction transfer by training mainly on Victorian criminal-law data and evaluating on US legal benchmarks.
AI.result: Contextual DPO improves the ability of reward models to evaluate grounded legal answers, but results depend strongly on how preference data is constructed. Length-balanced augmentation yields large gains in grounded legal evaluation. The best setup—combining length-balanced legal and general contextual preference data—improves performance by up to +25.6 percentage points over baseline. Models refined on Victorian criminal-law data also transfer, improving grounded evaluation on US legal benchmarks, including +16.2 percentage points on Housing Statute QA.
AI.conclusion: Specialized, context-aware reward models are crucial for evaluating legal RAG systems, especially under noisy or insufficient evidence. Their framework and LegalRewardBench offer a reproducible way to build and test such models. Carefully designed contextual preference data, particularly with length balancing and mixed legal/general sources, substantially boosts grounded evaluation and even transfers across legal jurisdictions.

title: Moral Rebel Agents: Decision-Making Under Conflicting Obligations
summary: Autonomous agents are typically obliged to follow user-assigned tasks. However, strict obedience may conflict with moral obligations that arise during execution. This paper investigates \textbf{moral rebellion}: the ability of an autonomous agent to deviate from a user-assigned task when morally justified. We formalize five agent architectures: an \textit{amoral agent} that pursues assigned tasks without considering moral obligations, and four forms of \textbf{moral rebel agency}: (1) \textit{utilitarian agents} that opportunistically maximize task outcomes; (2) \textit{deontic} agents that enforce normative constraints; (3) \textit{utilitarian-deontic} (UD) agents that combine deontic constraints with utilitarian reasoning; and (4) \textit{dutiful} agents that additionally preserve commitments to assigned tasks. We implement these architectures within a hierarchical task network planning framework and evaluate them in a Mini Search-and-Rescue domain that exposes trade-offs among assigned-task completion, opportunistic rescue, and norm compliance. Our empirical results show that the proposed agents exhibit distinct trade-offs among rescue results, assigned-task completion, and norm compliance. In particular, the preservation of task commitments emerges as an important dimension of moral rebellion, for which the UD and dutiful agents produce substantially different behaviors despite their shared utilitarian and deontological foundations. These findings highlight the importance of commitment-aware moral reasoning for autonomous agents operating in morally consequential environments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and evaluates ‘moral rebellion’ in autonomous agents: the capacity to deviate from user-given tasks when morally justified, comparing several moral architectures.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents typically follow user-assigned tasks blindly, which can lead to morally problematic behavior when those tasks conflict with emerging moral obligations. There is a need to systematically model and compare how agents can justifiably deviate from instructions to act morally.
AI.method: The authors formalize five agent architectures—amoral, utilitarian, deontic, utilitarian-deontic (UD), and dutiful—each with different ways of balancing task obedience and moral considerations. They implement these within a hierarchical task network (HTN) planning framework and test them in a Mini Search-and-Rescue domain that creates conflicts between finishing assigned tasks, rescuing additional victims, and complying with norms.
AI.result: All agent types exhibit distinct behavioral trade-offs between rescue performance, completion of the assigned task, and adherence to norms. Notably, UD and dutiful agents, which share utilitarian and deontic reasoning, nonetheless show substantially different behaviors because of how they treat commitments to assigned tasks.
AI.conclusion: Commitment to user-assigned tasks is a key dimension in designing morally aware autonomous agents. Moral architectures that explicitly reason about and preserve commitments, in addition to combining utilitarian and deontological principles, are crucial for agents operating in morally sensitive environments.

title: Quantifying the Generation Modality Gap in Speech-Text Language Models
comment: Accepted to SLT 2026, extended version with appendix
summary: Pure speech language models often lag behind text and speech-text language models in generating coherent content, but this gap is difficult to quantify because speech and text systems are typically evaluated with different metrics and trained on different data. We study the speech-text modality gap in a family of spoken language models, based on flow matching for continuous acoustic feature generation. We construct a unified generation-based evaluation suite that compares speech-only, text-only, and speech-text language models trained on matched data distributions and evaluated in matched generation settings. We evaluate generated continuations along multiple dimensions: semantic coherence, measured by transcribing generated speech and scoring it with a reference language model; local phonetic structure, measured by phone n-gram distributional statistics; speaker consistency and acoustic quality; and emotion-based distributional metrics. Across datasets, we find that joint speech-text modeling substantially improves semantic coherence. However, the improvement is not uniform across metrics: phone-level metrics change only modestly, speaker similarity and predicted quality are lower for speech-text continuations, while emotion-based distributional metrics improve. Compared with larger-scale speech-only models, our speech-text model closes much of the scaling gap in transcript-based semantic coherence, suggesting that text provides an efficient semantic training signal for spoken language modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper compares pure speech, pure text, and joint speech-text language models on matched data and evaluation, showing that adding text greatly improves the semantic coherence of generated speech but has mixed effects on other acoustic metrics.
AI.motivation: Speech-only language models generate less coherent content than text or speech-text models, yet this gap is hard to measure because systems differ in training data and evaluation metrics. The authors want a fair, unified way to quantify the "modality gap" between speech and text, and to understand how joint speech-text training affects different aspects of generated speech (semantics, phonetics, speaker, emotion).
AI.method: They build a family of spoken language models using flow-matching for continuous acoustic feature generation, in three variants: speech-only, text-only, and joint speech-text. All are trained on matched data distributions. They then design a unified, generation-based evaluation suite that measures: (1) semantic coherence via ASR transcripts of generated speech scored by a reference LM; (2) local phonetic structure via phone n-gram statistics; (3) speaker consistency and acoustic quality via similarity and quality predictors; and (4) emotion via distributional metrics over predicted emotions in generated speech. They run comparisons across multiple datasets and also compare to larger-scale speech-only models to study scaling effects.
AI.result: Joint speech-text models achieve substantially better semantic coherence than speech-only models across datasets, largely closing the scaling gap with much larger speech-only models on transcript-based semantic metrics. However, phone-level statistics change only slightly, speaker similarity and predicted acoustic quality are actually lower for speech-text generations, while emotion-related distributional metrics improve. This shows that text primarily strengthens high-level semantics rather than uniformly improving all aspects of speech generation.
AI.conclusion: Text is an efficient and powerful training signal for improving the semantic coherence of spoken language models, allowing smaller joint speech-text models to match or approach the coherence of much larger speech-only models. Yet, multimodal training brings trade-offs: it does not dramatically alter low-level phonetic patterns, may hurt speaker consistency and perceived quality, and selectively benefits emotional expressiveness.
