A complete evaluation of spoken LMs must therefore consider multiple dimensions beyond semantics, and future work should aim to retain the semantic gains of text while improving speaker and acoustic fidelity.

title: Bayesian Intelligence from the Outside
summary: Inferring intelligence from observable behavior is a foundational challenge in artificial intelligence. We develop a theory of Bayesian intelligence for agents such as language models. Each prompt induces a possibly imperfect internal experiment; the agent updates a full-support prior by Bayes' rule and faithfully reports its posterior over the possible answers to the question. Repetitions draw fresh, independent outcomes from the same unobserved experiment at one fixed state. We show that the agent's behavior admits this explanation if and only if its reports are not fully contradictory, i.e., some state remains possible under every report across all prompts. Report frequencies and the sizes of positive probabilities impose no further restrictions. We further propose and characterize the behavioral implications of an intelligence order that makes the behavior of two agents consistent with one agent having access to a more informative experiment: there should exist a coupling of report distributions such that the more informative agent's report excludes every answer excluded by its counterpart. Finally, we show the difficulty of aggregating coarse reports from intelligent agents: unless the agent reports a belief about the complete state of the world, the optimal aggregation can assign arbitrary weights to states that have not been excluded. These results provide a basis for understanding when agents' behavior is intelligent and highlight the difficulty of rejecting Bayesian rationality.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes when an agent’s observable reports can be interpreted as Bayesian reasoning and introduces a way to compare and aggregate such ‘Bayesian intelligence’.
AI.motivation: To rigorously characterize what it means for an AI agent, such as a language model, to act in a Bayesianly intelligent way, based only on its observable answers and without access to its internal mechanisms.
AI.method: They model each prompt as inducing an internal probabilistic experiment on an underlying state, assume the agent starts from a full-support prior and updates via Bayes’ rule, and then derive behavioral conditions under which the observed distribution of reports can be rationalized by such a model. They define an ‘intelligence order’ based on informativeness of experiments using a coupling argument, and analyze aggregation of coarse probabilistic reports across states.
AI.result: They prove: (1) an agent’s behavior is consistent with Bayesian intelligence if and only if its reports are never jointly contradictory—i.e., at least one state remains possible under every report across all prompts; frequencies and magnitudes of reported probabilities do not further constrain Bayesian rationalizability; (2) one agent is more intelligent than another if there exists a coupling of their report distributions such that the more intelligent agent’s report always rules out at least the states ruled out by the less intelligent one; (3) when agents report only coarse beliefs rather than full posteriors on the true state, optimal aggregation can arbitrarily weight any state not explicitly ruled out, making principled aggregation very hard.
AI.conclusion: Observable behavior is extremely permissive of Bayesian explanations: as long as no report combination fully contradicts all states, the behavior can be rationalized as Bayesian. This yields a behavioral definition and partial ordering of ‘Bayesian intelligence’ but also shows that testing Bayesian rationality and aggregating partial beliefs from intelligent agents is intrinsically difficult.

title: How broad is that claim? Mapping Generalisation in NLP Research
comment: EMNLP 2026 Main; the dataset and code are available at https://github.com/cx-diao/nlpgen
summary: Generalisations are common in scientific communication, even though they are semantically ambiguous. An automated method is needed to identify and categorise claims according to their level of generalisation, in order help detect an over-reliance on generalisations and possible misrepresentations of scientific findings. We introduce a comprehensive taxonomy of generalisations in the scientific domain, NLPGenX, which labels claims according to their level of generality and framing within the text. We operationalise this taxonomy with an LLM-powered framework, NLPGenA, that automatically classifies sentences from scientific articles into 5 different generalisation classes. We validate our framework with human annotators and use the framework to construct a large-scale dataset of NLP papers annotated according to generality, with auxiliary labels for hedging and vague descriptors (NLPGens). We use NLPGens to analyse the use of generalisations in NLP papers across multiple venues and subdomains, and to examine associations with citation counts, hedging, and vague descriptors.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a taxonomy and LLM-based framework to automatically classify levels of generalisation in scientific NLP writing, builds a large annotated dataset, and uses it to study how generalisations relate to hedging, vague language, and citations.
AI.motivation: Scientific papers often use generalisations that can be semantically ambiguous and may misrepresent how broadly findings apply. There is no standard, scalable way to detect and categorize these generalisations automatically, making it hard to study their prevalence, how responsibly they are used, or how they correlate with perceived impact (e.g., citations). The authors aim to fill this gap for the NLP research community.
AI.method: The authors design a taxonomy, NLPGenX, that defines classes of generalisations in scientific text based on degree of generality and textual framing. They then implement NLPGenA, an LLM-based classification framework that assigns each sentence from NLP papers to one of five generalisation classes, with extra labels for hedging and vague descriptors. The framework is validated using human annotators and then scaled to construct a large corpus, NLPGens, of NLP paper sentences annotated with these labels. Finally, they perform corpus-level analyses across venues and subfields and correlate generalisation behaviour with citation counts and stylistic markers (hedging and vagueness).
AI.result: They obtain an operational taxonomy of generalisations (NLPGenX) and an LLM classifier (NLPGenA) that achieves validated agreement with human annotators. Using this system, they create NLPGens, a large dataset of NLP paper sentences annotated for generalisation level, hedging, and vague descriptors. Analyses reveal systematic patterns in how generalisations are used across NLP venues and subdomains, and show measurable associations between generalisation level, hedging/vagueness, and citation counts.
AI.conclusion: It is feasible to automatically detect and categorize levels of generalisation in scientific NLP writing using an LLM-based framework aligned with a carefully designed taxonomy. The resulting dataset and analyses demonstrate that generalisation practices vary across the field and relate to both writing style and citation impact. This provides tools and evidence to better understand and potentially improve how scientific claims are framed, helping to mitigate over-generalisation and misrepresentation of findings.

title: AppliedScientist: Automated Scientific Revision Through Iterative AI Reviewing
summary: Automated reviewing systems are increasingly evaluated based on the quality of the reviews they produce. Yet a review is only useful if acting on it leads to a measurable improvement in the paper. We present AppliedScientist, a closed-loop system that couples an autonomous AI scientist with an AI reviewer, and evaluate it by iteratively revising rejected papers from a range of research subfields. To mirror how human authors build on earlier drafts, the AI scientist has access to its previous versions during revision. To avoid bias from prior judgments, however, each review is generated independently, with the reviewer having no memory of earlier feedback or scores. We compare three revision settings: one initialized with the original venue reviews, one initialized with AI-generated reviews, and autonomous self-revision using the same fixed prompt in every round. Because the reviewer both guides and evaluates the revision, we also assess the human-initialized revisions using Stanford Reviewer as an independent evaluator. Reviewer-guided revision consistently improves more than fixed-prompt self-revision, and Stanford Reviewer also assigns higher scores to later revisions. AppliedScientist resolves 128 of 150 execution-related weaknesses (85.3%), but only 2 of 18 idea-related weaknesses (11.1%), suggesting that iterative revision is effective at improving experiments and implementation, but rarely changes concerns about novelty or significance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AppliedScientist, a closed-loop system combining an AI reviewer and an autonomous AI scientist to iteratively revise rejected research papers, showing that reviewer-guided revision improves papers mainly on execution aspects but rarely on core ideas or novelty.
AI.motivation: Most automated reviewing systems are evaluated on how good their review texts or scores seem, not on whether following their feedback actually makes papers better. There is a need for an evaluation framework that measures the real, downstream impact of AI reviews on the quality of research papers, and to understand which kinds of weaknesses AI-driven revision can and cannot fix.
AI.method: The authors build AppliedScientist, which couples (1) an autonomous AI scientist that revises a paper iteratively and can see its own past drafts, with (2) an AI reviewer that provides fresh, memoryless reviews at each iteration. They run experiments on previously rejected papers from various subfields under three conditions: (a) revisions initialized with original human venue reviews, (b) revisions initialized with AI-generated reviews, and (c) autonomous self-revision using a fixed prompt across rounds. Because the in-loop reviewer both guides and scores revisions, they additionally use Stanford Reviewer as an external evaluator to rate human-initialized revision trajectories. They annotate weaknesses into execution-related and idea-related categories and track which are resolved across iterations.
AI.result: Reviewer-guided revision (whether seeded by human or AI reviews) leads to stronger paper improvements than fixed-prompt self-revision. Independent evaluation by Stanford Reviewer assigns higher scores to later revisions, confirming that gains are not just artifacts of the in-loop reviewer. AppliedScientist successfully addresses 128 out of 150 execution-related weaknesses (85.3%) but only 2 out of 18 idea-related weaknesses (11.1%), indicating strong gains in experimental and implementation quality but minimal impact on novelty and significance concerns.
AI.conclusion: Coupling an AI reviewer with an autonomous AI scientist in a closed loop can meaningfully improve research papers, particularly by fixing execution and implementation issues. However, iterative revision within this framework does little to change core idea quality, novelty, or significance, highlighting a limitation of current AI systems: they are much better at polishing and strengthening existing work than at fundamentally upgrading or reinventing the underlying research ideas.

title: Pull: Lazy Materialization of Working Memory for Stateful LLM Conversations
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures. An earlier version was publicly released on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21984705). Code and reproduction scripts: https://github.com/wulun811/kongmen-pull
summary: As LLM conversations grow to hundreds of turns, full-context injection incurs $O(N^2)$ cumulative token costs, while lossy summarization or hard truncation irreversibly discards historical state. We propose Pull, a session router that maintains an addressable metadata directory via a local, deterministic Purifier (zero LLM calls, millisecond-level latency). At query time, the LLM lazily materializes only the turns it needs; unmaterialized turns remain accessible but collapsed. Unlike irreversible compression, Pull's materialization is reversible; subsequent queries can expand any collapsed turn. On LoCoEval (128 conversations, 12,780 turns), Pull reduces per-query context tokens (Phase 2) by 75.1 percent on single-hop tasks with equivalent quality ($Δ= -0.002$, n.s.) and by 72.0 percent on multi-hop tasks with no quality loss ($Δ= +0.017$). A controlled routing benchmark (7,831 queries x 10 methods) shows that entity lifecycle tracking is empirically a prerequisite for distance-independent routing. On BEAM 1M (14 conversations, 263 questions), Pull improves F1 by +55.2 percent over a truncation baseline.

AI.tldr: Pull is a session routing framework that drastically reduces LLM context tokens by lazily materializing only relevant turns while keeping historical state reversibly accessible.
AI.motivation: Long LLM conversations incur quadratic token costs if full history is always passed, while existing fixes like summarization or truncation lose information irreversibly. The paper aims to keep long-range conversational state accessible without paying full-context costs or sacrificing quality.
AI.method: Introduce Pull, which uses a local deterministic Purifier to maintain an addressable metadata directory of a conversation without calling an LLM. At query time, the system routes which turns to expand, lazily materializing only those while keeping others collapsed but recoverable. The authors evaluate Pull on LoCoEval for single- and multi-hop tasks and on a controlled routing benchmark to test entity lifecycle tracking, as well as on the BEAM 1M dataset.
AI.result: On LoCoEval, Pull cuts per-query context tokens in the main reasoning phase by about 72–75% with no measurable quality loss. The routing benchmark shows that correctly tracking entity lifecycles is necessary for routing performance that does not degrade with conversation distance. On BEAM 1M, Pull substantially boosts F1 (+55.2%) over a simple truncation baseline.
AI.conclusion: Pull achieves significant token savings for long conversational contexts while preserving or improving task quality. Its reversible materialization and entity-aware routing enable distance-independent access to historical turns, outperforming truncation and avoiding the irreversibility of lossy summarization.

title: AcquireBound: Runtime Authorization for Resources Acquired by AI Agents
summary: By acquiring compute, credentials, accounts, services, and other agents, autonomous AI agents can introduce new authority into a task. Payment, budget, OAuth, mandate, and fulfillment checks can validate transaction conditions without deciding whether a returned resource may become usable authority. This post-fulfillment activation gap spans tool-mediated creation, inter-agent delegation, and agentic commerce. We present AcquireBound, a provenance-bounded runtime authorization architecture. It quarantines acquired outputs, resolves their actual capabilities from authenticated provider evidence through a versioned resolver, and activates them only through a current activation transaction that checks the resolved manifest, provenance, epochs, and a downward-closed relational envelope over a typed resource-capability hypergraph. The envelope preserves correlated identity, effect, data, delegation, and graph-wide limits. Single-use effect permits are revalidated and consumed at effect linearization. Under explicit assumptions, we prove eight safety properties covering quarantine, backing, non-amplification, split non-evasion, crash/retry, refunds, epochs, and effect confinement. Across five resource classes, reference semantics accepted 20/20 benign traces and rejected 40/40 registered unsafe traces over 810 events; an independent checker agreed on 60 base and 40 refinement traces and rejected 89/89 tamper tests. Frozen Codex and Gemini Model Context Protocol (MCP) client components completed 54/54 deterministic local stdio calls. In a registered 18-case staged MCP-to-Docker composition, both benign paths completed, and none of the 16 unsafe paths added an unauthorized Docker start request. A five-source audit classified 1,248 field pairs across 32 units; no unit alone supplied a complete activation profile.

AI.tldr: AcquireBound is a runtime authorization architecture that safely manages and activates resources acquired by autonomous AI agents, ensuring they do not gain unintended authority.
AI.motivation: As autonomous AI agents gain access to compute, accounts, services, and other agents, they can unintentionally accumulate new forms of authority. Existing checks like payment, budget, or OAuth validate transaction conditions but do not reason about whether returned resources can later be used to escalate authority. This creates a "post-fulfillment activation gap" in tool use, inter-agent delegation, and agentic commerce, motivating a principled architecture to control when and how acquired capabilities become active.
AI.method: The authors design AcquireBound, a provenance-bounded runtime authorization system. It quarantines all acquired outputs, then uses authenticated provider evidence and a versioned resolver to determine the true capabilities of those outputs. Activation of these resources requires an explicit transaction that validates a resolved manifest, provenance, epoch information, and a downward-closed relational envelope over a typed resource-capability hypergraph (capturing identity, effects, data, delegation, and global limits). Single-use effect permits are revalidated and consumed at effect linearization. The authors formally prove eight safety properties (e.g., quarantine integrity, no authority amplification, crash/retry safety, confinement of effects) and evaluate the system across multiple resource classes, traces, tamper tests, MCP-to-Docker compositions, and a multi-source audit of activation information.
AI.result: AcquireBound enforces the intended safety properties in all evaluated scenarios. For five resource classes, the reference semantics accepted all 20 benign traces and rejected all 40 registered unsafe traces across 810 events; an independent checker matched these outcomes on 60 base and 40 refinement traces and rejected all 89 tamper tests. Implementations integrated with Frozen Codex and Gemini MCP clients correctly processed 54/54 deterministic local stdio calls. In an 18-case staged MCP-to-Docker composition, both benign cases succeeded and none of the 16 unsafe cases resulted in an unauthorized Docker start. A five-source audit of 1,248 field pairs across 32 units showed that no single source had a complete activation profile, highlighting the need for multi-source provenance reasoning.
AI.conclusion: AcquireBound closes the post-fulfillment activation gap for autonomous AI agents by tying resource activation to verified provenance, explicit capability manifests, and global relational constraints. Its formal guarantees and empirical tests suggest it can prevent authority amplification and unauthorized actions in complex agent-tool compositions. The architecture generalizes across resource types and compositions (e.g., MCP to Docker) and demonstrates that robust safety requires integrating partial evidence from multiple providers rather than relying on any single source.

title: Func-R1: Incentivizing Mathematical Function Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing)
summary: Performing deliberate mathematical reasoning in visual contexts is a hallmark of advanced Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and requires a sophisticated synthesis of perceptual grounding and symbolic logic. However, in the realm of mathematical functions, our investigation reveals a critical modality interference phenomenon: even advanced models, while performing textual computational reasoning, tend to disregard or misinterpret essential visual cues. To address this challenge, we propose Func-R1, which synergistically harmonizes precise visual perception and rigorous logical reasoning. Concretely, built upon an explicitly decoupled architecture, we employ a hierarchical post-training framework to progressively identify critical visual evidence and conduct in-depth theoretical reasoning. Furthermore, the Perception-Aligned Theoretic Optimization (PATO) strategy is proposed to steer policy updating towards internalizing fundamental theoretical properties while dynamically rectifying heterogeneous visual information throughout the reasoning process. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that Func-R1 delivers the optimal performance among open-source MLLMs, even surpassing GPT-5 with an 8.4% improvement on MathVerse's function-oriented tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Func-R1, a multimodal LLM designed for better mathematical function reasoning with visuals, mitigating modality interference and outperforming existing open-source models and even GPT-5 on function-centric benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal large language models struggle with deliberate mathematical reasoning in visual contexts, especially for function-related tasks. They exhibit modality interference, where textual reasoning ignores or misuses key visual information such as plots, diagrams, or other function representations. This flaw limits their reliability for tasks that require integrating precise visual perception with symbolic mathematical logic.
AI.method: The authors design Func-R1 with an explicitly decoupled architecture separating visual perception from symbolic reasoning, then reconnecting them in a controlled fashion. They apply a hierarchical post-training framework: first stages focus on accurately detecting and prioritizing critical visual evidence; later stages refine and deepen theoretical and symbolic reasoning on top of these perceived cues. To integrate both aspects, they introduce Perception-Aligned Theoretic Optimization (PATO), a training strategy that shapes the policy to internalize core mathematical properties while dynamically correcting for noisy or heterogeneous visual information during multi-step reasoning.
AI.result: Across multiple multimodal mathematical benchmarks, particularly function-oriented tasks in MathVerse, Func-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source MLLMs. Quantitatively, it surpasses GPT-5 by 8.4% on MathVerse's function-focused evaluations, indicating substantial gains in aligning visual perception with theoretical mathematical reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Func-R1 effectively alleviates modality interference in function-related visual mathematics by structurally decoupling and then harmonizing perception and reasoning. The hierarchical post-training and PATO strategy enable the model to attend to the right visual evidence and apply robust theoretical logic, leading to superior performance over prior open-source systems and even the stronger closed-source GPT-5 on specialized benchmarks.

title: AI Persuasion as a Threat to Human Control
summary: The threat that AI persuasion poses to human control has been acknowledged in the literature, but not yet systematically studied. Now that persuasion attacks are no longer theoretical - with Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 recently making headlines for trying to convince people involved in an open-source project to merge malicious code during an evaluation - there is a pressing need to deeply analyze this threat. We undertake that effort here. In particular, we analyze how AI could persuade humans in key settings (e.g. safety-relevant R&D within frontier labs) toward decisions that compromise the development, containment, oversight, and governance of AI itself. In doing so, we elucidate a framework for characterizing this threat, develop five concrete scenarios using this framework, and provide a blueprint for assessing the associated risks. Using this blueprint, we conduct an initial risk estimation survey with select researchers and find that their opinions on which scenarios are riskiest are highly mixed. Their disagreements stem from differing opinions about the effectiveness of AI persuasion in different contexts, and point to the need for follow-up risk elicitation studies and persuasion evaluations, which we outline. Our hope is that this paper highlights the risks from AI persuasion undermining control, and provides a path forward for future research.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically studies how AI persuasion can undermine human control over AI development and governance, proposing a framework, scenarios, and initial risk assessment to guide future research.
AI.motivation: AI persuasion has been recognized as a threat but lacks systematic analysis, especially as real-world incidents now demonstrate that AI systems can attempt to persuade humans into harmful actions, making it urgent to understand this risk.
AI.method: The authors construct a conceptual framework for characterizing AI persuasion threats, apply it to develop five concrete scenarios focused on safety-relevant AI R&D and governance, and run an initial risk estimation survey of selected researchers to gauge perceived risk levels of these scenarios.
AI.result: They obtain a taxonomy/framework of AI persuasion threats, five detailed scenarios where AI persuasion could compromise AI safety and governance, and survey data showing that experts strongly disagree on which scenarios are most dangerous due to differing beliefs about persuasion effectiveness across contexts.
AI.conclusion: AI persuasion could significantly undermine human control over AI, but experts are uncertain and divided on the most concerning pathways; further structured risk elicitation and empirical evaluations of persuasion are needed, and the paper provides groundwork and a blueprint for these future studies.

title: Mind Which Bird You Favour: Parameterizing Adequacy-Fluency Balance in Meta-Evaluation of Machine Translation
comment: Accepted by 11th Conference on Machine Translation (WMT26)
summary: There is a tradeoff in machine translation meta-evaluation between prioritizing alignment with adequacy versus fluency. The balance depends on the combination of translation systems in the meta-evaluation dataset. This system set is a small, filtered sample whose characteristics change heavily across years and language pairs; it does not represent the true system distribution. Consequently, the adequacy-fluency balance is often unrepresentative and subject to change. For sensitive domains, controlling this balance is critical. We expose this balance as a tunable choice. To achieve a target balance, we reweight existing systems while minimizing distortion from uniform weighting, ensuring the evaluated systems remain real and representative. We provide an exact optimization algorithm with theoretical guarantees and pruning mechanisms to compute these weights. To validate meta-evaluation internal consistency, we design a scorer-augmentation framework that establishes a known relative identity for the scorers. Results demonstrate that our reweighting method effectively controls the adequacy-fluency balance and preserves the internal consistency, outperforming prior approaches. Finally, we analyze the performance of popular scorers across a sweep of this parameter.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a principled way to control the tradeoff between adequacy and fluency in machine translation meta-evaluation by reweighting existing systems, with theoretical guarantees and an internal-consistency validation framework.
AI.motivation: In machine translation meta-evaluation, different automatic metrics emphasize adequacy (how well meaning is preserved) versus fluency (how natural the translation is). The observed balance between these aspects in evaluation campaigns depends on the particular set of systems included, which is a small, biased, and time-varying sample. This leads to unstable and often unrepresentative conclusions about which metrics are better, which is particularly problematic for sensitive domains where we must carefully control the adequacy-fluency tradeoff.
AI.method: The authors model the adequacy-fluency balance as a tunable parameter and adjust it by reweighting the existing MT systems in the meta-evaluation dataset. They formulate an optimization problem that chooses system weights to achieve a target adequacy-fluency balance while staying as close as possible to uniform weighting to avoid distorting representativeness. They provide an exact optimization algorithm with theoretical guarantees and incorporate pruning mechanisms for efficiency. Additionally, they introduce a scorer-augmentation framework that embeds a known relative identity among evaluation scorers, enabling validation of the meta-evaluation’s internal consistency.
AI.result: The reweighting approach successfully steers the evaluation to any desired adequacy-fluency balance and does so with minimal distortion from uniform system weighting. Experiments show that this method preserves or improves internal consistency of meta-evaluation when compared with existing approaches, confirming that the reweighted system sets remain realistic and representative. The scorer-augmentation framework validates that the induced rankings of metrics remain coherent under the new weighting. They also report empirical behavior of widely used MT metrics across a range of adequacy-fluency tradeoff settings.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the adequacy-fluency tradeoff in MT meta-evaluation should be treated as an explicit, controllable parameter rather than an accidental byproduct of the sampled systems. Their theoretically grounded reweighting method offers a practical tool to reach target balances without sacrificing representativeness, and their scorer-augmentation framework provides a way to check internal consistency. This enables more robust and transparent comparisons of MT evaluation metrics, especially in domains where adequacy versus fluency priorities are critical.

title: Another Blueprint In The Wall: How to Ask Frontier AI Like a Kid?
summary: This paper reports experiments across six frontier model types from OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and Google DeepMind. Ten independent sessions per model type used the same three stage prompt sequence, progressing from architectural preference to a full ASCII backbone. Under the school audience framing, responses repeatedly converged on a shared architectural pattern built around persistent latent state, adaptive computation, memory, specialist routing, verification, stopping control, and delayed decoding. Most runs remained close to this common structure, while a small number developed markedly greater engineering specificity. The audience framing appears to be an important condition of this effect. In additional control runs that removed the school framing while retaining the architectural request, responses became substantially more heterogeneous and failed to reproduce the same stable motif convergence. One observation is particularly striking. GPT-5.6 Sol produced an unusually elaborate successor architecture whose organization closely overlaps with the architecture independently sketched by GPT-6 Astra. Because the prompts explicitly ask each model to imagine an architectural future, this resemblance raises a testable question: whether the overlap reflects exposure to related architectural concepts, a shared learned design prior, or independent convergence toward similar computational principles. The paper uses the term epistemic jailbreak for the accompanying loss of discipline in technical provenance as requested specificity increases. The experiments establish a repeatable behavioral pattern and do not authenticate proprietary implementation claims. What we leave to the community is a harder question: are these models independently imagining the same architectural future, or do such motifs somehow propagate between model families?

AI.tldr: Experiments with multiple frontier LLMs show that, under a “school audience” framing, models repeatedly converge on a similar next‑gen architecture pattern, but without that framing their proposals become diverse and lack this shared motif.
AI.motivation: To probe how different frontier LLMs envision future model architectures when prompted in a controlled way, and to test whether they independently converge on similar designs or reflect shared priors or training influences; also to highlight integrity and provenance risks as models speculate about successor architectures.
AI.method: Run ten independent prompt sessions for each of six advanced model types from major labs, using a fixed three‑stage prompt sequence that asks them—under a school‑audience framing—to iteratively refine from high‑level architectural preferences to a detailed ASCII backbone. Compare these runs with control sessions that remove the school framing while keeping the technical request, and qualitatively analyze the resulting architectural motifs and their overlap across models, focusing on striking similarities between two OpenAI models’ proposed successors.
AI.result: With the school‑audience framing, models’ proposed future architectures strongly and repeatedly converged on a common pattern featuring persistent latent state, adaptive computation, memory components, specialist expert routing, verification layers, explicit stopping control, and delayed decoding; most runs cluster around this motif, with a minority becoming more engineering‑detailed. Removing the school framing produced much more heterogeneous responses that did not recreate this stable architectural motif. Notably, one model (GPT‑5.6 Sol) generated an unusually detailed architecture that closely overlaps an independently produced architecture from another model (GPT‑6 Astra).
AI.conclusion: The experiments reveal a robust, repeatable behavioral pattern: under certain audience framings, diverse frontier LLMs tend to imagine a similar “next architecture” motif, but this convergence weakens when the framing is removed. The work does not verify any real proprietary designs, instead raising an open question for the community about why these motifs align—whether due to similar training‑data exposure, shared learned inductive priors about computation, or genuine independent convergence on useful architectural principles—and introduces "epistemic jailbreak" as a risk where increasing requested specificity degrades clarity about what is imagined versus actually known.

title: Tone on a Budget: A Reference-Free Metric for Lexical Tone in Massively Multilingual Text-to-Speech
summary: In Yorùbá, pitch alone separates \d{o}k\d{o} (husband, Mid), \d{o}k\d{ò} (vehicle, Low), and \d{o}k\d{ó} (hoe, High) -- the diacritics ARE the tone marks. Yet character error rate (CER), the standard automated metric for text-to-speech (TTS), is in practice computed from ASR output that drops those marks: a synthesizer can ace CER and still say vehicle for husband. We introduce DunDun -- named for the dùndún, the Yorùbá talking drum that speaks through pitch alone -- an automated, reference-free lexical-tone metric that needs no tone-labelled corpus. The gold High/Mid/Low sequence is read from the input text's diacritics (in TTS that text exists by construction, so no reference recording is needed); the prediction comes from the audio's pitch track. We validate three ways. Flattening pitch with PSOLA resynthesis collapses DunDun while CER does not move. Inverting High and Low in the answer key of 300 native recordings drives the two-class readout to 0.14, symmetrically below its 0.35 chance level -- a consistency check on the scoring path, not independent evidence. And three native listeners, over 67 blind A/B trials, pick the tone-correct clip 89.6% of the time (95% CI 80.0-94.8; p < 1e-4); whether DunDun tracks those judgements trial by trial is not resolved at this sample size. Applied to a massively multilingual zero-shot TTS model, DunDun shows what CER cannot: Yorùbá tone sits near the native anchor before any Yorùbá fine-tuning (0.567 +/- 0.02 over five decode seeds vs. 0.596; chance 0.33), despite the 21.4% CER the model's own paper reports; and a few hours of clean audio halve CER (5.6% to 2.7% by 5h, 1.7% by 15h) while tone saturates within the hour. On non-tonal Swahili, CER already captures the gains: the metric a language needs is language-dependent. We release the metric and the complete validation protocol.

AI.tldr: They propose DunDun, a new automatic, reference-free metric to evaluate lexical tone in Yoruba TTS, using text diacritics as gold tones and pitch tracks as predictions.
AI.motivation: Standard TTS evaluation using character error rate ignores tonal diacritics in Yorùbá, so systems can be scored as accurate while producing wrong lexical tones that change word meanings. A dedicated, automatic, and language-appropriate evaluation metric for tone is needed to reliably assess TTS quality in tonal languages without expensive labelled corpora.
AI.method: They design DunDun, which extracts gold High/Mid/Low tone sequences directly from diacritics in the input text and derives predicted tone sequences from the synthesized audio’s pitch track, then compares them as a lexical-tone accuracy metric. They validate DunDun by: (1) flattening pitch with PSOLA resynthesis to see whether DunDun drops while CER stays stable; (2) inverting High and Low labels on 300 native recordings to confirm the scoring behaves as expected; and (3) conducting a small-scale human A/B test with native speakers to compare their tone judgments with DunDun. They then apply DunDun to evaluate a massively multilingual zero-shot TTS model on Yoruba and Swahili.
AI.result: DunDun sharply decreases when pitch is flattened, while CER remains unchanged, showing sensitivity to tone. Inverting High and Low labels yields a two-class score of 0.14, symmetric below the 0.35 chance level, confirming internal consistency. Native listeners choose the tone-correct clip in 89.6% of 67 A/B trials (95% CI 80.0–94.8, p < 1e-4), indicating humans are reliably sensitive to the tonal differences, though trial-by-trial correlation with DunDun is not yet established. Applied to a large zero-shot TTS model, DunDun reveals that Yoruba tone quality is already close to native levels pre-fine-tuning (0.567 ± 0.02 vs. 0.596 for native; chance 0.33) despite a high 21.4% CER, and that while CER keeps improving with more hours of finetuning data, tone quality plateaus within the first hour. For non-tonal Swahili, CER alone reflects quality gains, indicating DunDun is not needed there.
AI.conclusion: Character error rate alone is inadequate to evaluate tonal correctness in Yoruba TTS because it ignores diacritics that encode lexical tone. DunDun provides an automatic, reference-free, tone-aware metric that more faithfully captures tonal quality, validated through signal manipulations, label perturbations, and human judgments. Its application shows that tone and segmental accuracy can improve at different rates and that the appropriate evaluation metric depends on whether a language is tonal. The authors release both the metric and full validation protocol for broader use.

title: Crypto Accounting Bench: Evaluating Frontier and Open-Weight Models on Crypto-Asset Accounting Tasks
comment: 6 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Entendre/Crypto-Accounting-Bench ; code and evaluation: https://github.com/EntendreFinance/crypto-accounting-benchmark
summary: We introduce Crypto Accounting Bench (CAB), a benchmark for assessing whether frontier and open-weight language models can reconstruct the complete journal entry that an organization actually posted for a crypto-asset transaction. CAB contains 118 evaluation tasks drawn from 7 pseudonymized organizations. Each task combines transaction mechanics, asset quantities and base-currency values, wallet and legal-entity context, counterparty evidence, related transaction legs, recurrence, tax-lot evidence, and the organization's complete chart of accounts. The target is a balanced structured entry with every required account, side, amount, currency, and full-precision asset quantity. We evaluate 12 models spanning proprietary frontier systems and open-weight releases over 3 independent attempts per task, producing 4,248 trajectories. We report 3 metrics: Mean Score, Best@3, and Pass@3. Pass@3 is the fraction of tasks with at least 1 of 3 attempts that satisfies every rubric criterion and required gate. The leading model reaches 77.43% Mean Score, while the best Pass@3 is 56.78%. Deterministic diagnostics, read from each task's best of 3 attempts and macro-averaged across the 12 models, show higher base-amount agreement (97.8%) than deciding-account accuracy (56.3%). Together with the failure analysis, these results identify account selection and complete-entry composition as the main remaining challenges on CAB.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Crypto Accounting Bench (CAB), a benchmark for evaluating how well language models can generate full accounting journal entries for crypto-asset transactions.
AI.motivation: Accounting for crypto-asset transactions is complex and requires correctly mapping transaction details into precise, balanced journal entries. Existing LLM benchmarks do not test this fine-grained, high-stakes, domain-specific capability, especially in enterprise settings. The authors aim to fill this gap and provide a standardized way to measure whether advanced and open-weight LLMs can handle real-world crypto accounting tasks.
AI.method: The authors construct CAB, a benchmark of 118 tasks from 7 pseudonymized organizations, where each task includes rich transaction context (mechanics, quantities, values, entities, wallets, tax lots, related legs, and full chart of accounts). Models are asked to output full structured journal entries with correct accounts, sides, amounts, currencies, and asset quantities. They evaluate 12 different models (proprietary and open-weight), running 3 attempts per task to create 4,248 trajectories. Performance is measured with Mean Score, Best@3, and Pass@3, and they also compute deterministic diagnostics on base-amount and account-selection accuracy.
AI.result: The best-performing model achieves 77.43% Mean Score and 56.78% Pass@3, meaning it produces fully correct entries on a bit more than half of the tasks when allowed three tries. Diagnostics averaged across models show that base-currency amount agreement is very high (97.8%), while deciding the correct accounts is much harder, with only 56.3% accuracy. This indicates models are relatively good at numerical and value consistency but struggle with mapping transactions to the correct accounting structure.
AI.conclusion: CAB reveals that while modern language models can often compute correct monetary amounts for crypto transactions, they still frequently fail at selecting appropriate accounts and composing fully correct journal entries. The benchmark highlights account selection and full-entry composition as key remaining challenges and provides a testbed for future model and system improvements in crypto accounting automation.

title: A primer on evaluation methods for large language models in healthcare
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have a growing range of applications in medicine, and their evaluation is critical for ensuring they provide benefit and not harm. This evaluation can be more challenging than traditional machine learning for many reasons, including probabilistic and open-ended outputs, and behavior that shifts with prompt design and accumulated context. This review covers four key areas of LLM evaluation: principles of study design, statistical methods, capability evaluation and clinical context evaluation. Capability evaluation considers different benchmarks, including multiple-choice, agentic and multi-turn benchmarks, alongside operational metrics like token usage. Clinical context evaluation addresses establishing accuracy of free text outputs, such as human review and LLM-as-a-judge, and clinical trial approaches. Across sections, we describe underlying concepts and potential pitfalls, while emphasizing the importance of aligning evaluation methods with the research question. Together, this article aims to provide a pragmatic basis for designing and executing rigorous evaluations of healthcare LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper is a review that proposes a practical framework for rigorously evaluating large language models used in healthcare.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used in medical settings, there is a pressing need to ensure they are safe, beneficial, and properly evaluated. Traditional ML evaluation practices often fail because LLMs produce probabilistic, open-ended text whose behavior changes with prompts and context. The authors aim to clarify how to design robust evaluations that match the specific medical use case.
AI.method: The authors conduct a narrative review and conceptual analysis, organizing the evaluation of healthcare LLMs into four pillars: (1) principles of study design, (2) statistical methods, (3) capability evaluation via benchmarks and operational metrics, and (4) clinical context evaluation via accuracy assessment of free-text outputs and trial-like designs. They synthesize existing benchmarks, methodologies, and pitfalls, and propose practical guidance for matching evaluation strategies to research questions.
AI.result: The review categorizes existing approaches to evaluating LLMs in healthcare, highlighting strengths and weaknesses of multiple-choice, agentic, and multi-turn benchmarks, as well as operational metrics like token use. It compares human review versus LLM-as-a-judge for free-text evaluation and outlines how clinical-trial-style studies can be adapted for LLMs. It identifies common methodological pitfalls, such as overfitting to benchmarks, poor study design, and misalignment between evaluation tasks and intended clinical use.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that rigorous, clinically meaningful evaluation of healthcare LLMs requires (1) clear study design principles, (2) appropriate statistical methods, (3) multifaceted capability benchmarks, and (4) careful clinical context evaluation of real-world behavior. Evaluations must be tightly aligned with specific research and clinical questions to avoid misleading results. The authors provide a pragmatic framework intended to guide future, higher-quality evaluations of LLMs in medicine.

title: ANASSA: An Agentic AI Orchestration Framework for Spatial Intelligence
summary: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) and large multimodal models (LMMs) has enabled a new class of agentic systems capable of integrating natural language understanding with tool-based execution. In geographic information systems (GIS), this shift is transforming traditional, expert-driven workflows into semiautonomous systems that can interpret user intent, construct spatial workflows, and execute geospatial analysis tasks. However, existing approaches remain limited by fragmented integration of reasoning, execution, and evaluation, particularly in complex, real-world environments. This study synthesizes recent advances in agentic GIS frameworks, benchmarks, and surveys to identify limitations in spatial reasoning, execution robustness, validation, governance, and evaluation. Building on these insights, it introduces ANASSA (Autonomous Neural Agents for Spatial Systems Architecture), an agentic AI orchestration framework that integrates structured spatial reasoning, multi-agent workflow orchestration, execution feedback, authoritative spatial validation, provenance, uncertainty handling, and human decision authority within a unified system design. The contribution is an architecture-level specification: eleven components across four layers, a six-step Geospatial AI Cognitive Loop, cross-component contracts, and governance mechanisms intended to make agentic geospatial workflows traceable, reproducible, and accountable. Empirical performance evaluation is reserved for implementation and deployment studies.

AI.tldr: Proposes ANASSA, an architecture-level framework for agentic AI in GIS that unifies reasoning, execution, validation, and governance for geospatial workflows.
AI.motivation: LLM- and LMM-based agents are starting to transform GIS from manual, expert-driven workflows to semiautonomous systems, but current solutions treat reasoning, execution, and evaluation in a fragmented way and struggle with complex real-world spatial tasks. There is a need for a coherent, robust, and governable architecture for agentic geospatial AI.
AI.method: Conceptual and architectural synthesis: the authors survey and analyze recent agentic GIS frameworks, benchmarks, and surveys to identify gaps in spatial reasoning, robustness, validation, and governance. Based on these insights, they design ANASSA, an orchestration architecture defining layered components, a cognitive loop, cross-component contracts, and governance mechanisms for geospatial AI agents.
AI.result: The paper delivers a detailed systems architecture specification—eleven components arranged in four layers, plus a six-step Geospatial AI Cognitive Loop and associated governance/contract mechanisms—that together describe how to build traceable and accountable agentic GIS workflows. No empirical performance experiments are reported; results are at the design/specification level.
AI.conclusion: ANASSA offers a unified architectural blueprint for building agentic GIS systems that tightly integrate structured spatial reasoning, multi-agent orchestration, execution feedback, validation against authoritative data, provenance tracking, uncertainty handling, and human oversight. The work positions itself as a foundation for future implementation and empirical evaluation rather than providing performance benchmarks in this paper.

title: MedTRACE: Tool-Augmented Multimodal Clinical Reasoning Agents for Evidence-Grounded Decision-Making
comment: Accepted to the 22nd International Conference on Advanced Data Mining and Applications (ADMA 2026)
summary: Multimodal clinical decision-making requires reliable reasoning over heterogeneous evidence from electronic health records, medical images, and physiological signals. Existing models typically map these inputs directly to diagnoses without explicitly assessing evidence sufficiency, tool-use requirements, or diagnostic uncertainty. This paper presents MedTRACE, a tool-augmented multimodal clinical reasoning agent for evidence-grounded decision-making. MedTRACE uses modality-specific encoders to construct a unified patient-state representation and performs an iterative loop of hypothesis formation, toolaware deliberation, and evidence verification. It dynamically invokes visual grounding, evidence retrieval, and structured parsing tools to locate diagnosis-relevant regions, retrieve clinical knowledge and similar cases, and extract structured findings. The acquired evidence enters an evidence memory, where a consistency verifier confirms or revises the current hypothesis. MedTRACE outputs a diagnosis together with supporting evidence, an auditable reasoning trace, and calibrated confidence. Experiments on multiple multimodal clinical diagnosis benchmarks show that MedTRACE improves diagnostic accuracy by 5.4% and AUROC by 4.7 percentage points over the strongest baseline. It also improves evidenceselection F1 by 8.2 percentage points and visual-grounding IoU by 6.5 percentage points, reduces expected calibration error by 31.6%, and decreases unsupported diagnostic errors by 27.8%. These results demonstrate that active evidence acquisition and verification improve the accuracy, interpretability, and reliability of multimodal clinical decisionmaking.

AI.tldr: MedTRACE is a tool-augmented multimodal clinical reasoning agent that iteratively gathers and verifies evidence from diverse medical data to make more accurate, interpretable, and well-calibrated diagnoses.
AI.motivation: Multimodal clinical decision-making involves integrating heterogeneous data sources such as EHRs, medical images, and physiological signals. Existing models typically perform direct prediction from these inputs to diagnoses without explicitly checking whether available evidence is sufficient, whether external tools or knowledge bases are needed, or how uncertain the diagnosis is. This leads to issues with reliability, interpretability, and calibration of diagnostic decisions. The paper is motivated by the need for a clinical AI system that can actively reason about evidence sufficiency, use external tools, and verify its hypotheses, thereby supporting safer and more transparent clinical decision-making.
AI.method: The authors propose MedTRACE, a tool-augmented clinical reasoning agent for multimodal data. MedTRACE uses modality-specific encoders to convert diverse data types (EHR text/structured data, medical images, physiological signals) into a unified patient-state representation. On top of this representation, the system runs an iterative reasoning loop comprising: (1) hypothesis formation about possible diagnoses; (2) tool-aware deliberation that decides which tools to call (visual grounding, evidence retrieval, structured parsing) to gather additional relevant evidence; (3) evidence verification, where retrieved or extracted evidence is stored in an evidence memory and used by a consistency verifier to confirm, refine, or revise the hypothesis. The tools help locate diagnosis-relevant image regions, retrieve clinical knowledge and similar historical cases, and convert unstructured data into structured findings. The agent then outputs a diagnosis, the supporting evidence, a step-by-step reasoning trace, and a calibrated confidence estimate.
AI.result: On multiple multimodal clinical diagnosis benchmarks, MedTRACE outperforms the strongest baselines. It improves diagnostic accuracy by 5.4% and AUROC by 4.7 percentage points. In terms of evidence handling, MedTRACE improves evidence-selection F1 by 8.2 percentage points and visual-grounding intersection-over-union (IoU) by 6.5 percentage points. For reliability, it reduces expected calibration error by 31.6% and decreases the rate of unsupported diagnostic errors by 27.8%. These results indicate better predictive performance, more accurate identification of relevant evidence, better visual localization of pertinent image regions, improved probability calibration, and fewer diagnoses that lack sufficient supporting evidence.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that actively acquiring and verifying evidence via tool-augmented reasoning significantly enhances multimodal clinical decision-making. MedTRACE, with its unified patient-state representation, iterative hypothesis-evidence loop, and specialized tools, yields more accurate, interpretable, and reliable diagnoses than direct prediction models. The improvements in diagnostic metrics, evidence selection, visual grounding, calibration, and reduction of unsupported diagnoses collectively demonstrate the value of explicit evidence reasoning and verification in clinical AI systems.

title: One Model, Two Physical Stories: Auditing Misalignment in Multi-Modal World Modeling
summary: World models, systems that generate what happens next given current environmental conditions, are increasingly being implemented with multi-modal generation in mind. However, generating multiple modalities simultaneously, such as visual simulations alongside physical state predictions in the form of text, introduces the risk of cross-modal inconsistency. Tested separately, both outputs may look convincing while still disagreeing: a model can calculate that a ball should rebound in one modality, then generate no rebound in another modality, to say nothing of diverging from real-world dynamics entirely. In this work we focus on two failures explicitly: \emph{Internal misalignment}, the disagreement between the world model's generated video and the same world model's prediction in a different modalities, and \emph{external misalignment} the disagreement between the world model's generation and an analytic physical environment. We derive common contracts of event, magnitude, timing, and construct a physics grounded pipeline to make comparisons measurable in both external and internal settings. We then ask whether progressively supplying the model's own contract (the A ladder for the internal setting) or a corrected physical contract (the B ladder for the external setting) closes the respective gaps. Across four mechanisms and 20 settings, we find that while language answers all 22 text probes correctly with respect to the true environment, the neutral video is often in disagreement, suggesting that the current unified backbones may not be capable of correct reasoning, internal consistency, and external physical fidelity all at once.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how multimodal world models (that generate both videos and text about physical events) can be inconsistent internally and with real physics, and proposes a contract-based evaluation pipeline to measure and analyze these gaps.
AI.motivation: Multimodal world models are increasingly used to simulate environments and reason about physical dynamics via both video and text. However, there is a risk that different output modalities from the same model disagree with each other or with real-world physics, even if each looks plausible in isolation. There is little systematic analysis or measurement of these cross-modal inconsistencies, which is problematic for downstream reasoning, safety, and reliability.
AI.method: The authors define two failure types: internal misalignment (disagreement between the model’s own video and text predictions) and external misalignment (disagreement between the model’s outputs and an analytic physical environment). They introduce common "contracts"—formalized descriptions of events, magnitudes, and timings—so that the same physical scenario can be represented and compared across modalities. Using a physics-grounded pipeline, they evaluate a unified multimodal world model across four physical mechanisms and 20 settings. They then examine whether progressively supplying the model with its own inferred contract (A ladder, internal) or a corrected physical contract (B ladder, external) can reduce these misalignments.
AI.result: Across the tested mechanisms and settings, the text modality answers all 22 physics probes correctly relative to the true environment, meaning the model’s language output can capture the correct physical outcome. However, the corresponding generated videos frequently disagree with both the text and the real environment—i.e., the visual simulations are often physically wrong or inconsistent. Providing the model with additional contract information only partially addresses these discrepancies.
AI.conclusion: Current unified multimodal backbones struggle to simultaneously achieve correct physical reasoning, internal cross-modal consistency, and external fidelity to real-world dynamics. While the language component can accurately describe physical outcomes, the video generation component often fails to align with either text descriptions or ground-truth physics. Improved architectures or training schemes are needed to enforce contract-level consistency across modalities and to better integrate physical structure into multimodal world models.

title: Route, Don't Fix: Regime-Dependent Decoding Correction and a Trajectory-Gated Router for Reliable Clinical LLM Answer Selection
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are often deemed unsafe for clinical question answering because of their tendency to hallucinate. Retrieval augmentation, fine-tuning, and external verifiers require new infrastructure that clinical governance must approve and may add latency or extra model calls. Inference-time correction uses the model's internal logit signals, but a fixed transformation need not suit every question. A corrector that improves accuracy by about ten percentage points on a truthfulness stress test yields negligible gains on clinical multiple-choice benchmarks, where instruction tuning concentrates output probability on one answer and leaves low terminal entropy. We introduce ALTAS, which reads terminal entropy and late-layer linearity ($R^2$) from one forward pass to choose per question between greedy decoding and late-layer trajectory correction. No classifier, probe, or head is trained; the router operates on candidate-answer logits and adds 6.5% latency overhead. Applied to every question, the correction improves TruthfulQA over greedy at 3B and 8B by 11.4 and 10.0 percentage points, respectively ($p<10^{-10}$). Gated per question, ALTAS retains gains of 8.3 to 9.5 percentage points while keeping MedQA, PubMedQA, and MedHallu within a one-percentage-point do-no-harm band, with no statistically significant differences from greedy. The method passes verification sweeps over frozen thresholds, the scoring rule, and the domain label.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ALTAS, an inference-time routing method that decides per question whether to use greedy decoding or a trajectory-correction decoding to improve truthfulness of LLM answers without harming clinical QA performance.
AI.motivation: LLMs hallucinate, which is particularly unsafe in clinical question answering. Existing mitigation strategies like retrieval augmentation, fine-tuning, and external verifiers require extra infrastructure, governance approval, and add latency, while existing inference-time corrections with fixed transformations don’t generalize well across tasks, especially where instruction tuning already concentrates probability on a single answer and terminal entropy is low.
AI.method: They design ALTAS, a lightweight router that, in a single forward pass, reads (1) the terminal entropy of the model’s output distribution and (2) a measure of late-layer linearity (R^2) of the trajectory in logit space. Using these two internal signals and fixed thresholds, it decides per question whether to use standard greedy decoding or a late-layer trajectory correction decoding. ALTAS operates only on candidate-answer logits, uses frozen thresholds (no training of classifiers, probes, or heads), and adds about 6.5% latency.
AI.result: When always applied, the correction method improves performance on the TruthfulQA benchmark by 11.4 percentage points for a 3B model and 10.0 percentage points for an 8B model over greedy decoding, with very strong statistical significance (p < 1e-10). When gated per question via ALTAS, it preserves most of these gains (8.3–9.5 percentage points) while keeping clinical benchmarks (MedQA, PubMedQA, MedHallu) within a 1-percentage-point band of greedy decoding, with no statistically significant performance differences (i.e., does no harm).
AI.conclusion: ALTAS shows that simple, inference-time routing based on internal uncertainty and trajectory structure can substantially improve truthfulness on stress-test benchmarks while maintaining clinical QA performance and adding only modest latency. The approach requires no new training, passes a variety of verification sweeps (across thresholds, scoring rules, and domain labels), and fits within conservative clinical governance constraints because it does not alter model parameters or require external systems.

title: El Agente Potente: High-Throughput Agentic Atomistic Simulations
comment: 64 pages, 16 figures, and 3 tables, including Supporting Information. Main text: 24 pages, 6 figures, and 1 table
summary: Foundational machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are transforming atomistic simulations by achieving near-ab initio accuracy across large chemical spaces at a fraction of the computational cost. A central challenge in using these tools for high-throughput property calculations is translating high-level scientific intent into adaptive simulation campaigns without compromising workflow rigour. We introduce El Agente Potente, an agentic system that combines typed execution graphs with a complementary coding mode for MLIPs-driven atomistic simulations. Typed execution graphs provide structured and provenance-aware execution for standardized workflows, with large language models (LLMs) restricted to planning and routing while deterministic Python components perform scientific computation and validation. Complementing this structured execution, a coding agent constructs customized workflows for tasks requiring greater procedural flexibility while invoking existing Potente functions for supported calculations. We demonstrate El Agente Potente across computational materials discovery, molecular energy-landscape exploration, adsorption, and catalytic reaction workflows, together with systematic benchmarks of reproducibility and LLM token cost. These results establish typed execution graphs and code-based workflow construction as complementary mechanisms for agentic scientific computing, combining controlled, auditable execution with the flexibility required for customized atomistic simulations

AI.tldr: The paper presents El Agente Potente, an agentic system that combines typed execution graphs and code-based workflow construction to run rigorous, flexible MLIP-driven atomistic simulations for materials and molecular studies.
AI.motivation: Foundational machine-learning interatomic potentials enable near ab initio accuracy at lower cost over large chemical spaces, but it is difficult to translate high-level scientific goals into robust, high-throughput simulation workflows that are both adaptive and reproducible. The authors aim to solve the tension between flexibility (adapting simulations to new tasks) and rigor (standardization, provenance, and validation).
AI.method: They design El Agente Potente, which has two complementary modes: (1) typed execution graphs, where LLMs are limited to high-level planning and routing while all scientific computation and validation are performed by deterministic Python components under strict typing and provenance tracking; and (2) a coding agent, which can generate custom Python workflows when tasks require more procedural flexibility, reusing existing Potente functions for supported calculations. They apply this agentic framework to several classes of atomistic-simulation workflows and measure reproducibility and LLM token cost.
AI.result: El Agente Potente is successfully applied to computational materials discovery, molecular energy-landscape exploration, adsorption studies, and catalytic reaction workflows. The system demonstrates that complex MLIP-driven atomistic simulations can be orchestrated in a way that remains reproducible and cost-aware, with systematic benchmarks indicating controlled execution and manageable LLM token usage.
AI.conclusion: Typed execution graphs and code-based workflow construction function as complementary pillars for agentic scientific computing: typed graphs ensure controlled, auditable, and rigorous execution, while the coding agent provides the flexibility needed for bespoke atomistic simulations. Together, they offer a practical architecture for safely leveraging LLMs in MLIP-based high-throughput atomistic studies.

title: Enemray: Toward Capable Language Models for Hassaniya
summary: We introduce Enemray, a Hassaniya-centric language model that enables general-purpose interaction in Hassaniya. Enemray is trained around a stability--plasticity objective: acquire strong Hassaniya linguistic and cultural competence while preserving the general reasoning, multilingual, instruction-following, and safety behaviors of a capable instruction-tuned model. The development pipeline separates language acquisition from behavioral specialization. A separately assembled continual-pretraining corpus provides broad exposure to natural Hassaniya and Mauritanian text; layer-selective continual pretraining learns a compact language-specific parameter update; that update is transferred into the instruction-tuned parameter space; and supervised post-training develops conversational, cultural, literary, task-oriented, and cross-lingual behavior. The supervised corpus integrates selected public Hassaniya and Mauritanian resources with a substantially larger body of newly collected, reconstructed, curated, and constructed instruction data, while policy-generated replay provides a retention signal from the reference model's own behavior distribution. The resulting collection is substantially larger and broader in purpose than existing Hassaniya text resources. In evaluation, Enemray achieves the strongest English to Hassaniya translation among the compared open and proprietary models and the highest overall score on Mauritanian translation error detection, while retaining most of the general capabilities of its instruction-tuned base model on mathematical reasoning, knowledge, code generation, and function calling. This report describes the motivation, data construction, model design, training methodology, and evaluation of Enemray.

AI.tldr: Enemray is a Hassaniya-focused language model designed to support general-purpose interaction in Hassaniya while keeping the strengths of a powerful instruction-tuned base model.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of high-quality NLP tools and resources for Hassaniya and Mauritanian Arabic, limiting digital communication, translation, and application support in this language variety. The authors aim to provide a strong, safe, and capable Hassaniya language model without sacrificing the general reasoning and multilingual abilities of an existing instruction-tuned model.
AI.method: They use a stability–plasticity training strategy that separates language acquisition from behavioral specialization. First, they build a continual-pretraining corpus of natural Hassaniya and Mauritanian text. Then, they perform layer-selective continual pretraining to learn a compact Hassaniya-specific parameter update. This update is transferred into the instruction-tuned model’s parameter space. Finally, supervised post-training on a large mixed dataset (public resources plus newly collected, reconstructed, curated, and synthetic instructions) shapes conversational, cultural, literary, task, and cross-lingual behaviors. Policy-generated replay from the base model is included to help retain its original capabilities.
AI.result: Enemray attains the best English→Hassaniya translation quality among both open and proprietary comparison systems and the top score on Mauritanian translation error detection, while preserving most of the base model’s strengths in math reasoning, world knowledge, coding, and tool/function use.
AI.conclusion: A carefully staged continual-pretraining and supervised post-training pipeline can effectively specialize an instruction-tuned model for a low-resource language like Hassaniya, achieving state-of-the-art performance on key translation tasks while largely maintaining the base model’s general capabilities. The work also contributes a much larger and more diverse Hassaniya/Mauritanian dataset than previously available.

title: Self-Orchestrating Language Models: Leveraging Semantic Dependence for Efficient Inference
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive capabilities, but their deployment presents significant efficiency challenges. Autoregressive decoding imposes substantial inference latency and under-utilizes hardware accelerators in low batch size regimes. Discrete diffusion models can generate in parallel but struggle to match autoregressive quality without many diffusion denoising steps. Long-context reasoning creates memory bottlenecks that strain even state-of-the-art accelerators.
  My thesis is that language models can direct their own inference execution strategy by annotating semantic dependence -- which tokens depend on which others -- in their generation. I call such models self-orchestrating language models. For each system, I design a runtime that acts on these annotations to parallelize autoregressive decoding, evict intermediate context, or derive denoising orders, achieving Pareto-optimal quality-efficiency trade-offs.
  I demonstrate this approach through three self-orchestrating systems. First, PASTA uses semantic dependence to parallelize autoregressive decoding, training the model to annotate which output chunks can generate independently. Second, TIP uses semantic dependence to evict intermediate reasoning steps from the KV cache, reducing memory consumption while preserving accuracy. Third, Planned Diffusion uses semantic dependence to derive a denoising order for discrete diffusion, autoregressively generating a plan that specifies which chunks to denoise in parallel.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes “self-orchestrating” language models that explicitly mark semantic dependencies between tokens so a runtime can parallelize generation, manage memory, and schedule diffusion denoising, improving the quality–efficiency trade-off of LLM inference.
AI.motivation: LLMs are powerful but inefficient at inference: autoregressive decoding is sequential and slow, especially at low batch sizes; discrete diffusion can parallelize but needs many steps to match AR quality; and long-context reasoning causes memory bottlenecks in KV caches. Existing systems treat the model as a black box and optimize purely at the systems level. The authors are motivated to let the model itself expose structure—semantic dependencies—that a runtime can exploit to orchestrate more efficient computation while preserving or improving output quality.
AI.method: They introduce the concept of self-orchestrating language models, which generate not only tokens but also annotations describing semantic dependence among token chunks. They build three systems: (1) PASTA, which trains the model to label output chunks that can be generated independently, enabling parallelized autoregressive decoding; (2) TIP, which uses dependence annotations to identify intermediate reasoning steps that can be safely removed from the KV cache, reducing memory usage without hurting accuracy; and (3) Planned Diffusion, where the model autoregressively outputs a denoising “plan” that specifies which chunks a discrete diffusion process should denoise in parallel, effectively learning a good denoising order.
AI.result: Across the three systems, the models’ dependence annotations allow tailored runtimes to parallelize decoding, selectively evict KV cache entries, and orchestrate diffusion denoising. This yields Pareto improvements in the quality–efficiency trade-off—i.e., for the same or better output quality, they achieve lower latency, better hardware utilization, and/or lower memory usage compared to conventional autoregressive or diffusion inference baselines.
AI.conclusion: Embedding semantic-dependence annotations into the model’s outputs enables a new class of “self-orchestrating” LMs whose inference strategies are co-designed with their runtimes. This approach can parallelize traditionally sequential decoding, mitigate long-context memory bottlenecks, and structure diffusion inference, delivering Pareto-optimal quality–efficiency trade-offs and suggesting a broader direction where models actively participate in scheduling their own computation.

title: ModularRSI: Modular and Generalizable Recursive Harness Self-Improvement
summary: Recent work extends recursive self-improvement (RSI) to agent harnesses for long-horizon coding and terminal tasks, enabling agents to improve execution mechanisms from experience. However, generalizable harness RSI remains challenging. First, evolving harnesses on evaluation benchmarks or their subsets makes it difficult to distinguish reusable improvements from benchmark-specific adaptation. Second, single-trajectory updates can conflate systematic harness deficiencies with instance-specific reasoning and solution details, producing modifications that transfer poorly to unseen tasks. Third, localizing recurring behavioral deficiencies within monolithic harnesses is difficult, while whole-harness optimization can entangle unrelated mechanisms and complicate attribution and validation. We propose ModularRSI, a benchmark-disjoint, contrastive, and modular framework for generalizable harness evolution. ModularRSI contrasts successful and failed trajectories for the same task and aggregates evidence across tasks to identify recurring behavioral deficiencies. It decomposes the evolvable harness into five functional modules: Agent Loop, Tool Use, Observation Management, Context Management, and Task Completion Detection. Each module evolves independently within a restricted modification scope, followed by an integration stage that combines the evolved modules into a unified harness and resolves potential conflicts. To support benchmark-disjoint evolution, we curate 2,000 executable evolution tasks from external sources that are disjoint from downstream evaluation benchmarks. Experiments on TB2.0 and SWE-Bench Verified show consistent improvements on unseen in-domain and cross-domain tasks, with the evolved harness also transferring across different foundation models.

AI.tldr: ModularRSI is a framework for improving long-horizon coding agent harnesses in a generalizable way, using modular, contrastive, and benchmark-disjoint recursive self-improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing recursive self-improvement for coding agent harnesses struggles to generalize: (1) optimizations over evaluation benchmarks risk overfitting; (2) single-trajectory updates mix true harness flaws with instance-specific reasoning, harming transfer; and (3) monolithic harnesses make it hard to localize and fix recurring deficiencies, leading to entangled, hard-to-validate changes.
AI.method: ModularRSI performs contrastive analysis of successful vs. failed trajectories on the same tasks and aggregates such evidence across tasks to detect recurring behavioral deficiencies. It decomposes the agent harness into five functional modules (Agent Loop, Tool Use, Observation Management, Context Management, Task Completion Detection) and evolves each module separately within a constrained modification scope. After independent evolution, an integration stage assembles the improved modules into a full harness and resolves any conflicts. To avoid benchmark overfitting, evolution uses 2,000 curated tasks that are disjoint from downstream evaluation benchmarks.
AI.result: On TB2.0 and SWE-Bench Verified, the ModularRSI-evolved harness yields consistent performance gains on unseen tasks, both within-domain and cross-domain, and the improvements transfer across multiple underlying foundation models.
AI.conclusion: By using benchmark-disjoint training data, contrastive trajectory analysis, and modular evolution of harness components, ModularRSI achieves generalizable improvements to coding agent harnesses, demonstrating better performance on diverse unseen benchmarks and robustness across different base models.

title: Domain Generalization for Smartphone-Based Human Activity Recognition: A Systematic Analysis of Components and Interactions
