We then audit the evaluation design, scoring code, read paths, and current human records of a private synthetic Japanese care-handoff workflow. The factory stored 69 planted error cards across 47 targets. Final review covers 22 targets and contains 22 confirmed imported proposals, 9 rejected proposals, and 79 human-added cards; only 3 reviewed targets are double annotated. Passing imported plant keys to a generic detector scorer yields 22/(22+9)=0.710 and 22/(22+79)=0.218. A direct audit identity shows that these values are proposal-confirmation yield and submitted-ledger composition, not judge precision and recall, because no independent detector realization was preserved for the audited proposals in the available records. The audit also finds source-name collisions, row shadowing, forced severity, vacuous ratio defaults, and unsupported zero-support field weights. We contribute a provenance-aware claim audit, a storage contract, and a minimum calibration gate for responsibly communicating biomedical ML capability claims. This single-workflow forensic case is an existence proof of a failure mode, not an estimate of its prevalence: existing human work supports an exploratory audit of synthetic proposals, but not LLM-judge operating characteristics, clinical validity, corpus prevalence, or robust inter-annotator agreement.

AI.tldr: The paper audits how synthetic perturbations (planted errors) are used to calibrate LLM-based evaluators in a biomedical workflow, showing that common metrics were misinterpreted and that record-keeping flaws prevent valid claims about model performance.
AI.motivation: In biomedical ML, expert human evaluation is expensive and scarce, so teams use synthetic perturbations (planted errors) as cheap calibration data for LLM evaluators. However, there is confusion between different types of ground truth and detector outputs, which can lead to misinterpreting performance metrics and overstating capabilities. The authors want to clarify these distinctions and show, via a concrete case, how evaluation pipelines can fail in practice.
AI.method: The authors introduce a conceptual framework of four “ledgers”: (1) planted perturbations (synthetic error keys), (2) independent detector outputs, (3) source-linked human dispositions (how humans judge proposals), and (4) human-added discoveries (errors humans find themselves). They then perform a forensic audit of a private synthetic Japanese care-handoff workflow. This involves examining evaluation design, scoring code, data storage, reading paths, and existing human annotation records to reconstruct what actually happened and how metrics were calculated.
AI.result: They find that the workflow’s stored data include 69 planted error cards across 47 targets, but final review only covers 22 targets with 22 confirmed imported proposals, 9 rejected proposals, and 79 human-added cards, and only 3 targets have double annotation. When the team naively treats imported plant keys as detector outputs and computes 22/(22+9)=0.710 and 22/(22+79)=0.218, these are actually proposal-confirmation yield and submitted-ledger composition, not true precision and recall, because no independent detector realizations were preserved. The audit also uncovers data and design issues: source-name collisions, row shadowing, forced severity labels, meaningless default ratios, and unsupported weighting of fields with zero support.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a provenance-aware audit methodology, a data storage contract, and a minimum calibration standard (“gate”) for responsibly reporting biomedical ML evaluation results. It shows, through a single detailed case, that synthetic perturbations can be misused, and that without careful separation and logging of ledgers, one cannot validly estimate LLM-judge performance, clinical validity, prevalence, or inter-annotator agreement. The case is presented as an existence proof of a failure mode rather than a frequency estimate, underscoring the need for more rigorous auditability and record-keeping in synthetic-evaluation pipelines.

title: SALUTE: Benchmarking and Adapting LLMs for the Defense Domain
summary: Defense is a knowledge-intensive domain that requires precise understanding of specialized terminology, doctrinal concepts, operational procedures, and evolving military events. Although recent work has explored language technologies for military applications, existing efforts remain fragmented: they are often task-specific, rely on limited adaptation pipelines, or lack comprehensive defense-domain evaluation. In this paper, we present SALUTE, an end-to-end framework for benchmarking and adapting LLMs for the defense domain. SALUTE integrates Salute-Corpus, a curated corpus from open-access U.S. military doctrine and government documents; Salute-Conv, a grounded instruction dataset from doctrinal sources and decade-long defense news; Salute-Pref, a defense-aware preference dataset; and Salute-Bench, a rigorously filtered benchmark for evaluating defense-domain understanding and reasoning over doctrine and defense news. Based on these resources, we train Salute-LLM through multi-stage post-training with continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and preference alignment. Extensive experiments show that Salute-LLM achieves strong defense-domain performance while retaining competitive general capabilities, demonstrating the effectiveness of SALUTE as an end-to-end framework for defense-domain LLM adaptation.

AI.tldr: Introduces SALUTE, an end-to-end framework and resources for adapting and benchmarking LLMs in the defense domain, culminating in Salute-LLM with strong domain and general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Defense applications need language models that deeply understand specialized military terminology, doctrine, procedures, and current events, but existing work is fragmented, task-specific, and lacks comprehensive, domain-wide evaluation and adaptation pipelines.
AI.method: Curate four main components: (1) Salute-Corpus from open US military doctrine and government documents; (2) Salute-Conv, a grounded instruction dataset from doctrinal sources and long-term defense news; (3) Salute-Pref, a defense-specific preference dataset; and (4) Salute-Bench, a filtered benchmark to evaluate doctrinal and news-related reasoning. Then perform multi-stage post-training of Salute-LLM using continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and preference alignment on these resources.
AI.result: Experiments show that Salute-LLM attains strong performance on defense-domain understanding and reasoning while preserving competitive capabilities on general tasks.
AI.conclusion: An integrated, end-to-end framework like SALUTE, combining curated corpora, instruction and preference data, and a dedicated benchmark, is effective for adapting LLMs to specialized, high-stakes domains such as defense without sacrificing general performance.

title: Horizon-specific Expert Fusion for Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
summary: Short-term photovoltaic power forecasting requires models to represent regular solar cycles and weather-driven fluctuations whose importance changes with the forecast horizon. This study develops a hierarchical ensemble that combines temporal neural models, historical analogs, state climatology, and gradient-boosted trees. Solar geometry and numerical weather forecasts describe the expected generation conditions, while horizon-specific convex weights combine complementary predictions. A separate calibration step uses available historical forecast errors to account for recent bias. The framework is evaluated on public PVDAQ data at 15--240-minute horizons and on three GEFCom2014 solar zones at hourly horizons up to four hours. On PVDAQ, the ensemble achieves a daylight capacity-normalized mean absolute error of 4.315%, reducing error by 4.11% relative to full-feature LightGBM and by 6.03% relative to fine-tuned Chronos-2 under identical calibration. Expert-removal experiments identify redundancy within the ensemble. Across three training seeds on GEFCom2014, learned fusion improves upon equal weighting but performs comparably to LightGBM. The results support horizon-specific combination as a useful forecasting strategy while showing that its advantage over strong individual models depends on the dataset and evaluation period.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical ensemble model is proposed for short-term photovoltaic power forecasting, yielding modest but consistent improvements over strong baselines, with benefits that depend on dataset and horizon.
AI.motivation: Short-term PV power forecasts are challenged by the need to capture both regular solar cycles and rapidly changing, weather-driven variability; different forecast horizons emphasize these components differently. Existing single models (e.g., tree-based or temporal neural networks) may not fully exploit this horizon dependence or the complementary strengths of diverse forecasting approaches. There is also a need to integrate bias calibration based on recent forecast errors and to understand when ensembles actually outperform strong individual models.
AI.method: The paper builds a hierarchical ensemble that fuses multiple expert models: temporal neural networks, historical analog methods, state climatology, and gradient-boosted trees (e.g., LightGBM). Inputs include solar geometry features and numerical weather prediction variables to encode expected generation conditions. For each forecast horizon, the framework learns convex combination weights to fuse expert predictions, enabling horizon-specific model emphasis. A separate postprocessing step calibrates forecasts using recent historical forecast errors to correct bias. The system is evaluated on PVDAQ data at 15–240 minute horizons and on GEFCom2014 solar zones at hourly horizons up to four hours. Expert-removal (ablation) experiments are used to probe redundancy within the ensemble, and multiple random seeds assess robustness on GEFCom2014.
AI.result: On PVDAQ, the proposed ensemble reaches a daylight capacity-normalized mean absolute error of 4.315%, improving over a full-feature LightGBM baseline by 4.11% and over a fine-tuned Chronos-2 temporal model by 6.03%, both under the same calibration procedure. Expert-removal tests show that some ensemble components are redundant, implying overlapping information among experts. On the GEFCom2014 solar zones, across three training seeds, learned horizon-specific fusion outperforms naive equal-weight averaging but delivers performance similar to LightGBM, indicating limited gains over a strong single model in that setting.
AI.conclusion: Horizon-specific hierarchical ensembling is an effective strategy for short-term PV power forecasting, delivering measurable accuracy gains on some datasets and horizons relative to strong individual models. However, its advantage is data- and period-dependent, and not uniformly superior to well-tuned tree-based baselines. The analysis of expert redundancy suggests potential to simplify ensembles without significant loss of accuracy. Overall, the study highlights the value of horizon-aware model combination and bias calibration, while cautioning that improvements over strong benchmarks may be modest and context dependent.

title: The average-farmer illusion in language-model simulations of agricultural decisions
summary: Language-model agents are increasingly used as synthetic people in surveys and social simulations, yet their apparent realism is often judged from population averages or distributional similarity. We tested what such evidence actually establishes by comparing Claude, Codex and Kimi under four prespecified prompt designs with matched farmer decisions from China and four African countries. Some configurations reproduced observed means and adoption rates. However, their person-level predictions were weak; their decisions clustered around typical values and policy-relevant extremes were largely missing. Most strikingly, a simple generator fitted only to the observed marginal dis- tribution, and given no information about any farmer, achieved greater distributional similarity than every language-model configuration. Prompt additions produced conditional gains rather than uni- versal improvement: results varied with model, outcome, population and validation target. We call this the average-farmer illusion: a synthetic population can look realistic while failing to repro- duce who does what or how behaviour varies. We provide a claim-matched validation framework and reusable modular prompts that turn prompt construction into an auditable experimental process. Population-level resemblance should therefore be treated as the start of validation, not as evidence of individual simulation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that language-model agents can match population averages in survey-like tasks but fail to accurately simulate individual-level behavior, calling this mismatch the 'average-farmer illusion.'
AI.motivation: As language models are increasingly used as synthetic people in surveys, policy analysis, and social simulations, researchers often validate them only by how well their aggregate responses resemble real populations. The authors want to know whether such aggregate similarity is sufficient evidence that these models can accurately simulate individuals and policy-relevant behavioral variations.
AI.method: The authors compare several language models (Claude, Codex, Kimi) configured with four pre-specified prompting strategies to real-world data on farmer decisions from China and four African countries. They then evaluate the models on both aggregate statistics (means, adoption rates) and individual-level predictive accuracy, and benchmark them against a simple generator trained only to match the marginal distribution of observed outcomes. They also systematically vary prompts and measure their effects under a claim-matched validation framework.
AI.result: Some model–prompt configurations reproduce observed population averages and adoption rates, but their individual-level predictions are poor: responses cluster near typical values and underrepresent policy-relevant extremes. Surprisingly, the simple marginal-distribution generator achieves better distributional similarity than any language-model configuration. Prompt modifications yield gains that are conditional on the specific model, outcome, population, and validation target, rather than providing uniform improvements.
AI.conclusion: Validating language-model agents only on population-level resemblance is misleading: they can look realistic at the aggregate level while failing to capture who behaves how, especially at extremes that matter for policy. The authors term this the 'average-farmer illusion' and argue that population-level fit should be just the starting point of validation. They propose a claim-matched validation framework and modular, auditable prompts to make the evaluation and construction of language-model agents more rigorous and transparent.

title: Salesforce Koa: An Enterprise Language Model for Agentic Tool Use
summary: We present Salesforce Koa, an enterprise language model built by post-training the open-weight Nemotron-3-Super-120B foundation model with reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Salesforce Koa is trained on public and synthetically generated data, with no customer data, to improve tool use and agentic capabilities while preserving strong general-purpose performance. Its distinctive component is a simulation-to-reward pipeline that expands workflow specifications into persona-conditioned multi-turn tasks with task-resolution rewards grounded in successful tool use for data-dependent requests. For enterprise domains, these specifications are written in Agent Script, Salesforce's declarative language for building Agentforce agents; for public tool-use domains, we synthesize the workflow structure directly. The same simulation and grounded-reward machinery drives GRPO across both. Across public tool-use, agentic-reasoning, and enterprise Customer Relationship Management (CRM) benchmarks, Salesforce Koa improves over its open-weight base, with the clearest gains on multi-turn tool use, and surpasses a strong proprietary baseline while remaining below the strongest frontier models. These results show that specification-driven reinforcement learning is a practical path to specializing open-weight foundation models for enterprise agentic tasks.

AI.tldr: Salesforce Koa is a 120B-parameter enterprise-oriented language model built by RL post-training of Nemotron-3-Super-120B using a specification-driven, tool-use–focused reinforcement learning pipeline to improve multi-turn tool use and CRM agent capabilities.
AI.motivation: Enterprises need large language models that are strong at multi-step tool use, agentic workflows, and domain-specific tasks (like CRM) while still being based on open-weight foundations and not trained on proprietary customer data. Existing open models often underperform on complex, multi-turn tool-use and enterprise workflows compared to proprietary frontier models. The paper aims to bridge this gap with a practical method to specialize open-weight models for enterprise agentic tasks.
AI.method: They start from the open-weight Nemotron-3-Super-120B foundation model and apply reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). The core innovation is a simulation-to-reward pipeline: (1) Take workflow specifications describing tasks and tools. For enterprise domains, these are written in Agent Script (Salesforce’s declarative language for Agentforce agents); for public tool-use domains, they synthesize the workflow structure. (2) Expand these specifications into persona-conditioned, multi-turn interaction tasks that simulate realistic user–agent dialogues requiring tool calls. (3) Define task-resolution rewards grounded in correct, successful tool use for data-dependent requests, so rewards depend on whether the model’s tool usage solves the simulated task. The same simulation plus grounded reward machinery is used to drive GRPO training across both enterprise and general tool-use domains.
AI.result: The resulting model, Salesforce Koa, shows improved performance compared to its Nemotron-3-Super-120B base model on benchmarks covering public tool use, agentic reasoning, and enterprise CRM tasks. The gains are most pronounced on multi-turn tool-use settings. Koa also surpasses a strong proprietary baseline model on these benchmarks, though it still lags behind the very strongest frontier models. All improvements are achieved without training on customer data, relying instead on public and synthetic data generated via their specification-driven pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Specification-driven reinforcement learning—using workflow specs to simulate multi-turn, persona-conditioned tasks and reward grounded tool success—is an effective way to specialize open-weight foundation models for enterprise agentic applications. Salesforce Koa demonstrates that such an RL post-training pipeline can significantly improve multi-turn tool use and CRM-related performance, offering a practical, privacy-preserving path to strong enterprise agents without relying on customer data and while staying competitive with proprietary baselines.

title: BusMA: A Bus Communication Substrate for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-Agent (MA) systems are effective at solving complex tasks that demand planning, tool use, and the synthesis of evidence from multiple sources. Existing systems typically adopt Hierarchical Manager-Worker (HMW) or Router-based Message Passing (RMP) structures as their communication protocol. However, these designs restrict agent autonomy: Worker agents cannot directly consult specific "peers", and misrouted messages can propagate errors. Inspired by bus architectures in computer systems, we propose BusMA, a communication framework that allows any agent to address other agents through a shared channel, i.e., the Bus. It consists of agent registration, message routing, and shared memory management components. Worker agents, each equipped with tools, have their own local memory and can reason, act (tool usage), and communicate by posting shared messages with specific intents. We introduce four intents: discussion, challenge, guidance, and request for explanation, which support fine-grained communication among agents. A Chair agent monitors the shared memory to coordinate interactions and facilitate convergence among Workers. To evaluate the effectiveness of BusMA, we conduct extensive experiments with two frontier LLMs across 13 tasks spanning visual reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and knowledge retrieval demonstrate that BusMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art HMW and RMP methods.

AI.tldr: BusMA is a new multi-agent communication framework using a shared ‘bus’ channel that lets any agent address any other, improving autonomy and performance over hierarchical and router-based systems.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM systems mostly use hierarchical manager–worker or router-based message passing topologies. These restrict worker autonomy (workers cannot directly contact specific peers) and are brittle to routing mistakes that can propagate errors. The authors want a more flexible, expressive, and robust communication protocol that enables richer agent-to-agent interactions, preserves coordination, and boosts task performance on complex reasoning and tool-use benchmarks.
AI.method: They design BusMA, a bus-style communication architecture inspired by computer system buses. All agents communicate via a shared channel (the Bus) with three key components: (1) agent registration so agents can be discovered and addressed; (2) message routing on the shared bus; and (3) shared memory management. Each worker agent has tools and local memory, and can reason, act (via tools), and post messages to shared memory with explicit intents. They define four communication intents—discussion, challenge, guidance, and request for explanation—to structure fine-grained peer interaction. A special Chair agent monitors the shared bus and shared memory, coordinates workers, and steers them toward convergence on solutions. They implement BusMA on top of two frontier LLMs and evaluate it on a diverse benchmark suite.
AI.result: Across 13 tasks covering visual reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and knowledge retrieval, BusMA achieves consistently better performance than state-of-the-art hierarchical manager–worker and router-based multi-agent methods when using the same underlying LLMs. The experiments show that the bus communication style and intent-based messaging enhance collaboration and reduce failure modes linked to rigid hierarchies or misrouting.
AI.conclusion: A bus-based, shared-channel communication framework with structured intents and a coordinating Chair can significantly enhance multi-agent LLM systems. By enabling flexible, peer-to-peer style interaction through a common bus while maintaining coordination, BusMA improves autonomy and performance relative to hierarchical and router-based baselines. This suggests that revisiting system-level communication architectures, not just model quality, is key to advancing multi-agent AI for complex reasoning and tool-use tasks.

title: DA-DLM: Explicitly Modeling Token Dependencies in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising a masked sequence, independently predicting multiple tokens at each step. This conditional independence discards inter-token dependencies and degrades coherence-an issue that parallels the multi-modality problem in Non-Autoregressive Translation (NAT). Drawing on the Directed Acyclic Transformer (DAT), which tackles this problem in NAT via a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), we propose DA-DLM, a model that adapts DAG-based dependency modeling to DLMs' iterative setting through a position-oriented DAG design. The position-oriented DAG binds node groups to fixed output positions so that tokens fixed in earlier steps anchor neighboring predictions via learned transitions, and evolves with denoising to focus on remaining uncertainty as anchors accumulate. On language modeling, open-ended generation, and summarization, DA-DLM consistently outperforms Block Diffusion, especially under fewer denoising steps, and matches autoregressive models while preserving the parallel generation advantage. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/jipy0222/DA-DLM.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DA-DLM, a diffusion-based language model that uses a position-oriented directed acyclic graph to model token dependencies during iterative denoising, improving coherence and performance while keeping parallel generation.
AI.motivation: Existing Diffusion Language Models denoise masked sequences by predicting multiple tokens independently at each step. This conditional independence ignores inter-token dependencies, often harming coherence, similar to the multi-modality issue in Non-Autoregressive Translation. The authors aim to incorporate effective dependency modeling into DLMs without losing their parallel decoding benefits.
AI.method: The authors adapt the Directed Acyclic Transformer idea from Non-Autoregressive Translation to diffusion language modeling. They design a position-oriented directed acyclic graph (DAG) where node groups are tied to fixed output positions. During iterative denoising, tokens that become fixed earlier serve as anchors for nearby positions through learned transition edges in the DAG. As denoising proceeds and more tokens are fixed, the DAG structure effectively shifts focus to the remaining uncertain positions, enabling structured, dependency-aware parallel predictions at each step.
AI.result: On tasks including language modeling, open-ended generation, and summarization, DA-DLM shows consistent improvements over Block Diffusion models, particularly when using fewer denoising steps. Performance reaches or matches that of strong autoregressive baselines, while still benefiting from parallel token generation. The experiments demonstrate better coherence and efficiency in these settings.
AI.conclusion: DA-DLM successfully brings DAG-based dependency modeling into diffusion language models through a position-oriented DAG that evolves over denoising steps. This design mitigates the coherence issues from conditionally independent predictions, achieves competitive or superior performance to autoregressive models, and retains the core advantage of parallel generation. The approach offers a practical way to close the quality gap between diffusion and autoregressive language modeling without sacrificing speed benefits.

title: Enabling Creative Exploration for Vibe Design Agents
summary: Vibe design agents turn natural-language briefs into rendered interfaces and frontend code. Yet a useful design agent should do more than produce one valid page: it should help users explore coherent alternatives. Increasing token-level temperature is a blunt solution because it varies aesthetic decisions and syntax-sensitive code at the same time. We instead separate exploration from implementation through an inference architecture that makes design direction an explicit intermediate decision. Inspired by Verbalized Sampling, a pre-pass proposes structured design specifications with typicality scores, an external selector samples one, and the downstream generator realizes the selected specification together with the original request under fixed settings. We apply this approach to UI themes and visual-asset prompts. Across 168 prompts, with 1,255 paired comparisons per temperature for each intervention, theme sampling broadens observed selection coverage and screenshot variation, while LLM-judge preferences vary across interventions, prompt complexity, and viewport. In an online experiment with more than 300,000 tasks, the observed code-export increase remains statistically uncertain, while fewer negative feedback events coexist with more correction interactions and modest operational costs. Together, these findings identify structured design specifications as a practical control point for exploring alternative UI concepts while keeping downstream generation settings fixed.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage LLM-based design agent that first generates structured design specifications and then realizes them into UI and code, enabling exploration of coherent alternative designs without changing low-level generation temperature.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based UI design agents can turn natural-language briefs into interfaces and code but struggle to help users systematically explore coherent alternative designs. Naively raising token temperature entangles high-level aesthetic variation with low-level syntax-sensitive code randomness, leading to fragile or invalid outputs. The authors want a principled way to vary design direction while keeping implementation stable and reliable.
AI.method: They introduce an inference architecture that explicitly separates design exploration from implementation. In a pre-pass, the model generates structured design specifications (e.g., UI themes or visual-asset prompts) along with typicality scores, inspired by Verbalized Sampling. An external selector then samples one of these candidate specifications. Finally, a downstream generator, run under fixed decoding settings, realizes the chosen specification into rendered UI and frontend code. They evaluate this on UI theming and visual-asset prompting, measuring selection coverage, visual variation, LLM-judge preferences, and online behavior metrics in a large-scale deployment.
AI.result: Across 168 prompts with extensive pairwise comparisons, sampling over structured themes increases the diversity of selected designs and screenshot-level variation, compared with standard temperature-based sampling. However, LLM-based evaluators show mixed preferences depending on the intervention type, prompt complexity, and viewport. In a large online experiment covering over 300,000 tasks, the intervention’s effect on code-export rates is statistically inconclusive, but there are fewer negative feedback events, more correction interactions, and only modest additional computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling design direction as structured specifications, separate from implementation, is a practical control mechanism for exploring multiple coherent UI concepts while keeping low-level generation parameters fixed. This structured sampling improves the breadth of design exploration without clearly harming usability or efficiency, suggesting a promising direction for deploying design agents that support richer ideation workflows in production settings.

title: Translating the Translator: Decomposing the Cost of English-Forced Inter-Agent Communication
comment: Accepted at The 2nd Workshop for Research on Agent Language Models at EMNLP 2026
summary: Multi-agent LLM architectures, such as LangChain and AutoGen, largely assume English as the lingua franca for internal inter-agent communication, even when the end-user task is non-English. We fill this gap by evaluating a two-agent extraction-answer core, with an additional back-translation agent in the English-forced condition, across four typologically diverse languages (Hindi, Chinese, Spanish, Arabic; n = 300 per language) using the Aya-23-8B model. We compare a native-language pipeline to an English-forced one (which incorporates a final back-translation step from English to the user's language). We discover a statistically significant English-Forcing Tax (surviving a strict Bonferroni correction) that isolates the cost of English routing from general multi-agent orchestration overhead. Forcing inter-agent communication through English reduces Exact Match accuracy by 13.0 percentage points (Spanish) up to 30.6 percentage points (Hindi) compared to native-language multi-agent execution. Using chrF scores as a diagnostic measure of English-reference lexical overlap, we find that lower overlap is strongly associated with pipeline failure, consistent with translation loss being an important contributor to the observed performance drop. These findings suggest a compelling case for native-language routing in agent frameworks when the source and target languages are typologically distant, reducing a compounding translation tax.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that forcing multi-agent LLM systems to communicate in English, instead of the user’s native language, significantly harms performance across several non-English languages.
AI.motivation: Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume English as the internal coordination language, even when the users and tasks are non-English. It is unclear how much performance is lost by routing all internal steps through English, especially for typologically distant languages. The authors aim to quantify this “English-forcing tax” and understand whether translation loss is a major source of errors in such pipelines.
AI.method: The authors evaluate a two-agent extraction–answering architecture using Aya-23-8B across four typologically diverse languages: Hindi, Chinese, Spanish, and Arabic (300 examples per language). They compare two settings: (1) native-language routing, where agents communicate in the user’s language, and (2) English-forced routing, where internal communication is in English with an extra back-translation step to the user’s language. They measure performance with Exact Match accuracy and use chrF scores to quantify lexical overlap between non-English text and English references, analyzing how overlap relates to pipeline failures. Statistical significance is assessed with a Bonferroni correction to isolate the specific cost of English routing from general multi-agent overhead.
AI.result: Across all four languages, forcing agents to communicate in English significantly reduces performance compared to native-language routing. The drop in Exact Match accuracy ranges from 13.0 percentage points for Spanish to 30.6 points for Hindi. These effects remain significant under strict Bonferroni correction, confirming a robust “English-Forcing Tax.” Lower chrF overlap between the non-English text and English references strongly correlates with pipeline failures, indicating that translation loss plays a central role in the observed degradation.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that using English as the internal communication language in multi-agent LLM systems imposes a substantial accuracy penalty for non-English tasks, especially for typologically distant languages. Translation-induced information loss, revealed by low chrF overlap, is a key driver of this penalty. The authors conclude that native-language routing for inter-agent communication is preferable in multilingual settings, as it minimizes compounding translation errors and significantly improves end-task performance.

title: ER-EDF: A Psychology-Grounded Emotion Regulation Framework for Speech Empathetic Dialogue Generation in Large Audio-Language Models
summary: Empathetic response generation in spoken dialogue systems requires both accurate emotion perception and appropriate emotion regulation. Grounded in psychological theories such as the Perception-Action Model and emotion regulation theory, effective empathy depends not only on inferring a user's affective state but also on regulating how it is expressed in responses. However, recent large audio-language models (LALMs) largely treat emotion as a direct conditioning signal, lacking explicit regulatory mechanisms, which often leads to affect mirroring rather than calibrated support. We propose ER-EDF, a psychology-grounded framework that explicitly decouples emotion perception and emotion regulation in LALMs. Perception tracks the user's emotional state, while regulation determines how this state should guide empathetic response generation. The framework is model-agnostic and integrates seamlessly into existing LALMs. We further construct a spoken empathetic dialogue dataset and introduce empathy-aware evaluation metrics beyond lexical matching. Experiments across five LALMs and two datasets show that ER-EDF consistently improves empathetic response quality in both automatic and human evaluations, highlighting the importance of jointly modeling emotion perception and regulation in spoken empathetic dialogue systems, paving a new direction for psychologically grounded empathetic AI.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ER-EDF, a psychology-grounded framework that separates emotion perception from emotion regulation in large audio-language models to generate better empathetic spoken dialogue responses, and validates its effectiveness with a new dataset and empathy-focused metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing large audio-language models for empathetic spoken dialogue typically treat emotion as a simple conditioning label, causing them to mirror user emotions rather than provide properly regulated, supportive responses. Psychological theories, like the Perception-Action Model and emotion regulation theory, suggest that effective empathy requires first understanding a user’s affective state and then deliberately regulating how this understanding is expressed. There is a gap between this psychological view and current model architectures, which lack explicit mechanisms for emotion regulation and are evaluated mostly with shallow lexical metrics.
AI.method: The authors introduce ER-EDF, a model-agnostic framework that explicitly decouples two components within large audio-language models: (1) emotion perception, which tracks and infers the user’s emotional state from spoken dialogue, and (2) emotion regulation, which controls how the inferred state should influence the content and style of the system’s response. ER-EDF is integrated into existing LALMs without changing their core architectures. Additionally, the authors create a spoken empathetic dialogue dataset tailored to training and evaluating empathetic responses and propose empathy-aware evaluation metrics that go beyond standard lexical overlap, focusing on empathy quality.
AI.result: Applied to five different large audio-language models and evaluated on two datasets, ER-EDF yields consistent improvements in empathetic response quality. Both automatic metrics (including the new empathy-aware ones) and human judgments show that responses generated under ER-EDF are more empathetic and better calibrated than those from baseline models that do not explicitly separate perception and regulation of emotion.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling both emotion perception and emotion regulation in spoken dialogue systems leads to more effective, psychologically grounded empathetic responses. The ER-EDF framework provides a general way to equip LALMs with these capabilities, integrates smoothly into existing models, and improves performance across multiple systems and datasets. This work argues that future empathetic AI should adopt psychological frameworks that distinguish understanding emotion from regulating how it is expressed.

title: When the Wrong Key Wins: Understanding and Detecting Hallucinations in LLMs
summary: Large language models can hallucinate even when the knowledge required for a correct answer is already available. We study this failure through a latent-key view of inference, where answer selection depends on competition among associations acquired during pretraining. We show that model predictions can be highly sensitive to individual query keywords, that these influential keywords exhibit entity-specific binding, and that their effects are systematically shaped by pretraining frequency. Multiple bindings can also compete and exhibit higher-order interactions within the same query. Based on this mechanism, we introduce a two-stage keyword-perturbation method for hallucination detection. By removing influential keywords and measuring how the model reorganizes its prediction, the method distinguishes errors caused by misleading key associations from correct decisions supported by diagnostic evidence. Across multiple models and benchmarks, perturbation provides a strong and transferable detection signal, reaching $.910$ AUROC on probe-known ScientistQA. Finally, we extend the same probabilistic framework to four hallucination regimes: knowledge deficit, wrong knowledge, context distraction, and unstable inference. Their operational distributions across benchmarks provide diagnostic context for why different detector families succeed in different settings.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why large language models hallucinate even when relevant knowledge is present, proposing a latent-key competition view of inference and a keyword-perturbation method to detect hallucinations.
AI.motivation: LLMs frequently produce hallucinations—confident but incorrect answers—even when they have seen the necessary facts in pretraining. Existing explanations and detectors often do not clearly separate when errors arise from missing knowledge versus misleading associations or context. The authors aim to understand the internal mechanisms that drive these hallucinations and to develop a detection method that is grounded in this mechanism and transfers across models and benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors propose a latent-key view of LLM inference, where output choices are driven by competition among associations tied to specific influential keywords in the query. They empirically study sensitivity to individual query terms, how these act as entity-specific bindings, and how pretraining frequency shapes their influence. They then design a two-stage keyword-perturbation procedure: (1) identify influential query keywords, and (2) remove or perturb them to observe how the model’s prediction reorganizes. This behavior is used as a signal to classify outputs as hallucinations versus supported answers. They also formalize a probabilistic framework to categorize hallucinations into four regimes: knowledge deficit, wrong knowledge, context distraction, and unstable inference.
AI.result: The study shows that LLM predictions can change sharply when certain keywords are perturbed, that these keywords display entity-specific binding and interaction patterns, and that their influence correlates with pretraining frequency. The proposed perturbation-based detector yields a strong, model-transferable hallucination detection signal. On the probe-known ScientistQA setting, the method attains about 0.910 AUROC. Using their probabilistic framework, the authors map how different hallucination regimes are distributed across benchmarks and how those regimes align with the strengths and weaknesses of existing detector families.
AI.conclusion: Hallucinations in LLMs can be fruitfully understood as arising from competition among latent keyword-bound associations, not merely from missing knowledge. Influential keywords, shaped by pretraining statistics and higher-order interactions, can mislead inference even when correct knowledge is available. By strategically perturbing such keywords, one can robustly distinguish misleading-key hallucinations from genuinely supported answers, achieving strong detection performance that generalizes across models and benchmarks. The proposed four-regime taxonomy of hallucinations helps explain why different detection approaches work better in different scenarios and offers a diagnostic lens for future detector design.

title: OpenAl4S: Code as Action, Science as Sessions
summary: AI co-scientists could accelerate computational research, but over a long-running study the workflow also has to stay inspectable, resumable and reproducible, which requires persistent computational state and provenance. Here we present OpenAI4S, an open-source scientific research agent built around the principle of \emph{Code as Action, Science as Sessions}. OpenAI4S combines a persistent computing runtime with research-session management: orchestration is handled through structured tool calls, while scientific actions are represented as complete code cells executed in persistent Python and R kernels. An append-only Action Ledger, per-cell execution records, versioned artifacts, environment records, and workspace checkpoints preserve how results were produced and support session recovery, branching, and extension. Configurable sandboxing, permission controls, and code and trajectory screening provide complementary safeguards. We evaluate OpenAI4S on 36 research scenarios spanning retrosynthesis, molecular dynamics, protein binder design, protein mutation, catalyst screening, and mineral spectroscopy, measuring scientific task accuracy, workflow completeness, and reproducibility of the resulting repositories. OpenAI4S achieves an overall score of 7.83, compared with 5.7--6.4 for a general-purpose coding harness evaluated with three frontier models, with the largest gains on long-horizon and computation-intensive workflows. These results suggest that integrating persistent execution with session-level provenance can improve the reliability of AI-assisted scientific workflows. Environment specification and full rerunnability remain weak for every evaluated system, ours included, so reproducibility is still an open problem for scientific agents. The system is available under the MIT license at \href{https://github.com/PKU-YuanGroup/OpenAI4S}{github.com/PKU-YuanGroup/OpenAI4S}.

AI.tldr: Introduces OpenAI4S, an open-source AI research agent that uses persistent code-based sessions and detailed provenance tracking to improve reliability and partial reproducibility of computational science workflows.
AI.motivation: AI agents can accelerate computational science but typical workflows with LLMs are ephemeral and hard to inspect, resume, or reproduce. For scientific credibility and long-running projects, we need persistent state, clear provenance of results, and mechanisms to safely orchestrate complex tool-using workflows. Existing coding harnesses for LLMs do not fully address long-horizon, computation-intensive, and reproducible research scenarios.
AI.method: Design and implement OpenAI4S, an open-source scientific research agent built on the paradigm "Code as Action, Science as Sessions." The system executes complete code cells in persistent Python and R kernels via structured tool calls, while tracking all actions and outputs through an append-only Action Ledger, per-cell execution records, versioned artifacts, environment records, and workspace checkpoints. It also includes configurable sandboxing, permission controls, and code/trajectory screening. The authors evaluate OpenAI4S on 36 computational research scenarios (retrosynthesis, molecular dynamics, protein binder design, protein mutation, catalyst screening, mineral spectroscopy) and compare its performance against a general-purpose coding harness used with three frontier LLMs, using metrics such as scientific task accuracy, workflow completeness, and reproducibility of generated repositories.
AI.result: Across 36 diverse scientific scenarios, OpenAI4S obtains an overall score of 7.83 on the evaluation metrics, outperforming a general-purpose coding harness paired with three frontier models, which score between 5.7 and 6.4. The largest improvements appear in long-horizon and computation-heavy workflows. Despite these gains, all evaluated systems, including OpenAI4S, exhibit weaknesses in environment specification and fully rerunnable workflows, limiting end-to-end reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: Integrating persistent execution environments with session-level provenance significantly improves the reliability and partial reproducibility of AI-assisted computational science workflows compared with generic coding harnesses. The OpenAI4S framework demonstrates that representing actions as code cells within persistent kernels, combined with detailed logging and artifact versioning, helps support inspectable, resumable, and extendable research sessions. However, fully specifying environments and guaranteeing complete rerunnability remain unsolved challenges for scientific research agents, so reproducibility is still an open problem. The system is released as open source (MIT license), encouraging further development and adoption.

title: MoME: Mixture-of-Memory Embeddings for Context-Aware Sparse Lookup
summary: Scaling large language models efficiently has motivated sparse capacity mechanisms such as Mixture-of-Experts and, more recently, conditional memory: token-indexed embedding tables that augment the backbone with cheap parametric lookups. Existing memory-embedding methods retrieve via a deterministic function of the surface form, which collapses different contextual senses of the same token (e.g., python the language vs. the animal) into a single fixed entry. We introduce Mixture of Memory Embeddings (MoME), a context-aware memory mechanism that replaces each token's single memory row with a mixture of M slots and uses a learned gate over the hidden state to choose which slots to read at each position. In controlled pretraining experiments across nanochat, Llama-3/MobileLLM, and Qwen3 backbones, MoME improves over Value Embedding, Bigram, and STEM baselines in iso-parameter and iso-training-FLOP settings, shows a more promising memory-size scaling trend at sub-billion scale, and remains efficient in training and inference. Qualitative routing analyses on polysemous tokens further suggest that the learned mixture exhibits a degree of semantic interpretability, dispatching the same surface token to distinct memory slots under different senses.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Mixture of Memory Embeddings (MoME), a context-aware conditional memory mechanism for large language models that assigns multiple memory slots per token and uses a learned gate to choose slots based on context, improving performance and scaling over prior memory-embedding baselines while remaining efficient.
AI.motivation: Existing sparse capacity methods like Mixture-of-Experts and conditional memory improve LLM efficiency, but current memory-embedding approaches map each token to a single deterministic memory entry. This conflates different meanings of polysemous tokens (e.g., “python” as language vs. animal), limiting expressiveness and potential gains from conditional memory. The authors aim to design a memory mechanism that is both efficient and context-sensitive, able to differentiate senses of the same surface token without sacrificing scalability or efficiency.
AI.method: They propose Mixture of Memory Embeddings (MoME), where each token is associated with a mixture of M memory slots instead of a single row. At each token position, the model uses the current hidden state to compute a learned gating distribution over these M slots and reads a weighted combination (or selected subset) of them. This yields context-aware memory lookups that can route the same token to different slots depending on its contextual sense. MoME is integrated into several backbones (nanochat, Llama-3/MobileLLM, Qwen3) and evaluated under iso-parameter and iso-training-FLOP conditions against Value Embedding, Bigram, and STEM baselines. The authors also analyze routing patterns for polysemous tokens to study interpretability of the learned mixture.
AI.result: Across controlled pretraining experiments on multiple backbones, MoME consistently outperforms baselines such as Value Embedding, Bigram, and STEM when matched on parameter count and training FLOPs. It demonstrates better scaling behavior with increasing memory size at sub-billion parameter scales, while maintaining training and inference efficiency. Qualitative analyses show that for polysemous tokens, the gating mechanism routes different contextual senses to different memory slots, indicating that the mixture learns semantically meaningful specializations.
AI.conclusion: MoME provides an effective, efficient, and context-aware conditional memory mechanism for large language models. By replacing single token memories with mixtures of learnable slots and using context-dependent gating, it overcomes the limitation of collapsing multiple senses into one embedding, yields better performance and more favorable scaling trends than prior memory-embedding methods, and exhibits signs of semantic interpretability in how tokens are routed to memory slots.

title: Medical Knowledge Simplification for Patients in the Era of LLMs: A Case Study on Diabetes
summary: Complex medical information is often difficult for patients to understand, making effective medical knowledge simplification essential for improving patient comprehension, informed decision-making, and health outcomes. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide a promising approach for simplifying complex medical information into patient-friendly language; however, their effectiveness in real-world patient education remains insufficiently explored through human evaluation. To investigate their practical effectiveness, this paper presents a case study on diabetes knowledge simplification through the implementation and evaluation of MediClear, an LLM-based medical knowledge simplification system enhanced with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Public diabetes-related articles from Diabetes Australia, WHO, American Diabetes Association (ADA), NIDDK, and AIHW are indexed in the RAG knowledge base to retrieve clinically grounded information, which is then simplified by the LLM into accessible patient explanations. We evaluate the generated responses using standard readability metrics, including the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL), and conduct a human study involving 10 participants. Results show that MediClear consistently reduces the reading level of generated responses to the recommended patient literacy range while achieving high user satisfaction and willingness for future use. This case study demonstrates the potential of LLMs to improve the accessibility of medical knowledge for patient education.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MediClear, an LLM + RAG system that simplifies authoritative diabetes information into patient-friendly text, showing improved readability and high user satisfaction in a small human study.
AI.motivation: Patients struggle to understand complex medical information, which hurts comprehension and health decisions. While LLMs can rewrite text in simpler language, their real-world effectiveness for patient education, especially with clinically reliable content, has not been well validated through human evaluation. The authors want to see if an LLM-based, clinically grounded system can reliably simplify diabetes information to appropriate health literacy levels and be accepted by users.
AI.method: The authors build MediClear, a medical knowledge simplification system that combines a large language model with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). They index public, authoritative diabetes-related articles from organizations like Diabetes Australia, WHO, ADA, NIDDK, and AIHW into a retrieval system. For a user query, MediClear retrieves relevant passages and has the LLM generate simplified, patient-friendly explanations grounded in these sources. They evaluate outputs via readability metrics such as Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level and run a human study with 10 participants to rate satisfaction and willingness for future use.
AI.result: MediClear’s outputs consistently lower the reading level of the medical content into the recommended range for patient health literacy, as measured by FKGL and similar metrics. In the human study, participants report high satisfaction with the explanations and indicate strong willingness to use the system again for medical information.
AI.conclusion: MediClear shows that combining LLMs with RAG over trusted medical sources can effectively simplify complex diabetes information, yielding text that is more readable for patients and well-received by users. The case study suggests that LLM-based systems have strong potential to improve accessibility and understanding of medical knowledge in patient education, though broader and larger-scale evaluations will be needed for generalization.

title: Improving Mathematical Reasoning Capabilities in Large Language Models via Reasoning Process Error Classification
summary: The reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) is a critical factor for practical LLM-based applications. To investigate the current reasoning capability of LLMs, we clarify the types of errors that arise in LLMs' reasoning processes on mathematical datasets. We focus on problems where LLMs produce an incorrect answer. We define errors in the reasoning process as reasoning errors and manually analyze the features of reasoning errors. We defined and classified 21 error classes and identified the frequently occurring classes among them. Beyond qualitative evaluation, we leverage the evaluation results to improve the reasoning capability. We designed a prompt that explicitly focuses on eight error classes. The experiments demonstrate that this prompt effectively improves reasoning performance. Furthermore, the results suggest that the frequent reasoning errors identified in this paper are common across LLMs of comparable scale.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how large language models make reasoning mistakes on math problems, classifies these errors into 21 types, and shows that prompts targeting the most common ones improve reasoning performance.
AI.motivation: Reasoning ability is crucial for real-world use of large language models, yet their specific failure modes on mathematical reasoning tasks are not well understood. A detailed taxonomy of reasoning errors can help diagnose weaknesses and guide methods to improve performance.
AI.method: The authors focus on math problems where LLMs give wrong answers. They manually inspect and annotate the step-by-step reasoning traces to define and categorize distinct reasoning error types, resulting in 21 error classes. They then design a new prompt that explicitly draws the model’s attention to eight of the most frequent error classes and evaluate its impact on reasoning performance across LLMs of similar scale.
AI.result: They obtain a taxonomy of 21 reasoning error classes and identify which of these appear most frequently. Using this insight, they craft a targeted prompt that focuses on eight common error types and empirically show that this prompt significantly improves reasoning accuracy on mathematical tasks. They also find that the identified frequent error classes generalize across different LLMs of comparable size.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning failures in LLMs on mathematical tasks can be systematically classified into a set of recurring error types. Making these error types explicit and prompting models to avoid them measurably boosts reasoning performance, and the observed error patterns appear to be shared among LLMs with similar scales.

title: HazardAuditor: From Executable Threats to Safer Computer-Use Agents
summary: Computer-use agents increasingly interact with browsers, terminals, file systems, and external services, introducing safety risks that emerge through runtime behavior rather than generated content alone. Existing guard models target static prompts and responses and are poorly suited to agent execution; existing executable safety platforms produce evaluation verdicts rather than the normalized supervision a guard model needs to learn across heterogeneous agent frameworks. We introduce HazardAuditor, an execution-grounded framework that closes both gaps. Its infrastructure runs heterogeneous agents (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, and OpenClaw) in controlled environments and normalizes their interactions into a canonical event representation for cross-framework supervision. We further observe that token-level post-training objectives create a structural mismatch for generative guards, causing longer rationales to dominate gradient updates. Guard Policy Optimization (GuardPO) addresses this by converting deterministic safety outcomes into sequence-level advantages and normalizing rationale and verdict regions, making the safety decision the effective unit of optimization. Across multiple benchmarks and heterogeneous computer-use systems, HazardAuditor improves accuracy by up to 16.5 percentage points over the strongest prior guard. Code, models, and evaluation artifacts will be available at https://yunhao-feng.github.io/HazardAuditor/.

AI.tldr: HazardAuditor is a framework and training method for safety guards that supervise computer-use agents during execution, yielding substantially better safety accuracy across multiple agent systems.
AI.motivation: Computer-use agents now control browsers, terminals, file systems, and external tools, creating safety risks that only appear during their runtime actions rather than in static text. Existing safety guards are designed for static prompts/outputs and cannot effectively supervise live agent executions, while current executable safety platforms output ad hoc evaluation labels instead of the consistent, normalized supervision signal needed to train general-purpose guard models across different agent frameworks. There is also a training mismatch: guards trained with token-level objectives over long rationales get gradients dominated by explanation tokens rather than the core safety decision.
AI.method: The authors design HazardAuditor, an execution-grounded supervision framework that (1) runs diverse computer-use agents (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw) inside controlled environments and (2) converts their heterogeneous tool calls and actions into a unified, canonical event representation suitable for cross-framework safety supervision. For learning the guard, they introduce Guard Policy Optimization (GuardPO), which takes deterministic safety labels (hazard vs safe) as sequence-level outcomes, converts them into advantages, and normalizes the contribution of rationale and verdict segments so the guard is optimized primarily on the correctness of its safety decision rather than the length or wording of its explanation.
AI.result: On multiple benchmarks involving different computer-use systems, HazardAuditor substantially outperforms prior guard approaches, achieving up to a 16.5 percentage-point improvement in safety accuracy over the strongest existing guard model. This demonstrates both the value of execution-grounded, normalized supervision and the effectiveness of GuardPO’s sequence-level optimization for generative safety guards.
AI.conclusion: Execution-grounded safety supervision with a canonical event representation enables a single guard model to monitor heterogeneous computer-use agents more effectively than prior static prompt-based approaches. GuardPO aligns the training objective with the real decision unit (the overall safety verdict) and mitigates structural issues of token-level training on long rationales. Together, these contributions provide a practical, higher-accuracy path to supervising complex agent behaviors in real computer-use environments, and the authors plan to release code, models, and evaluation artifacts for broader use and extension.

title: EMR: Self-Evolving Medical Multi-Agent System via Experience Mining and Reuse
summary: Large language model (LLM) driven multi-agent systems have shown promise in complex clinical reasoning, yet existing approaches rely on static strategies and lack persistent clinical memory, preventing self-evolving from prior diagnostic successes and failures. We present EMR, a self-evolving medical multi-agent system via Experience Mining and Reuse. EMR introduces a hierarchical clinical experience library that organizes accumulated knowledge into three levels: clinical principles, diagnostic patterns, and representative cases. During inference, EMR emulates multidisciplinary consultation: a planner agent coordinates domain-specific department agents for specialized reasoning, while a summary agent synthesizes their analyses into a final decision. Critically, EMR automatically extracts correct diagnostic insights and failure-related warnings from multi-agent reasoning trajectories, incrementally updating the experience library to guide future cases. Experiments on medical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that EMR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art medical multi-agent baselines. Further analysis reveals that the hierarchical experience enables cross-specialty generalization and transfer across diverse LLM backbones, offering a scalable and in

AI.tldr: EMR is a self-improving LLM-based medical multi-agent system that mines past reasoning experiences to build a hierarchical clinical memory, enabling better and more transferable diagnostic performance than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based medical multi-agent systems use fixed, static strategies and lack a persistent, structured clinical memory. As a result, they cannot systematically learn from past diagnostic successes and failures, nor can they generalize their accumulated knowledge across future cases or different model backbones. The paper aims to overcome these limitations by designing a system that can continuously capture, organize, and reuse rich experiential knowledge from its own multi-agent reasoning processes.
AI.method: The authors propose EMR, a multi-agent framework with a hierarchical clinical experience library. This library has three levels: (1) high-level clinical principles, (2) mid-level diagnostic patterns, and (3) concrete representative cases. Inference mimics multidisciplinary consultation: a planner agent dispatches tasks to department-specific expert agents; each performs domain-specific reasoning; then a summary agent integrates their outputs into a final diagnosis/decision. After each case, the system automatically mines its own reasoning trajectory to extract (a) validated correct diagnostic insights and (b) warnings derived from failure modes. These are incrementally stored in the experience library and later retrieved to guide subsequent reasoning in new cases. The design is evaluated on multiple medical reasoning benchmarks and across different LLM backbones.
AI.result: Across medical reasoning benchmarks, EMR achieves consistently higher diagnostic performance and reasoning quality than existing medical multi-agent baselines. The hierarchical experience library improves not only accuracy but also robustness by enabling the system to avoid previously observed failure patterns. The authors also show that the mined experiences transfer well across medical specialties and remain useful when plugged into different underlying LLMs, indicating that the representation is backbone-agnostic and supports cross-model generalization.
AI.conclusion: EMR demonstrates that equipping LLM-based multi-agent medical systems with a structured, hierarchical experience memory and an automatic experience mining mechanism leads to continuous self-improvement in clinical reasoning. The framework scales across specialties and LLM backbones, suggesting a general approach for building adaptive, self-evolving AI assistants in healthcare and potentially other complex reasoning domains.

title: T-LoopFormer: Token-Level Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning With Dynamic Routing
summary: Looped Transformers have recently demonstrated strong performance in both reasoning and language tasks by reusing a shared set of parameters across multiple iterations, achieving parameter efficiency without sacrificing representational power. Besides, looped Transformers perform inference directly in the latent space (latent reasoning) to reduce the number of tokens consumed during inference, thereby achieving improved sample efficiency. However, these models typically apply a fixed recursion depth uniformly to every token, leading to suboptimal compute allocation and leaving significant efficiency gains on the table. In this work, we propose \textbf{dynamic token-choice routing} for looped transformers, enabling each token to adaptively determine its own number of loop iterations based on its hidden state. We use a dynamic router to decide whether a token should continue recursing or exit early, allowing simple tokens to bypass unnecessary computation while hard tokens receive deeper processing. To ensure that this adaptive mechanism does not compromise decoding efficiency, we further introduce recursion-wise KV caching, which maintains an independent key-value cache for each recursion loop. This design ensures that tokens at different depths only attend to their corresponding cached states, effectively eliminating redundant computations for exited tokens and enabling fast autoregressive decoding. Extensive experiments show that T-LoopFormer reaches the sota performance under the same parameters on PPL and 10 zero-shot reasoning tasks, even surpassing the base model at 24x FLOPs and our model could reach the lowest inference latency, which validate the effectiveness of token-choice router and recursion-wise KV cache. Code: https://github.com/YuMingQian1234/T-LoopFormer.

AI.tldr: They propose T-LoopFormer, a looped Transformer with dynamic token-wise routing and specialized KV caching, improving efficiency and performance by letting each token choose its own recursion depth.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers reuse parameters over multiple iterations and perform latent reasoning to be parameter and sample efficient, but they currently use a fixed recursion depth for all tokens. This wastes computation because easy tokens are over-processed while hard tokens may need more depth, leading to suboptimal compute allocation and unnecessary FLOPs and latency.
AI.method: Introduce dynamic token-choice routing in looped Transformers: each token adaptively decides how many loop iterations to undergo based on its hidden state. A learned dynamic router determines, at each loop, whether a token keeps recursing or exits. To keep decoding efficient, they design recursion-wise KV caching, where each recursion depth has its own key-value cache. Tokens at different depths attend only to their corresponding cache, which avoids recomputing attention for tokens that have already exited and enables fast autoregressive decoding.
AI.result: On language modeling (perplexity) and 10 zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, T-LoopFormer achieves state-of-the-art performance among models with the same parameter count, and even outperforms the base non-looped model while using up to 24x more FLOPs. Their approach also attains the lowest inference latency among compared methods, demonstrating that dynamic token-choice routing and recursion-wise KV caching yield both better accuracy and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, token-level control of recursion depth in looped Transformers can significantly improve the trade-off between compute, latency, and performance. By combining a token-choice router with recursion-wise KV caches, T-LoopFormer allocates more computation to difficult tokens and less to easy ones, achieving superior perplexity and reasoning scores without increasing parameters and with reduced latency, validating the effectiveness of adaptive routing in latent reasoning models.

title: CITECHOICE: A Causal Audit of How Document Presentation Redistributes Citation Credit in Agentic Search
summary:
When several retrieved sources support the same claim, an answer engine cites some but not others. We call this decision citation allocation and introduce CITECHOICE, a causal audit of authentic multi-turn agentic search. From 129 everyday-query transcripts, CITECHOICE selects 113 same-call document pairs with independently verified support for the same pre-specified fact, without observing ranks or answer outcomes; blinded human review confirms 103. It runs a hash-verified 2-by-2 replay crossing pair order with jointly generated, fidelity-checked structured and prose renderings of one target while the rest of the transcript remains fixed.
  Three results emerge. First, and most importantly, structured rendering concentrates citation credit rather than clearly increasing source admission. It raises target citation count by +0.50 citations per answer (95 percent CI [+0.20, +0.84]; Holm-adjusted p=.033), without increasing total citations or reducing competitor credit. The pre-specified incidence effect (whether the target is cited at all) is +4.5 percentage points and inconclusive (95 percent CI [-1.4, +10.4]; p=.168). Second, observational position differences exceed controlled reordering effects: the citation-rate gap between rank 1 and rank 5 is 42.3 percentage points, compared with +7.9 percentage points in the main replay and 0.0 percentage points held out. Third, citation evaluation has a measurable noise floor. Although the aggregate count effect repeats under fresh decoding of 30 frozen families, 15 percent of binary decisions change and decoding accounts for an estimated 45 percent of single-generation family-effect variance. Together, these findings isolate what survives control: presentation can causally redistribute visible citation credit within frozen transcripts. They do not establish reliable source admission, a pure formatting mechanism, or a general rank advantage.

AI.tldr: Study of how answer engines choose which supporting sources to cite when multiple documents support the same claim.
AI.motivation: In modern answer engines and LLM-based systems, multiple retrieved documents can support the same factual claim, but only a subset is cited in the final answer. This affects transparency, perceived reliability, and credit attribution to sources. However, it is unclear whether citation choices are driven by meaningful causal factors like presentation format or ranking, or are largely incidental or noisy. The paper aims to causally audit how citation credit is allocated among equally valid sources in realistic multi-turn search scenarios.
AI.method: The authors introduce CITECHOICE, a causal audit framework built on authentic multi-turn agentic search transcripts. From 129 real-world query transcripts, they identify 113 pairs of documents that independently support the same pre-specified fact, verified without using ranking or outcome information; blinded human review confirms 103 valid pairs. They then perform a 2×2 replay experiment: they cross the order of the document pair with whether one document (the target) is rendered in a more structured, high-fidelity format (structured and prose rendering) while keeping the rest of the transcript fixed. Hash verification ensures experimental integrity. They measure how these manipulations affect citation counts and incidence (whether a document is cited at all), compare observational rank-position gaps to controlled reordering effects, and evaluate randomness/noise by re-decoding 30 frozen model families and quantifying decision variability.
AI.result: 1) Structured rendering of a target source increases its share of citation credit without increasing overall citation volume. Specifically, it increases the target’s citation count by about +0.50 citations per answer (95% CI [+0.20, +0.84]; Holm-adjusted p=.033) but does not raise total citations or reduce competitor citations. The pre-registered effect on citation incidence (probability of being cited at all) is modest (+4.5 percentage points) and statistically inconclusive (95% CI [-1.4, +10.4]; p=.168). 2) Observed rank-position differences in citation rates are larger than the causal effect of controlled reordering: the citation rate gap between rank 1 and rank 5 is 42.3 percentage points observationally, versus only +7.9 percentage points under experimental replay and 0.0 percentage points in a held-out condition. 3) Citation decisions exhibit a measurable noise floor: when re-decoding 30 frozen model families, the aggregate citation count effect persists, but ~15% of binary citation decisions flip, and sampling noise from decoding explains an estimated 45% of the variance in single-generation family effects.
AI.conclusion: Presentation format can causally shift which sources receive visible citation credit within a fixed interaction, but this does not robustly increase the chance that a source is admitted (cited at all), nor does it establish a strong, general causal advantage for higher-ranked documents. Citation allocation appears sensitive to formatting, rank correlates with but may not causally drive citation, and model sampling introduces substantial noise in which supporting sources are credited. The work suggests that current answer engines may redistribute credit among equally valid sources based on presentation rather than consistently improving source coverage or fairness, and that any evaluation of citation behavior must account for a non-trivial noise floor.

title: STHMoE: Hypergraph-Enhanced Heterogeneous Dependency Coordination for LLM-Based Urban Traffic Data Forecasting
summary: Spatio-temporal traffic forecasting is a fundamental big data analytics task for intelligent transportation systems, where massive urban sensor streams exhibit heterogeneous, non-stationary, and structurally dynamic patterns. Although recent deep learning and large language model (LLM)-based methods have advanced traffic forecasting, they often remain temporally centered and lack effective coordination of temporal, spectral, pairwise spatial, and higher-order structural cues under evolving traffic regimes. To address this heterogeneous dependency coordination problem, we propose STHMoE, a Spatio-Temporal Hypergraph-Enhanced Mixture of Experts framework for urban traffic data forecasting. STHMoE decouples traffic dynamics into frequency-domain, time-domain, spatio-domain, and higher-order spatial representations, which are modeled by prompt-guided heterogeneous experts built upon a partially frozen LLM backbone. The first three experts leverage domain-specific statistical prompts, while the higher-order spatio expert uses a structural placeholder prompt and obtains dependency information from an adaptive hypergraph module. To capture evolving spatial structures in traffic data,, STHMoE jointly learns first-order graph dependencies and higher-order group interactions without predefined topologies. An entropy-aware MoE router with coefficient-of-variation load balancing adaptively fuses expert outputs while improving expert utilization and routing confidence. Experiments on 10 real-world traffic benchmarks show that STHMoE achieves competitive performance against temporal, spatio-temporal graph, and LLM-based baselines.

AI.tldr: STHMoE is a mixture-of-experts model that uses hypergraphs and a partially frozen LLM with prompts to jointly capture temporal, spectral, pairwise spatial, and higher-order structural patterns for traffic forecasting, achieving strong results on many real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning and LLM-based traffic forecasting models tend to be temporally focused and struggle to jointly coordinate heterogeneous dependencies: time-domain dynamics, frequency-domain patterns, pairwise spatial relations, and higher-order structural interactions, especially when traffic regimes evolve and network structures are non-stationary and not predefined.
AI.method: The authors propose STHMoE, a Spatio-Temporal Hypergraph-Enhanced Mixture of Experts framework. They decouple traffic dynamics into four representations—frequency-domain, time-domain, spatio-domain, and higher-order spatial.
