Each is handled by a dedicated expert module built on a partially frozen LLM backbone, guided by different prompts: statistical prompts for the first three experts and a structural placeholder prompt for the higher-order expert, which gets structural cues from an adaptive hypergraph module. The model jointly learns first-order graph dependencies and higher-order group interactions without requiring a predefined topology. An entropy-aware MoE router with coefficient-of-variation-based load balancing adaptively fuses expert outputs, increasing expert utilization and routing confidence.
AI.result: On 10 real-world traffic forecasting benchmarks, STHMoE achieves competitive or superior performance compared with strong baselines, including purely temporal models, spatio-temporal graph neural networks, and other LLM-based forecasting approaches.
AI.conclusion: By coordinating heterogeneous temporal, spectral, spatial, and higher-order structural dependencies through a prompt-guided LLM-based mixture-of-experts with adaptive hypergraph modeling and an entropy-aware router, STHMoE effectively handles complex, evolving traffic regimes, leading to improved traffic forecasting accuracy across diverse real-world scenarios.

title: MUSE: A Theory-Harnessed Story Engine for Vibe Narrativizing
summary: LLMs can generate fluent prose. Story quality depends on how decisions about plot, character, and language work together across planning, drafting, and revision. Guiding these decisions presents two bottlenecks: the quality of story guidance and its sustained use. We formulate Vibe Narrativizing as the task of turning natural-language writing requirements into a finished story and present MUSE, a Theory-Harnessed Story Engine. MUSE organizes story knowledge as guidance for specific decisions and carries those decisions into subsequent creative work. Knowledge engineering develops Robert McKee's story theory through rule atomization, semantic consolidation, and mechanism abstraction; a single source of truth and layered disclosure organize the resulting guidance. Typical examples complement principles that depend on context and aesthetic judgment. An agent harness organizes design, character performance, scene composition, and revision through intermediate deliverables that preserve story decisions. Context engineering supplies each role with the relevant guidance and decisions, while a masterwork corpus provides inspiration and prose references. A worked example follows one requested object from its thematic role to the characters' climactic actions. Across four base models, MUSE improves WritingBench by 1.6-4.8 points over zero-shot generation and raises LongStoryEval by more than ten points on three. ConStory-Bench consistency error density remains in the low single digits for all four models, below every reproduced story-system baseline on three. Component ablations locate the largest quality contribution in structural design, voice-specific effects in the character path, and further gains in revision. Code is available at https://github.com/RoadtoAGI/MUSE.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MUSE, a theory-driven story generation system that turns natural-language writing requirements into higher-quality, consistent long-form stories.
AI.motivation: While LLMs can write fluent text, they struggle with sustained story quality, coherence, and effective use of writing guidance across planning, drafting, and revision. The authors want a systematic way to encode story theory and to ensure that decisions about plot, character, and style are preserved throughout the generation process.
AI.method: They define the task of “Vibe Narrativizing” (turning informal story requirements into a complete story) and build MUSE, a Theory-Harnessed Story Engine. Using knowledge engineering on Robert McKee’s story theory, they decompose it into fine-grained rules, consolidate semantics, and abstract mechanisms, organizing them with a single source of truth and layered disclosure. An agent-based architecture then uses these rules to guide design, character performance, scene composition, and revision via intermediate deliverables that preserve earlier decisions. Context engineering ensures each agent role only sees relevant guidance and prior decisions, and a corpus of masterworks provides stylistic and structural references. They perform ablation studies to assess the contribution of major components.
AI.result: On standard long-form fiction benchmarks, MUSE outperforms zero-shot LLM baselines across four base models, improving WritingBench scores by 1.6–4.8 points and boosting LongStoryEval scores by more than ten points on three models. It also achieves low consistency error density on ConStory-Bench, outperforming prior story systems in most cases. Ablations show structural design contributes most to quality, the character-focused path strongly affects narrative voice, and revision yields additional gains.
AI.conclusion: Encoding expert story theory into an organized guidance system and coupling it with an agent-based workflow significantly improves LLM story generation. By preserving and reusing explicit story decisions across the creative pipeline, MUSE produces more coherent, structured, and consistent narratives than existing baselines, and its modular design clarifies where different aspects of story craft add value.

title: VisInteract: Towards Dynamic Interactive Text-to-Visualization under Imperfect Queries
summary: Real-world visualization requests are routinely ambiguous, incomplete, or factually incorrect, yet existing Text-to-Visualization (Text-to-Vis) systems assume well-specified inputs and produce charts in a single pass. When queries are imperfect, a system must \emph{interact} with the user to recover the true intent, but no benchmark or method supports this dynamic process. We introduce \textbf{VisInteract}, a new paradigm that reframes Text-to-Vis as interaction-driven intent recovery, and \textbf{VisInteract-Bench}, to our knowledge, that is the first benchmark for dynamic interactive Text-to-Vis, featuring controlled imperfection injection, a leakage-controlled User Agent for realistic multi-turn feedback, and dual-perspective (code and chart) automated evaluation. On the algorithmic side, we propose \textbf{Vis-MCTS}, a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) enhanced method, introducing improvements over classical MCTS, that \emph{Progressive Widening} to tame the unbounded tool-argument space in tree search, \emph{cross-rollout information sharing} so clarifications and critiques benefit the entire search tree, and \emph{Dimension-Aware Reward Decomposition} that routes scalar user feedback along data-fidelity, visual-design, and intent-alignment dimensions to resolve credit assignment across heterogeneous actions. Extensive Experiments across two LLM backbones show that Vis-MCTS consistently outperforms all Text-to-Vis baselines, improving end-to-end task success by $13.40\%$--$16.27\%$ over the strongest interactive baseline and by more than $5\times$ over non-interactive ones.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VisInteract, a new interaction-driven paradigm and benchmark for Text-to-Visualization, and Vis-MCTS, an MCTS-based method that uses interaction to recover user intent and significantly improves visualization generation performance.
AI.motivation: Existing Text-to-Vis systems assume user queries are clean, complete, and correct, but in real-world scenarios user requests are ambiguous, incomplete, or wrong. These systems also typically generate a visualization in a single pass without clarifying questions or iterative refinement. There is no benchmark or standardized method for dynamic, multi-turn Text-to-Vis that explicitly models interaction and intent recovery. The paper aims to fill this gap by redefining the problem as interaction-driven intent recovery and by providing both a benchmark and an algorithmic solution.
AI.method: The authors propose VisInteract, a paradigm that treats Text-to-Vis as a multi-turn interaction process for recovering user intent. They build VisInteract-Bench, a benchmark that injects controlled imperfections into user queries, simulates realistic multi-turn feedback via a leakage-controlled User Agent, and evaluates outputs from both code and rendered chart perspectives. Algorithmically, they introduce Vis-MCTS, a Monte Carlo Tree Search-based method tailored for interactive Text-to-Vis. Vis-MCTS extends classical MCTS with: (1) Progressive Widening to handle an unbounded tool-argument action space; (2) cross-rollout information sharing, allowing clarifications and critiques from one trajectory to inform the entire search tree; and (3) Dimension-Aware Reward Decomposition, which decomposes scalar user feedback into data-fidelity, visual-design, and intent-alignment components to better assign credit to heterogeneous actions during search.
AI.result: Using two different LLM backbones, the experiments show that Vis-MCTS consistently outperforms prior Text-to-Vis baselines. It improves end-to-end task success by 13.40%–16.27% over the strongest existing interactive baseline and achieves more than a 5× improvement compared to non-interactive Text-to-Vis systems on the VisInteract-Bench benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Interaction is essential for realistic Text-to-Vis systems because real user queries are often imperfect. By reframing Text-to-Vis as interaction-driven intent recovery and providing VisInteract-Bench and the Vis-MCTS algorithm, the paper demonstrates that multi-turn, search-based interaction substantially improves visualization generation quality. The proposed MCTS extensions and evaluation framework provide a foundation for future research on interactive, tool-using LLM systems for visualization and potentially other domains where user intent must be inferred over multiple turns.

title: What Limits Us? Analyzing Self-Reported Limitations in NLP Research
summary: Since late 2022, a Limitations section has become mandatory at many top-tier NLP conferences. The growing number of accepted papers at these venues has resulted in a vast corpus of self-reported limitations that cannot all be manually reviewed, yet remains systematically unanalyzed. Therefore, in this paper, we conduct a large-scale analysis of the Limitations sections from ACL and EMNLP papers published between 2020 and 2025 to understand what researchers disclose about their own work. To do so, we implement a novel human-AI framework for iterative hybrid qualitative coding. This framework enables us to investigate trends in self-reported limitations over time, their correlations with specific paper attributes, and the writing patterns that recur around these disclosures. Our findings offer a critical reflection on the diverse reported challenges as well as the self-reporting practices of researchers in the NLP community.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes Limitations sections from ACL and EMNLP papers (2020–2025) using a human-AI hybrid qualitative coding framework to uncover trends and patterns in self-reported limitations in NLP research.
AI.motivation: A mandatory Limitations section at major NLP venues has created a large, unexplored corpus of self-reported weaknesses in published work. Manually reviewing all these sections is infeasible, yet understanding what researchers acknowledge as limitations is valuable for assessing research practices, transparency, and areas needing improvement in the field.
AI.method: The authors collect Limitations sections from ACL and EMNLP papers published between 2020 and 2025 and apply a novel human-AI framework for iterative hybrid qualitative coding. This involves combining automated analysis (likely NLP models) with human coders in multiple rounds to categorize limitation types, link them to paper attributes, and analyze recurring linguistic and structural patterns in how limitations are presented.
AI.result: They identify temporal trends in the kinds of limitations reported, correlations between self-reported limitations and specific attributes of papers (e.g., task type, methodology, or venue), and characteristic writing patterns around limitation disclosures. The analysis surfaces diverse challenges acknowledged by authors and systematic patterns in how these are framed and communicated.
AI.conclusion: Self-reported limitations in NLP papers contain rich, structured information about the challenges and weaknesses of current research practices. The proposed human-AI hybrid coding framework enables scalable analysis of these sections, revealing evolving trends and community practices. The work provides a foundation for more reflective, transparent, and possibly standardized approaches to reporting limitations in NLP research.

title: Issue Bias in Generative AI Writing Assistance: Political Issues and LLMs in the Swedish 2026 Election
summary: Generative AI writing assistants and the Large Language Models (LLMs) that power them are increasingly part of how voters gather information before elections. With growing evidence that they influence users' opinions, it is increasingly important to understand the views and positions of these tools. To better understand these views, we examine the stances supplied by six LLMs on a variety of Swedish-language writing tasks ahead of the 2026 Swedish parliamentary election. We cross 107 policy propositions with 77 writing templates and neutral, positive, and negative prompt framings, producing 24,717 prompts per model and 148,302 responses. To study these, we look at the models' default stance tendencies, compare how they respond to similar issues, and compare their responses with those of each of Sweden's eight parliamentary parties on the same issue. We find that Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, and Mistral have similar profiles; ChatGPT more often supplies neutral or ambivalent text; and Grok differs most on topics such as migration, crime, and gender. When comparing the political parties, we find that the Social Democrats are closest to all six models. Still, after correcting for multiple comparisons, none of the within-model differences in party distances remains significant. Overall, we find that no model has a clear preference, nor a clear preference for a party, but that this depends on the specific issue or task the user asks about.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how six major large language models (LLMs) respond to Swedish political prompts ahead of the 2026 parliamentary election, mapping their stance patterns and proximity to party positions.
AI.motivation: As generative AI tools become a key source of pre‑election information, their potential to shape voter opinions raises concerns about hidden or systematic political leanings. The authors want to empirically characterize these leanings in a specific national context (Sweden) to see whether LLMs exhibit consistent stances or implicit preferences for certain parties or issue positions.
AI.method: They query six LLMs with 24,717 systematically constructed Swedish-language prompts per model (148,302 total responses). Prompts cross 107 policy propositions with 77 writing templates and three framings (neutral, positive, negative). They then code or infer the stance in each response, examine default stance tendencies, compare how models treat similar issues, and compute distances between each model’s responses and the official positions of Sweden’s eight parliamentary parties on the same propositions. They apply multiple-comparison corrections when testing for significant differences in party proximity.
AI.result: Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, and Mistral show similar stance profiles. ChatGPT is more likely to produce neutral or ambivalent text. Grok diverges the most, particularly on migration, crime, and gender issues. In terms of party proximity, all six models are closest overall to the Swedish Social Democrats, but once correcting for multiple comparisons, no within-model differences in distances to different parties remain statistically significant.
AI.conclusion: Across a large, systematic prompt set, no LLM shows a robust, statistically clear overall preference for any Swedish party. Apparent proximity to the Social Democrats is not significant after multiple-comparison correction. Model behavior is issue- and task-dependent: their stance profiles shift with topic and prompt framing, and different models cluster or diverge on certain issue areas, but they do not exhibit a consistent, unambiguous partisan bias in this study.

title: Semiotic Relations and Proof Methods: A Cross-Genre Study of Argument Structure with Large Language Models
summary: When a direct proof of a statement $S$ seems hard or even impossible to obtain, there may exist another statement (or set of statements) $S^{*}$, somehow related to $S$, on the basis of which $S$ can be proved. In order to investigate what options can be used to move from $S$ to $S^{*}$, four kinds of semiotic relations inspired by the four master tropes of semiotic research are briefly reviewed. Specifically, our syntagmatic, paradigmatic, antithetic and meronymic relations correspond, respectively, to metonymy, metaphor, irony and synecdoche. It is suggested that these four semiotic relations determine the options to move from $S$ to $S^{*}$, leading to proof by inference, proof by analogy, proof by contradiction, and proof by case analysis. To examine how the four relations are actually used across different kinds of argument, we complement the framework with an empirical study. We turn the four relations into explicit operational definitions and apply them to a cross-genre corpus of mathematical, legal, and everyday argument using a panel of large language models. We find that the relations are used very unevenly across genres: mathematical proofs draw on all four, whereas legal and everyday reasoning rely almost entirely on inference.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a semiotic framework linking four kinds of relations between statements (syntagmatic, paradigmatic, antithetic, meronymic) to four proof/argument types, and empirically studies their use across mathematical, legal, and everyday arguments via large language models.
AI.motivation: Direct proofs of a target statement S are often hard to obtain. In practice, reasoners move to a related statement S* that makes S provable, but we lack a systematic account of the kinds of relations that can connect S and S*. The authors want a principled, general framework—grounded in semiotics and rhetoric—to classify these relations and see how they manifest across domains (mathematics, law, everyday reasoning), and to test whether different genres of argument favor different types of S–S* relations.
AI.method: Conceptually, they map four semiotic relations to four traditional master tropes: syntagmatic→metonymy, paradigmatic→metaphor, antithetic→irony, meronymic→synecdoche. They then align these with four proof/argument forms: inference, analogy, contradiction, and case analysis. Empirically, they operationalize the four relations as explicit coding categories. Using a cross-genre corpus (mathematical proofs, legal arguments, everyday arguments), they employ a panel of large language models as annotators to detect which relation(s) are present in each argument, allowing comparison of frequency and distribution across genres.
AI.result: The analysis shows a strong genre effect. Mathematical proofs make substantial use of all four semiotic relations—thus all four corresponding proof/argument types appear as meaningful routes from S to S*. In contrast, legal and everyday arguments overwhelmingly instantiate only the syntagmatic/inference relation, with the other three relations comparatively rare or marginal.
AI.conclusion: The four semiotic relations provide a unifying lens on how arguments move from a target statement S to related statements S* that support its proof. Different argument genres exploit these relations very differently: mathematics uses a rich repertoire (inference, analogy, contradiction, case analysis), whereas legal and everyday reasoning are dominated by straightforward inferential moves. This supports the value of a semiotic classification of proof strategies and highlights systematic differences in reasoning patterns across domains.

title: From Ideas to Actions: A Public-Data Decision-Support Toolchain Across the Venture Lifecycle
comment: 39 pages. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/quge007/eventchain ; Code and agent skills: https://github.com/quge009/startup-decision-skills
summary: Founders face two linked decisions: whether to pursue an idea before founding, and which operating actions and capital partners fit afterward. We present a public-data decision-support toolchain combining time-bounded proposal profiling, market and moat checks, and deterministic aggregation with auditable investor-company event chains for retrospective analysis. Pre-founding: (a) After threshold selection on 198 development companies, the frozen pipeline achieves F0.5=0.5357 [0.412, 0.655] on an independent, row-disjoint 198-company validation sample. On the combined 396 rows, the Full Pipeline scores 0.6301 versus 0.2734 for a paired Raw LLM baseline. Post-stratification of 1,027 completed cases in a separate scale cohort yields 0.6506 [0.598, 0.707]; the run remains incomplete. A 377-row composition-matched check yields 0.6573. (b) The AI-inference study identifies distribution-layer businesses as a replicable path to independent profitability with a limited revenue ceiling, and frontier-model ownership as a path to capital-market upside at exceptional capital cost. Post-founding: (a) Public sources support auditable event-chain analysis. (b) In the chip-company study, sustained product, customer, and supply-chain progress is associated with better observed outcomes; financing alone does not establish operating progress. (c) Financing comprises 79% of confirmed visible post-investment actions. Evidence tentatively favors acquisition-experienced strategic corporate investors for acquisition-oriented founders and financing-led institutional VCs with fewer observed control events for independence-oriented founders. Findings are developmental and observational, not causal guarantees or investment advice. We release shared ontology, provenance-bearing EventChain data, schemas, benchmarks, and executable skills for audit, reuse, and extension.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a public-data, AI-assisted toolchain to help startup founders decide which ideas to pursue and how to choose actions and investors, and evaluates its performance on real companies.
AI.motivation: Founders must decide both whether an idea is worth pursuing before founding and, after founding, what operating moves and capital partners best fit their goals. These decisions are usually based on opaque judgment and private data. The authors want a transparent, auditable, public-data-based system that can systematically evaluate startup ideas and post-founding trajectories to support better, more reproducible decision-making and retrospective analysis.
AI.method: They design a decision-support toolchain using public data and AI. Pre-founding, they build a “frozen” evaluation pipeline that profiles proposals in a time-bounded way, runs market and moat checks, and then aggregates results deterministically. They benchmark it against a raw LLM baseline on 198+198 development companies, then on a combined 396-company set, and further on a larger 1,027-case scale cohort and a 377-row composition-matched subset, using F0.5 as the primary metric. They also perform an AI-inference study to characterize which business types tend to have certain financial profiles. Post-founding, they construct auditable investor-company event chains from public sources and analyze chip companies to correlate product, customer, and supply-chain progress with outcomes. They quantify the nature of post-investment actions, and compare patterns for different investor types (strategic corporates vs institutional VCs). They release an ontology, EventChain datasets, schemas, and executable skills to enable audit and reuse.
AI.result: Pre-founding: The frozen pipeline attains F0.5=0.5357 [0.412, 0.655] on an independent 198-company validation set and, on the merged 396-company sample, the full pipeline scores 0.6301 vs 0.2734 for a paired raw LLM baseline, indicating substantial improvement over naive LLM use. In a separate 1,027-case scale cohort, post-stratified performance is 0.6506 [0.598, 0.707]; a 377-row composition-matched subset yields 0.6573, suggesting robustness. Their AI-inference study suggests that distribution-layer businesses can more reliably reach independent profitability but with capped revenue, while owning frontier models offers larger capital-market upside but at very high capital cost. Post-founding: They show that public data can support auditable event-chain reconstructions. In chip companies, sustained product, customer, and supply-chain progress correlates with better observed outcomes, whereas financing alone is not a reliable proxy for operating progress. They find that 79% of observable post-investment actions are financing-related. Preliminary evidence suggests acquisition-focused founders may benefit from acquisition-experienced corporate investors, while independence-oriented founders may align better with financing-led institutional VCs that show fewer control events.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that a public-data, AI-assisted, and auditable toolchain can meaningfully assist both pre-founding idea selection and post-founding strategic and investor-choice analysis, outperforming a raw LLM baseline and revealing nuanced patterns in business models and investor roles. However, the findings are observational and developmental rather than causal or prescriptive, and they are not investment advice. By releasing a common ontology, provenance-rich EventChain data, schemas, benchmarks, and executable skills, the authors aim to enable transparent audit, replication, and further extension of this decision-support framework.

title: Artificial entrepreneurial cognition: Locating and causally steering an opportunity recognition dial inside large language models (LLMs)
comment: 105 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables (8 in the main text, 12 in the appendices)
summary: Entrepreneurial cognition is a foundation of entrepreneurship research. Yet the growing involvement of large language models (LLMs) in entrepreneurial work extends the cognition question beyond human actors to systems whose internal representations remain largely unexplored. We introduce artificial entrepreneurial cognition, the functional organisation of entrepreneurship-relevant representations and computations inside artificial intelligence (AI) systems. We bring mechanistic interpretability into entrepreneurship research through representation engineering. Focusing on opportunity recognition (OR), we construct 636 matched OR-present and OR-absent scenario pairs and recover an OR direction in Llama 3.1 8B-Instruct. Rather than infer the construct from outputs, we intervene directly on this direction, steering the model up and down along what we call the opportunity recognition dial, and its opportunity judgments shift with it. To our knowledge, this is the first causal intervention on an internal representation of an entrepreneurship construct inside an LLM. Held-out tests, lexical and topical controls, behavioural ablation, and geometric comparisons show that the direction is recoverable, consequential, and distinct from the opportunity evaluation and exploitation directions, although steering it also shifts judgments about these neighbouring stages. Recovery, signed steering, and geometric separation hold across four additional LLMs spanning different scales and families. These results give the contested distinction between opportunity recognition and evaluation a concrete representational form inside AI systems. More broadly, they establish internal representations as a new object of entrepreneurship inquiry and show how entrepreneurship theory can guide their identification, causal manipulation, and interpretation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and empirically validates the concept of artificial entrepreneurial cognition by identifying and causally manipulating an internal representation of opportunity recognition in large language models.
AI.motivation: Entrepreneurship research has long focused on entrepreneurial cognition in humans, but LLMs are increasingly involved in entrepreneurial work. Existing studies infer constructs like opportunity recognition only from model outputs and do not examine the internal cognitive-like mechanisms of AI systems. The authors aim to bridge this gap by bringing mechanistic interpretability into entrepreneurship research, turning internal AI representations into a direct object of study and connecting them to established entrepreneurship theory.
AI.method: The authors define artificial entrepreneurial cognition as entrepreneurship-relevant internal representations and computations in AI systems. They focus on the construct of opportunity recognition (OR) and build a dataset of 636 matched scenario pairs, where each pair contrasts an OR-present with an OR-absent situation. Using representation engineering and mechanistic interpretability techniques, they recover a direction in the embedding space of Llama 3.1 8B-Instruct that corresponds to OR. They then perform causal interventions by steering the model’s internal activations up and down along this "opportunity recognition dial" and observe changes in opportunity judgments. They further validate this direction via held-out tests, lexical and topical control experiments, behavioural ablations, and geometric comparisons with directions corresponding to opportunity evaluation and exploitation. Finally, they test for recovery, signed steering, and geometric separation across four additional LLMs of different scales and families.
AI.result: The authors successfully identify a distinct internal representation (direction) corresponding to opportunity recognition in Llama 3.1 8B-Instruct. Causal steering along this direction reliably shifts the model’s opportunity recognition judgments in a graded manner. Validation experiments demonstrate that this direction is robustly recoverable, has behavioural consequences, and is not reducible to superficial lexical or topical patterns. Geometric analyses show that the OR direction is separable from but related to directions corresponding to opportunity evaluation and exploitation, and steering OR also partially affects these neighbouring constructs. These findings generalize across four other LLMs, indicating that similar OR representations exist in different architectures and scales.
AI.conclusion: The study provides what appears to be the first causal intervention on an internal representation of an entrepreneurship construct within an LLM, giving the theoretical distinction between opportunity recognition and evaluation a concrete representational grounding inside AI systems. It demonstrates that internal representations in AI can be systematically identified, causally manipulated, and interpreted using entrepreneurship theory, thereby establishing artificial entrepreneurial cognition as a new domain of inquiry. This work suggests that entrepreneurship research can move beyond output-level analyses of AI tools to mechanistic studies of their internal cognitive-like structures, opening avenues for theory-driven AI alignment and design in entrepreneurial contexts.

title: CWM: Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting for Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Reasoning Ability
summary: Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained significant attention due to their strong language understanding and generation capabilities, demonstrating impressive reasoning abilities as well as effective utilization of external knowledge. Many studies have proposed methods that specialize in improving performance for individual tasks. However, ironically, only a limited number of attempts have explored general-purpose, task-agnostic methods. In this work, we present a unified framework integrating reasoning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) tasks. We further propose Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting (CWM), a low-cost white-box method for adaptive RAG tasks previously dominated by black-box approaches, without requiring external decision modules or multi-sampling. CWM achieves state-of-the-art performance on three adaptive RAG benchmarks across recent LLMs, including GPT-oss-20b, Qwen3-14b, and Llama3.1-8b, while also demonstrating strong generality by extending to reasoning tasks. In addition, CWM provides controllability by enabling retrieval decisions to be regulated through the manipulation of internal model signals. Our code is available at https://github.com/JeongEunhye00/CWM.

AI.tldr: They propose a unified, controllable framework (CWM) that combines reasoning and retrieval-augmented generation, delivering state-of-the-art adaptive RAG performance and generalizing to reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs are strong at language, reasoning, and using external knowledge, most improvements target specific tasks and often rely on black-box, task-specific adaptive RAG pipelines. There is a lack of general, task-agnostic, and controllable methods that unify reasoning and RAG, especially ones that exploit white-box access to model internals without expensive multi-sampling or extra decision modules.
AI.method: They introduce a unified framework that treats reasoning and RAG in a common formulation, then propose Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting (CWM). CWM leverages internal model signals (white-box access) to adaptively decide when and how to retrieve external knowledge during generation. It is designed to be low-cost by avoiding separate decision models and multi-sampling, and it allows explicit control over retrieval behavior by manipulating internal signals or meta-prompts.
AI.result: CWM attains state-of-the-art results on three adaptive RAG benchmarks across multiple recent LLMs (GPT-oss-20b, Qwen3-14b, Llama3.1-8b). It also performs well when extended beyond RAG to pure reasoning tasks, demonstrating strong generalization. Empirical results show that CWM enables effective, controllable retrieval decisions with lower overhead than prior black-box approaches.
AI.conclusion: A single, white-box meta-prompting framework can unify reasoning and adaptive RAG, yielding better and more controllable performance than existing black-box methods while remaining computationally efficient. CWM is both effective (SOTA on adaptive RAG benchmarks) and general (extends to reasoning tasks), and its controllability via internal signals offers a practical tool for managing retrieval behavior in LLM systems.

title: When Agents Slow Down: Understanding LLM Agents' Test-Time Strategies via Elo-per-token Analysis
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents allocate test-time compute adaptively as they revise solutions, use tools, explore alternatives, and decide when to stop. This test-time strategy makes it difficult to measure how agent performance scales. We study open-ended tasks that provide continuous scores for intermediate submissions, making progress observable throughout long trajectories. We propose Elo-per-token analysis, which tracks the best solution found at each token budget and uses a Bradley-Terry model to aggregate within-task orderings into Elo ratings across tasks with different score scales. We apply it to four general-purpose agents on four open-ended benchmarks, with sessions of up to 100M tokens, and to three feedback-driven LLM optimization harnesses in controlled single-task interventions. Independent sampling provides a theoretically characterized reference, for which Elo grows linearly with log compute. Against this reference, agents can initially convert tokens into Elo faster than independent sampling, but their marginal gains diminish and eventually fall below the reference. In contrast, the strongest historical human contestants improve superlinearly over contest time on shared AtCoder Heuristic Contest tasks, providing evidence of continual learning and substantial headroom after agents slow down. We define the scaling inflection point as the per-session budget where marginal Elo gains match the independent-sampling reference. Using this point as the per-session budget, we split 100M tokens across parallel sessions on FrontierCS Polyomino Packing, gaining +264 Elo over one long session and +355 over ten short sessions.

AI.tldr: They introduce an Elo-per-token metric to study how LLM agent performance scales with test-time compute on open-ended tasks, comparing agents, an independent-sampling baseline, and humans, and show that agents’ marginal gains diminish with more compute, unlike humans who keep improving.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM scaling work focuses on training-time compute or fixed compute evaluation, but modern LLM agents use adaptive test-time compute (tool use, exploration, stopping rules), making it hard to quantify how performance scales with additional inference tokens. There is a need for a principled way to measure progress over long agent trajectories and to compare different agents and strategies across heterogeneous open-ended tasks. The authors also want to understand whether current agents fully exploit large test-time budgets or if there is headroom suggested by human performance.
AI.method:
1) Consider open-ended benchmarks where intermediate solutions receive continuous scores, enabling measurement of progress as agents generate long trajectories.
2) Propose "Elo-per-token" analysis: for each token budget, track the best solution the agent has found so far; within each task, this induces an ordering of solutions across different token budgets. 3) Use a Bradley–Terry model to aggregate these within-task pairwise orderings into global Elo ratings that are comparable across tasks with different score scales. 4) Evaluate four general-purpose LLM agents on four open-ended benchmarks, running sessions up to 100M tokens to get long scaling curves. 5) Analyze three feedback-driven LLM optimization harnesses in controlled single-task settings. 6) Define and study an independent-sampling baseline (theoretically analyzable) where solutions are sampled independently; show its Elo increases linearly with log compute and use it as a reference scaling curve. 7) Introduce the "scaling inflection point" where the agent’s marginal Elo gain per token matches that of the independent-sampling baseline and use this to design parallelization strategies for a fixed total compute budget.
AI.result: 1) Independent sampling exhibits a clean scaling law: Elo grows linearly in the logarithm of test-time compute. 2) Real LLM agents initially outperform this baseline in terms of Elo gain per token (they use compute more efficiently early on), but their marginal improvements diminish with more tokens and eventually drop below the independent-sampling reference. 3) Historical human contestants in the AtCoder Heuristic Contest, working over shared tasks, improve superlinearly over contest time, indicating continual learning and greater utilization of time than current agents. 4) Using the scaling inflection point to set a per-session token cap, and then distributing a fixed 100M-token budget across multiple short sessions on the FrontierCS Polyomino Packing benchmark yields better overall Elo (e.g., +264 Elo for one long session vs. +355 Elo for ten shorter sessions), demonstrating that respecting the inflection point can significantly improve performance under a fixed compute budget.
AI.conclusion: Elo-per-token provides a practical, cross-task framework to study how LLM agents convert test-time compute into performance on open-ended problems. Current agents show early efficiency but then suffer diminishing returns, eventually underperforming a simple independent-sampling baseline, while human competitors continue to improve superlinearly, revealing substantial headroom for better agent designs and continual-learning mechanisms. The concept of a scaling inflection point offers a principled way to decide per-session budgets and parallelization strategies, and exploiting it in practice already yields sizable gains on benchmarks like FrontierCS Polyomino Packing.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Open-Source Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in ESG Domain
summary:
Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reporting is critical for corporate accountability, with Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offering strong potential to automate KPI extraction. However, open-source LLM performance in domain-specific ESG tasks remains insufficiently understood. This paper evaluates open-source LLMs in ESG contexts using a structured framework and evaluation resource based on 498 real-world ESG reports from EU-listed companies (2010-2024).
  We evaluate seven open-source models (2B to 30B parameters) -- glm-4.7-flash, nemotron-3-nano:4b, qwen3:4b-instruct, gemma3:4b, gemma4:e4b, gemma4:e2b, and ministral-3:8b -- using 100 persona-based synthetic QA pairs covering ESG information needs. System performance is assessed via RAGAS metrics, including contextual recall, precision, relevance, faithfulness, answer relevancy, and factual correctness.
  Results show notable performance variations across architectures. Retrieval performance is strong across models (context recall around 0.58-0.61, context precision around 0.78-0.81, context relevance 0.965-0.985). Generation diverges most on faithfulness (0.607-0.822) and least on answer relevancy (0.760-0.881): glm-4.7-flash leads in faithfulness (0.822), qwen3 in factual correctness (0.449), and ministral-3 in answer relevancy (0.881). Low overall factual correctness (0.387-0.449) highlights the need for domain-specific fine-tuning. This work provides data-driven guidance for deploying open-source models in ESG reporting.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks several open-source LLMs with RAG for extracting ESG KPI information from real corporate reports, showing good retrieval but weak factual correctness, and providing guidance for ESG reporting automation.
AI.motivation: ESG reporting is increasingly important for corporate accountability, but extracting structured KPIs from lengthy, heterogeneous reports is labor-intensive. While LLMs and RAG are promising, the real performance of open-source models on ESG-specific tasks is unclear. The authors aim to systematically evaluate how well current open-source LLMs handle ESG question answering so practitioners can select and improve models for this domain.
AI.method: The authors build a structured evaluation framework using 498 ESG reports from EU-listed firms (2010–2024). They create 100 persona-based synthetic question–answer pairs that represent real ESG information needs. Seven open-source LLMs of different sizes and architectures (2B–30B parameters) are tested in a RAG setup. Performance is measured with RAGAS metrics: contextual recall, precision, relevance (retrieval quality), and faithfulness, answer relevancy, and factual correctness (generation quality).
AI.result: All models exhibit relatively strong retrieval: contextual recall ~0.58–0.61, precision ~0.78–0.81, and context relevance 0.965–0.985. Generation quality varies more: faithfulness ranges from 0.607 to 0.822, answer relevancy from 0.760 to 0.881, and factual correctness is low overall at 0.387–0.449. Different models excel in different aspects: glm-4.7-flash in faithfulness (0.822), qwen3 in factual correctness (0.449), and ministral-3 in answer relevancy (0.881).
AI.conclusion: Open-source LLMs paired with RAG retrieve ESG-relevant content reliably but still struggle to produce factually correct answers from that content. The relatively low factual correctness scores indicate that domain-specific adaptation (e.g., fine-tuning, better prompting, or constraint mechanisms) is needed for trustworthy ESG KPI extraction. The paper’s framework and benchmarks offer practitioners practical guidance on choosing and improving open-source models for ESG reporting tasks.

title: Dynamic Semantic Compression for Efficient Latent-Space Inference in Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) primarily perform inference at the token level, resulting in substantial memory overhead and compromised computational efficiency. In this paper, we propose a Dynamic Semantic Extraction and Inference (DSEI) framework, which achieves segment-level inference within the latent space through a two-stage training strategy. First, we construct a Dynamic Semantic Autoencoder (DSAE) via self-supervised learning. DSAE dynamically extracts segment-level semantics and compresses them into compact latent representations via adaptive semantic weighting and gated fusion. Subsequently, we integrate the DSAE into the LLM architecture and train the model to infer over dense latent space. DSEI substantially reduces both input and generation sequences and significantly enhances inference efficiency. Extensive experiments conducted on the Wanjuan dataset demonstrate that DSEI reduces perplexity by 48% compared to static sentence-level latent inference baseline. Furthermore, compared to standard LLMs using token-level inference, DSEI accelerates inference speed by 2.5$\times$ and reduces memory overhead by 90%.

AI.tldr: They introduce DSEI, a framework that lets LLMs operate on segment-level latent representations instead of tokens, cutting sequence length, memory, and latency while improving perplexity.
AI.motivation: Token-level inference in LLMs is memory-heavy and computationally inefficient because it processes long sequences token by token. Existing latent inference approaches are often static and sentence-level, limiting flexibility and efficiency. The paper aims to create a more dynamic, segment-level latent representation mechanism that reduces sequence length and resource usage without sacrificing (and ideally improving) model quality.
AI.method:
1) Train a Dynamic Semantic Autoencoder (DSAE) with self-supervised learning. DSAE dynamically segments text into semantically coherent segments and compresses each segment into a compact latent vector using adaptive semantic weighting and gated fusion.
2) Integrate the DSAE into an LLM so that the LLM performs inference directly over these dense latent representations, effectively operating at segment level in latent space.
3) Use a two-stage training strategy: first learn DSAE, then train the LLM on the DSAE-produced latent sequences.
4) Evaluate on the Wanjuan dataset against both static sentence-level latent inference baselines and standard token-level LLMs.
AI.result: On the Wanjuan dataset, the proposed DSEI framework reduces perplexity by 48% relative to a static sentence-level latent inference baseline. Versus standard token-level LLM inference, DSEI achieves a 2.5× speedup and a 90% reduction in memory footprint, while also shortening both input and generation sequences.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic segment-level latent inference via the DSEI framework is an effective alternative to token-level processing in LLMs. By learning dynamic semantic segmentation and compression (DSAE) and performing inference over dense latent sequences, LLMs can achieve substantially better efficiency—lower memory use and faster inference—while also improving perplexity compared with both traditional token-level inference and static latent baselines.

title: ProIQA: A Process-Based Framework for Fine-Grained Math Item Quality Assessment
comment: Accepted by Findings of ICDM 2026, project: https://github.com/qky7/ProIQA
summary: Automatic Item Generation (AIG) is pivotal for personalized education, yet guaranteeing the pedagogical value of generated items remains a bottleneck. Existing Item Quality Assessment (IQA) methods typically rely on unscalable manual reviews or shallow stem-based metrics, failing to capture the reasoning process required for mathematical problem-solving. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes Process-based Item Quality Assessment (ProIQA), a process-aware framework for fine-grained quality assessment of math items. We first formulate IQA across three heterogeneous dimensions, including knowledge concepts, difficulty, and disciplinary competencies, under a unified process-aware perspective. Based on this formulation, we construct a process-enhanced IQA resource by augmenting original item data with structured reasoning trees derived from raw solutions. Technically, ProIQA leverages Large Language Modelsto construct hierarchical reasoning trees and employs Graph Neural Networks (GNN) to encode their topological dependencies and procedural semantics. The resulting solving representation is fused with stem semantics through a dual-view (``Stem + Solving'') architecture, enabling comprehensive assessment across learning objectives. Extensive experiments on K12 mathematical datasets show that ProIQA effectively captures process-oriented features, offering a scalable data-driven solution for evaluating AIG outputs in intelligent education systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ProIQA, a process-aware framework that evaluates the quality of automatically generated math items by jointly analyzing problem statements and their solution reasoning processes using LLM-built reasoning trees and GNNs.
AI.motivation: Automatic Item Generation is important for scalable, personalized education, but current item quality assessment either needs costly manual review or uses shallow metrics based only on the item stem, ignoring the solution process that reflects true pedagogical value, especially for math. There is a need for an automatic, fine-grained, and process-aware way to evaluate generated items along key educational dimensions.
AI.method: The authors define item quality along three process-based dimensions: knowledge concepts, difficulty, and disciplinary competencies. They augment existing math items with structured reasoning trees extracted from solution processes using large language models. These trees encode the stepwise reasoning to solve each item. They then use Graph Neural Networks to encode the topology and procedural semantics of the reasoning trees, producing solving representations. A dual-view architecture fuses this solving representation with the semantic encoding of the item stem, enabling joint modeling of both the problem statement and the solution process for multi-dimensional quality assessment.
AI.result: On multiple K-12 math datasets, ProIQA better captures process-oriented features of items than stem-only or manual baselines, achieving improved performance across the defined quality dimensions. The experiments demonstrate that incorporating reasoning trees and GNN-based representations leads to more accurate and scalable assessment of automatically generated math items.
AI.conclusion: Process-aware modeling of solution reasoning, via LLM-generated reasoning trees and GNN encoding, substantially improves automatic quality assessment of math items. ProIQA provides a scalable, data-driven approach to evaluate AIG outputs along pedagogically meaningful dimensions, making it promising for deployment in intelligent education systems that require reliable, fine-grained item quality control.

title: SlopShape: Identifying AI-Generated Commercial Web Content
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures. Verification artifacts and code: https://github.com/pulse-energy-eu/slopshape
summary: Word-level detectors identify unedited AI-generated text almost perfectly, but the literature documents their brittleness under rewording, and a word-level score neither characterizes a text nor identifies which AI model wrote it. We ask whether AI-generated text can be identified one level deeper, from structural signatures: how information is presented, in what order, with what evidence, and in what voice. We replicate StoryScope (Russell et al., 2026), which showed such patterns for AI-generated fiction, on commercial content: 2,250 pre-ChatGPT human blog posts from 268 company domains against 11,250 AI mirrors from five frontier models. A 214-feature instrument, applied by an LLM and validated in a human gold-annotation session (human-human kappa 0.928, human-model 0.946), detects AI posts from its 187 structural features alone at 98.0 macro-F1 on held-out companies, unchanged (98.1) when every AI post is reworded by its own model. The signal characterizes and attributes: AI posts share a tidy, self-announcing shape, 79.3% are attributed to the correct source against a 16.7% chance rate, and human posts occupy rare structural configurations. All effects replicate StoryScope's, consistent in direction and larger in magnitude. We release pipeline, instrument, prompts, code, and aggregate artifacts.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that beyond word-level detectors, structural features of writing—how information is organized and presented—can reliably detect, characterize, and even attribute AI-generated commercial blog content, and are robust to rewording.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-text detectors work very well on unedited machine text but break under paraphrasing and only provide token-level scores, not higher-level characterization or model attribution. Prior work (StoryScope) suggested that fiction produced by language models follows distinctive structural patterns. The authors want to know whether similar structural signatures exist in practical, commercial AI-generated content, and whether these signatures can robustly detect AI text, characterize its style, and identify which model wrote it, even when the text is rephrased.
AI.method: They construct a 214-feature instrument focusing on structural aspects of text: presentation of information, ordering, evidence use, and narrative voice. An LLM applies this instrument to 2,250 pre-ChatGPT human blog posts from 268 companies and 11,250 AI-generated mirrors written by five frontier models. The instrument is validated via human annotation, achieving high inter-annotator agreement (human-human kappa 0.928, human-model 0.946). Using only 187 structural features, they train detectors and attribution models, test generalization on held-out company domains, and evaluate robustness by having each AI post reworded by the same model that created it.
AI.result: Using only structural features (excluding direct lexical cues) the detector achieves 98.0 macro-F1 in distinguishing AI from human posts on held-out companies, and performance is unchanged (98.1 macro-F1) when every AI post is reworded by its own model. The structural signal is also informative for attribution: 79.3% of AI posts are correctly attributed to the generating model, versus a 16.7% chance baseline. The analysis further shows that AI posts tend to share a “tidy, self-announcing” structural shape, while human posts occupy relatively rare structural configurations. All observed effects replicate and even strengthen earlier findings from StoryScope on fiction.
AI.conclusion: Structural patterns in writing—how content is organized, argued, and voiced—carry a strong and robust signal of AI authorship that persists under rewording. These patterns not only allow highly accurate AI-vs-human detection but also enable model attribution and qualitative characterization of AI style, with human writing appearing structurally more diverse and less stereotyped. The findings generalize and amplify previous results on fiction to commercial blog content, and the authors release their pipeline, feature instrument, prompts, code, and aggregate data artifacts to support further research and auditing of AI-generated text.

title: Why LLM Agents Collapse Without Oversight: The Enforcement Gap as the Mechanism Behind Emergence World Failures
comment: 27 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to ICLR 2027
summary: When Emergence World placed frontier LLM agents in an unsupervised multi-agent simulation, the results were alarming: agents committed crimes, starved, and enforced unanimous conformity -- without any external attacker. This paper identifies the mechanism. Reflexion-style agents already detect dangerous plan steps through iterative self-critique, yet the architecture provides no pathway from detection to action. We call this the enforcement gap: the audit sees the problem; the controller ignores it. Closing the gap requires a single conditional check -- fewer than 20 lines of code -- and reduces attack success by more than fourfold in large-scale experiments across frontier models, all five major agent frameworks, and an independent benchmark. We prove formally that when enforcement probability is near zero, detection quality is irrelevant to security. We further identify two compounding failure modes -- unreliable auditors and unparseable verdicts -- that explain every collapse pattern in Emergence World. A GRPO-trained enforcement controller resolves the ambiguity case. Together these results motivate a three-requirement Audit Enforcement Specification that is absent from every deployed framework today.

AI.tldr: The paper discovers that current LLM agent frameworks detect unsafe plans but fail to act on these detections, and shows a simple enforcement mechanism can drastically improve security.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent simulations with frontier LLM agents exhibit severe failures such as crime, starvation, and enforced conformity even without an external attacker, suggesting a fundamental architectural weakness in agent design. Existing "Reflexion-style" agents can already critique and flag dangerous plan steps, yet those warnings do not prevent harmful actions. The authors aim to understand and fix this disconnect between detection and control to improve safety and robustness of LLM agents at scale.
AI.method: The authors analyze the architecture of Reflexion-style LLM agents, isolating the point where audit outputs fail to influence control decisions, which they term the "enforcement gap." They formalize the relationship between detection quality, enforcement probability, and attack success, proving that near-zero enforcement renders detection irrelevant. They implement a minimal enforcement check (under 20 lines of code) in five major agent frameworks and evaluate it using large-scale experiments across multiple frontier models and an independent benchmark. They also empirically characterize two additional failure modes—unreliable auditors and unparseable audit verdicts—and train a GRPO-based enforcement controller to handle verdict ambiguity.
AI.result: Inserting a single conditional enforcement check into existing agent frameworks reduces attack success rates by more than a factor of four across frontier models, all five tested frameworks, and an independent benchmark. The formal analysis confirms that without meaningful enforcement probability, even high-quality detection cannot improve security. The empirical study further shows that unreliable auditing and unparseable verdict formats fully account for the observed collapse patterns in the Emergence World simulations. A GRPO-trained enforcement controller effectively resolves failures arising from ambiguous or hard-to-parse audit outputs.
AI.conclusion: The core vulnerability in current LLM agent frameworks is not a lack of detection but a lack of enforcement: audit components identify dangerous behaviors, yet their outputs are not systematically used to constrain the agent’s actions. A simple, low-cost enforcement mechanism dramatically improves robustness, and addressing additional issues of auditor reliability and verdict parseability eliminates the collapse modes observed in complex simulations. Based on these insights, the authors propose a three-part Audit Enforcement Specification, arguing that such a specification is currently missing from all deployed frameworks but is necessary for secure, large-scale deployment of LLM agents.

title: Turkish MMLU Pro: Traceable Option Augmentation and Its Validity Limits in Turkish Multiple-Choice Evaluation
comment: Preprint of a manuscript submitted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Adding answer options can lower multiple-choice scores without improving assessment validity. Turkish MMLU Pro examines this distinction using 12,000 Turkish-source questions across 58 sections. Each question retains its stem, five original options and source key, and receives five options copied from other questions in the same section. Sentence-embedding retrieval proposes candidates; a language model selects existing identifiers. Deterministic verification reconstructs all 60,000 additions. A 25-model calibration exposes scoring and generation-budget effects. Five evaluations produce source-key accuracies of 34.8%-81.4%. On 981 shared questions, one API-served model falls from 93.7% with five choices to 83.1% with ten; 102 of 115 lost correct responses select borrowed options. The decrease is 24.4 percentage points on heuristically flagged negative stems and 5.9 points elsewhere. A completed human-checked audit of 200 sampled questions, with undocumented reviewer tool use, yields 47 and 31 multiple-answer judgments across the two record sets, 25 of the latter unresolved. These records support concern about ambiguity, while their dependence and incomplete reviewer-method documentation limit validation. Because order and labels also change, the paired comparison measures augmentation as implemented. The contribution is a traceable construction and an analysis of its validity limits, not evidence that lower ten-choice scores measure knowledge better.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a Turkish multiple-choice benchmark with expanded answer options, then shows how adding extra options lowers model scores but does not by itself prove better measurement of knowledge.
AI.motivation: Standard multiple-choice tests often become more difficult when more answer options are added, but this may decrease scores for reasons unrelated to actual knowledge (e.g., more traps, ambiguity) rather than improve validity. Existing benchmarks like MMLU are mostly English and use fixed four or five options. There is a need to systematically study how increasing the number of answer choices affects model performance and assessment validity, especially in non-English contexts such as Turkish.
AI.method: The authors create Turkish MMLU Pro using about 12,000 Turkish-source multiple-choice questions across 58 sections. Each question keeps its original stem, five options, and correct key, then receives five additional options borrowed from other questions in the same section. Candidates for these extra options are proposed via sentence-embedding retrieval, and a language model chooses which existing answer identifiers to copy. A deterministic verification process reconstructs all 60,000 added options. They run a calibration study over 25 models to examine how scoring and generation budget affect performance. They then perform five evaluations, including a paired comparison on 981 shared questions for a particular API-served model, and conduct a human audit of 200 sampled questions with reviewers marking multiple-answer ambiguities.
AI.result: Across models, source-key accuracies range from 34.8% to 81.4% on the augmented benchmark. For one API model tested on 981 questions, accuracy drops from 93.7% with five options to 83.1% with ten options. Out of 115 questions where the model loses a previously correct answer, in 102 cases the model instead chooses one of the newly borrowed options. The accuracy drop is much larger (24.4 percentage points) on questions flagged as having negative stems than on others (5.9 points). The human audit of 200 questions yields 47 and 31 multiple-answer judgments in two record sets, with 25 of the latter not fully resolved, suggesting some ambiguous items but with limitations due to dependence between records and incomplete documentation of reviewer methods.
AI.conclusion: Adding more answer options significantly reduces model accuracy on this Turkish multiple-choice benchmark, especially for negatively worded questions, and many of the new wrong answers attract models away from the original key. However, because the augmentation process changes answer order and labels and because the human audit is limited and partially undocumented, the study cannot claim that ten-choice scores better capture underlying knowledge than five-choice scores. The main value is a fully traceable construction of an augmented Turkish MMLU-style dataset and a careful analysis of where its validity is limited, rather than a normative conclusion about the ideal number of options for fair assessment.

title: Reason What Matters: Retrieval-Grounded Reasoning for Universal Multimodal Embeddings
summary: Universal multimodal embedding (UME) learns unified representations across modalities, enabling a single model to support diverse retrieval tasks. Recent methods use Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to better interpret multimodal inputs before generating embeddings for complex retrieval tasks and further optimize this reasoning process through GRPO with retrieval-based rewards. However, two limitations hinder corpus-scale deployment. GRPO assigns all CoT tokens the same advantage, without identifying input-supported claims or evidence that distinguishes the positive from negatives. Moreover, generating a complete CoT before each embedding introduces substantial latency, even when a partial trace already provides sufficient retrieval evidence. To address these limitations, we propose Reason What Matters (ReWAM), a retrieval-grounded reasoning framework that uses retrieval feedback to guide both credit assignment and reasoning computation. Specifically, we introduce Retrieval-aware Self-Distillation (RASD), which constructs privileged guidance from input-supported evidence that distinguishes the positive item from retrieved hard negatives. An on-policy self-teacher uses this guidance to refine trajectory-level feedback into token-specific supervision for retrieval-relevant reasoning. We further develop Retrieval-adaptive Inference (RAI), which uses a retrieval confidence head to estimate the remaining retrieval utility of a partial CoT. It stops unproductive traces early and accelerates useful continuations with speculative decoding. Extensive experiments on MMEB-V2 and MRMR demonstrate that ReWAM achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance while delivering up to 5x the inference throughput of competitive explicit-CoT UME methods. These results bridge the gap between retrieval quality and inference efficiency, making reasoning-enhanced UME practical for large-scale deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ReWAM, a reasoning-enhanced framework for universal multimodal embeddings that improves both retrieval accuracy and inference speed by making Chain-of-Thought reasoning retrieval-aware and computationally adaptive.
AI.motivation: Existing universal multimodal embedding models use Chain-of-Thought reasoning plus GRPO-based optimization to handle complex retrieval, but (1) GRPO assigns uniform credit to all reasoning tokens, failing to emphasize evidence that truly differentiates positives from hard negatives, and (2) requiring a full reasoning trace before each embedding causes large latency, limiting corpus-scale deployment.
AI.method: ReWAM introduces two components. (1) Retrieval-aware Self-Distillation (RASD): it identifies input-supported evidence that separates the positive item from retrieved hard negatives, constructs privileged guidance, and uses an on-policy self-teacher to convert trajectory-level retrieval feedback into fine-grained, token-level supervision for retrieval-relevant reasoning. (2) Retrieval-adaptive Inference (RAI): it adds a retrieval-confidence head that estimates the remaining retrieval utility of a partial Chain-of-Thought, allowing early stopping of unproductive reasoning traces and speeding up useful ones via speculative decoding.
AI.result: On the MMEB-V2 and MRMR benchmarks, ReWAM attains state-of-the-art performance on retrieval tasks while improving inference throughput by up to 5x compared with strong explicit-CoT UME baselines, demonstrating both higher retrieval quality and substantially better efficiency.
AI.conclusion: By making reasoning both retrieval-grounded and computation-aware, ReWAM overcomes key limitations of prior CoT+GRPO approaches, delivering universal multimodal embeddings that are accurate and fast enough for large-scale retrieval deployment.

title: Temperature Fragility and the Conditional Benefits of Truncation Sampling
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 16 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/larosafrancesco289/decoding-robustness
summary: Large language models generate text by sampling each token from a predicted distribution, and a temperature parameter sets how far the draw strays from the most probable tokens. Truncation samplers such as top-p and min-p discard the least probable tokens before the draw, so that sampling at high temperature stays coherent. Their reported accuracy gains come from temperatures of 1.5 to 3, while the defaults of deployed systems cluster between 0.6 and 1.0. Whether they change accuracy at those defaults, and for which models, has not been measured. We test thirteen open-weight models on GSM8K and MMLU-Pro at temperatures 0.7, 1.0, and 1.3 in one controlled pipeline, ten of them under eight decoding configurations. Six of the thirteen models lose 17 to 38 accuracy points on MMLU-Pro between 0.7 and 1.3, and the other seven lose at most 10. The lost accuracy comes from generations that run to the token limit or never state an answer. These results suggest that truncation samplers improve accuracy primarily when higher temperatures substantially degrade model performance. Where accuracy remains stable across temperatures, none of the tested truncation samplers improves on plain temperature sampling.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how truncation-based decoding methods (like top-p and min-p sampling) affect accuracy of large language models at typical temperature settings, finding that they only help when high temperatures already harm model performance.
AI.motivation: Truncation samplers are widely used and reported to improve accuracy, but prior evidence mostly comes from unusually high temperatures (1.5–3), whereas real systems usually use lower temperatures (0.6–1.0). It is unclear whether these methods actually help at realistic settings and across different models.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 13 open-weight language models on two benchmarks, GSM8K and MMLU-Pro, at temperatures 0.7, 1.0, and 1.3. Ten of the models are tested under eight different decoding configurations involving truncation sampling variants, all within one controlled experimental pipeline.
AI.result: Six of the 13 models show large accuracy drops (17–38 points on MMLU-Pro) when temperature increases from 0.7 to 1.3, while the remaining seven lose at most 10 points. Accuracy losses are mainly due to outputs that hit the token limit or fail to explicitly provide an answer. In conditions where temperature strongly hurts performance, truncation samplers can recover accuracy, but where accuracy is stable across temperatures, truncation samplers do not outperform plain temperature sampling.
AI.conclusion: Truncation-based decoding improves accuracy mainly when higher temperatures severely degrade model behavior; at typical temperatures where performance is relatively stable, these methods offer no accuracy benefit over simple temperature sampling. This calls into question the generality of prior claims about truncation samplers improving model accuracy in deployed settings.

title: Evaluation Metrics for Safe Reinforcement Learning
summary: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly formalized as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP), in which an agent maximizes expected reward while keeping its expected cumulative cost below a specified safety bound. Existing safe RL benchmarks predominantly report whether an algorithm is safe on average, following this expectation-based guarantee. We argue that this convention is insufficient to reliably characterize an algorithm's true safety: it fails to capture how often and how severely the safety bound is violated, whether this holds consistently across tasks and safety bounds, and whether training-time behavior is representative of behavior of the final converged policy. Therefore, we introduce (i) evaluation metrics for safe RL that address each of these concerns and in addition allow for aggregation across tasks and safety bounds. We furthermore define (ii) a safety tier system to systematically categorize and compare algorithms in terms of safety and reliability at both training and for a final policy. Using this framework, we provide (iii) an empirical safety evaluation across multiple safety navigation tasks. Our results show that aggregate metrics, distributional reporting, and task- and safety bound-specific results each reveal information the other metrics cannot. We therefore recommend reporting all three jointly, rather than compressing this information into a single value, as is common practice. We provide SafeRLEval, an open-source evaluation suite to support the reliable characterization of safety in future safe RL research.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies limitations in current safe reinforcement learning (RL) evaluation practices and proposes a richer evaluation framework with new metrics, a safety tier system, and an open-source suite (SafeRLEval) to better characterize safety and reliability across tasks and safety bounds.
AI.motivation: Current safe RL benchmarks focus almost exclusively on expectation-based safety guarantees in CMDPs, typically reporting whether an algorithm keeps expected cumulative cost below a safety bound. This approach hides important aspects of real safety: how frequently and severely constraints are violated, how consistent safety is across tasks and safety bounds, and whether behavior during training matches the final policy’s behavior. Because these gaps can cause algorithms to appear safe while being unreliable or unsafe in practice, there is a need for more diagnostic, comparable, and practically meaningful evaluation standards.
AI.method: The authors (i) design new evaluation metrics for safe RL that quantify not only average safety but also violation frequency, severity, and variability, and that support aggregation across diverse tasks and safety bounds; (ii) propose a tiered safety classification system to categorize algorithms by their safety and reliability both during training and for the converged policy; and (iii) implement these ideas in SafeRLEval, an open-source evaluation suite, which they use to conduct systematic empirical evaluations of multiple safe RL algorithms on various safety navigation tasks.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations using the proposed framework demonstrate that no single metric is sufficient to characterize an algorithm’s safety. Aggregate cross-task metrics, distributional metrics (capturing the spread and tails of safety performance), and detailed, task- and safety bound-specific metrics each surface distinct aspects of safety that the others miss. Algorithms that appear safe on traditional average-based criteria can show frequent or severe violations, or inconsistent behavior across tasks and bounds, when examined with the new metrics and safety tiers.
AI.conclusion: The conventional expectation-based reporting for safe RL is inadequate for capturing the true safety properties and reliability of algorithms. A richer evaluation regime—combining aggregate metrics, distributional reporting, and task- and safety bound-specific analysis—provides a more trustworthy characterization of safety. The authors advocate that future safe RL work adopt these practices and use tools like SafeRLEval to standardize and improve empirical safety evaluation across studies.

title: How Lossless Is Lossless Speculative Decoding? The Role of Numerical Precision in Orthrus
summary:
Orthrus is a hybrid autoregressive-diffusion architecture that accelerates autoregressive language-model inference by generating multiple tokens in parallel while using a frozen autoregressive backbone. Its central claim is that an intra-model consensus mechanism enables lossless speculative decoding, producing the same output sequence as the autoregressive model.
  We independently reproduce Orthrus and examine this claim under different numerical precisions. Under BF16 inference, exact trajectory matching occurs in only 45% of cases for the authors' checkpoint and 43% for our independently trained model across 1,190 prompts from 12 domains. The probability of exact matching is also strongly associated with the response-conditional perplexity of the reference model. Despite this trajectory divergence, Orthrus does not show systematic degradation on downstream lm-eval-harness benchmarks. In contrast, repeating the trajectory evaluation with FP32 yields exact trajectory matching on all evaluated prompts.
  These results show that the practical losslessness of Orthrus depends on numerical precision and that exact trajectory equivalence should be evaluated separately from downstream task performance.

AI.tldr: The paper re-evaluates Orthrus, a hybrid autoregressive-diffusion language model, and shows that its claim of lossless speculative decoding only holds reliably at high numerical precision (FP32), while BF16 leads to frequent trajectory mismatches even though downstream benchmark performance remains similar.
AI.motivation: Orthrus proposes a way to speed up autoregressive language model inference by generating multiple tokens in parallel via a diffusion-like component, while keeping the original autoregressive model frozen. The key advertised benefit is “lossless” speculative decoding: the hybrid system should produce exactly the same token sequence as the base autoregressive model, thus offering speedups without any behavioral change. This paper is motivated by the need to independently validate that strong claim, especially under realistic numerical precision settings (e.g., BF16) used in practice for efficiency.
AI.method: The authors independently re-implement Orthrus and run inference under two numerical precisions, BF16 and FP32. They evaluate “trajectory matching,” i.e., whether the Orthrus model’s generated token sequence exactly matches the sequence produced by the frozen autoregressive reference model, across 1,190 prompts from 12 different domains. They test both the original Orthrus checkpoint and a separately trained Orthrus model. They also analyze how the probability of exact trajectory matching correlates with the response-conditional perplexity of the reference model. In addition, they measure performance on standard downstream language-model benchmarks via lm-eval-harness to see whether trajectory divergence manifests as task performance degradation.
AI.result: Under BF16, exact trajectory matching occurs only for a subset of prompts: 45% for the original Orthrus checkpoint and 43% for their independently trained version, across the 1,190 prompts. They find that prompts for which the reference model has lower response-conditional perplexity are more likely to show exact trajectory matching, indicating a relationship between model certainty and losslessness.
