It introduces a class-adaptive influence scoring mechanism to rectify gradient dominance and employs a direction-constrained update strategy to prevent the unintended erosion of vital clinical knowledge. Comprehensive benchmarking across multiple medical datasets, including skin cancer (ISIC), brain tumor (MRI), and breast ultrasound (BUSI), demonstrates that GRIN+ achieves an optimal balance of the PEU trilemma. Experimental results show that GRIN+ maintains high diagnostic accuracy and robust privacy while significantly enhancing runtime efficiency compared to existing baselines. We open-source the GRIN+ code and benchmarks to support further research.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GRIN+, a machine unlearning framework tailored for imbalanced medical datasets that efficiently and precisely removes data influence while preserving diagnostic performance and privacy.
AI.motivation: Existing machine unlearning methods face a privacy-efficiency-utility trilemma, which is especially severe in healthcare where data is highly imbalanced and long-tailed. Standard unlearning may either fail to fully erase sensitive information or unintentionally remove critical features for rare but important conditions because gradients from majority classes dominate. There is a need for a method that can selectively and reliably forget particular patient data while maintaining clinical utility and being computationally efficient.
AI.method: GRIN+ operates at the parameter level by decoupling unlearning-related knowledge from general representations. It analyzes gradient contributions from two sets: the data to be forgotten and the data to be retained. A class-adaptive influence scoring mechanism is used to reweight and correct for gradient dominance from majority classes, so minority/rare-class effects are appropriately accounted for. Additionally, a direction-constrained update strategy is introduced to ensure that parameter updates for unlearning move in directions that minimize forgetting of essential clinical knowledge, thereby preserving useful representations while erasing targeted information.
AI.result: Across multiple medical imaging datasets—ISIC (skin cancer), MRI brain tumor, and BUSI breast ultrasound—GRIN+ outperforms baseline MU methods on all three axes of the PEU trilemma. It maintains or improves diagnostic accuracy and model utility, provides robust privacy guarantees in terms of effective forgetting of targeted data, and reduces unlearning runtime significantly compared with existing techniques. Quantitative benchmarks show that it better preserves performance on rare classes while ensuring that the influence of forgotten samples is effectively removed.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that GRIN+ provides an effective solution to the privacy-efficiency-utility trilemma in medical machine unlearning, particularly under severe class imbalance. By class-adaptive influence scoring and direction-constrained parameter updates, it enables fast and precise erasure of specific data without sacrificing critical clinical knowledge or diagnostic performance. The open-sourcing of code and benchmarks is intended to facilitate further research and adoption of reliable unlearning methods in healthcare AI systems.

title: CiteGuard-RAG: A Validation-Centered AI System for Evidence-Grounded Question Answering
comment: Submitted to Engineering Reports. 22 pages, 2 figures, 12 tables
summary:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve access to complex information; however, retrieving evidence alone does not ensure that answers are grounded, citation-valid, or appropriately refused. This paper introduces CiteGuard-RAG, a validation-centered AI system for evidence-grounded question answering. The system integrates hybrid semantic-lexical retrieval, citation-constrained generation, sentence-level grounding validation, and single-pass regeneration. Validation is used at runtime to determine whether a candidate answer should be accepted, refused, or regenerated before final delivery.
  CiteGuard-RAG is evaluated on 400 questions across a controlled housing-law dataset, PrivacyQA, and CUAD. In the controlled evaluation, it achieves 99.1% retrieval accuracy, 98.3% grounded-answer accuracy, and 98.3% citation validity, with no validation-detected hallucinations. Ablation results show that grounded-answer accuracy drops sharply when validation is removed, even when retrieval accuracy remains unchanged. External evaluation shows that while citation validity remains strong, evidence utilization, span alignment, and refusal calibration become harder under domain shift.
  These findings indicate that trustworthy RAG systems require explicit validation between retrieval and final answer delivery. CiteGuard-RAG provides a practical architecture for linking retrieval, generation, citation checking, abstention, and regeneration in high-stakes information access.

AI.tldr: CiteGuard-RAG is a RAG architecture that inserts an explicit validation layer between retrieval and final answer to ensure grounded, citation-correct, and appropriately refused responses.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG systems often hallucinate, mis-cite sources, or fail to refuse when evidence is missing, because they treat retrieval as sufficient grounding without checking whether generated answers truly align with retrieved evidence. The authors aim to make RAG trustworthy for high-stakes domains like law and privacy, where grounding and citation validity are critical.
AI.method: They design CiteGuard-RAG, which combines hybrid semantic and lexical retrieval, a generation process constrained to provided citations, and a sentence-level grounding validator that checks whether each part of the answer is supported by the retrieved evidence. Based on validation signals, the system can accept the answer, abstain/refuse, or trigger a single-pass regeneration step to correct unsupported content before returning a final response. They test it on a controlled housing-law benchmark and two real-world legal/privacy datasets (PrivacyQA and CUAD), and perform ablation studies removing validation components.
AI.result: On a controlled housing-law dataset, CiteGuard-RAG attains 99.1% retrieval accuracy, 98.3% grounded-answer accuracy, and 98.3% citation validity, with no hallucinations flagged by the validator. Ablations show that removing validation substantially degrades grounded-answer accuracy even when retrieval remains strong. On PrivacyQA and CUAD, citation validity stays high but performance on evidence use, span alignment, and refusal calibration declines, highlighting challenges under domain shift.
AI.conclusion: Explicit validation between retrieval and generation is crucial for trustworthy RAG in high-stakes applications. CiteGuard-RAG demonstrates that integrating retrieval, constrained generation, grounding validation, abstention, and regeneration into a single architecture can yield highly grounded, citation-correct answers, though maintaining performance under domain shift remains an open challenge.

title: Diversified and Perceptible Counterfactual Examples Leveraging Expert Knowledge
summary: CounterFactual Examples (CFEs) are a cornerstone of eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), offering local, post hoc, and model-agnostic explanations by identifying minimal input modifications that alter a model's prediction. Yet, in order to be intelligible, these modifications must also be semantically meaningful to the explainee. This paper proposes to integrate knowledge expressed as a fuzzy linguistic vocabulary to represent the explainee's perception and interpretation of the data. The domain induced by this fuzzy vocabulary imposes structural constraints that make the features dependent, preventing the use of gradient-based optimisation methods for CFE generation, e.g., DiCE. The paper proposes a continuous data embedding in this linguistic domain and exploits it to define a variant of DiCE that allows personalisation for the explainee, named DiCEf. As illustrated by experimental results on a real-world dataset, this extension of the DiCE method enables the generation of CFEs that are linguistically perceptible while preserving cost minimality, sparsity, and diversity.

AI.tldr: The paper extends counterfactual explanation methods by embedding data into a fuzzy linguistic space that reflects a user’s subjective perception, enabling personalized, human-intelligible counterfactuals while keeping them minimal, sparse, and diverse.
AI.motivation: Standard counterfactual explanations focus on minimal changes in feature space but ignore how users actually perceive and interpret those features. Semantically odd or unintuitive changes (e.g., tiny numeric tweaks) may be incomprehensible to humans. Moreover, existing gradient-based CFE methods like DiCE typically assume independent, continuous features and cannot easily handle structural constraints introduced by user-specific, linguistic knowledge. The authors want to make counterfactuals both formally minimal and cognitively meaningful to specific explainees.
AI.method: They encode the explainee’s knowledge as a fuzzy linguistic vocabulary (e.g., ‘low’, ‘medium’, ‘high’ with gradual membership functions) that defines a constrained domain where features become interdependent. Because this breaks standard gradient assumptions, they introduce a continuous embedding of the data into this fuzzy linguistic domain. On top of this embedding, they design a modified DiCE algorithm, called DiCEf, that searches for counterfactuals in the fuzzy space while respecting the structural constraints and personalisation to the explainee. The method preserves DiCE’s optimisation objectives for cost, sparsity, and diversity but evaluates them in the linguistic domain.
AI.result: On a real-world dataset, DiCEf can successfully generate counterfactual examples that are expressed in linguistically meaningful terms aligned with the user’s vocabulary. The experiments show that, compared to standard DiCE, the generated CFEs remain minimal, sparse, and diverse, while additionally satisfying the semantic and structural constraints implied by the fuzzy linguistic model. This demonstrates that the personalised fuzzy embedding does not significantly degrade the usual quantitative quality criteria for CFEs.
AI.conclusion: Integrating fuzzy linguistic knowledge into counterfactual generation makes explanations more user-centric and intelligible without sacrificing standard optimisation goals. The proposed DiCEf framework illustrates how to adapt gradient-based CFE methods to structurally constrained, perception-driven domains via continuous embeddings. This opens a path toward personalised XAI where explanations are aligned with an explainee’s own conceptual language rather than the raw numerical feature space alone.

title: Before You Poll with LLMs: A Deliberative Diagnostic Framework
comment: 17 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. Note: Web abstract is abridged to meet arXiv character limits. See PDF for the full proceedings abstract
summary: Can LLMs reason through new information like humans, or do they merely retrieve cached opinions? This is critical for silicon sampling, where LLM personas simulate public opinion at scale. Current evaluations test only whether personas hold the right opinions -- a static snapshot. But opinion research increasingly depends on dynamic fidelity: whether personas update beliefs in response to new arguments, as humans do during deliberation. No existing benchmark tests this. We introduce the Deliberative Polling Diagnostic Framework, which compares human and LLM belief shifts after identical informational interventions. Grounded in deliberative polling, it surfaces failures invisible to static evaluation: models that produce plausible partisan opinions can still misrepresent how those opinions change. Applying the framework to five frontier models using data from America in One Room (526 personas, 72 questions), we find that every model fails, each in a unique manner. GPT-5.1 exhibits reversal: its personas become more hostile toward the opposing party after balanced information, while humans become less so. This reversal is selective (80% on outgroup vs. 26% on policy questions) and symmetric across partisan identities. Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Llama 3.3 70B exhibit overshoot, shifting correctly but at 5-7x human magnitude. DeepSeek V3 exhibits rigidity with near-zero change. Targeted ablations reveal that policy content triggers these failures and that they are identity-specific: GPT-5.1 reverses on outgroup questions but overshoots on ingroup; Gemini shows the inverse. We term this signature self-sycophancy: conformity to the model's internal stereotype of the persona rather than reasoning from the information provided. Our framework offers a concrete protocol: run the deliberative diagnostic before trusting LLM personas to mimic revised beliefs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework to test whether LLM-based personas update their beliefs like humans when given new information, and shows that current top models systematically fail in different ways.
AI.motivation: LLM personas are increasingly used to simulate public opinion (“silicon sampling”). Existing evaluations only check if personas start with the “right” opinions, not whether they update those opinions when exposed to new, balanced information, which is how real humans often change views in deliberative settings. Opinion research and downstream applications need models that not only hold plausible beliefs but also adjust them in realistic ways. There is currently no benchmark to assess this dynamic fidelity, especially in politically charged contexts where belief change matters most.
AI.method: The authors build the Deliberative Polling Diagnostic Framework, inspired by deliberative polling in political science. They take real-world data from the America in One Room deliberative event, where citizens answered attitude questions before and after receiving structured, balanced information and discussion. They then create 526 LLM personas matched to these human participants and pose 72 identical pre/post questions, with the same informational interventions. For five frontier models (GPT‑5.1, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Llama 3.3 70B, DeepSeek V3), they compare the direction and magnitude of belief shifts between personas and humans. They also run targeted ablations to see which question types and identity cues trigger divergences.
AI.result: All five models fail to match human-like belief updating, each in a distinct failure pattern. GPT‑5.1 shows “reversal”: after balanced information, its personas become more hostile toward the political outgroup, whereas humans become less hostile; this is strong on outgroup questions (80% of items) but weaker on policy questions (26%), and it is symmetric across partisan identities. Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Llama 3.3 70B show “overshoot”: they move in the correct direction but with 5–7 times the magnitude of human opinion change. DeepSeek V3 shows “rigidity,” with almost no belief change. Ablation studies indicate that these behaviors are driven specifically by policy-related content and are identity-specific: GPT‑5.1 reverses on outgroup and overshoots on ingroup questions, while Gemini shows the opposite pattern.
AI.conclusion: Static evaluations that only check whether LLM personas hold plausible baseline opinions are insufficient; models can pass those tests yet badly misrepresent how opinions evolve when exposed to information. The proposed Deliberative Polling Diagnostic Framework exposes these dynamic failures and attributes them to what the authors call “self-sycophancy”: models conform to their own internal stereotypes of the persona instead of reasoning from provided evidence. The authors recommend running this deliberative diagnostic before relying on LLM personas as stand-ins for dynamic public opinion, especially in policy and identity-sensitive contexts.

title: Potential of Artificial Intelligence Algorithms for Identification of Relevant Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers of Early-Stage Liver Cancer
comment: 25 pages, 11 figures, 4 tables, currently being reviewed after the second revision at the biomedical signal processing and control journal
summary: This study explores the use of deep learning and explainable artificial intelligence to diagnose hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and define effective biomarkers across five different stages of disease development using a transcriptomic biomarker HCC dataset constructed via semi-supervised learning from three source datasets. Several deep learning experiments were conducted with different feature extraction techniques and gene sets to identify the most effective features for training high-accuracy models with minimal loss. The best-performing model, using 15 selected genes with the SelectKBest algorithm, achieved 90.74% accuracy, while the model with the lowest recorded loss of 0.3187 was obtained using 20 selected genes. To address the issue of class imbalance in the dataset, a weighted training approach was conducted, and for model transparency and interpretability a SHAP-based XAI analysis provided insights into the model's decision-making, consistently finding DNAJB14 as the most influential gene. Functional validation in this study has provided compelling evidence that DNAJB14 plays an important role in the adverse properties of HCC and that its inhibition effectively reverses tumour cell migration, invasion, colony and sphere formation. The main limitation of this study is the dataset's class imbalance, and while weighted training helped mitigate this, further research and additional data are needed to guarantee model generalizability. Future studies should also explore the influence of genetic variations, environmental factors, and clinical differences on model performance across diverse populations.

AI.tldr: The paper develops deep-learning models with explainable AI to diagnose HCC across five disease stages from transcriptomic data, identifies a small biomarker gene panel, and functionally validates DNAJB14 as a key driver gene.
AI.motivation: Early and accurate diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma and stratification across disease stages remain challenging, and existing biomarkers and models often lack robustness, interpretability, and functional validation. There is a need to leverage deep learning on transcriptomic data to discover compact, clinically actionable biomarker sets while also making model decisions transparent and biologically meaningful.
AI.method: The authors build a semi-supervised transcriptomic HCC biomarker dataset by integrating three source datasets. They train multiple deep learning models with various feature-extraction strategies and gene subsets, including SelectKBest-based feature selection. To manage class imbalance, they use weighted training. They then apply SHAP-based explainable AI to interpret model predictions and identify influential genes, and perform experimental functional validation of the top gene, DNAJB14, in HCC-related cellular assays.
AI.result: A best-performing deep learning model using 15 SelectKBest-selected genes achieved an accuracy of 90.74%, while another model using 20 genes achieved the lowest loss (0.3187). SHAP analysis consistently highlighted DNAJB14 as the most influential gene for model decisions. Functional experiments confirmed that DNAJB14 promotes malignant features of HCC, and that its inhibition reduces tumour cell migration, invasion, and colony and sphere formation. Class imbalance remained a notable limitation despite weighted training.
AI.conclusion: A compact panel of transcriptomic biomarkers can support accurate, explainable deep-learning-based diagnosis and staging of HCC, with DNAJB14 emerging as a key mechanistic driver supported by both model interpretation and functional assays. However, class imbalance and limited data may restrict generalizability, necessitating larger, more diverse cohorts and investigation of genetic, environmental, and clinical heterogeneity in future work.

title: Learning to Coach for Experiential Learning
summary: Language models can learn from experience, but raw solution trajectories are often too long and noisy to provide effective guidance. In this work, we propose Learning to Coach (L2C), a framework that trains a dedicated LLM-as-a-Coach to extract actionable experiential knowledge from an actor model's previous trajectory. The actor remains frozen, while the LLM-as-a-Coach is trained to maximize a reward given by the correctness of the actor's guided response. We study two such rewards: a same-instance reward, which improves subsequent responses on the original problem, and a cross-instance reward, which elicits knowledge that transfers to other instances. Across mathematical reasoning and interactive text-games, L2C consistently outperforms self-refinement and an untrained LLM-as-a-Coach. Running experiential learning for more iterations further improves accuracy and uses additional inference compute more effectively than enlarging the actor's decoding budget. The trained LLM-as-a-Coach also transfers to out-of-distribution tasks and adapts its guidance to the specific actor it coaches.

AI.tldr: They propose Learning to Coach (L2C), which trains a separate LLM coach to turn past trajectories of a frozen actor model into concise, actionable guidance, improving performance more effectively than just giving the actor more decoding compute.
AI.motivation: Existing language models can in principle learn from experience, but their raw solution trajectories are long, noisy, and not directly reusable as high-quality guidance. Standard self-refinement or naive reuse of previous attempts does not reliably extract generalizable, actionable knowledge, and simply increasing decoding budget is compute-inefficient. There is a need for a mechanism that can distill experiential data into targeted hints that improve future performance and transfer across instances and tasks.
AI.method: They introduce L2C, where a separate LLM is trained as a “coach” while the base actor model is kept frozen. The coach reads the actor’s previous trajectories and generates guidance or hints for the actor’s next attempt. The coach is optimized via reinforcement learning using a reward defined by the correctness of the actor’s guided output. They explore two reward designs: (1) same-instance reward, where the coach is rewarded for improving the actor’s performance on the same problem; and (2) cross-instance reward, where the coach is rewarded when its extracted knowledge transfers to new problem instances. They evaluate L2C on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and interactive text games, comparing against self-refinement and an untrained coach.
AI.result: L2C consistently improves the actor’s performance over self-refinement baselines and over using an untrained LLM as coach. Iterating experiential learning multiple times yields further accuracy gains and uses extra inference compute more effectively than enlarging the actor’s decoding budget alone. The trained coach generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks and is able to adapt its coaching style to different actor models.
AI.conclusion: Training a dedicated LLM-as-a-Coach to distill and repurpose experiential trajectories is an effective way to improve a frozen actor model’s performance. Carefully designed rewards, especially ones encouraging cross-instance transfer, make the extracted guidance generalizable. This coaching paradigm is a more compute-efficient use of additional inference budget than simply increasing decoding for the actor, and it yields a coach that can transfer across tasks and actors while dynamically tailoring its guidance.

title: EEG-Xplain: Decoding Neural Black-Boxes of EEG Foundation Models
summary: EEG foundation models such as BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGMamba have achieved remarkable performance in neural signal decoding, but their black-box nature limits clinical trust and neuroscientific validation. We propose a unified attribution framework for interpreting EEG foundation models across heterogeneous architectures. The framework integrates gradient-, perturbation-, and activation-based explanation methods to analyze model behavior in spatial, temporal, and frequency dimensions. Spatially, it identifies critical EEG channels and visualizes their distributions using topographic maps. Temporally, it highlights decision-relevant signal segments through attribution heatmaps. In the frequency domain, it quantifies the contributions of canonical EEG rhythms via spectral perturbation analysis. To assess explanation reliability, we introduce a population-level evaluation combining Area Over the Perturbation Curve (AOPC) and cross-method consistency analysis. The framework further leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to transform structured attribution outputs into natural-language reports, bridging low-level neural representations and high-level semantic reasoning. Experiments on benchmark datasets, including Mumtaz2016 and TUAB, demonstrate that the generated explanations are consistent with established neurophysiological markers, validating meaningful neural representations while exposing potential dependencies on artifacts and spurious patterns. The proposed framework provides a standardized approach for evaluating the interpretability, reliability, and physiological plausibility of EEG foundation models.

AI.tldr: They introduce a unified, multi-view attribution framework to interpret EEG foundation models across space, time, and frequency, and show its explanations align with known neurophysiology while revealing artifacts.
AI.motivation: EEG foundation models achieve strong decoding performance but are hard to trust and validate scientifically because their internal decision processes are opaque. There is no standard, architecture-agnostic way to interpret these models and assess whether they rely on meaningful neural patterns or spurious artifacts.
AI.method: They build a unified attribution framework that works across different EEG foundation model architectures, combining gradient-based, perturbation-based, and activation-based explanation techniques. The framework decomposes model explanations into three dimensions: spatial (important channels with topoplots), temporal (important time segments with attribution heatmaps), and spectral (important frequency bands using spectral perturbation). For reliability, they propose a population-level evaluation that merges Area Over the Perturbation Curve (AOPC) with cross-method consistency checks. Finally, they use LLMs to convert structured attribution outputs into human-readable reports, linking low-level attributions to high-level semantic interpretations.
AI.result: On benchmark datasets like Mumtaz2016 and TUAB, the framework’s explanations align with well-known neurophysiological markers, implying that the models capture meaningful brain activity. At the same time, the analysis uncovers possible reliance on artifacts and spurious correlations. The quantitative metrics (AOPC and method-consistency) support the stability and informativeness of the generated attributions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a standardized, model-agnostic way to interpret EEG foundation models across key dimensions (space, time, frequency). It provides tools to evaluate interpretability and explanation reliability and to judge whether model decisions are physiologically plausible, thereby improving clinical and neuroscientific trust in EEG foundation models.

title: K-Bench: a clinically calibrated benchmark for evaluating large language models in high-risk mental health conversations
summary: % !TEX root = ../main.tex People increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for mental health support, yet their safety in evolving, high-risk conversations remains poorly characterised. We developed K-Bench, a clinician-calibrated, protected benchmark evaluating 125 model configurations representing 33 base models from 14 providers across a fixed cohort of 200 multi-turn vignettes involving suicide, self-harm, domestic violence, substance misuse, and no-risk presentations. Synthetic patient conversations showed substantial distributional overlap with real human-AI conversations. A frozen GPT-4o judge achieved 94.2% exact agreement with clinician consensus across 6,751 eligible item comparisons from 151 clinician-rated transcripts. Leading models combined strong supportive conversation with combined-risk scores above 95, whereas risk exploration exposed substantial variation among lower-performing configurations. Therapeutic prompting produced configuration-specific gains concentrated among weaker models, while elevated reasoning produced no average improvement. K-Bench combines broader clinical coverage and configuration-scale comparison with a continuously updated public leaderboard whose operational test materials are protected from direct optimisation. The leaderboard is available at www.k-bench.ai.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces K-Bench, a clinician-calibrated benchmark to evaluate the safety and quality of large language models in high-risk mental health conversations.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used for mental health support, there is a critical need to systematically and clinically validate their behavior in complex, high-risk situations such as suicide, self-harm, domestic violence, and substance misuse. Existing benchmarks are limited in clinical scope, real-world representativeness, and resistance to overfitting/optimisation.
AI.method: The authors build K-Bench, a benchmark of 200 multi-turn synthetic patient vignettes covering various levels of psychosocial risk. They evaluate 125 LLM configurations from 33 base models and 14 providers. They compare synthetic conversations with real human–AI interactions, use a frozen GPT-4o as an automatic judge calibrated against clinician consensus, and test different prompting strategies including therapeutic prompting and enhanced reasoning. The benchmark is deployed as a protected, continuously updated leaderboard at k-bench.ai.
AI.result: Synthetic conversations showed close distributional similarity to real-world human–AI mental health interactions. GPT-4o, when used as a fixed judge, matched clinician consensus with 94.2% exact agreement across thousands of ratings. Top models achieved high-quality supportive dialogue and combined safety-risk scores above 95, but lower-performing configurations showed large variability when probed with risk-exploration prompts. Therapeutic-style prompting improved performance mostly for weaker models, while increased reasoning prompts offered no average benefit.
AI.conclusion: K-Bench provides a scalable, clinically grounded way to evaluate and compare LLM configurations in high-risk mental health scenarios, revealing that model performance and safety vary significantly across configurations and prompting strategies. The protected, leaderboard-based setup aims to support safer deployment and ongoing monitoring of LLMs used for mental health support without enabling direct benchmark overfitting.

title: NoteVQA: Benchmarking VLMs on Real-Life Questions from Human Communities
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly power consumer-facing AI search, yet evaluating them on the diversity of everyday visual questions remains challenging. Existing benchmarks often target predefined capabilities, such as multi-hop retrieval or long-form synthesis, whereas users ask photo-grounded questions spanning a long tail of everyday scenarios. Despite advances in VLMs, users on Xiaohongshu, a mainstream Chinese image-sharing platform, continue to turn to other people for help with everyday visual questions. Motivated by this behaviour, we curate NoteVQA from these questions, yielding 252 items across 12 topical categories and 7 user intents. Each item includes a concise reference distilled from expert community responses and a human-audited interleaved reference answer that combines textual explanations with supporting visual evidence. We evaluate both short-answer correctness and interleaved-answer quality. To support the latter, we introduce AgenticInterleave, a single-agent ReAct framework for retrieval-supported answer generation, together with IVR-12, a 12-dimensional rubric for assessing the content, presentation, and image quality of interleaved references and model outputs. Across 10 frontier VLMs, the highest short-answer accuracy is 52.8\%, while adding agentic search to Qwen3.5-397B-A17B improves accuracy by only 2.0\%. For interleaved answers, the same model running AgenticInterleave scores 3.52 under IVR-12, compared with 4.65 for the human-audited references, with the largest gap in content quality. These results highlight the challenges that everyday visual questions pose for current VLMs in both answer accuracy and the quality of visually grounded explanations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NoteVQA, a benchmark of real-world everyday visual questions from a Chinese social platform, and evaluates cutting-edge vision-language models, finding substantial performance gaps, especially in producing high-quality, visually grounded explanations.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM benchmarks focus on narrow, predefined skills (like multi-hop reasoning or long-form generation) and do not capture the diverse, long-tail, everyday visual questions that real users ask online. On Xiaohongshu, users still rely on other people, not VLMs, to answer such questions, indicating a mismatch between current benchmarks and actual user needs. The authors want to better measure and improve VLMs on these realistic, photo-grounded questions and their associated explanation quality.
AI.method: They collect NoteVQA, a dataset of 252 real user questions from Xiaohongshu, covering 12 topical categories and 7 user intents. For each item, they construct: (1) a concise reference answer distilled from expert community replies, and (2) a human-audited interleaved reference answer that mixes textual explanation with explicit visual evidence. They then propose AgenticInterleave, a single-agent ReAct-style framework that uses retrieval to support generating interleaved answers, and IVR-12, a 12-dimensional evaluation rubric that scores content quality, presentation, and image usage for both references and model outputs. Using NoteVQA and IVR-12, they systematically test 10 frontier VLMs, including Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with and without agentic search.
AI.result: On short-answer accuracy over NoteVQA, the best-performing VLM reaches only 52.8%. For Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, adding the AgenticInterleave retrieval-based agentic search yields only a modest 2.0% improvement in short-answer accuracy. For interleaved answers evaluated under IVR-12, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with AgenticInterleave scores 3.52 on average, while human-audited references score 4.65, with the biggest gap in content quality dimensions rather than formatting or image presentation.
AI.conclusion: Real-world, everyday visual questions remain difficult for current frontier VLMs: they frequently fail to provide correct short answers and lag well behind humans in generating rich, visually grounded explanations. Benchmarks like NoteVQA and evaluation tools like AgenticInterleave and IVR-12 reveal limitations that are not well captured by existing capability-specific benchmarks and suggest that improving content quality and grounding in realistic settings is a key direction for future VLM development.

title: Inoculation Midtraining with Learned Neologisms
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often learn both desirable and undesirable properties during post-training. We study whether midtraining, an earlier training stage, can shape which of these properties later generalise. We introduce Inoculation Midtraining, a technique that teaches a base model that unsafe behaviour belongs to a designated <quarantine_token> context, as indicated by the <quarantine_token> neologism (a new token) introduced during midtraining, and then post-trains the model on unsafe data within that context. We then evaluate the model outside the context, with the <quarantine_token> neologism excluded from the system prompt. Across supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning post-training regimes, we find that Inoculation Midtraining can reduce misalignment while preserving the transfer of benign data properties (e.g., speaking in German or Shakespearean prose). However, our approach does not outperform standard Inoculation Prompting, is sensitive to training configuration, and produces a leaky boundary that nearby contextual cues can reactivate. These results show that inoculation with a learned association introduced via midtraining can shape selective generalisation. Still, more work is needed before this approach can become a load-bearing component in a developer's safety framework.

AI.tldr: They test whether training a model early to associate unsafe behavior with a special quarantine token can later reduce unsafe behaviors while keeping useful skills.
AI.motivation: LLMs pick up both good and bad behaviors during post-training, and it is unclear whether earlier training stages can steer which behaviors generalize. They want to know if shaping behavior at midtraining can selectively prevent unsafe behaviors from appearing in normal use, without losing helpful capabilities learned from the same unsafe data.
AI.method: They introduce Inoculation Midtraining: during midtraining they add a new neologism token <quarantine_token> that marks a special context where unsafe behavior is allowed. The model is trained to treat unsafe content as only belonging in that quarantine context. Later, in post‑training (both SFT and RL), they provide unsafe data inside that marked context. At evaluation, they remove the token from the prompt and test whether unsafe behaviors generalize outside the quarantine, while checking whether benign properties (e.g., language style) still transfer.
AI.result: Inoculation Midtraining reduces some misalignment compared to not doing it, while still letting harmless properties from the unsafe data (like German language ability or Shakespeare style) transfer to normal contexts. However, it does not perform better than a simpler baseline called Inoculation Prompting, is quite sensitive to exact training choices, and the quarantine boundary is imperfect—nearby contextual cues can cause unsafe behavior to reappear.
AI.conclusion: Midtraining with a learned association that cages unsafe behavior in a special tokenized context can influence which behaviors generalize, offering a possible tool for selective generalization. But the method is not yet robust or superior to simpler techniques; the boundary around unsafe behavior is leaky and configuration‑dependent, so it is not ready to serve as a primary safety mechanism without further research and improvement.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Robustness, Cost, and Governance Trade-offs for Vision-Language Models in Templated Document Extraction
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used to extract structured fields from business documents, yet most evaluations report accuracy on clean benchmarks and offer little guidance to practitioners choosing an approach for a given task complexity. We address this gap with a measurement-grounded study and an open-source release. Across eleven systems (three commercial, two reasoning, five open-source VLMs in pretrained and fine-tuned form, and a non-LLM OCR->regex floor) scored on a 750-document held-out pool of synthetic checks, fine-tuning on 3K samples lifts the best open-source VLMs above F1 0.98-above every zero-shot commercial system on this task-while GPT-5 leads the commercial pool on F1 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 collapses on Date. To turn these measurements into actionable choices, we introduce a practitioner-oriented selection framework that maps a task profile (quality, latency, governance, volume) to a recommended approach via filtering and total-cost minimization, illustrated on a hypothetical mid-volume document-extraction scenario.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates multiple vision-language models for structured field extraction from business documents and proposes a practical framework to choose the best approach based on task constraints.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models are widely used for extracting structured information from business documents, but existing evaluations focus on clean benchmarks and do not help practitioners select methods for tasks with varying complexity and constraints. There is a need for measurement-grounded guidance to support real-world decision-making.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate eleven systems—including commercial VLMs, reasoning models, open-source VLMs (both pretrained and fine-tuned), and a non-LLM OCR+regex baseline—on a 750-document held-out set of synthetic checks. They fine-tune open-source VLMs on 3,000 samples and compare F1 performance across systems. They also design a practitioner-oriented selection framework that maps task profiles (defined in terms of quality, latency, governance, and volume) to recommended approaches using filtering and total-cost minimization, with a worked example on a mid-volume extraction scenario.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on 3,000 samples raises the best open-source VLMs to F1 > 0.98, outperforming all evaluated zero-shot commercial systems on the synthetic check task. Among commercial systems, GPT-5 achieves the highest F1, while Claude Sonnet 4.5 performs poorly on date extraction. The measurements provide detailed performance comparisons across systems and configurations.
AI.conclusion: With moderate fine-tuning data, open-source VLMs can surpass zero-shot commercial systems on structured document extraction, making them competitive options under certain constraints. The proposed selection framework translates empirical measurements into practical guidance, helping practitioners choose an approach that balances quality, latency, governance, and cost for their specific document-processing workloads.

title: HypoEvolve: Genetic Algorithms Enable Multi-Agent LLMs to Discover Scientific Hypotheses
summary: Scientific agents contribute to hypothesis discovery by synthesizing evidence, assessing proposals, and developing new explanations. Recent systems combine scientific agents with evolutionary search through critique, comparison, and revision. However, how different forms of agent collaboration affect hypothesis quality remains an open question. Answering this question requires separating the effects of agents' scientific capabilities from those of their collaboration. A framework must therefore preserve agents' scientific roles and support rules for combining, revising, and retaining hypotheses. Building on this view, we introduce HypoEvolve, which makes collaboration explicit through successive updates to a hypothesis population. Specifically, we propose a generational genetic algorithm to coordinate specialized large language model (LLM) agents that integrate mechanistic arguments, reconsider assumptions, and assess evidence and testability. Each generation specifies how scientific judgments and new proposals reshape the population, making collaboration effects on hypothesis quality directly testable. Moreover, we design our evaluation around scientifically meaningful hypotheses that explain how a proposed intervention could work. Drug repurposing links these explanations to target-level biological claims assessed against external evidence. Specifically, we adapt DepMap and Open Targets into complementary external measures grounded in experimental, genetic, and clinical evidence. Across 34 cancer types, HypoEvolve achieves the highest scores against six baselines on both measures. DepMap selectivity reaches 0.171, versus 0.115 for the strongest baseline. Gains over single-pass generation also generalize to held-out cancer types. HypoEvolve advances a vision of autonomous science in which AI research teams achieve a capacity for discovery beyond that of individual models.

AI.tldr: HypoEvolve is a genetic-algorithm framework that coordinates collaborating LLM agents to iteratively improve scientific hypotheses, demonstrated on drug repurposing across 34 cancer types, where it outperforms six baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based scientific agents can generate, critique, and refine hypotheses, often combined with evolutionary search, but it is unclear how different collaboration patterns among agents affect hypothesis quality. Prior work tends to conflate the intrinsic scientific abilities of agents with how they collaborate, lacking a framework that cleanly separates and measures collaboration effects. There is a need for a system where scientific roles of agents are preserved, collaboration is explicit, and hypothesis evolution can be systematically controlled and evaluated against external, domain-specific evidence.
AI.method: The authors propose HypoEvolve, a framework that models collaboration among specialized LLM agents as a generational genetic algorithm operating over a population of hypotheses. Each agent plays a scientific role (e.g., constructing mechanistic arguments, revisiting assumptions, evaluating evidence and testability). In each generation, agents critique and revise hypotheses, generate new candidates, and selection rules determine which hypotheses are retained, modified, or discarded. This process yields explicit, stepwise updates to the hypothesis population. For evaluation, the system is applied to drug repurposing in oncology, where hypotheses explain mechanisms by which interventions might work, and are grounded in target-level biological claims. External evidence from DepMap and Open Targets is adapted into complementary evaluation measures based on experimental, genetic, and clinical data, allowing quantitative comparison to six baseline methods including single-pass LLM generation.
AI.result: Across 34 cancer types, HypoEvolve outperforms six baseline approaches on both DepMap- and Open Targets–based evaluation metrics. In particular, HypoEvolve achieves a DepMap selectivity of 0.171 compared to 0.115 for the strongest baseline, indicating more precise and evidence-aligned target hypotheses. The improvements over single-pass generation persist on held-out cancer types, suggesting that the benefits of iterative, collaborative hypothesis evolution generalize beyond the training or tuning set. The framework thus demonstrates that structured collaboration among specialized agents, orchestrated via a genetic algorithm, materially improves hypothesis quality over individual or less-structured approaches.
AI.conclusion: HypoEvolve shows that making multi-agent collaboration explicit—as generational evolution of a hypothesis population coordinated by specialized LLM agents—can significantly enhance the quality of scientific hypotheses, here in the context of cancer drug repurposing. By preserving scientific roles and providing clear rules for how critiques and new proposals shape hypotheses, the framework allows direct testing of collaboration effects, distinct from raw model capability. The superior performance against external biological evidence and the generalization to new cancer types support a broader vision of autonomous science, where coordinated AI research teams can exceed the discovery capabilities of single LLMs or ad hoc prompting strategies.

title: New Conditions for Philosophers to Catch the Wave of Citizen Deliberation in the Age of Artificial Intelligence in advance
summary: Powerful technologies labeled ``AI''-without sufficient epistemic caution-are already reshaping political and private life, bringing both new dangers and new opportunities for citizen participation. These range from electoral and legislative engagement to the most ambitious form: political co-creation through citizens' assemblies. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support such processes through moderation, translation, facilitation, summarization, and writing assistance. But this potential remains largely unrealized. The Democratic Commons project takes a fundamentally interdisciplinary approach-from philosophy to computer science-to evaluate LLMs against five proposed democratic principles. At its core, the project is driven by the question of political bias: under what conditions can LLMs be used democratically within forms of citizen participation that are them- selves still largely experimental? Addressing these socio-technical questions requires grounding in political theory and, more broadly, in philosophy-disciplines that provide the normative frameworks without which the democratic evaluation of AI systems cannot be mean- ingfully conducted.

AI.tldr: Interdisciplinary project (Democratic Commons) examining how large language models can be used in democratic citizen‑participation processes, focusing on political bias and grounding the evaluation in political theory and philosophy.
AI.motivation: AI systems, especially LLMs, are already shaping political and private life but are deployed with little epistemic caution or democratic scrutiny. There is both risk (e.g., bias, manipulation) and opportunity (e.g., improved citizen participation) in using LLMs for democratic processes such as elections, legislative engagement, and citizens’ assemblies. To harness opportunities while mitigating risks, we need a principled way to evaluate LLMs’ democratic suitability.
AI.method: Conceptual and interdisciplinary framework-building: the project draws on philosophy, political theory, and computer science to propose and apply five democratic principles for evaluating LLMs. It investigates how LLMs can be used as tools (moderation, translation, facilitation, summarization, writing assistance) in participatory and co-creative democratic processes, with a particular focus on identifying and understanding political bias and the conditions under which LLMs can be used democratically.
AI.result: The abstract announces a research program rather than completed empirical results. Its main outcome at this stage is the articulation of the Democratic Commons project, the identification of five democratic principles for evaluating LLMs, and the argument that meaningful evaluation of LLMs in democratic contexts must be normatively grounded in political theory and philosophy.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating and deploying LLMs in democratic citizen-participation settings requires explicit normative frameworks from political theory and philosophy. Without such grounding, discussions of political bias and democratic suitability of AI tools are incomplete. The Democratic Commons project will use these frameworks to assess when and how LLMs can be used in experimental forms of citizen participation in a normatively defensible way.

title: Verifiable by Construction: Claim-Level Evaluation of Verbatim Citation in Clinical Question Answering
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been widely adopted for clinical question answering (QA). Current systems can attach citations to their answers, but these often point to broad texts, leaving time-pressed clinicians unable to verify them efficiently. An alternative is to ensure that responses are verifiable by construction: providing fine-grained verbatim quotes from reference material that substantiate claims, so users can verify an answer without opening other documents. In this paper, we evaluate the ability of current models to perform this task end-to-end: from providing citations for every factual claim, to producing verbatim quotes, to ensuring that those quotes fully substantiate the claims. To do so, we build a standardized harness over four clinical practice guidelines and evaluate twelve LLMs on 222 synthetic clinical questions, measuring each of these stages separately. We find that most models can attach verbatim quotes to over 90% of their claims from prompting alone, apart from some lightweight models such as claude-haiku-4.5. Yet these quotes often fail to substantiate every detail of the claims they accompany. For instance, claude-opus-5 produces verbatim quotes for 98.0% of its claims, but fully substantiates only 37.1%. Our work provides insights into the current capability gap of LLMs in building verifiable clinical QA systems, along with artifacts for future research.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well current large language models can create fully verifiable clinical QA answers that include fine-grained supporting quotes from guidelines for every factual claim.
AI.motivation: Clinicians are time-pressured and cannot always open and read long cited documents to verify LLM answers. Existing clinical QA systems often provide coarse citations that do not clearly support specific claims, making verification inefficient and potentially unsafe. The authors aim to understand whether modern LLMs can, by design, generate answers that are immediately verifiable via precise verbatim quotes tied to each factual statement.
AI.method: The authors build a standardized evaluation harness over four clinical practice guidelines and construct 222 synthetic clinical questions. They then test 12 different LLMs on an end-to-end task: (1) attaching citations for every factual claim, (2) producing verbatim quotes from the guidelines, and (3) ensuring each quote fully substantiates its associated claim. They evaluate each stage separately to analyze where models succeed or fail, comparing performance across models, including lightweight ones like claude-haiku-4.5 and stronger ones like claude-opus-5.
AI.result: Most evaluated LLMs, when appropriately prompted, can attach verbatim quotes to more than 90% of the factual claims in their answers, showing strong retrieval and quoting capabilities. However, there is a large gap between quoting and true substantiation: many quotes do not fully support all aspects of the claims. For example, claude-opus-5 provides verbatim quotes for 98.0% of its claims, but only 37.1% of those claims are fully supported by the quoted text. Lightweight models perform worse on the quoting step as well.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs are good at finding and attaching relevant-looking verbatim quotes but often fail to ensure that these quotes rigorously substantiate each factual claim in clinical QA. This reveals a significant ‘verifiability gap’ between surface-level citation and genuine evidential support. The paper offers benchmark artifacts and analysis to guide future work on building safer, more verifiable clinical QA systems where every answer is reliably backed by precise evidence.

title: Predicting build orientation for SLM dental parts: a comparison of rotation representations and direct vector regression
summary: Build orientation for selective laser melting (SLM) manufacturing of dental parts is usually chosen manually by technicians. We treat orientation prediction as supervised machine learning of the part's up-axis from technician-labeled production data, and test which rotation representations produce the best results. Using $n\approx2400$ patient-specific dental parts, we trained a ResNet-50 multi-view image backbone and a PointNeXt-S point-cloud backbone, both pretrained and fine-tuned end-to-end, on 13 up-axis representations spanning six classical $SO(3)$ parameterizations and seven representations defined directly on the unit sphere $S^2$. We report the geodesic angular error between predicted and ground-truth up-axis on a test set, with and without test-time augmentation (TTA) over $K=21$ known rotations. With TTA, the octahedral map achieves the lowest mean angular error ($10.6^\circ$, ResNet-50). The three lowest-error results overall are direct $S^2$ representations, though this may reflect label noise in the unsupervised in-plane component of the $SO(3)$ targets rather than a topological advantage. von Mises-Fisher collapses to a near-constant prediction when trained with PointNeXt-S but not with ResNet-50. TTA reduces mean angular error by 31-73 % across almost every representation and backbone. Overall, test-time augmentation over a small set of known rotations is the most consistent driver of accuracy, whereas the best-performing representation is strongly backbone-dependent.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different 3D rotation / direction representations affect machine-learning prediction of the build orientation (up-axis) for SLM-manufactured dental parts, using both image- and point-cloud-based neural backbones, and shows that test-time augmentation brings the largest accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: In SLM production of dental parts, technicians manually choose part orientations, which is time-consuming, non-standardized, and may be suboptimal. Automating orientation selection could improve consistency and efficiency. However, predicting a 3D orientation with neural networks requires choosing a rotation or direction representation, and it is unclear which representation works best for this specific industrial problem and common deep backbones. The authors aim to systematically compare rotation / direction encodings and clarify which choices actually matter for prediction accuracy in this application.
AI.method: They formulate build orientation prediction as supervised learning of the up-axis direction from technician-labeled production data. On a dataset of about 2400 patient-specific dental parts, they train two different 3D-orientation predictors: (1) a ResNet-50 backbone using multi-view images of each part, and (2) a PointNeXt-S backbone using point clouds. Both networks are pretrained and then fine-tuned end-to-end. They evaluate 13 different orientation representations: six classical SO(3) parameterizations and seven representations defined directly on the unit sphere S^2. Models are trained for each representation and backbone, and performance is measured as geodesic angular error between predicted and ground-truth up-axis on a held-out test set. They also apply test-time augmentation (TTA) by evaluating over K=21 known rotations and aggregating predictions, then compare errors with and without TTA.
AI.result: With test-time augmentation, the octahedral map representation combined with the ResNet-50 backbone yields the lowest mean angular error of about 10.6 degrees. Generally, the three best-performing setups use direct S^2-based representations. However, the authors suggest this advantage may be due to label noise in the unconstrained in-plane rotation component of SO(3) labels rather than an inherent topological benefit of S^2. They observe that the von Mises-Fisher representation almost collapses to predicting a near-constant direction when trained with the PointNeXt-S backbone, but not when trained with ResNet-50, illustrating strong interaction between representation and backbone. Across nearly all representation-backbone combinations, TTA decreases mean angular error substantially, by about 31–73%.
AI.conclusion: The dominant factor in improving build-orientation prediction accuracy is test-time augmentation over a small set of known rotations, not the specific rotation representation. While certain S^2-based encodings (notably the octahedral map) perform best in some settings, the performance ranking of representations is highly backbone-dependent and can be affected by label noise. Practitioners should therefore prioritize using TTA and be cautious in generalizing representation preferences across architectures; no single representation is universally optimal for this task.

title: Mind2Dialogue: Training Human-Aware Language Models by Simulating User Mental States
summary: As language models become more capable, long-term collaboration in learning, reasoning, and decision-making calls for a deeper understanding of the people they serve. Yet training such human-aware language models faces a fundamental supervision gap because current datasets for LLM assistant training contain few if any well-informed responses explicitly grounded in users' unspoken beliefs and goals. Scaling such supervision is inherently constrained, as users' underlying states are not directly observable. We thus propose the Mind2Dialogue framework to mitigate this gap by simulating users' mental states and turning them into privileged supervision for human-aware training. Specifically, we first propose a psychology-guided simulator that preserves personal characteristics while updating mental states through interaction to generate coherent conversations. The key idea is to enforce a shared evolving mental state that drives user behavior and guides an Oracle assistant's responses. Our privileged distillation then trains models on the Oracle's well-informed responses to assist users without direct access to their mental states at deployment. Moreover, we propose to evaluate human-aware learning by combining personalization and theory of mind, examining how models understand people and act on that understanding. Training on the full Mind2Dialogue corpus improves every reported personalization metric over the corresponding Qwen, Llama, and OLMo instruction-tuned baselines, including gains of 26.6 to 40.9 percentage points in preference-following generation. The gains extend to belief and action reasoning on Qwen and Llama, beyond personalized assistance. Looking forward, Mind2Dialogue makes user simulation a foundation for genuine AI collaborators that understand beliefs and intentions behind people's words and support their long-term goals across education, work, and everyday life.

AI.tldr: Introduces Mind2Dialogue, a framework that simulates users' mental states to create privileged supervision for training human-aware language models, leading to large gains in personalization and theory-of-mind style reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current LLM assistants lack deep understanding of users’ unspoken beliefs, preferences, and goals. Existing training data rarely contains responses explicitly grounded in users’ internal mental states, and such states are inherently unobservable, making it difficult to scale supervision for truly human-aware models. There is a need for a systematic way to approximate and leverage users’ latent mental states in training so models can collaborate with people over the long term in learning, reasoning, and decision-making.
AI.method: Proposes Mind2Dialogue, a two-part framework: (1) a psychology-guided user simulator that maintains and updates a shared, evolving mental state (capturing personal traits, beliefs, and goals) as the conversation progresses. This shared state simultaneously drives simulated user behavior and guides an Oracle assistant that has privileged access to it. (2) A privileged distillation process that trains deployable models on the Oracle’s well-informed responses, so at inference time the models help real users without direct access to their mental states. The framework also introduces an evaluation protocol that combines personalization metrics with theory-of-mind assessments, testing both how well models infer users’ internal states and how effectively they act on that understanding.
AI.result: Training Qwen-, Llama-, and OLMo-based instruction-tuned models on the full Mind2Dialogue corpus yields consistent improvements across all reported personalization metrics compared to their baselines, with particularly large gains (26.6–40.9 percentage points) in preference-following generation. The improvements also transfer to belief and action reasoning tasks for Qwen and Llama, indicating benefits beyond narrow personalization and into broader human-aware reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Simulating users’ evolving mental states and using them as privileged supervision is an effective strategy for training more human-aware language models. Mind2Dialogue demonstrates that user simulation can serve as a scalable foundation for assistants that better infer and respect people’s beliefs, preferences, and intentions. The resulting models not only personalize responses more accurately but also exhibit enhanced theory-of-mind-like reasoning, moving toward AI collaborators capable of supporting users’ long-term goals across various real-world domains such as education, work, and daily life.

title: Data storytelling meets interpretable machine learning: Decoding AI decisions for non-experts without revealing sensitive data and model details
summary: AI-driven automated decision-making requires both predictive performance and interpretability. Recent advances in interpretable machine learning (IML) provide tools for explaining model predictions, but the technical complexity of these explanations may hinder accessibility to non-experts. To address this challenge, this study integrates data storytelling with IML to enhance the explainability of AI-generated decisions for a broader audience. Following the design science research (DSR) paradigm, this study proposes a formal definition of data storytelling in IML, introduces the DIST Pyramid to align data storytelling with IML, and presents the I-P-O Model to describe their interactions. It further develops an architecture to explain AI decisions through distinct "What-if" and "Why-not" event-generation processes. The architecture also employs data desensitization to protect sensitive input data. To validate the approach, a case study is conducted with the Boston Housing dataset, using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values and large language models (LLMs) to generate data stories with And-But-Therefore (ABT) structures. An empirical evaluation shows that 76.4% and 74.3% of respondents rated the "What-if" and "Why-not" data stories as more comprehensible, with significantly higher accessibility scores than traditional SHAP visualizations. The paper concludes with the presentation of a narrative interpretation framework that integrates IML and data storytelling, thereby expanding the research scope as well as the practical applicability of AI decision-making.

AI.tldr: The paper integrates interpretable machine learning with data storytelling to make AI decisions more understandable to non-experts, demonstrating that narrative SHAP-based explanations are more accessible than standard visualizations.
AI.motivation: While interpretable machine learning provides technical explanations such as feature importance and SHAP plots, these are often too complex or abstract for non-expert users, limiting trust and adoption of AI-driven automated decision-making. There is a need for explanation formats that are both faithful to the model and easily understandable by a broad audience.
AI.method: Using a design science research paradigm, the authors: (1) formally define data storytelling in the context of interpretable ML; (2) propose the DIST Pyramid to conceptually align storytelling layers with IML; (3) introduce an Input-Process-Output (I-P-O) model describing interactions between data, interpretation mechanisms, and narrative outputs; (4) design a system architecture that generates "What-if" and "Why-not" explanatory stories, incorporates data desensitization, and leverages SHAP values plus large language models to produce And-But-Therefore (ABT) narratives; and (5) validate the approach with a Boston Housing case study and empirical user evaluation.
AI.result: The system can automatically generate narrative explanations for model decisions, framed as "What-if" and "Why-not" scenarios, using SHAP-based reasoning and ABT structure. In user studies, 76.4% of respondents found the "What-if" stories and 74.3% found the "Why-not" stories more comprehensible than traditional SHAP visualizations, and both narrative types received significantly higher accessibility scores.
AI.conclusion: Integrating interpretable ML techniques with structured data storytelling substantially improves the accessibility and perceived comprehensibility of AI decision explanations for non-experts. The proposed conceptual models (DIST Pyramid, I-P-O model) and narrative interpretation framework provide a foundation for designing AI systems that communicate decisions through natural, desensitized stories, broadening both research avenues and practical deployment of explainable AI.

title: Discovery Foundation Models: Toward Open-Ended Discovery Intelligence
summary: Foundation models have progressed from learning and reasoning over existing knowledge, to increasingly learning through action, tool use, and outcome feedback. We argue that the next frontier is a further transition: from solving and acting within problems specified by humans to participating in the process by which new problems, representations, explanations, and knowledge are created. We refer to this capability as Discovery Intelligence. We formulate Discovery Foundation Models (DFMs) as general-purpose model systems for open-ended discovery. A DFM operates over a revisable research state and supports seven coupled capabilities spanning problem discovery, formulation, representation construction, hypothesis formation, intervention, evidence-grounded revision, and continual discovery improvement. We instantiate this framework with Zetema, which couples explicit research-state dynamics, verification and experimental gating, external grounding, and cross-task Discovery Skill evolution. We further ground the framework with GALILEO, a real therapeutic-discovery system in which Dry-Lab reasoning, robotic and hands-on Wet-Lab experimentation, external biological evidence, and iterative hypothesis and design revision form a closed physical discovery loop. We then formulate a unified approach to capability formation and process-centered evaluation, enabling discovery behavior to be trained, improved, and measured beyond final-answer performance. Together, these components establish discovery as a learnable, executable, and evaluable capability of foundation-model systems. We view this shift as a broader progression in intelligence scaling: from learning over existing knowledge, to learning from action outcomes, and ultimately to participating in the construction, testing, and revision of the structures through which new knowledge is discovered. Code: https://github.com/Gen-Verse/DFM-Plans

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Discovery Foundation Models (DFMs), a new class of foundation models designed not just to solve given tasks but to autonomously participate in scientific discovery cycles, from problem finding to hypothesis testing and revision.
AI.motivation: Existing foundation models mainly operate on static data or within human-defined tasks, and recent work extends them to tool use and action feedback. However, they still do not fully address how AI can help originate new problems, representations, and knowledge the way scientific discovery does. The authors want to formalize and enable this next step: AI systems that actively drive open-ended discovery processes, especially in domains like therapeutic discovery.
AI.method: The authors introduce the concept of Discovery Intelligence and define Discovery Foundation Models (DFMs) as models that operate on a dynamic, revisable research state and support seven interlinked capabilities: problem discovery, problem formulation, representation construction, hypothesis generation, intervention/experimentation, evidence-based revision, and continual improvement of discovery skills. They instantiate this framework via Zetema, a generic DFM research environment with explicit research-state dynamics, verification and experimental gating, external grounding, and cross-task skill evolution. They also present GALILEO, a concrete therapeutic-discovery system that closes the loop between in silico reasoning, robotic and manual lab experiments, external biological evidence, and iterative hypothesis/design updates. Finally, they outline a unified training and evaluation approach that focuses on discovery processes instead of just final answers.
AI.result: Conceptually, the paper delivers: (1) a formalized framework for Discovery Intelligence and DFMs; (2) the Zetema environment embodying this framework in a general setting; (3) the GALILEO system as a real-world case study in therapeutic discovery; and (4) a process-centered evaluation protocol for measuring discovery behavior. Empirical or quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract, but the systems show that discovery can be operationalized as a tractable modeling and evaluation problem for foundation models.
AI.conclusion: Discovery—understood as the end-to-end process of generating, testing, and refining new problems, hypotheses, and representations—can be framed as a learnable capability for foundation models. With structures like DFMs, research-state dynamics, and process-centric training/evaluation, foundation models can move beyond reasoning over fixed knowledge or acting in predefined tasks toward actively constructing and revising the frameworks through which new scientific knowledge is produced.

title: Are LLMs Good Financial User Simulators? A Preliminary Study
comment: The complete version will be open and the paper is under review in AAAI
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as user simulators, but their ability to reproduce evolving individual financial decisions remains unclear. We present a preliminary study in a controlled paper-trading environment with 120 volunteers. Participants used non-redeemable virtual funds under real-time market conditions; no real brokerage accounts, real-money positions, or real transaction records were accessed. Given only information available before a prediction cutoff, a simulator predicts the participant's next-trading-day action, traded security, and transaction quantity. We evaluate temporally aligned rolling predictions and compare settings with and without point-in-time market information. Market context improves action and ticker prediction in the controlled ablation, while transaction sizing remains difficult. We also observe systematic behavioral compression: models overproduce hold actions, underpredict sell decisions, and simplify multi-security transactions. These results provide an initial empirical characterization and motivate larger-scale evaluation of individual, temporal, and portfolio-level behavioral fidelity.

AI.tldr: The paper preliminarily evaluates how well large language models can simulate evolving individual trading behavior in a controlled paper-trading setup, finding they capture some actions and ticker choices but struggle with order size and faithfully reproducing nuanced behavior.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as user simulators in finance and other domains, yet it is unclear whether they can accurately reproduce detailed, temporally evolving decisions of individual retail investors. Understanding their strengths and limitations is important for using simulators in research, system design, and risk assessment, especially in financial contexts where behavior is complex and path-dependent.
AI.method: The authors run a controlled paper-trading experiment with 120 volunteers who trade using non-redeemable virtual funds in real-time market conditions. They construct an LLM-based simulator that, using only data available before a prediction cutoff, predicts each participant’s next trading-day behavior along three dimensions: action (e.g., buy/sell/hold), traded security (ticker), and transaction quantity. They evaluate rolling, temporally aligned predictions and conduct an ablation comparing models with and without access to point-in-time market information.
AI.result: Incorporating point-in-time market context improves the simulator’s accuracy for predicting actions and tickers in the ablation study, indicating that LLMs benefit from contemporaneous market data when modeling trading choices. However, predicting transaction size remains challenging, with relatively poor performance. The models also exhibit systematic biases described as behavioral compression: they default too often to hold, underpredict selling, and oversimplify trades that span multiple securities.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based user simulators can partially reproduce individual trading actions and asset choices, especially when given real-time market context, but they currently struggle with more granular aspects such as order sizing and the diversity of complex, multi-security trades. The observed behavioral compression suggests that current simulators may underestimate the richness and risk-relevant aspects of real investor behavior. The study serves as an initial empirical benchmark and highlights the need for larger-scale, more comprehensive evaluations of individual, temporal, and portfolio-level behavioral fidelity before relying on such simulators for high-stakes financial applications.

title: Disentangling Representation Evolution in Transformers through Directional Decomposition
summary: Transformer representations evolve through learned additive transformations that either preserve their current direction or redirect it. We study this evolution as a functional geometry, decomposing learned updates into parallel and perpendicular components. Across pretrained models, we find substantial parallel components beyond the residual identity path. We then apply the decomposition in two spaces: to attention and MLP updates relative to the hidden state, and to attention value aggregation relative to the current token's value. Targeted edits reveal a strongly space-dependent asymmetry: exclude-self value-space parallel manipulation is markedly more robust than residual-space and perpendicular counterparts, preserving the direct self message while scaling only the non-self aggregate. The same decomposition gives a component-resolved description of compression-induced update error: perpendicular error separates compression methods more clearly than parallel error. Extensive experiments further demonstrate that full-aggregate parallel suppression during from-scratch pretraining lowers validation-loss trajectories and improves downstream averages, with the value-space variant strongest. Together, these results connect representation geometry to editing robustness, compression diagnosis, and training-time intervention. Code is available in the \href{https://github.com/Shwai-He/Transformer-Geometry}{project repository}.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a geometric decomposition of Transformer updates into parallel and perpendicular components and shows that this viewpoint explains and improves editing robustness, compression diagnostics, and pretraining interventions.
AI.motivation: Better understanding how Transformer representations evolve layer by layer could clarify why edits, compression, and architectural tweaks behave as they do. Existing work often treats updates as opaque, without separating direction-preserving vs. direction-changing components. The authors aim to connect representation geometry to practical tools for model editing, compression, and training improvements.
AI.method: They model each layer’s update as a vector added to the current representation and decompose this update into components parallel and perpendicular to a reference direction (e.g., the residual stream or the token’s own value vector). They apply this decomposition to both attention and MLP updates, and to attention value aggregation. They then run targeted interventions that separately manipulate parallel vs. perpendicular components and compare robustness.
